# Foreword

It was the autumn of 1989—a few weeks before the Berlin wall came down, President George H. W. Bush was president, and the American Mathematical Society decided to outsource T X programming to Frank Mittelbach and me. 

Why did the AMS outsource TEX programming to us? This was, after all, a decade before the words “outsourcing” and “of-shore” entered the lexicon. There were many American TEX experts. Why turn elsewhere? 

For a number of years, the AMS tried to port the mathematical typesetting features of AMS-T X to L<sup>A</sup>T X, but they made little progress with the AMSFonts. Frank and I had just published the New Font Selection Scheme for L<sup>A</sup>TEX, which went a long way to satisfy what they wanted to accomplish. So it was logical that the AMS turned to us to add AMSFonts to L<sup>A</sup>T X. Being young and enthusiastic, we convinced the AMS that the AMS-T X commands should be changed to conform to the L<sup>A</sup>T X standards. Michael Downes was assigned as our AMS contact; his insight was a tremendous help. 

We already had L<sup>A</sup>TEX-NFSS, which could be run in two modes: compatible with the old LAT<sub>E</sub>X or enabled with the new font features. We added the reworked AMS-TEX code to L<sup>A</sup>TEX-NFSS, thus giving birth to AMS-L<sup>A</sup>TEX , released by the AMS at the August 1990 meeting of the International Mathematical Union in Kyoto. 

AMS-L<sup>A</sup>TEX was another variant of L<sup>A</sup>TEX. Many installations had several L<sup>A</sup>TEX variants to satisfy the needs of their users: with old and new font changing commands, with and without AMS-L<sup>A</sup>TEX , a single and a multi-language version. We decided to develop a Standard L<sup>A</sup>TEX that would reconcile all the variants. Out of a group of interested people grew what was later called the L<sup>A</sup>TEX3 team—and the L<sup>A</sup>TEX3 project got underway. The team’s first major accomplishment was the release of L<sup>A</sup>T Xe in June 1994. This standard L<sup>A</sup>T X incorporates all the improvements we wanted back in 1989. It is now very stable and it is uniformly used. 

Under the direction of Michael Downes, our AMS-L<sup>A</sup>T X code was turned into AMS packages that run under L<sup>A</sup>TEX just like other packages. Of course, the L<sup>A</sup>TEX3 team recognizes that these are special; we call them “required packages” because they are part and parcel of a mathematician’s standard toolbox. 

Since then a lot has been achieved to make an author’s task easier. A tremendous number of additional packages are available today. The L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X Companion, 2nd edition, describes many of my favorite packages. 

George Grätzer got involved with these developments in 1990, when he got his copy of AMS-L<sup>A</sup>TEX in Kyoto. The documentation he received explained that AMS-L<sup>A</sup>TEX is a L<sup>A</sup>TEX variant—read Lamport’s L<sup>A</sup>TEX book to get the proper background. AMS-L<sup>A</sup>TEX is not AMS-TEX either—read Spivak’s AMS-TEX book to get the proper background. The rest of the document explained in what way AMS-L<sup>A</sup>TEX difers from L<sup>A</sup>TEX and AMS-TEX. Talk about a steep learning curve ... 

Luckily, George’s frustration working through this nightmare was eased by his lengthy e-mail correspondence with Frank and lots of telephone calls to Michael. Three years of labor turned into his first book on L<sup>A</sup>TEX, providing a “simple introduction to AMS-L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X ”. This edition is more mature, but preserves what made his first book such a success. Just as in the first book, Part I, Mission Impossible, is a short introduction for the beginner. Chapter 1, Short Course, dramatically reducing the steep learning curve of a few weeks to a few hours in only 30 pages. Chapter 2, And a few more things. . . adds a few more advanced topics useful already at this early stage. 

The rest of the book is a detailed presentation of everything you may need to know. George “teaches by example”. You find in this book many illustrations of even the simplest concepts. For articles, he presents the L<sup>A</sup>TEX source file and the typeset result. For formulas, he discusses the building blocks with examples, presents a Formula Gallery, and a Visual Guide for multiline formulas. 

Going forth and creating “masterpieces of the typesetting art”—as Donald Knuth put it at the end of the T Xbook—requires a fair bit of initiation. This is the book for the L<sup>A</sup>T X beginner as well as for the advanced user. You just start at a diferent point. 

The topics covered include everything you need for mathematical publishing. 

Instructions on creating articles, from the simple to the complex 

Converting an article to a presentation 

Customize L<sup>A</sup>TEX to your own needs 

The secrets of writing a book 

Where to turn to get more information 

The many examples are complemented by a number of easily recognizable features: 

Rules which you must follow 

Tips on what to be careful about and how to achieve some specific results 

Experiments to show what happens when you make mistakes—sometimes, it can be dificult to understand what went wrong when all you see is an obscure L<sup>A</sup>TEX message 

This book teaches you how to convert your mathematical masterpieces into typographical ones, giving you a lot of useful advice on the way. How to avoid the traps for the unwary and how to make your editor happy. And hopefully, you’ll experience the fascination of doing it right. Using good typography to better express your ideas. 

If you want to learn L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X, buy this book and start with the Short Course. If you can have only one book on L<sup>A</sup>TEX next to your computer, this is the one to have. And if you want to learn about the world of L<sup>A</sup>TEX packages as of 2004, also buy a second book, the L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X Companion, 2nd edition. 

Peine Schopf 

Rainer Schöpf 

LAT<sub>E</sub>X3 team 

# Preface to the fifth edition

My book Practical L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X [42] was published last year. Many of the changes in this fifth edition are based on Practical L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X and on my articles “What Is New in L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X?” in the Notices of the American Mathematical Society [36–41] and [43]. 

Part I. Short Course of the fourth edition was revised under the title Chapter 1. Short Course. I renamed Part I: Mission Impossible. This part now has a second chapter: And a few more things ... The new Chapter 1 is what you absolutely, unquestionably must know to write your first T X document. It’s only 30 pages long, should not take more than a few hours to read and understand. No typing is necessary, the files you need are provided for you, see Section 1.1.2. 

T<sup>h</sup>e new C<sup>h</sup>apter 2 adds a <sup>f</sup>ew more top<sup>i</sup>cs t<sup>h</sup>at <sup>i</sup>s <sup>h</sup>e<sup>l</sup>p<sup>f</sup>u<sup>l</sup> to <sup>k</sup>now suc<sup>h</sup> as t<sup>h</sup>e aux files, what is their role, how to handle them. It deals in some detail with error messages. Finally, it contains Brian Davey’s list of L<sup>A</sup>TEX mistakes most often made by authors. 

To create “vector graphics” illustrations (see page 343 for an example), many users switched to Till Tantau’s TikZ package. We introduce TikZ in Chapter 13. We hope that the few commands we discuss are suficient to get you started. 

I carefully revised all the material in this book. One would think that this is not necessary in a fifth edition. But as Fred says, there are infinitely many typos in any book, and even our best eforts remove only finitely many. And so many of the links have changed. . . 

Finally, I should mention that I renamed the awkward user-defined commands to custom commands. How come I have not thought of this before? 

Toronto, ON, Canada 

George Grätzer 

# Introduction

## Is this book for you?

This book is for the mathematician, physicist, engineer, scientist, linguist, or technical typist who has to learn how to typeset articles containing mathematical formulas or diacritical marks. It teaches you how to use L<sup>A</sup>TEX, a typesetting markup language based on Donald E. Knuth’s typesetting language TEX, designed and implemented by Leslie Lamport, and greatly improved under the guidance of AMS. 

Part I provides a quick introduction to L<sup>A</sup>TEX, from typing examples of text and math to typing your first article such as the sample article on page 4 and creating your first presentation such as the sample presentation—four slides of which you find in Figure 1.5—in a very short time. The rest of the book provides a detailed exposition of LAT<sub>E</sub>X. 

L<sup>A</sup>TEX has a huge collection of rules and commands. While the basics in Part I should serve you well in all your writings, most articles and presentations also require you to look up special topics. Learn Part I well and become passingly familiar with the rest of the book, so when the need arises you know where to turn with your problems. 

You can find specific topics in the Short Contents, the detailed Contents, and the Index. 

Mathematicians find L<sup>A</sup>TEX very strange. A typical article in mathematics deals with a field defined by a few axioms, and the topic of the article needs only a few more. In contrast, L<sup>A</sup>TEX has hundreds of axioms. We try to ease the transition by introducing at the start as few commands as possible. For instance, we introduce presentations with only five new commands. 

## What is document markup?

When you work with a word processor, you see your document on the computer monitor more or less as it looks when printed, with its various fonts, font sizes, font shapes (e.g., roman, italic) and weights (e.g., normal, boldface), interline spacing, indentation, and so on. 

Working with a markup language is diferent. You type the source file of your article in a text editor, in which all characters appear in the same font. To indicate changes in the typeset text, you must add text markup commands to the source file. <sup>For instance</sup>, <sup>to em</sup>p<sup>hasize the</sup> p<sup>hrase</sup> detailed description <sup>in a LAT</sup>E<sup>X source file</sup>, type 

\emph{detailed description} 

The \emph command is a markup command. The marked-up text yields the typeset output 

detailed description 

In order to typeset math, you need math markup commands. As a simple example, consider the formula $\textstyle { \int { \sqrt { \alpha ^ { 2 } + x ^ { 2 } } } d x }$ . To mark it up in L<sup>A</sup>TEX, type 

$\int \sqrt{\alpha $\hat { \bf \theta } ^ { \langle 2 \rangle } + \hat { \bf \theta } \hat { \bf \phi } ^ { \langle 2 \rangle \dagger } \hat { \bf \theta } , \mathrm { d } { \bf x } \hat { \bf \theta }$ 

You do not have to worry about determining the size of the integral symbol or how to construct the square root symbol that covers $\alpha ^ { 2 } + x ^ { 2 }$ . L<sup>A</sup>TEX does it all for you. 

## The three layers

The markup language we shall discuss comes in three layers: TEX, L<sup>A</sup>TEX, and the AMS packages, described in detail in Appendix C. Most L<sup>A</sup>TEX installations automatically place all three on your computer. You do not have to know what comes from which layer, so we consider the three together and call it L<sup>A</sup>TEX. 

## The three platforms

Most of you run L<sup>A</sup>TEX on one of the following three computer types: 

A Windows computer, a computer running Microsoft Windows 

A Mac, a Macintosh computer running OS X 

A computer running a UNIX variant such as Solaris or Linux 

The L<sup>A</sup>T X source file and the typeset version both look the same independent of what computer you have. However, the way you type your source file, the way you typeset it, and the way you look at the typeset version depends on the computer and on the L<sup>A</sup>TEX implementation you use. 

## What’s in the book?

Part I is Mission Impossible; it helps you to get started quickly with L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X, to type your first articles, to make your first presentations, and it prepares you to tackle L<sup>A</sup>TEX in more depth in the subsequent parts. 

Chapter 1 is the Short Course. You start writing your first article—as typeset on page 4—and prepare yourfirst presentation—see some of the slides typeset on page 27. This chapter introduces how L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X uses the keyboard and how to type text. You do not need to learn much to understand the basics. Text markup is quite easy. You also learn math markup, which is not so straightforward. Several sections in this chapter ease you into mathematical typesetting. There is a section on the basic building blocks of math formulas. Another one discusses equations. Finally, we present the two simplest multiline formulas, which should cover most of your everyday needs. We also cover the elements of presentations with a simple example. 

In Chapter 2, we explain how things work, the structure of L<sup>A</sup>T X, the auxiliary files, the logical and visual design of an article, L<sup>A</sup>T X error messages. Finally, we present a long list of dos and don’t to help you write good L<sup>A</sup>TEX. 

Part II introduces the two most basic skills for writing with L<sup>A</sup>TEX in depth, typing text and typing math. 

Chapters 3 and 4 introduce text and displayed text. Chapter 3 is especially important because, when you type a L<sup>A</sup>TEX document, most of your time is spent typing text. The topics covered include special characters and accents, hyphenation, fonts, and spacing. Chapter 4 covers displayed text, including lists and tables, and for the mathematician, proclamations (theorem-like structures) and proofs. 

Typing math is the heart of any mathematical typesetting system. Chapter 5 discusses inline formulas in detail, including basic constructs, delimiters, operators, math accents, and horizontally stretchable lines. The chapter concludes with the Formula Gallery. 

Math symbols are covered in three sections in Chapter 6. How to space them, how to build new ones; we introduce the new set of some 2,000 STIX math symbols. We also look at the closely related subjects of math alphabets and fonts. Then we discuss tagging and grouping equations. 

L<sup>A</sup>TEX knows a lot about typesetting an inline formula, but not much about how to display a multiline formula. Chapter 7 presents the numerous tools L<sup>A</sup>TEX ofers to help you do that. We start with a Visual Guide to help you get oriented. 

Part III discusses the parts of a L<sup>A</sup>T X document. In Chapter 8, you learn about the structure of a L<sup>A</sup>T X document. The most important topics are sectioning and crossreferencing. In Chapter 9, we discuss the amsart document class for articles. In partic-<sup>ular</sup>, <sup>I</sup> p<sup>resent the title</sup> p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>e information. Cha</sup>p<sup>ter 9 also features</sup> secondarticle.tex, <sup>a sam</sup>p<sup>le article for</sup> amsart, <sup>somewhat more advanced than</sup> firstarticle.tex <sup>t</sup>yp<sup>e-</sup> set on page 4. You can learn a lot about L<sup>A</sup>TEX just by reading the source file one paragraph at a time and seeing how that paragraph is typeset. We conclude this chapter with a brief description of the AMS distribution, the packages and document classes, 

<sup>of</sup> <sup>which</sup> amsart <sup>is</sup> <sup>a</sup> p<sup>art.</sup> 

In Chapter 10 the most commonly used legacy document classes are presented, article, report, <sup>and</sup> letter (<sup>the</sup> book <sup>class is discussed in Cha</sup>p<sup>ter 17</sup>), <sup>alon</sup>g <sup>with</sup> <sup>a descri</sup>p<sup>tion of the standard LAT</sup>E<sup>X distribution. Althou</sup>g<sup>h</sup> article <sup>is not as so</sup>p<sup>histi-</sup> <sup>cated as</sup> amsart, <sup>it is commonl</sup>y <sup>used for articles not meant for</sup> p<sup>ublication.</sup> 

In Part IV, we start with Chapter 11, discussing PDF files, hyperlinks, and the hyperref package. This prepares you for presentations, which are PDF files with hyperlinks. In Chapter 12 we utilize the beamer package for making L<sup>A</sup>TEX presentations and Chapter 13 introduces its sister package TikZ for illustrations. 

Part V (Chapter 14) introduces techniques to customize L<sup>A</sup>TEX: custom commands and environments created by users, and command files. We present a sample <sup>command file</sup>, newlattice.sty, a<sup>nd a version of the second sam</sup>p<sup>le article utilizin</sup>g this command file. You learn how parameters that afect L<sup>A</sup>TEX’s behavior are stored in counters and length commands, how to change them, and how to design your own custom lists. A final section discusses the pitfalls of customization. 

In Part VI (Chapters 15 and 16), we discuss the special needs of longer documents. Two applications, contained in the standard L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X distribution, BIBT<sub>E</sub>X and MakeIndex, make compiling large bibliographies and indexes much easier. 

<sup>LAT</sup>E<sup>X</sup> p<sup>rovides the</sup> book <sup>and the</sup> amsbook <sup>document classes to serve as founda-</sup> tions for well-designed books. We discuss these in Chapter 17. Better quality books have to use document classes designed by professionals. 

You will probably find yourself referring to Appendices A and B time and again. They contain the math and text symbol tables. You can also find them in the samples file. 

Appendix C relates some historical background material on L<sup>A</sup>TEX. It gives you some insight into how L<sup>A</sup>TEX developed and how it works. Appendix D discusses the many ways we can find L<sup>A</sup>TEX material on the Internet. Appendix E is a short introduction to the use of PostScriptfonts in a L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X document. Appendix F briefly describes the use of L<sup>A</sup>TEX for languages other than American English. 

L<sup>A</sup>TEX on an iPad is introduced in Appendix G. 

Finally, Appendix H discusses what we left out, points you towards some areas for further reading, and mentions some recent developments. 

Lots of sample files help you save typing examples, see Section 1.1.2. You also get PDF files of Mission Impossible, the symbol tables, and the STIX symbols. 

## Mission statement

This book is a guide for typesetting mathematical documents within the constraints imposed by L<sup>A</sup>TEX, an elaborate system with hundreds of rules. L<sup>A</sup>TEX allows you to perform almost any mathematical typesetting task through the appropriate application of its rules. You can customize L<sup>A</sup>TEX by introducing custom commands and environments and by changing L<sup>A</sup>TEX parameters. You can also extend L<sup>A</sup>TEX by invoking packages 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/637fc1cf-16f2-479a-94ce-1647e65477cb/4951c29cf965cc492ac12527a804bff5c2df6aed4f8b0295486db31c8911cf66.jpg)


that accomplish special tasks. 

It is not my goal 

to survey the hundreds of L<sup>A</sup>TEX packages you can utilize to enhance L<sup>A</sup>TEX 

to teach how to write TEX code to create your own packages 

to discuss how to design beautiful documents by writing document classes 

The definitive book on the first topic, as of 2004, is Frank Mittelbach and Michel Goosens’s The L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X Companion, 2nd edition [56] (in collaboration with Johannes Braams, David Carlisle, and Chris Rowley). The second and third topics still await authoritative treatment. 

## Conventions

To make this book easy to read, I use some simple conventions: 

Explanatory text is set in this typeface: Times. 

Computer Modern typewriter is used to show what you should type, as well as messages from LaTeX. All the characters in this typeface have the same width, making it easy to recognize. 

I also use Computer Modern typewriter to indicate 

– <sup>Commands</sup> (\newpage) 

– <sup>Environments</sup> (\align) 

– <sup>Documents</sup> (firstarticle.tex) 

– <sup>Document classes</sup> (amsart) 

– <sup>Document class o</sup>p<sup>tions</sup> (draft) 

– <sup>Folders or directories</sup> (work) 

– The names of packages—extensions of L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X (verbatim) 

When I show you how something looks when typeset, I use Computer Modern, T X’s standard typeface: 

I think you find this typeface suficiently diferent from the other typefaces I have used. The strokes are much lighter so that you should not have much dificulty recognizing typeset L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X material. When the typeset material is a separate paragraph or paragraphs, corner brackets in the margin set it of from the rest of the text—unless it is a displayed formula. 

For explanations in the text, such as 

Compare if with iff, typed as iff and if{f}, respectively. 

the same typefaces are used. Because they are not set of spatially, it may be a little more dificult to see that if is set in Computer Modern roman (in Times, it looks like this: if ), whereas iff is set in the Computer Modern typewriter typeface. Compare: if, if, iff, and a larger version: if, if, iff. 

I usually introduce commands with examples, such as 

\\[22pt] 

However, it is sometimes necessary to define the syntax of a command more formally. For instance, 

\\[length ] 

where length, typeset in Computer Modern typewriter italic font, represents the value you have to supply. 

Good luck and have fun.

# Short course

It happens to most of us. We live a happy life without L<sup>A</sup>TEX and then, all of a sudden, we have to do something urgent that requires it. 

If you are a student, maybe your professor turned to you and said “I need the solutions to these exercises typed up and distributed to the class by tomorrow” and the solutions are chock-full of formulas, dificult to do in Word. 

Or you are a researcher whose documents have always been typed up by a secretary. You have to attend a conference and give a presentation. Your secretary is on vacation. 

In my case, it was a letter (this was before e-mail) from the American Mathematical Society, in which they informed me that my paper, written in Word, was accepted for publication. The AMS will publish the paper in nine months. However, a L<sup>A</sup>TEX version would be published in three months! So I had to learn L<sup>A</sup>TEX in a hurry. 

The mission, should you choose to accept it, is to get started really fast in L<sup>A</sup>TEX. Our goal is to produce in L<sup>A</sup>TEX the little article printed on the next page. 

Relax, this chapter will not self-destruct in five seconds. 

# A TECHNICAL RESULT FOR CONGRUENCES OF FINITE LATTICES

G. GRATZER<sup>¨</sup> 

Abstract. We present a technical result for congruences on finite lattices. 

## 1. Introduction

In some recent research, G. Cz´edli and I, see [1] and [2], spent quite an efort in proving that some equivalence relations on a planar semimodular lattice are congruences. The number of cases we had to consider was dramatically cut by the following result. 

Theorem 1. Let L be a finite lattice. Let δ be an equivalence relation on L with intervals as equivalence classes. Then δ is a congruence relation iff the following condition and its dual hold: 

$\left( \mathrm { C } _ { + } \right)$ If x is covered by $y , z \in L$ and $x \equiv y$ (mod δ), then $z \equiv y + z { \pmod { \delta } }$ 

## 2. The proof

We prove the join-substitution property: if $x \leq y$ and $x \equiv y$ (mod δ), then 

$$
x + z \equiv y + z \pmod {\delta}.\tag{1}
$$

Let $\boldsymbol { U } = [ x , y + z ]$ . We induct on length $U ,$ , the length of U. 

Let $I = [ y _ { 1 } , y + z ]$ and $J = [ z _ { 1 } , y + z ]$ . Then length I and length $J <$ < length U. Hence, the induction hypothesis applies to I and $\delta \rceil I ,$ and we obtain that $w \equiv y + u$ (mod δ). By the transitivity of δ, we conclude that 

$$
z _ {1} \equiv y + w \pmod {\delta}.\tag{2}
$$

Therefore, applying the induction hypothesis to J and $\delta 7 J ,$ , we conclude (1). 

## References



[1] G. Cz´edli, Patch extensions and trajectory colorings of slim rectangular lattices. Algebra Uni versalis 88 (2013), 255–280. 





[2] G. Gra¨tzer, Congruences of fork extensions of lattices. Acta Sci. Math. (Szeged), 57 (2014), 417–434.

## 1.1 Getting started

## 1.1.1 Your L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X

Are you sitting in front of your computer that has a L<sup>A</sup>TEX implementation? If you use a UNIX computer, you surely are. If you are in front of a Windows computer or a Mac, p<sup>oint</sup> y<sup>our</sup> <sup>Internet</sup> <sup>browser</sup> <sup>at</sup> tug.org<sup>.</sup> <sup>Choose</sup> <sup>to</sup> <sup>download</sup> <sup>MikTeX</sup> <sup>for</sup> <sup>a</sup> <sup>Windows</sup> computer and MacTeX for a Mac. Follow the easy instructions (and be patient, these are big downloads) and you are done. 

Even better, find a friend who can help. 

## 1.1.2 Sample files

We work with a few sample documents. Download them from the Springer page for this book: 

http://www.springer.com/us/book/9783319237954 

I suggest you create a <sup>f</sup>o<sup>l</sup>der, samples, on your computer to store t<sup>h</sup>e down<sup>l</sup>oaded sample files, and another folder called work, where you will keep your working files. Copy the documents from the samples to the work folder as needed. In this book, the samples and workfolders refer to thefolders you created. 

<sup>One of the sam</sup>p<sup>le files is</sup> sample.cls<sup>. Make sure it is in the</sup> work <sup>folder when</sup> you typeset a sample document. 

## 1.1.3 Editing cycle

Watch a friend type a document in L<sup>A</sup>TEX and learn the basic steps. 

1. A text editor is used to create a L<sup>A</sup>T X sourcefile. A source file might look like this: 

\documentclass{amsart} 

\begin{document} 

Then $\delta$ is a congruence relation. I can type formulas! \end{document} 

Note that the source file is diferent from a typical word processor file. All characters are displayed in the same font and size. 

2. Yourfriend “typesets” the sourcefile (tells the application to produce a typeset version) and views the result on the monitor: 

Then � is a congruence relation. I can type formulas! 

3. The editing cycle continues. Your friend goes back and forth between the source file and the typeset version, making changes and observing the results of these changes. 

4. The file is viewed/printed. View the typeset version as a pdf file or print it to get a paper version. 

If L<sup>A</sup>TEX finds a mistake when typesetting the source file, it records this in the log file. The log window (some call it console) displays a shorter version. 

Various L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X implementations have diferent names for the source file, the text editor, the typeset file, the typeset window, the log file, and the log window. Become familiar with these names, so you can follow along with our discussions. 

## 1.1.4 Typing the source file

A source file is made up of text,formulas, and instructions (commands) to L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X. For instance, consider the following variant of the first sentence of this paragraph: 

A source file is made up of text, formulas (e.g., 

$\sqrt{5}$), and \emph{instructions to} \la. 

This typesets as 

A source file is made up of text, formulas $( \mathrm { e . g . , } \sqrt { 5 } )$ , and instructions to L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X. L 

In this sentence, the first part 

A source file is made up of text, formulas (e.g., 

is text. Then 

$\sqrt{5}$ 

is a formula 

), and 

is text again. Finally, 

\emph{instructions to} \la. 

The instruction \emph is a command with an argument, while the instruction \LaTeX is a command without an argument. Commands, as a rule, start with a backslash ( \ ) and te<sup>ll</sup> L<sup>A</sup>TEX to do somet<sup>hi</sup>ng spec<sup>i</sup>a<sup>l</sup>. In t<sup>hi</sup>s case, t<sup>h</sup>e command \emph emp<sup>h</sup>as<sup>i</sup>zes <sup>i</sup>ts argument (the text between the braces). Another kind of instruction to L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X is called an environment. For instance, the commands 

\begin{center} 

\end{center} 

enclose a center environment; the contents (the text typed between these two commands) are centered when typeset. 

In practice, text, formulas, and instructions (commands) are mixed. For example, 

My first integral: $\int \zeta^{2}(x) \, dx$. 

is a mixture of all three; it typesets as 

My first integral: $\int \zeta^2 (x)dx$ . 

Creating a document in L<sup>A</sup>TEX requires that we type in the source file. So we start with the keyboard, proceed to type a short note, and learn some simple rules for typing text in LAT<sub>E</sub>X. 

## 1.2 The keyboard

The following keys are used to type the source file: 

$$
\begin{array}{l l l} \text {a - z} & \text {A - Z} & 0 - 9 \\ + = * / () [ ] \end{array}
$$

You can also use the following punctuation marks: 

$$
, \quad ; \quad . \quad ? \quad ! \quad : \quad " \quad , -
$$

and the space bar, the Tab key, and the Return (or Enter) key. 

Finally, there are thirteen special keys that are mostly used in L<sup>A</sup>TEX commands: 

$$
\#    \% \& \sim \_ \hat {} \backslash \{\} @" |
$$

If you need to have these characters typeset in your document, there are commands to produce them. For instance, the dollar sign, $ is typed as \$, the underscore, _ , is typed as \_, and the percent sign, %, is typed as \%. Only @ requires no special command, type @ to print @; see Sections 3.1.2 and B.4. 

There are also commands to produce composite characters, such as accented characters, for example ä, which is typed as \"{a}. L<sup>A</sup>T X prohibits the use of other keys on your keyboard unless you have special support for it. See the text accent table in Sections 3.4.7 and B.2. If you want to use accented characters in your source file, then y<sup>ou must use the</sup> inputenc p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>e.</sup> 

Tip The text accent table looks formidable. Don’t even dream of memorizing it. You will need very few. When you need a text accent, look it up. I know only one: \"a (LOL). If you use a name with accented characters, figure out once how to type it, and then any time you need it you can just copy and paste (chances are that the name is in your list of references). 

## 1.3 Your first text notes

We start our discussion on how to type a note in L<sup>A</sup>TEX with a simple example. Suppose you want to use L<sup>A</sup>TEX to produce the following: 

It is of some concern to me that the terminology used in multi-section math courses is not uniform. 

In several sections of the course on matrix theory, the term “hamiltonianreduced” is used. I, personally, would rather call these “hyper-simple”. I invite others to comment on this problem. 

To produce this typeset document, create a new file in your work folder with <sup>the name</sup> textnote1.tex<sup>. T</sup>yp<sup>e the followin</sup>g, <sup>includin</sup>g <sup>the s</sup>p<sup>acin</sup>g <sup>and linebreaks</sup> shown, but not the line numbers: 

```latex
% Sample file: textnote1.tex
\documentclass{sample}
\begin{document}
It is of some concern to me that
the terminology used in multi-section
math courses is not uniform.
In several sections of the course on matrix theory, the term
'hamiltonian-reduced' is used.
I, personally, would rather call these
'hyper-simple'. I invite others
to comment on this problem.
\end{document} 
```

<sup>Alternativel</sup>y, <sup>co</sup>py <sup>the</sup> textnote1.tex <sup>file from the</sup> samples <sup>folder</sup> (<sup>see</sup> p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>e 5</sup>)<sup>.</sup> 

<sup>The first line of</sup> textnote1.tex <sup>starts with</sup> %<sup>. Such lines are called</sup> comments and are ignored by L<sup>A</sup>TEX. Commenting is very useful. For example, if you want to add some notes to your source file and you do not want those notes to appear in the typeset version of your document, begin those lines with a %. You can also comment out part of a line: 

simply put, we believe % actually, it’s not so simple 

Everything on the line after the % character is ignored by L<sup>A</sup>TEX. 

Line 2 specifies the document class, sample (the special class we provided for the sample documents), which controls how the document is formatted. 

<sup>The text of the note is t</sup>yp<sup>ed within the</sup> document <sup>environment</sup>, <sup>that is</sup>, <sup>between</sup> \begin{document} <sup>and</sup> \end{document}<sup>.</sup> 

<sup>Now t</sup>yp<sup>eset</sup> textnote1.tex<sup>. You should</sup> g<sup>et the t</sup>yp<sup>eset document as shown.</sup> As you can see from this example, L<sup>A</sup>TEX is diferent from a word processor. It disregards the way you input and position the text, and follows only the formatting instructions given by the document class and the markup commands. L<sup>A</sup>TEX notices when you put a blank space in the text, but it ignores how many blank spaces have been typed. L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X does not distinguish between a blank space (hitting the space bar), a tab (hitting the Tab key), and a single carriage return (hitting Return once). However, hitting Return twice gives a blank line; one or more blank lines mark the end of a paragraph. There is also a command for a new paragraph: \par. 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/637fc1cf-16f2-479a-94ce-1647e65477cb/5c3a7e65b0e6937134ad51c60f0d2950cc607538ccbcaa0da47168cb158d130b.jpg)


L<sup>A</sup>TEX, by default, fully justifies text by placing a flexible amount of space between words—the interword space—and a somewhat larger space between sentences—the intersentence space. If you have to force an interword space, you can use the $\updownarrow _ { \sqcup }$ command (in L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X books, we use the symbol $\sqcup$ to mean a blank space). The ˜ (tilde) command also forces an interword space, but with a diference: it keeps the words on the same line. This command produces a tie or nonbreakable space. 

Note that on lines 11 and 13, the left double quotes is typed as two left single quotes and the right double quote is typed as two right single quotes, apostrophes. 

We numbered the lines of the source file for easy reference. Sometimes you may want the same for the typeset file. This is really easy. Just add the two lines 

\usepackage{lineno} 

\linenumbers 

<sup>after the</sup> \documentclass <sup>line and</sup> y<sup>ou</sup> g<sup>et:</sup> 

1 It is of some concern to me that the terminology used in multi-section math 2 courses is not uniform. 

3 In several sections of the course on matrix theory, the term “hamiltonian 

4 reduced” is used. I, personally, would rather call these “hyper-simple”. I invite 

5 others to comment on this problem. 

Next, we produce the following note: 

January 5, 2015 

From the desk of George Grätzer 

February 7–21 please use my temporary e-mail address: 

Type t<sup>h</sup>e source <sup>fil</sup>e, w<sup>i</sup>t<sup>h</sup>out t<sup>h</sup>e <sup>li</sup>ne numbers. Save <sup>i</sup>t <sup>i</sup>n your work <sup>f</sup>o<sup>l</sup>der as textnote2.tex (textnote2.tex <sup>can also be found in the</sup> samples <sup>folder</sup>)<sup>:</sup> 

```latex
% Sample file: textnote2.tex
\documentclass{sample}
\begin{document}
\begin{flushright}
\today
\end{flushright}
\textbf{From the desk of George Gr\"{a}tzer}
February 7--21 \emph{please} use my temporary e-mail address:
\begin{center}
\texttt{George\_Gratzer@yahoo.com}
\end{center}
\end{document} 
```

This note introduces several additional text features of LAT<sub>E</sub>X. 

The \today command (in line 6) to display the date on which the document is typeset, so you will see a date diferent from the date shown above in your own typeset document (see also Section 3.4.8). 

The environments to rightjustify (lines 5–7) and center (lines 12–14) text. 

The commands to change the text style, including the \emph command (line 10) to emphasize text, the \textbf command (line 8) for bold text (text bold font), and <sup>the</sup> \texttt <sup>command</sup> (<sup>line 13</sup>) <sup>to</sup> p<sup>roduce</sup> typewriter style <sup>text. These are</sup> commands with arguments. 

The form of the L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X commands. As we have noted already, almost all L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X commands start with a backslash ( \ ) followed by the command name. For instance, \textbf <sup>is a command and</sup> textbf <sup>is the command name. The command name is</sup> terminated by the first non-alphabetic character, that is, by any character other than a–z or A–Z. 

The multiple role of hyphens: Double hyphens are used for number ranges. For example, 7--21 (in line 10) typesets as 7–21. The punctuation mark – is called an en dash. Use triple hyphens for the em dash punctuation mark—such as the one in this sentence. 

Special rules for special characters (see Section 1.2), for accented characters, and for some European characters. For instance, the accented character ä is typed as \"{a}. ## 1.4 Lines too wide

L<sup>A</sup>TEX reads the text in the source file one line at a time and typesets the entire paragraph when the end of a paragraph is reached. Occasionally, L<sup>A</sup>T X gets into trouble when trying to split the paragraph into typeset lines. To illustrate this situation, modify textnote1.tex<sup>. In the second sentence</sup>, <sup>re</sup>p<sup>lace</sup> term <sup>b</sup>y strange term<sup>. Now save</sup> <sup>this modified file in</sup> y<sup>our</sup> work <sup>folder usin</sup>g <sup>the name</sup> textnote1bad.tex (<sup>or co</sup>py <sup>the</sup> <sup>file from the</sup> samples <sup>folder</sup>)<sup>.</sup> 

<sup>T</sup>yp<sup>esettin</sup>g textnote1bad.tex, y<sup>ou obtain the followin</sup>g<sup>:</sup> 

1 It is of some concern to me that the terminology used in multi-section math 2 courses is not uniform. 

3 In several sections of the course on matrix theory, the term “hamiltonian-4 reduced” is used. I, personally, would rather call these “hyper-simple”. I invite 5 others to comment on this problem. 

The first line of paragraph two is too wide. In the log window, L<sup>A</sup>TEX displays the following messages: 

Overfull \hbox (15.38948pt 

```txt
`overfull \nbox (15.38948pt
too wide) in paragraph at lines 9--15 []\0T1/cmr/m/n/10 In sev-eral
sec-tions of the course on ma-trix theory, the strange term
``'hamiltonian-
```

It informs you that the typeset version of this paragraph has a line that is 15.38948 points too wide. L<sup>A</sup>T X uses points (pt) to measure distances; there are about 72 points in 1 inch. Then it identifies the source of the problem: L<sup>A</sup>TEX did not properly hyphenate the word hamiltonian-reduced because it (automatically) hyphenates a hyphenated word only at the hyphen. 

What to do, when a line is too long? 

```txt
Tip Your first line of defense: reword the offending line. Write
The strange term “‘hamiltonian-reduced’” is used in several sections of the course on matrix theory.
and the problem goes away.
Your second line of defense: insert one or more optional hyphen commands (\-), which tell LATEX where it can hyphenate the word. Write:
hamil\-tonian-reduced 
```

we assume that the function is defined and continuous in a neighborhood of �. L

This note introduces several basic concepts of formulas in L<sup>A</sup>TEX. 

<sup>There are two kinds of math formulas and environments in</sup> formulanote.tex<sup>:</sup> 

– Inline formulas; they open and close with $ or open with \( and close with \). 

– Displayed math environments; they open with \[ and close with \]. (We will introduce many other displayed math environments in Section 1.7 and Chapter 7.) 

L<sup>A</sup>TEX uses its own spacing rules within math environments, and completely ignores the white spaces you type, with two exceptions: 

– <sup>S</sup>p<sup>aces that terminate commands. So in</sup> $\infty a$ <sup>the s</sup>p<sup>ace is not i</sup>g<sup>nored</sup>; $\inftya$ produces an error. 

– Spaces in the arguments of commands that temporarily revert to regular text. \text is such a command; see Sections 1.6 and 5.4.6. 

The white space that you add when typing formulas is important only for the readability of the source file. 

A math symbol is invoked by a command. For example, the command for ∞ is \infty and the command for → is \to. The math symbols are organized into tables in Appendix A; <sup>see also</sup> SymbolTables.pdf <sup>in the</sup> samples <sup>folder.</sup> 

Some commands, such as <sub>\sqrt</sub>, need arguments enclosed b<sub>y {</sub> and <sub>}</sub>. To t<sub>yp</sub>eset √5, <sup>t</sup>yp<sup>e</sup> $\sqrt{5}$, <sup>where</sup> \sqrt <sup>is the command and</sup> 5 <sup>is the ar</sup>g<sup>ument.</sup> 

Some commands need more than one argument. To get 

$$
\frac {3 + x}{5}
$$

type 

\[ 

\frac{3+x}{5} 

\] 

<sup>where</sup> \frac <sup>is the command</sup>, 3+x <sup>and</sup> 5 <sup>are the ar</sup>g<sup>uments.</sup> 

There is no blank line before a displayed formula!

## 1.6 The building blocks ofaformula

```txt
A formula (inline or displayed) is built from components. We group them as follows: Arithmetic Binomial coefficients Congruences Delimiters Ellipses Integrals Math accents Matrices Operators Roots Text In this section, I describe each of these groups, and provide examples illustrating their 
```

In this section, I describe each of these groups, and provide examples illustrating their use. Read carefully the groups you need! 

Arithmetic We type the arithmetic operations $a + b , a - b , - a , a / b ,$ and �� in the natural way: $a + b$, $a - b$, $-a$, $a / b$, and $a b$ (the spaces are typed only for readability). 

If you wish to use ⋅ or × for multiplication, as in �⋅� or �×�, use \cdot or \times, respectively. The formulas �⋅� and �×� are typed as $a \cdot b$ and $a \times b$. 

Displayed fractions, such as 

$$
\frac {1 + 2 x}{x + y + x y}
$$

<sup>are t</sup>yp<sup>ed with</sup> \frac<sup>:</sup> 

```latex
[\frac{1 + 2x}{x + y + xy}] 
```

Subscripts and superscripts Subscripts are typed with _ and superscripts with ˆ (caret). Subscripts and superscripts should be enclosed in braces, that is, typed between { and }. To get $a _ { 1 }$ , type $a_{1}$. Omitting the braces in this example causes no harm, but to get $a _ { 1 0 } ,$ you must type $a_{10}$. Indeed, $a_10$ is typeset as $a _ { 1 } 0 .$ 

There is one symbol, the prime (’), that is automatically superscripted in a formula. To get $f ^ { \prime } ( x )$ , just type $\$ 123,456$ . (On many keyboards, the symbol on the key looks like this: `) 

See Section 5.4.1 for more detail. 

Binomial coeficients Binomial coeficients are typeset with the \binom command. \binom{a}{b + c} <sup>is here inline:</sup> $\scriptstyle { \binom { a } { b + c } }$ , whereas 

$$
\binom{a}{b + c}
$$

is the displayed version. 

See Section 5.4.2 for more detail. 

Congruences The two most important forms are 

$$
\begin{array}{l l} a \equiv v (\text {mod} \theta) & \text {typed as} \\ a \equiv v (\theta) & \text {typed as} \end{array} \quad \begin{array}{l l} \text {\$a \equiv v \pmod{\theta}} \\ \text {\$a \equiv v \pmod{\theta}} \end{array}
$$

See Section 5.6.2 for more detail. 

Delimiters Parentheses and square brackets are examples of delimiters. They are used to delimit some subformulas, as in $\$ 123,456$ , which typesets as $[ ( a * b ) +$ $( c * d ) ] ^ { 2 }$ . L<sup>A</sup>TEX can be instructed to expand them vertically to enclose a formula such as 

$$
\left(\frac {1 + x}{2 + y ^ {2}}\right) ^ {2}
$$

which is typed as 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \backslash [ \\ \text {   left(  \frac{1   +   x}{2   +   y^{2}} \}   \text {   right) } ^{2} \} } \\ \backslash ] \end{array}
$$

<sup>The</sup> \left( <sup>and</sup> \right) <sup>commands tell LAT</sup>E<sup>X to size the</sup> p<sup>arentheses correctl</sup>y, <sup>rela-</sup> tive to the size of the formula inside the parentheses; sometimes the result is pleasing, sometimes not. 

We dedicate Section 5.5 to this topic. 

Ellipses In a formula, the ellipsis is printed either as low (or on-the-line) dots: 

$$
F (x _ {1}, \dots , x _ {n}) \quad \text { is   typed   as } \quad F (x _ {-} \{1 \}, \backslash \text { dots }, x _ {-} \{n \})
$$

or as centered dots: 

� + ⋯ + � is typed as 

$$
\mathbb {S} x _ {-} \{1 \} + \backslash d o t s + x _ {-} \{n \}
$$

<sup>Use</sup> \cdots <sup>and</sup> \ldots <sup>if</sup> \dots <sup>does not work as ex</sup>p<sup>ected.</sup> 

See Section 5.4.3 for more detail. 

Integrals The command for an integral is \int. The lower limit is specified as a subscript and the upper limit is specified as a superscript. For example, the formula $\textstyle \int _ { 0 } ^ { \pi }$ sin � �� = 2 is typed as 

$\int_{0}^{\pi} \sin x$ , dx = 2 

where \, is a spacing command. 

The formula looks bad without the spacing command: $\textstyle \int _ { 0 } ^ { \pi }$ sin ��� = 2. 

See Section 5.4.4 for more complicated integrals. 

Math accents The four most frequently used math accents are: 

ā    typed as $bar{a}$ $\hat{a}$ typed as $hat{a}$ ā    typed as $tilde{a}$ $\vec{a}$ typed as $vec{a}$ 

See Section 5.7 for more detail. See Sections 5.7 and A.8 for complete lists. 

Matrices You type the matrix

## 1.7.1 Equations

<sup>The</sup> equation <sup>environment creates a dis</sup>p<sup>la</sup>y<sup>ed formula and automaticall</sup>y g<sup>enerates an</sup> equation number. The equation

You can choose to have equations numbered within each section—(1.1), (1.2), . . . , in Section 1; (2.1), (2.2), . . . , in Section 2; and so on—by including, in the preamble (see Sections 1.8 and 5.3), the command 

## \numberwithin{equation}{section}

<sup>The</sup> equation* <sup>environment is the same as the dis</sup>p<sup>la</sup>y<sup>ed formula o</sup>p<sup>ened with</sup> \[ <sup>and</sup> <sup>closed with</sup> \] <sup>we discussed in Section 1.5. Sometimes</sup> y<sup>ou ma</sup>y <sup>want to use</sup> equation* <sup>for</sup> the ease of deleting the *-s if you wish.

<sup>Th</sup>e <sup>n</sup>u<sup>mb</sup>e<sup>r</sup> o<sup>f</sup> t<sup>hi</sup>s <sup>f</sup>o<sup>rm</sup>u<sup>l</sup>a <sup>i</sup>s <sup>r</sup>e<sup>f</sup>e<sup>r</sup>e<sup>n</sup>ce<sup>d</sup> w<sup>i</sup>t<sup>h</sup> t<sup>h</sup>e \ref co<sup>mm</sup>a<sup>nd</sup>. <sup>I</sup>ts page <sup>i</sup>s <sup>r</sup>e<sup>f</sup>e<sup>r</sup> <sup>enced usin</sup>g <sup>the</sup> \pageref <sup>command. For exam</sup>p<sup>le</sup>, <sup>to</sup> g<sup>et</sup> 

type (see Sections 1.3 and Section 3.4.3 for ~) 

see~(\ref{E:firstIntegral}) on page~\pageref{E:firstIntegral}.

## Absolute referencing

Equations can also be tagged by attaching a name to the formula with the \tag command. The tag replaces the equation number. 

For example, 

(Int) 

$$
\int_ {0} ^ {\pi} \sin x d x = 2
$$

is typed as 

```latex
\begin{equation}
    \int_{0}~{\pi} \sin x \, dx = 2 \tag{Int}
\end{equation} 
```

Tags are absolute. This equation is always referred to as (Int). Equation numbers, on the other hand, are relative, they may change when the file is edited. 

## 1.7.3 Aligned formulas

L<sup>A</sup>TEX has many ways to typeset multiline formulas. We discuss three constructs in this section: simple alignment, annotated alignment, and cases. For more constructs, see Chapter 7. 

<sup>For sim</sup>p<sup>le and annotated ali</sup>g<sup>nment we use the</sup> align <sup>environment. Each line in the</sup> align <sup>environment is a se</sup>p<sup>arate e</sup>q<sup>uation</sup>, <sup>which LAT</sup>E<sup>X automaticall</sup>y <sup>numbers.</sup> 

## Simple alignment

Simple alignment is used to align two or more formulas. To obtain the formulas 

(2) 

$$
\begin{array}{c} {r ^ {2} = s ^ {2} + t ^ {2},} \\ {2 u + 1 = v + w ^ {\alpha}.} \end{array}\tag{3}
$$

type the following, using \\ as the line separator and & as the alignment point: 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \text {   begin   } \{\text { align } \} \\ \quad r ^ {\{2 \}} \& = s ^ {\{2 \}} + t ^ {\{2 \}}, \\ \quad 2 u + 1 \& = v + w ^ {\{\alpha \}}. \\ \text {   end   } \{\text { align } \} \end{array} \quad \begin{array}{l} \text {   label   } \{\text { E:Pyth } \} \backslash \% \text { eqref   } \{\text { E:Pyth } \} \\ \text {   label   } \{\text { E:alpha } \} \% \text { eqref   } \{\text { E:alpha } \} \end{array}
$$

Figure 1.1 may help visualize the placements of the ampersands. 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/637fc1cf-16f2-479a-94ce-1647e65477cb/50ca15c7481a87b1d62f30a44ccd929e834f4e5d52b6a2de3a2c3da41eb3d0a2.jpg)



Figure 1.1: Simple alignment: source and typeset.


These formulas are numbered (2) and (3) because they are preceded by one numbered equation earlier in this section. 

<sup>The</sup> align <sup>environment can also be used to break a lon</sup>g <sup>formula into two or more</sup> parts. Since numbering both lines in such a case would be undesirable, you can prevent t<sup>h</sup>e <sup>n</sup>u<sup>mb</sup>e<sup>rin</sup>g o<sup>f</sup> t<sup>h</sup>e seco<sup>nd</sup> <sup>lin</sup>e <sup>b</sup>y us<sup>in</sup>g t<sup>h</sup>e \notag co<sup>mm</sup>a<sup>nd</sup> <sup>in</sup> t<sup>h</sup>e seco<sup>nd</sup> pa<sup>r</sup>t o<sup>f</sup> t<sup>h</sup>e formula. For example, 

$$
\begin{array}{c} {h (x) = \int \left(\frac {f (x) + g (x)}{1 + f ^ {2} (x)} + \frac {1 + f (x) g (x)}{\sqrt {1 - \sin x}}\right) d x} \\ {= \int \frac {1 + f (x)}{1 + g (x)} d x - 2 \tan^ {- 1} (x - 2)} \end{array}\tag{4}
$$

is typed as follows: 

$$
\begin{array}{l}\begin{array}{r l}&\begin{array}{r l}&h(x) \&=\backslash int \left(\backslash frac\{f(x)+g(x)\}\{1+f^{\{2\}}(x)\} \\ &\quad+\backslash frac\{1+f(x)g(x)\}\{\sqrt{1-\sin x}\}\end{array}\\ &\quad\backslash right)\backslash,dx\backslash label\{E:longInt\}\backslash\%\backslash eqref\{E:longInt\}\end{array}\\&=\backslash int \backslash frac\{1+f(x)\}\{1+g(x)\}\backslash,dx\\&-2\tan^{-1}(x-2)\notag\\end\begin{array}{r l}&\end{array}
$$

The rules for simple alignment are easy to remember. 

## Rule Simple alignments

<sup>Use the</sup> align <sup>environment.</sup> 

Separate the lines with \\. 

In each line, indicate the alignment point with &, one & per line. If the alignment point is adjacent to an =, +, and so on, place the & before to ensure proper spacing. 

<sup>Place a</sup> \notag <sup>command in each line that</sup> y<sup>ou do not wish numbered.</sup> 

<sup>If no line should be numbered</sup>, <sup>use the</sup> align* <sup>environment.</sup> 

<sup>Place a</sup> \label <sup>command in each numbered line</sup> y<sup>ou can want to reference with</sup> \ref, \eqref, <sup>or</sup> \pageref<sup>.</sup> 

## Annotated alignment

Annotated alignment allows you to align formulas and their annotations, that is, explanatory text, separately: 

```latex
(5)    x = x ∧ (y ∨ z)    (by distributivity)
    = (x ∧ y) ∨ (x ∧ z)    (by condition (M))
    = y ∨ z

This is typed as
\begin{align}
    x &= x \wedge (y \vee z)
    &&\text{(by distributivity)}\label{E:Align}%\eqref{E:Align}\
    &= (x \wedge y) \vee (x \wedge z)
    &&\text{(by condition (M))} \notag \\
    &= y \vee z \notag
\end{align} 
```


Figure 1.2 may help visualize the placements of the ampersands.


## Rule Annotated alignment

The rules for annotated alignment are similar to the rules of simple alignment. In each line, in addition to the alignment point marked by &, there is also a mark for the start of the annotation: . 

## 1.7.4 Cases

<sup>The</sup> cases <sup>construct is a s</sup>p<sup>ecialized matrix. It has to a</sup>pp<sup>ear within a math environment</sup> <sup>such as the</sup> equation <sup>environment or the</sup> align <sup>environment. Here is a t</sup>yp<sup>ical exam</sup>p<sup>le:</sup> 

$$
f (x) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} - x ^ {2}, & \text {if} x <   0; \\ \alpha + x, & \text {if} 0 \leq x \leq 1; \\ x ^ {2}, & \text {otherwise.} \end{array} \right.
$$

It is typed as follows: 

```latex
\[
f(x) =
\begin{cases}
-x^{-2}, &\text{if $x < 0$;} \\
\alpha + x, &\text{if $0 \leq x \leq 1$;} \\
x^{-2}, &\text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\] 
```

<sup>The rules for usin</sup>g <sup>the</sup> cases <sup>environment are the same as for matrices. Se</sup>p<sup>arate the</sup> lines with \\ and indicate the annotation with &. 

## 1.8 The anatomy of a document

<sup>To be</sup>g<sup>in</sup>, <sup>we use the sam</sup>p<sup>le document</sup> firstarticle.tex (<sup>in the</sup> samples <sup>folder</sup>) <sup>to ex-</sup> amine the anatomy of an document. 

Every L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X document has two parts, the preamble and the body. The preamble of a document is everything from the first line of the source file down to the line 

\begin{document} 

The body is the contents of the document environment. For a schematic view of a document, see Figure 1.3.

The preamble contains instructions afecting the entire document. The only required <sup>command in the</sup> p<sup>reamble is the</sup> \documentclass <sup>command. There are other commands</sup> (<sup>such as the</sup> \usepackage <sup>commands</sup>, <sup>see Section 8.2</sup>) <sup>that must be</sup> p<sup>laced in the</sup> p<sup>reamble</sup> if they are used, but such commands do not have to be present in every document. 

<sup>Here</sup> <sup>is</sup> <sup>the</sup> p<sup>reamble</sup> <sup>and</sup> <sup>to</sup>p <sup>matter</sup> <sup>of</sup> firstarticle<sup>:</sup> 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/637fc1cf-16f2-479a-94ce-1647e65477cb/88f5f6dbefd549a05d100e91d1a138a465ae07638cd5bc29188c1f9f7383a3bb.jpg)



Figure 1.3: A schematic view of a document.

<sup>You</sup> <sup>find</sup> <sup>the</sup> <sup>source</sup> <sup>file</sup>, firstarticle.tex, <sup>in</sup> <sup>the</sup> samples <sup>folder</sup> <sup>and</sup> <sup>the</sup> <sup>t</sup>yp<sup>eset</sup> <sup>document</sup> on page 4. 

To simplify the discussion in Part I, we discuss only one document class for articles: amsart<sup>. You ma</sup>y <sup>come across its</sup> p<sup>redecessor</sup>, article, <sup>which handles a limited set of</sup> commands for the preamble and the top matter and displays them diferently. ## 1.9 Your own commands

Over time, L<sup>A</sup>TEX can be adjusted to fit your needs. You add packages to enable L<sup>A</sup>TEX to do <sup>new thin</sup>g<sup>s</sup> (<sup>such as the</sup> graphicx p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>e</sup>, <sup>see Sections 1.10 and 8.4.3</sup>) <sup>and introduce</sup> y<sup>our</sup> own commands to facilitate typing and make the source file more readable. 

<sup>We can add two new commands to the sam</sup>p<sup>le article</sup> firstarticle.tex<sup>:</sup> 

\newcommand{\pdelta}{\pmod{\delta}} 

\DeclareMathOperator{\length}{length} 

So instead of 

$x \equiv y \pmod{\delta}$+ 

we can type 

$x \equiv y \pdelta$ 

<sup>and instead of</sup> length\,$U$, <sup>we can t</sup>yp<sup>e</sup> $\length U$ (<sup>see Section 14.1.6</sup>)<sup>. Notice how</sup> the spacing is now done by L<sup>A</sup>T X! 

We’ll dedicate Chapter 14 to customizing L<sup>A</sup>TEX.

## 1.11 The anatomy ofa presentation

Chances are, one of your first exposures to L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X was watching a presentation. The presenter used a pdf document produced by L<sup>A</sup>T X and opened it with Adobe Reader. He went from “slide” to “slide” by pressing the space bar. Figure 1.4 and Figure 1.5 show four slides of a presentation. 

In L<sup>A</sup>TEX, you use a presentation package—really, a document class—to prepare the PDF file. We use Till Tantau’s BEAMER. 

Here are the first few lines—the preamble and the Title slide—of the source file of <sup>our sam</sup>p<sup>le</sup> p<sup>resentation</sup>, firstpresentation.tex (<sup>see</sup> firstpresentation.tex <sup>in the</sup> samples <sup>folder</sup>, <sup>alon</sup>g <sup>with</sup> Louisville.tex, <sup>the full</sup> p<sup>resentation</sup>)<sup>:</sup> 

\documentclass[leqno]{beamer} 

\usetheme{Warsaw} 

\DeclareMathOperator{\Princ}{Princ} 

\begin{document} 

\title{The order of principal congruences} 

\author{G. Gr\"atzer} 

\date{} 

\maketitle

Figure 1.5: Slides 3 and 4


\usetheme{Warsaw} p<sup>rovides a flavor. It is followed b</sup>y <sup>the Title slide</sup>, p<sup>rovidin</sup>g <sup>the</sup> title and the author. 

T<sup>h</sup>e \title command may be <sup>l</sup>onger, <sup>i</sup>t may conta<sup>i</sup>n a<sup>ll</sup> t<sup>h</sup>e add<sup>i</sup>t<sup>i</sup>ona<sup>l i</sup>n<sup>f</sup>ormat<sup>i</sup>on you <sup>ma</sup>y <sup>want to dis</sup>p<sup>la</sup>y<sup>. Here is the</sup> \title <sup>command of</sup> Louisville.tex<sup>:</sup>

```latex
\title[The order of principal congruences of a bounded lattice]
{The order of principal congruences\\
of a bounded lattice.\\
AMS Fall Southeastern Sectional Meeting\\
```

Note that the \title has two parts. The first, in [], is the short title, repeated in the bottom line on every slide. The second, in {}, is the title for the front page. 

The rest of the presentation source file is divided into twoframes with the structure: 

Each frame produces a “slide” (or more). Here is the first frame:

\begin{frame}
\frametitle{Summary}
We characterize the order of principal congruences
of a bounded lattice
as a bounded ordered set.
We~also state a number of open problems in this new field.
\medskip

arXiv: 1309.6712
\end{frame}

The command \frametitle gives the slide its title: Summary, see Slide 2 in Figure 1.4. In the body of the frame, you type regular L^TEX.
    To produce Slides 3 and 4, it would be natural to try

\begin{frame}
\frametitle{Theorem 1}
For a bounded lattice $L$, the order $Princ K$$ is bounded.
We now state the converse.
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}
\frametitle{Theorem 1}
For a bounded lattice $L$, the order $Princ K$$ is bounded.
We now state the converse.
\begin{theorem}
Let $P$ be an order with zero and unit.
Then there is a bounded lattice~$K$ such that
\[ P \cong \Princ K.
\]
If $P$ is finite, we can construct $K$ as a finite lattice.
\end{theorem}
\end{frame}

which produces the two frames of Figure 1.6.
    This is really jarring to watch. The two lines of the new Slide 3 jump up more than two lines as they transition to Slide 4.
    Here is how we produce Slides 3 and 4 of Figure 1.5:

\begin{frame}
\frametitle{Theorem 1}
For a bounded lattice $L$, the order $Princ K$$ is bounded.
We now state the converse.
\pause
\begin{theorem}

There is only one new command to learn: \pause; it produces from this frame two slides. 

<sup>The</sup> \pause <sup>in this frame s</sup>p<sup>lits the contents of the frame into two</sup> p<sup>arts. The first slide</sup> is typeset from the first part as if the second part was also present. The second slide is typeset from both parts. So the transition from the first slide to the second is smooth, see Figure 1.5. 

<sup>You can have more than one</sup> \pause <sup>in a frame. Use</sup> \pause <sup>also to dis</sup>p<sup>la</sup>y <sup>a list one</sup> item at a time.

# And a few more things. . .

If life was perfect, we would not need this chapter. You would write perfect L<sup>A</sup>TEX, based on Chapter 1, no need to study how L<sup>A</sup>TEX works, what error messages mean... But life is not perfect, you will make mistakes, L<sup>A</sup>TEX will send messages, plain and mysterious. 

In this chapter, we briefly explain how things work, the structure of L<sup>A</sup>TEX, the auxiliary files, the logical and visual design of an article, L<sup>A</sup>TEX error messages. See Appendix C for more detail. Finally, we present a long list of dos and don’t to help you write good L<sup>A</sup>TEX. 

## 2.1 Structure

L<sup>A</sup>TEX’s core is a programming language called TEX, created by Donald E. Knuth, which provides low-level typesetting instructions. TEX comes with a set of fonts called Computer Modern (CM). The CM fonts and the T<sub>E</sub>X programming language form the foundation of a typical T X system. T X is extensible—new commands can be defined in terms of more basic ones. LAT X is one of the best known extensions of T X. 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/637fc1cf-16f2-479a-94ce-1647e65477cb/4888fc65dc651d29dc44897e23a46bf94d9712526df7f1bbab669b8859a216cb.jpg)



Figure 2.1: The structure of LAT<sub>E</sub>X.


The visual layout of a L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X document is primarily determined by the document class, <sup>such as</sup> amsart, article <sup>for articles</sup>, amsbook, book <sup>for books. Man</sup>y j<sup>ournals</sup>, publishers, and schools have their own document classes for formatting articles, books, and theses. 

Extensions of L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X are called packages. They provide additional functionality by adding new commands and environments, or by changing the way previously defined commands and environments work. It is essential that you find the packages that make your work easier. The L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X Companion, 2nd edition [56] discusses a large number of the most useful packages as of 2004. 

The structure of L<sup>A</sup>TEX is illustrated in Figure 2.1. This figure suggests that in order to work with a L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X document, you first have to install T<sub>E</sub>X and the CM fonts, then L<sup>A</sup>T X, and finally specify the document class and the necessary packages. The p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>es must include</sup> amsmath, amsthm, <sup>and so on. Of course</sup>, y<sup>our LAT</sup>E<sup>X installation</sup> already includes all of these. 

## 2.2 Auxiliary files

Figure 2.2 illustrates the steps in the production of a typeset document. 

You start by opening an existing L<sup>A</sup>TEX source file or creating a new one with a text <sup>editor. For this discussion</sup>, <sup>the source file is called</sup> myart.tex<sup>. Once the source file</sup> is ready, you typeset it. Depending on the document class options you choose and the packages the document loads, you end up with at least three additional files:

Figure 2.2: Using LAT<sub>E</sub>X.

```txt
see Theorems 1 and 3. 
```

<sup>2.</sup> myart.aux <sup>The</sup> <sup>auxiliar</sup>y <sup>file</sup>, <sup>used</sup> <sup>b</sup>y <sup>LAT</sup>E<sup>X</sup> <sup>for</sup> <sup>internal</sup> <sup>bookkee</sup>p<sup>in</sup>g, <sup>includin</sup>g cross-references and bibliographic citations. 

<sup>3.</sup> myart.log <sup>The</sup> log <sup>file. LAT</sup>E<sup>X records the t</sup>yp<sup>esettin</sup>g <sup>session in the</sup> log <sup>file</sup>, <sup>inc</sup> luding any warnings and messages that appear on your monitor in the log window. 

Your computer uses a video driver to display the typeset article on your monitor and a printer driver to print the typeset article on a printer. The video and printer drivers are computer and L<sup>A</sup>TEX implementation dependent. 

It should be emphasized that of the three applications used, only one is the same for all computers and all implementations. 

L<sup>A</sup>TEX always uses the aux file from the last typesetting. Here is an example. Your <sup>article has Theorems 1</sup> (<sup>with</sup> \label{T:first}) <sup>and 2</sup> (<sup>with</sup> \label{T:main})<sup>. The</sup> aux <sup>file has the two lines:</sup>

So the reference 

see Theorems \ref{T:first} and \ref{T:first}.

## 2.3 Logical and visual design

<sup>The t</sup>yp<sup>eset version of</sup> firstarticle.tex <sup>looks im</sup>p<sup>ressive on</sup> p<sup>. 4. To</sup> p<sup>roduce such</sup> articles, you need to understand that there are two aspects of article design: visual and logical. 

<sup>As an exam</sup>p<sup>le</sup>, <sup>let us look at a theorem from</sup> firstarticle.tex (<sup>see the t</sup>yp<sup>eset</sup> form of the theorem on page 4). You tell L<sup>A</sup>TEX that you want to state a theorem by <sup>usin</sup>g <sup>a</sup> theorem <sup>environment:</sup> 

\begin{theorem}\label{T:technical} 

Let $L$ be a finite lattice. 

\end{theorem} 

The logical part of the design is choosing to define a theorem by placing mate-<sup>rial inside a</sup> theorem <sup>environment. For the visual desi</sup>g<sup>n</sup>, <sup>LAT</sup>E<sup>X makes hundreds of</sup> decisions. Could you have specified all of the spacing, font size changes, centering, numbering, and so on? Maybe, but would you want to? And would you want to repeat that process for every theorem in your document? 

Even if you did, you would have spent a great deal of time and energy on the visual design of the theorem rather than on the logical design of your article. The idea behind L<sup>A</sup>TEX is that you should concentrate on what you have to say and let L<sup>A</sup>TEX take care of the visual design. 

This approach allows you to easily alter the visual design by changing the document class (or its options, see Sections 9.5, 10.1.2, and 17.1). Section 9.1 provides some examples. If you code the visual design into the article—hard coding it, as a programmer would say—such changes are much harder to accomplish, for you and for the journal publishing the article. 

For more on this topic, see Section C.4. 

## 2.4 General error messages

Now that you are ready to type your first document, we give you some pointers on using LAT<sub>E</sub>X. 

You will probably make a number of mistakes in your first document. These mistakes fall into the following categories: 

1. Typographical errors, which L<sup>A</sup>TEX blindly typesets. 

2. Errors in formulas or in the formatting of the text. 

3. Errors in your instructions to L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X, that is, in commands and environments. 

Typographical errors can be corrected by viewing and spell checking the source file, finding the errors, and then editing the typeset file. Mistakes in the second and third categories may trigger errors during the typesetting process, such as lines too wide of Section 1.4.

Experiment 1. <sup>In</sup> firstarticle.tex, g<sup>o to line 19</sup> (<sup>use the</sup> Go to Line <sup>command</sup> <sup>of</sup> y<sup>our editor</sup>) <sup>and remove the closin</sup>g <sup>brace so that it reads</sup> \begin{abstract

Tip L<sup>A</sup>T X’s messages are not very useful with displayed formulas. Comment out some of the lines to try to localize the problem. 

Tip Typeset often. 

Typesetting my book First Steps into L<sup>A</sup>T X with the closing brace of the first \caption <sup>command on line 480 of the source file missin</sup>g, <sup>I</sup> g<sup>et the error messa</sup>g<sup>e</sup> 

```txt
! Text line contains an invalid character.
1.1227 ...pletely irreducible^^? 
```

where the reference is to line 1227, about 700 lines removed from the actual error. However, if the only thing I did before typesetting was to insert that figure with its incorrect caption command, at least I would know where to look for errors. If you make a dozen changes and then typeset, you may not know where to start. 

## 2.5 Errors in math

Even in such a simple note there are opportunities for errors. To help familiarize yourself with some of the most commonly seen L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X errors in formulas, we introduce mis-<sup>takes into</sup> formulanote.tex<sup>.</sup> 

Experiment 1 <sup>In line 6 of</sup> formulanote.tex, <sup>delete the third</sup> $ <sup>s</sup>y<sup>mbol</sup>; <sup>save the</sup> <sup>file under the name</sup> formulanotebad1.tex <sup>in the</sup> work <sup>folder.</sup> 

<sup>T</sup>yp<sup>eset</sup> formulanotebad1.tex<sup>. LAT</sup>E<sup>X</sup> g<sup>enerates the followin</sup>g <sup>messa</sup>g<sup>e:</sup> 

```txt
! Missing $ inserted.
<inserted text>
    $
1.6 as $(u, v)$ and (u, \infty)
$ . Such an interval 
```

<sup>LAT</sup>E<sup>X reads</sup> (u, \infty) <sup>as text</sup>; <sup>but the</sup> \infty <sup>command instructs LAT</sup>E<sup>X to t</sup>yp<sup>eset</sup> a math symbol, which can only be done in a formula. So L<sup>A</sup>TEX ofers to put a $ in front of \infty while typesetting the source file—it does not put the $ in the source file itself. L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X attempts a cure, but in this example it comes too late, because the formula should start just before (u. 

Experiment 2 <sup>In line 16 of</sup> formulanote.tex, <sup>delete the second</sup> } <sup>s</sup>y<sup>mbol and save</sup> <sup>it under the name</sup> formulanotebad2.tex <sup>in the</sup> work <sup>folder. This introduces an error:</sup> the closing brace of the subscript (see page 14) is missing. Now typeset the note. You get the message 

Missing } inserted.
<inserted text>
}
1.12 such as $\lim_{x \to \infty f(x)}$ 

L<sup>A</sup>TEX reports that a closing brace (}) is missing, but it is not sure where the brace should be. L<sup>A</sup>T X noticed that a subscript started with {, but it reached the end of the formula before finding a closing brace }. To remedy this, you must look in the formula for an opening brace { that is not balanced, and insert the missing closing brace }. Make the necessary change and typeset again to view the diference. 

Experiment 3 In mathnote.tex, delete the two $ signs in line 19, that is, replace $a$ by a. Typeset the file. It typesets with no errors. Here is the last line of the typeset file you get: 

we assume that the function is defined and continuous in a neighborhood of a. 

instead of 

we assume that the function is defined and continuous in a neighborhood of �. L 

This is probably the error most often made by beginners. There is no message by L<sup>A</sup>TEX and the typeset version looks good. Notice the diference in the shape of the letter a in the two cases. You need sharp eyes to catch such an error. 

Tip After an error is corrected, L<sup>A</sup>TEX can refuse to typeset your document. If your docu-<sup>ment is</sup> document.tex, <sup>look in the same folder for the</sup> auxiliary file document.aux that was created by L<sup>A</sup>TEX. Delete document.aux and typeset twice. See Section 2.2. 

## 2.6 Your errors: Davey’s Dos and Don’ts

Based on his many years of experience correcting L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X articles for the journal Algebra Universalis, Brian Davey collected the L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X mistakes most often made by authors. Here are some items from his list, divided into three categories. 

## Commands

1. Place ALL custom commands and environments in the preamble! If you have trouble with custom commands, then you know where to find them. 

<sup>2. Don’t use</sup> \def; <sup>rather use</sup> \newcommand <sup>or</sup> \renewcommand<sup>.</sup> 

\def <sup>is a T</sup>E<sup>X command. It is like</sup> \newcommand (<sup>see Sections 1.9 and 14.1</sup>), <sup>but it</sup> can redefine an existing command. Redefining your own commands is bad enough, redefining a TEX command can be a disaster. 

3. Do not simply type the name of an operator into a formula. Declare the appropriate operator; see Sections 1.9 and 14.1. For instance, do not type $length I$; it typesets as �����ℎ�. It should be length �, <sup>t</sup>yp<sup>ed as</sup> $\length I$<sup>. Of course</sup>, y<sup>ou have to add</sup> 

\DeclareMathOperator{\length}{length} 

to the preamble (see Section 1.8). 

4. When you send a document to a coauthor or submit an article to a journal, remove all the custom commands not used. This is a real time saver for your coauthor and editor. 

```latex
\medskip
\hspace {*6pt} Please, display this text.
\medskip
but rather
\begin{itemize}
\item[] Please, display this text.
\end{itemize}
or
\begin{quote}
Please, display this text.
\end{quote} 
```

## Text

1. Do not produce a list with horizontal and vertical spacing commands. Use a list environment; see Sections 3.8 and 4.2. 

<sup>2. Do not t</sup>yp<sup>e numbers for citations and internal references. Use</sup> \cite{...} <sup>for</sup> <sup>citations</sup> <sup>and</sup> \ref{...} <sup>for</sup> <sup>references.</sup> <sup>For</sup> <sup>references</sup> <sup>to</sup> <sup>e</sup>q<sup>uations</sup>, <sup>use</sup> \eqref; see Sections 1.7.1 and 5.3. 

<sup>3. Do not number</sup> p<sup>roclamations</sup> (<sup>see Section 4.4</sup>)<sup>. Use the standard</sup> amsart <sup>environ-</sup> ments for theorems, and so on, and let L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X number them. 

4. When writing a document for a journal requiring a document class file, do not 

(a) change any of the size parameters: for instance, do not use options like 12pt to <sup>chan</sup>g<sup>e the font size or the</sup> \setlength <sup>command to chan</sup>g<sup>e an</sup>y p<sup>arameter of</sup> the page size; 

(<sup>b</sup>) <sup>insert</sup> <sup>vertical</sup> <sup>white</sup> <sup>s</sup>p<sup>ace</sup> <sup>via</sup> \bigskip, \smallskip, \vskip, \vspace, <sup>etc</sup>, nor via your own custom commands. Do not adjust horizontal space without a very good reason. 

So if you want to display some text: 

Please, display this text. 

don’t do this: 

<sup>5. Do not leave a blank line before</sup> \end{proof} <sup>or before a text environment</sup> (<sup>see</sup> Section 4.1). 

<sup>6. Do not use the</sup> geometry p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>e.</sup> 

## Formulas

1. Do not leave a blank line before a displayed formula. 

2. Don’t use the symbol | in a set description, use the binary relation \mid; see Section 5.5.4. For instance, $\backslash \{ \begin{array} { r } { \textbf { x } \ | \ \textbf { x } ^ { > } 2 \ < \ 2 \ \backslash \} } \end{array}$ typesets as $\{ x | x ^ { 2 } < 2 \}$ . The correct form is $\{ x \mid x ^ { 2 } < 2 \}$ , typed as $\{x \mid $\mathbf { x } \hat { } 2 < 2 \setminus \} \Phi$ 

3. Don’t put punctuation marks inside an inline math environment. For instance, sin �. typed as $\sin x.$; use $\sin x$. This typesets as sin �. Notice the smaller space between “sin �.” and “typed” and the wider space between <sup>“</sup>$\sin x$.<sup>” and “This”</sup>; <sup>see Sections 1.3 and 3.2.2.</sup> 

4. Don’t use two or more displayed formulas one after another. Use an appropriate <sup>environment such as</sup> \align, \alignat, \gather, <sup>and so on</sup> (<sup>see Section 7.1.1</sup>)<sup>.</sup> 

<sup>5. Don’t use</sup> \left\{, \right\}, \left(, \right), <sup>and so on</sup>, <sup>b</sup>y <sup>default</sup> (<sup>see</sup> p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>e</sup> <sup>15</sup> <sup>and</sup> <sup>Section</sup> <sup>5.5.1</sup> <sup>for</sup> <sup>the</sup> <sup>commands</sup> \left <sup>and</sup> \right)<sup>.</sup> <sup>Even</sup> <sup>when</sup> \left <sup>and</sup> \right <sup>do</sup> <sup>not</sup> <sup>chan</sup>g<sup>e</sup> <sup>the</sup> <sup>size</sup> <sup>of</sup> <sup>the</sup> <sup>s</sup>y<sup>mbol</sup>, <sup>the</sup>y <sup>add</sup> <sup>extra</sup> <sup>s</sup>p<sup>ace</sup> after the closing delimiter. 

<sup>6. Use</sup> \colon <sup>for functions. For instance</sup>, $f(x) \colon x \to $\tt { x } ^ { \sim } 2 \$ 1$ typesets as $f ( x ) : x \to x ^ { 2 }$ . If you type $f $( { \bf x } ) { \mathrm { ~  ~ : ~ } } { \bf x } { \mathrm { ~  ~ \backslash ~ t o ~ } } { \bf x } ^ { \setminus 2 \Phi } .$ , you get $f ( x ) : x \stackrel { \textstyle \ w } { \to } x ^ { 2 }$ ; the spacing is bad. 

7. Use \[ and \] (or equation*) to type a displayed math environment (see Section 1.7) rather than the old TEX $$ matched by $$. While display math produced via the latter does work properly most of the time, there are some L<sup>A</sup>T X commands <sup>that do not</sup>; <sup>for exam</sup>p<sup>le</sup>, \qedhere<sup>.</sup> 

<sup>8. Do not use the</sup> center <sup>environment to dis</sup>p<sup>la</sup>y <sup>formulas.</sup> 

<sup>9. Use</sup> \dots <sup>first and let LAT</sup>E<sup>X make the decision whether to use</sup> \dots <sup>or</sup> \cdots; <sup>see</sup> p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>e 15 and Section 5.4.3. If LAT</sup>E<sup>X</sup> g<sup>ets it wron</sup>g, <sup>then use</sup> \cdots <sup>or</sup> \ldots<sup>.</sup> 

up 10. If you can, avoid constructs (for instance, ) in inline formulas that disrupt the regular line spacing. Although L<sup>A</sup>TEX automatically leaves room for it, it does not look good, as a rule.
