# Typing text

In Chapter 1, we briefly discussed how to type text in a document. Now we take up this topic more fully. 

This chapter starts with a discussion of the keyboard in Section 3.1 and continues with the rules for spaces in Section 3.2. We cover a very important topic that must precede any in-depth discussion of L<sup>A</sup>T X, how to control L<sup>A</sup>T X with commands and environments, in Section 3.3. 

A document may contain symbols that cannot be found on your keyboard. In Section 3.4, we show how to get these symbols in our typeset documents by using commands. 

Some other characters are defined by L<sup>A</sup>TEX as command characters. For example, the % character plays a special role in the source document. In Section 3.5.1, you will see how % is used to comment out lines. In Section 3.5.2, we introduce the command for footnotes. 

In Section 3.6, we discuss the commands (and environments) for changing fonts, their shapes and sizes. In Section 3.7, you learn about lines, paragraphs, and pages. The judicious use of horizontal and vertical spacing is an important part of document formatting, and also the topic of Section 3.8. In Section 3.9, you learn how to typeset text in a “box”, which behaves as if it were a single large character. 

To help the discussion along, we shall use the terms text mode and math mode to distinguish between typesetting text and math. 

## 3.1 The keyboard

Most of the keys on your computer’s keyboard produce characters, while others are function or modifier keys. 

## 3.1.1 Basic keys

The basic keys are grouped as follows: 

Letters The 52 letter keys: 

```txt
a b c ... z A B C ... Z 
```

Digits The ten digits: 

```txt
1 2 ... 9 0 
```

<sup>Old-st</sup>y<sup>le di</sup>g<sup>its are available with the</sup> \oldstylenums <sup>command. The next line</sup> shows the default digits followed by the old style digits: 1234567890 1234567890 typed as 

1234567890 \quad \oldstylenums{1234567890} 

Punctuation There are nine punctuation marks: 

```txt
，；．？！：‘，- 
```

The first six are the usual punctuation marks. The ‘ is the left single quote— also known as the grave accent—while ’ doubles as the right single quote and apostrophe (see Section 3.4.1). The - key is the dash or hyphen (see Sections 3.4.2 and 3.4.9). 

Parentheses There are four: 

( ) [ ] 

( and ) are parentheses; [ and ] are called (square) brackets. 

Math symbols Seven math symbols correspond to keys. The math symbols are: 

```txt
* + = - < > / 
```

The last four characters have a role also in text mode: 

The minus sign − corresponds to the hyphen key, - (see Section 3.4.9). 

The math symbols < and > correspond to the keys < and >; use them only in math mode. 

Note that there is also a version of colon (:) for math formulas (see Sections 6.1 and A.2). 

Space keys Pressing the space bar gives the space character. Pressing the tab key gives the tab character. When typesetting the source file, L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X does not distinguish between these two. Pressing the Return key gives the end-of-line character. These keys produce invisible characters that are normally not displayed on your monitor by the text editor. Diferent computer systems have diferent end-of-line characters, which may cause some problems when transferring files from one system to another. A good text editor translates end-of-line characters automatically or on demand. Section 3.2.1 explains how L<sup>A</sup>TEX handles the invisible characters. 

When explaining some rules of L<sup>A</sup>TEX, sometimes it is important to show if a space is required. In such cases, I use the symbol verb* ␣ to indicate a space, for instance, $\mathtt { \backslash i n _ { \perp } u t }$ and $\setminus \cup \cdot$ 

The tilde ˜ produces a nonbreakable space or tie (see Section 3.4.3). 

## 3.1.2 Special keys

There are 13 special keys on the keyboard: 

$$
\#    \% \& \sim \_ \hat {} \backslash \{\} @" |
$$

They are mostly used to give instructions to L<sup>A</sup>TEX and some are used in math mode (see Chapter 5), and some in BIBT<sub>E</sub>X (see Chapter 15). See Section 3.4.4 on how to print these characters in text. Only @ requires no special command, type @ to print @. 

## 3.1.3 Prohibited keys

Keys other than those discussed in Sections 3.1.1 and 3.1.2 are prohibited! Specifically, do not use the computer’s modifier keys—Control, Alt, Escape, and others—to produce special characters, such as accented characters. L<sup>A</sup>T X will either reject or misunderstand them. Prohibited characters may not cause problems in some newer L<sup>A</sup>TEX implementations. They may just print $\mathrm { i } \mathrm { { f } _ { \mathrm { { i } } } }$ if your source file has $\mathrm { i f } \mathrm { i } .$ , and ignore the invisible invalid characters. However, for portability reasons, you should avoid using prohibited characters. The babel package provides support for using some modifier keys (see Appendix F). 

```txt
1.222 completely irreducible^? 
```

Tip If there is a prohibited character in your document, you may receive a message such as 

! Text line contains an invalid character. 

Delete and retype the ofending word or line until the error goes away. 

## 3.2 Words, sentences, and paragraphs

Text consists of words, sentences, and paragraphs. In text, words are separated by one or more spaces, which may include a single end-of-line character (see the rule, Spacing in text), or by parentheses and punctuation marks. A group of words terminated by a period, exclamation point, or question mark forms a sentence (not all periods terminate a sentence, see the discussion in Section 3.2.2). A group of sentences terminated by one or more blank lines constitutes a paragraph. 

## 3.2.1 Spacing rules

Here are the most important L<sup>A</sup>TEX rules about spaces in text in the source file. 

## Rule Spacing in text

1. Two or more spaces in text are the same as one. 

2. A tab or end-of-line character is the same as a space. 

3. A blank line, that is, two end-of-line characters separated only by spaces and tabs, indicates the end of a paragraph. The \par command is equivalent. 

4. Spaces at the beginning of a line are ignored. 

Rules 1 and 2 make cutting and pasting text less error-prone. In your source file, you do not have to worry about the line length or the number of spaces separating words or sentences, as long as there is at least one space or end-of-line character separating any two words. Thus 

```txt
You do not have to worry about the number of spaces separating words, as long as there is at least one space or end-of-line character separating any two words.   
produces the same typeset text as 
```

You do not have to worry about the number of spaces 

separating words, as long as there is at least one space 

or end-of-line character separating any two words. 

However, 

the number of spaces separating words, 

as long 

and 

the number of spaces separating words, 

as long 

produce diferent results: 

the number of spaces separating words, as long 

the number of spaces separating words , as long 

Notice the space between “words” and the comma in the second line. That space was produced by the end-of-line character in accordance with Rule 2. 

It is very important to maintain the readability of your source file. L<sup>A</sup>TEX may not care about the number of spaces or line length, but you, your coauthor, and your editor might. 

Rule 3 contradicts Rules 1 and 2, consider it an exception. Sometimes—especially when defining commands and environments (see Sections 14.1 and 14.2)—it is more convenient to indicate the end of a paragraph with \par. 

## 3.2.2 Periods

L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X places a certain size space between words—the interword space—and a somewhat larger space between sentences—the intersentence space. To know which space to use, L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X must decide whether or not a period indicates the end of a sentence. 

## Rule 1 Period

To L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X, a period after a capital letter, for instance, A. or caT., signifies an abbreviation or an initial. Generally, every other period signifies the end of a sentence. 

This rule works most of the time. When it fails—for instance, twice with e.g.—you need to specify the type of space you want, using the following two rules. 

## Rule 2 Period

I<sup>f</sup> an abbrev<sup>i</sup>at<sup>i</sup>on does not end w<sup>i</sup>t<sup>h</sup> a cap<sup>i</sup>ta<sup>l l</sup>etter, <sup>f</sup>or <sup>i</sup>nstance, etc., and <sup>i</sup>t <sup>i</sup>s not t<sup>h</sup>e last word in the sentence, then follow the period by an interword space (\␣) or a tie (˜), if appropriate (see Section 3.4.3). 

Recall that $\nu _ { \sf U }$ provides an interword space. 

The result was first published, in a first approximation, in the Combin.\ Journal. The result was first published, in a first approximation, in the Combin. Journal. 

prints as 

The result was first published, in a first approximation, in the Combin. Journal. The result was first published, in a first approximation, in the Combin. Journal. 

Notice that Combin. in the first line is followed by a regular interword space. The intersentence space following Combin. in the second line is a little wider; it is an error. 

A tie (or nonbreakable space)—see also Section 3.4.3—is more appropriate than \␣ in phrases such as Prof. Smith, typed as Prof.~Smith, and pp. 271–292, typed as pp.~271--292<sup>.</sup> 

Tip <sup>The</sup> thebibliography <sup>environment handles</sup> p<sup>eriods</sup> p<sup>ro</sup>p<sup>erl</sup>y<sup>. You do not have to</sup> mark periods for abbreviations (in the form .\␣) in the name of a journal, so 

Acta Math. Acad. Sci. Hungar. 

is correct. 

## Rule 3 Period

If a capital letter is followed by a period and is at the end of a sentence, precede the period with \@. 

For example, 

(1) follows from condition~H\@. We can proceed\\ 

(1) follows from condition~H. We can proceed 

prints: 

(1) follows from condition H. We can proceed 

(1) follows from condition H. We can proceed 

Notice that there is not enough space after H. in the second line. 

Most typographers agree on the following rule (see, for instance, The Elements of Typographic Style by Robert Bringhurst [8], p. 30): 

<table><tr><td>Rule ■ EnvironmentsAn environment starts with the command\begin{name}and ends with\end{name}Between these two commands is the content of the environment, affected by the definition of the environment.</td></tr></table>

## 3.3 Commanding L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X

## Rule 4 Period

Add no space or a thin space (\,) within strings of initials and be consistent. 

So W.H. Lampstone with no space or W. H. Lampstone with thin space is preferred over W. H. Lampstone. My personal choice is W. H. Lampstone with thin space. 

To make all intersentence spaces equal to the interword space—as required in French typography—you can use the command 

\frenchspacing 

To switch back to using spaces of diferent sizes, give the command 

\nonfrenchspacing 

## 3.3 Commanding LAT<sub>E</sub>X

How do you command L<sup>A</sup>TEX to do something special for you, such as starting a new line, changing emphasis, or displaying the next theorem? You use commands and special pairs of commands called environments, both briefly introduced in Section 1.1.4. 

Most, but not all, commands have arguments, which are usually fairly brief. Environments have contents, the text between the \begin and \end commands. The contents of an environment can be several paragraphs long. 

## 3.3.1 Commands and environments

<sup>The</sup> \emph{text } command <sup>instructs LAT</sup>E<sup>X to em</sup>p<sup>hasize its ar</sup>g<sup>ument</sup>, text. <sup>The</sup> \& command has no argument; it instructs L<sup>A</sup>TEX to typeset & (see Section 3.4.4). 

The flushright environment instructs L<sup>A</sup>TEX to right justify the content, the text between the two commands 

\begin{flushright} 

\end{flushright} 

<sup>The content of the</sup> document <sup>environment is the bod</sup>y <sup>of the article</sup> (<sup>see</sup> Section 1.8) and the content of the environment is the abstract. 

## Rule Commands

A L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X command starts with a backslash, \, and is followed by the command name. The name of a command is either a single non-alphabetic character other than a tab or end-of-line character or a string of letters, that is, one or more letters. 

So # and ’ are va<sup>li</sup>d command names. T<sup>h</sup>e correspond<sup>i</sup>ng commands \# and \’ are <sup>used in Sections 3.4.4 and 3.4.7</sup>, <sup>res</sup>p<sup>ectivel</sup>y<sup>.</sup> input <sup>and</sup> date <sup>are also valid command</sup> <sup>names. However</sup>, input3, in#ut, <sup>and</sup> in␣ut <sup>are not valid names because</sup> 3, #, <sup>and</sup> ␣ should not occur in a multicharacter command name. Note that ␣ is a command name, the command \␣ produces a blank. 

L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X has a few commands, for instance, $ (see Section 5.1) that do not follow this <sup>namin</sup>g <sup>scheme</sup>, <sup>that is</sup>, <sup>the</sup>y <sup>are not of the form</sup> \name<sup>. See also Section 14.1.9 for</sup> special commands with special termination rules. 

## Rule Command termination

LAT<sub>E</sub>X finds the end of a command name as follows: 

If the first character of the name is not a letter, the name is the first character. 

If the first character of the name is a letter, the command name is terminated by the first nonletter. 

If the command name is a string of letters, and is terminated by a space, then L<sup>A</sup>TEX discards all spaces following the command name. 

<sup>While</sup> input3 <sup>is an invalid name</sup>, \input3 <sup>is not an incorrect command. It is the</sup> \input <sup>command followed b</sup>y <sup>the character</sup> 3, <sup>which is either</sup> p<sup>art of the text followin</sup>g the command or the argument of the command. 

<sup>LAT</sup>E<sup>X also allows some command names to be modified with</sup> *<sup>. Such command</sup> are referred to as *-ed commands. Many commands have *-ed variants. \hspace* is an often-used *-ed command (see Section 3.8.1). 

## Rule Command and environment names

Command and environment names are case sensitive. \ShowLabels is not the same as \showlabels<sup>.</sup> 

## Rule Arguments

Optional arguments are enclosed in brackets, [ ]. 

Commands may have arguments, typed in braces immediately after the command. The argument(s) are used in processing the command. 

Accents provide very simple examples. For instance, \’{o}—which produces ó— consists of the command \’ and the argument o (see Section 3.4.7). In the command 

\bibliography{article1} 

<sup>the</sup> <sup>command</sup> <sup>is</sup> \bibliography <sup>and</sup> <sup>the</sup> <sup>ar</sup>g<sup>ument</sup> <sup>is</sup> article1 (<sup>see</sup> <sup>Section</sup> <sup>15.2.2</sup>)<sup>.</sup> 

Sometimes, if the argument is a single character, the braces can be dropped: \’o also typesets as ó. 

<sup>Some</sup> <sup>environments</sup> <sup>also</sup> <sup>have</sup> <sup>ar</sup>g<sup>uments.</sup> <sup>For</sup> <sup>exam</sup>p<sup>le</sup>, <sup>the</sup> alignat <sup>environment</sup> (see Section 7.5.4) is delimited by the commands 

\begin{alignat}{2} 

and 

\end{alignat} 

The argument, 2, is the number of columns—it could be any number 1, 2, ... A command or env<sup>i</sup>ronment may <sup>h</sup>ave more t<sup>h</sup>an one argument. T<sup>h</sup>e \frac command (see Sec tion 5.4.1) has two, $\frac{1}{2}$ typesets as ${ \frac { 1 } { 2 } } .$ <sup>. The custom command</sup> \con <sup>has</sup> three (see Section 14.1.2). 

Some commands and environments have one or more optional arguments, that is, arguments that may or may not be present. The \sqrt command (see Section 5.4.5) has an o<sub>p</sub>tional ar<sub>g</sub>ument for s<sub>p</sub>ecif<sub>y</sub>in<sub>g</sub> roots other than the s<sub>q</sub>uare root. To <sub>g</sub>et √<sup>3</sup> 25, <sup>t</sup>yp<sup>e</sup> \sqrt[3]{25}<sup>. The</sup> \documentclass <sup>command has an ar</sup>g<sup>ument</sup>, <sup>the name of</sup> a document class, and an optional argument, a list of options (see Section 8.2), for instance, 

\documentclass[12pt,draft,leqno]{amsart} 

Tip If you get an error when using a command, check that: 

1. The command is spelled correctly, including the use of uppercase and lowercase letters. 

<sup>5. The</sup> p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>e</sup> p<sup>rovidin</sup>g <sup>the command is loaded with the</sup> \usepackage <sup>command.</sup> 

Most errors in the use of commands are caused by breaking the termination rule. <sup>We can illustrate some of these errors with the</sup> \today <sup>command</sup>, <sup>which</sup> p<sup>roduces</sup> today’s date. You have already seen this command in Section 1.3 (see also Section 3.4.8). The correct usage is 

\today\ is the day 

or 

\today{} is the day 

which both typeset in the following form 

July 19, 2015 is the day 

<sup>In the first case</sup>, \today <sup>was terminated b</sup>y \␣, <sup>the command that</sup> p<sup>roduces an interword</sup> space. In the second case, it was terminated by the empty group { }. 

<sup>If there is no s</sup>p<sup>ace after the</sup> \today <sup>command</sup>, <sup>as in</sup> 

\todayis␣the␣day 

you get the message 

! Undefined control sequence. 

l.3 \todayis the day 

<sup>LAT</sup>E<sup>X thinks that</sup> \todayis <sup>is the command</sup>, <sup>and</sup>, <sup>of course</sup>, <sup>does not reco</sup>g<sup>nize it.</sup> 

I<sup>f</sup> you type one or more spaces a<sup>f</sup>ter \today: 

\today␣␣is␣the␣day 

L<sup>A</sup>TEX interprets the two spaces as a single space by the first space rule (see page 48), and <sup>uses that one s</sup>p<sup>ace to delimit</sup> \today <sup>from the text that follows it. So LAT</sup>E<sup>X</sup> p<sup>roduces</sup> 

July 19, 2015is the day 

Section 14.1.9 discusses how best to avoid such errors. 

## 3.3 Commanding L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X

Tip If a command—or environment—can have an optional argument and 

none is given, and 

the text following the command starts with [, 

then type this as {[}. 

This may happen, for instance, with the command \item (see page 103). To get an example for an environment, see Section 7.6.1 for subsidiary math environments and page 211 for the alignment options. See what happens if no option is given but the math starts, say, with [x]. 

## 3.3.2 Scope

A command issued inside a pair of braces { } has no efect beyond the right brace, except for the rare global commands (see Section 3.3.3). You can have any number of pairs of braces: 

{ ... { ... { ... } ... } ... } 

The innermost pair containing a command is the scope of that command. The command <sup>has no efect outside its sco</sup>p<sup>e. We can illustrate this conce</sup>p<sup>t usin</sup>g <sup>the</sup> \bfseries command that switches the font to boldface: 

{some text \bfseries bold text} no more bold 

typesets as 

some text bold text no more bold 

<sup>The commands</sup> \begin{name } <sup>and</sup> \end{name } <sup>bracketin</sup>g <sup>an environment act</sup> also as a pair of braces. In particular, $, \[, and \] are special braces. 

## Rule Braces

1. Braces must be balanced: An opening brace has to be closed, and a closing brace must have a matching opening brace. 

2. Pairs of braces cannot overlap. 

Violating the first brace rule generates warnings and error messages. If there is one more opening brace than closing brace, the document typesets, but you get a warning: 

(\end occurred inside a group at level 1) 

For two or more unmatched opening braces, you are warned that \end occurred inside a group at level 2, and so on. There is a tendency to disregard such warnings since your article is already typeset and the unmatched opening brace may be dificult to find. However, such errors may have strange consequences. At one point in the writing of my second L<sup>A</sup>TEX book, there were two extra opening braces in Chapter 2.4. As a result, the title of Chapter 7 was placed on a page by itself! So it is best not to disregard such warnings. 

If you have one unmatched closing brace, you get a message such as 

## ! Too many }’s

<sup>If s</sup>p<sup>ecial braces</sup>, <sup>sa</sup>y, \begin{name} <sup>and</sup> \end{name}, <sup>do not balance</sup>, y<sup>ou</sup> g<sup>et</sup> an error message: 

! LaTeX Error: \begin{name} on input line 21 ended by \end{document}. 

## or

! LaTeX Error: \begin{document} ended by \end{name}. 

To illustrate the second rule, here are two simple examples of overlapping braces. 

## Example 1

```latex
{\bfseries some text
\begin{lemma}
    more text} final text
\end{lemma} 
```

## Example 2

{some \bfseries text, then math: $\sqrt{2} }, \sqrt{3}$ 

<sup>In Exam</sup>p<sup>le 1</sup>, <sup>the sco</sup>p<sup>e of</sup> \bfseries <sup>overla</sup>p<sup>s the braces</sup> \begin{lemma}, \end{lemma} <sup>In Exam</sup>p<sup>le 2</sup>, <sup>the sco</sup>p<sup>e of</sup> \bfseries <sup>overla</sup>p<sup>s the s</sup>p<sup>ecial braces</sup> $ and $. Example 1 is easy to correct: 

```latex
{\bfseries some text}
\begin{lemma}
    {\bfseries more text}
    final text
\end{lemma} 
```

Example 2 may be corrected as follows: 

{some \bfseries text, then math:} $\sqrt{2}, \sqrt{3}$ 

Actuall<sub>y</sub>, √2 does not even have a bold version (see Section 6.4.3). 

If the braces do overlap and they are of the same kind, L<sup>A</sup>TEX simply misunderstands the instructions. The closing brace of the first pair is regarded as the closing brace of the second pair, an error that may be dificult to detect. L<sup>A</sup>TEX can help if special braces overlap. Typesetting Example 1 gives the message 

! Extra }, or forgotten \endgroup. l.7 more text } 

final text 

## 3.3.3 Types of commands

It may be useful at this point to note that commands can be of various types. 

Some commands have arguments, and some do not. Some commands efect change only in their arguments, while some commands declare a change. 

<sup>For instance</sup>, \textbf{This is bold} <sup>t</sup>yp<sup>esets the</sup> p<sup>hrase</sup> This is bold <sup>in</sup> bold type: This is bold and has no efect on the text following the argument of the com-<sup>mand. On the other hand</sup>, <sup>the command</sup> \bfseries <sup>declares that the text that follows</sup> should be bold. This command has no argument. I call a command that declares change a command declaration. So \bfseries is a command declaration, while \textbf is not. As a rule, command declarations are commands without arguments. 

Commands with arguments are called long if their argument(s) can contain a blank line or a \par command; otherwise they are short. For example, \textbf is a short <sup>command. So are all the to</sup>p <sup>matter commands discussed in Section 9.2. The</sup> \parbox command, discussed in Section 3.9.4, is long. 

Finally, as discussed in Section 3.3.2, the efect of a command remains within its scope. This is true only of local commands. There are also some global commands, <sup>such as the</sup> \setcounter <sup>command described in Section 14.5.1.</sup> 

## Fragile commands

As a rule, L<sup>A</sup>TEX reads a paragraph of the source file, typesets it, and then goes on to the next paragraph (see Section C.4). Some information from the source file, however, is separately stored for later use. Examples include the title of an article, which is reused as a running head (Section 9.2.1); titles of parts, sections, subsections, and other sectioning commands, which are used in the table of contents (Sections 17.2 and 8.4.1); footnotes (Section 3.5.2); table and figure captions (Section 8.4.3), which are used in lists of tables and figures (Section 8.4.3); and index entries (Chapter 16). 

These are movable arguments, and certain commands embedded in them must be protected from damage while being moved. L<sup>A</sup>TEX commands that need such protection are called fragile. The inline math delimiter commands \( and \) are fragile, while $ is not. 

<sup>In a movable ar</sup>g<sup>ument</sup>, <sup>fra</sup>g<sup>ile commands must be</sup> p<sup>rotected with a</sup> \protect command. Thus 

The function $\backslash ( \mathrm { ~ \ f ~ } ( \mathbf { x } \hat { \mathbf { \Xi } } \{ 2 \} ) \mathrm { ~ \ } \backslash )$ 

is not an appropriate section title, but 

The function \protect \( f(x^{2}) \protect \) 

is. So is 

The function $f(x^{2})$ 

To be on the safe side, you should protect every command that might cause problems in a movable argument. Section 17.2 shows an example of what happens if a fragile command is not protected. Alternatively, use commands declared with 

\DeclareRobustCommand 

<sup>This command works the same wa</sup>y <sup>as</sup> \newcommand <sup>but the command defined is</sup> robust, that is, not fragile. 

## 3.4 Symbols not on the keyboard

A typeset document may contain symbols that cannot be typed. Some of these symbols may even be available on the keyboard but you are prohibited from using them (see Section 3.1.3). In this section, we discuss the commands that typeset some of these symbols in text. 

## 3.4.1 Quotation marks

To produce single and double quotes, as in 

‘subdirectly irreducible’ and “subdirectly irreducible” 

type 

‘subdirectly irreducible’ and ‘‘subdirectly irreducible’’ 

Here, ‘ is the left single quote and ’ is the right single quote. Note that the double quote is obtained by pressing the single quote key twice, and not by using the double quote key. If you need single and double quotes together, as in “She replied, ‘No.’ ”, separate them with \, (which provides a thin horizontal space, see Section 3.8.1): 

```txt
“‘She replied, ‘No.’\,”” 
```

## 3.4.2 Dashes

Dashes come in three lengths. The shortest dash, called a hyphen, is used to connect words: 

Mean-Value Theorem 

This phrase is typed with a single dash: 

Mean-Value Theorem 

A medium-sized dash, called an en dash, is typed as -- and is used 

For number ranges; for instance, the phrase see pages 23–45, is typed as 

see pages~23--45 

Note: ˜ is a nonbreakable space or tie (see Section 3.4.3). 

In place of a hyphen in a compound adjective when one of the elements of the adjective is an open compound (such as New York) or hyphenated (such as non-English). For instance, the phrase Schmidt–Freid adjoint, is typed as 

Schmidt--Freid adjoint 

A long dash—called an em dash—is used to mark a change in thought or to add emphasis to a parenthetical clause, as in this sentence. The two em dashes in the last sentence are typed as follows: 

```txt
A long dash---called an \emph{em dash}---is used 
```

In math mode, a single dash is typeset as the minus sign − (a binary operation) with some spacing on both sides, as in 15 − 3 or the “negative” as in −3; this is discussed in Sections 3.1.1 and 5.4.1. 

Note that there is no space before or after an en dash or em dash. 

## 3.4.3 Ties or nonbreakable spaces

A tie or nonbreakable space or blue space is an interword space that cannot be broken across lines. For instance, when referencing P. Neukomm in an article, you do not want the initial P. at the end of a line and the surname Neukomm at the beginning of <sup>the next line. To</sup> p<sup>revent such an occurrence</sup>, y<sup>ou should t</sup>yp<sup>e</sup> P.~Neukomm<sup>.</sup> 

<sup>If</sup> y<sup>our ke</sup>y<sup>board does not have</sup> ~, <sup>use the</sup> \nobreakspace <sup>command instead</sup>, <sup>and</sup> <sup>t</sup>yp<sup>e</sup> P.\nobreakspace Neukomm<sup>. The followin</sup>g <sup>exam</sup>p<sup>les show some t</sup>yp<sup>ical uses:</sup> 

Theorem~\ref{T:main} in Section~\ref{S:intro} 

Donald~E. Knuth 

assume that $f(x)$ is (a)~continuous, (b)~bounded 

the lattice~$L$ 

Sections~\ref{S:modular} and~\ref{S:distributive} 

In~$L$, we find 

Of course, if you add too many ties, as in 

Peter~G.~Neukomm% Incorrect! 

L<sup>A</sup>TEX may send you a line too wide message (see Sections 1.4 and 3.7.1). 

<sup>The</sup> <sup>tie</sup> (˜) <sup>absorbs</sup> <sup>s</sup>p<sup>aces</sup>, <sup>so</sup> <sup>t</sup>yp<sup>in</sup>g P.␣~␣Neukomm <sup>works</sup> j<sup>ust</sup> <sup>as</sup> <sup>well.</sup> <sup>This</sup> feature is convenient when you add a tie during editing.

The characters corresponding to nine of the 13 special keys (see Sections 1.2 and 3.1.2) are produced by typing a backslash (\) and then the key, as shown in Table 3.1.

\texttt{\textbackslash}

For a typewriter style backslash you can use the \bsl com-<sup>mand introduced in Section 14.1.1 or the</sup> \texttt{\symbol{92}} <sup>command intro-</sup> duced later in this section.

## 3.4.5 Ellipses

The text ellipsis, . . . , is produced using the \dots command. Typing three periods produces ... (notice that the spacing is wrong).\dots is one of several commands that can be used to create ellipses in formulas (see Section 5.4.3). 

## 3.4.6 Ligatures

Certain groups of characters, when typeset, are joined together—such compound characters are called ligatures. There are five ligatures that L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X typesets automatically (if you use the Computer Modern fonts): f, fi, fl, fi, and fl. 

If you want to prevent L<sup>A</sup>TEX from forming a ligature, separate the characters with <sup>the command</sup>\textcompwordmark<sup>. Com</sup>p<sup>are</sup> if <sup>with</sup> iff, <sup>t</sup>yp<sup>ed as</sup> iff <sup>and</sup> 

if\textcompwordmark f 

Enclosing the second character in braces ({}) is a crude method of preventing the liga ture, as used in Formula 4 of the Formula Gallery (see Section 5.10). This method, in some instances, may interfere with L<sup>A</sup>TEX’s hyphenation algorithm. 

## 3.4.7 Accents and symbols in text

L<sup>A</sup>TEX provides 15 European accents. Type the command for the accent ( \ and a character), followed by the letter (in braces) on which you want the accent placed (see Table 3.3). For example, to get Grätzer György, type 

Gr\"{a}tzer Gy\"{o}rgy 

and to get Ö type \"{O}. 

To place an accent on top of an i or a j, you must use the dotless version of i and j. These are obtained by the commands \i and \j: \’{\i} typesets as í and \v{\j} typesets as ˇj. Tables 3.4 and 3.5 list some additional text symbols and European characters available in L<sup>A</sup>TEX when typing text. Using localized versions of L<sup>A</sup>TEX, you get more accented and combined characters such as the Catalan geminated ell (see Appendix F). 

<sup>Note that the</sup> \textcircled <sup>command</sup> (<sup>in Table 3.5</sup>) <sup>takes an ar</sup>g<sup>ument. It seems</sup> to work best with a single lowercase character, like ○ or<sup>a</sup> ○. Capitals such as� ○ are not<sup>A</sup> ver<sub>y</sub> satisfactor<sub>y</sub>. Section 3.9.6 ex<sub>p</sub>lains how to create the s<sub>y</sub>mbol ○A . 

## 3.4.8 Logos and dates

\TeX produces T X, \LaTeX produces L<sup>A</sup>T X, and \LaTeXe produces L<sup>A</sup>T Xe (the original name of the current version of L<sup>A</sup>T X). The \AmS command produces the logo ${ \mathcal { A } } \ M S .$ 

Remember to type $\mathrm { \nabla { \cdot } T e X \backslash } _ { \sqcup }$ or \TeX{} if you need a space after T X (similarly for the others). A better way to handle this problem is discussed in Section 14.1.1. 

LAT X also stores some useful numbers:

## 3.4.9 Hyphenation

LAT<sub>E</sub>X reads the source file one line at a time until it reaches the end of the current paragraph and then tries to balance the lines (see Section C.2.2). To achieve this goal, L<sup>A</sup>TEX hyphenates long words using a built-in hyphenation algorithm, a database stored <sup>in the</sup> hyphen.tex <sup>file</sup>, <sup>and a lon</sup>g \hyphenation <sup>list in the AMS document classes.</sup> If you use a document class not containing such a list, copy the hyphenation list from amsart.cls <sup>to</sup> y<sup>our document.</sup> 

## Rule Optional hyphen

If you find that L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X cannot properly hyphenate a word, put optional hyphens in the word. An optional hyphen is typed as \- , and allows L<sup>A</sup>TEX to hyphenate the word where the optional hyphen is placed—and only at such points—if the need arises. 

<sup>Exam</sup>p<sup>les:</sup> data\-base,an\-ti\-thet\-ic, set\-up Note that: 

Optional hyphens prevent hyphenation at any other point in the word. 

Placing an optional hyphen in a particular occurrence of a word does not afect the hyphenation of any other occurrences of that word. 

## Rule Hyphenation specifications

List the words that often need help in a command: 

\hyphenation{set-up as-so-ciate} 

All occurrences of the listed words following this command in your document are hyphenated as specified. 

<sup>Note that in the</sup> \hyphenation <sup>command the h</sup>yp<sup>hens are desi</sup>g<sup>nated b</sup>y - <sup>and</sup> not by \-, and that the words are separated by spaces not by commas. 

You must use optional hyphens for words with accented characters, as in 

Gr\"{a}t\-zer 

<sup>Such words cannot be included in a</sup> \hyphenation <sup>list</sup> (<sup>unless</sup> y<sup>ou use the T1 font</sup> encoding—see Appendix F). 

## Rule Preventing hyphenation

To prevent hyphenation of a word, put it in the argument of a \text command or place <sup>it unh</sup>yp<sup>henated in a</sup> \hyphenation <sup>command.</sup> 

For example, type 

\text{database} 

<sup>if</sup> y<sup>ou</sup> <sup>do</sup> <sup>not</sup> <sup>want</sup> <sup>this</sup> <sup>instance</sup> <sup>of</sup> database <sup>h</sup>yp<sup>henated</sup>, <sup>or</sup> <sup>t</sup>yp<sup>e</sup> 

\hyphenation{database} 

if you do not want L<sup>A</sup>TEX to hyphenate any occurrence of the word after this command <sup>in</sup> y<sup>our document. Of course</sup>, <sup>t</sup>yp<sup>in</sup>g data\-base <sup>overrides the</sup> g<sup>eneral</sup> p<sup>rohibition for</sup> this one instance. 

<sup>You</sup> <sup>can</sup> <sup>have</sup> <sup>an</sup>y <sup>number</sup> <sup>of</sup> \hyphenation <sup>commands</sup> <sup>in</sup> y<sup>our</sup> <sup>document.</sup> 

C Tip L<sup>A</sup>TEX does not break a hyphenated word except at the hyphen, nor does it break a word followed by or preceding an em dash or en dash (see Section 3.4.2). L<sup>A</sup>TEX often needs help with such words. 

Sometimes a hyphen in a phrase should not be broken. For instance, the phrase �-complete lattice should not be broken after �; so type it as 

\text{$\mathfrak{m}$-com}\-plete lattice 

(<sup>see Section 6.4.2 for</sup> \mathfrak)<sup>.</sup> 

<sup>Use the</sup> \nobreakdash <sup>command</sup> (p<sup>laced before the h</sup>yp<sup>hen</sup>) 

\nobreakdash- \nobreakdash-- \nobreakdash--- 

to prevent such breaks. For example, 

pages~24\nobreakdash--47 

Since L<sup>A</sup>TEX does not hyphenate a hyphenated word except at the hyphen, 

\nobreakdash-

prevents the hyphenation of the whole word as though it were enclosed in a \text command. The form 

\nobreakdash-\hspace{0pt} 

allows the normal hyphenation of the word that follows the hyphen. For example, 

$\mathfrak{m}$\nobreakdash-\hspace{0pt}complete lattice 

<sup>allows the word</sup> complete <sup>to be h</sup>yp<sup>henated.</sup> 

This coding of the phrase �-complete lattice is a natural candidate for a custom command (see Section 14.1.1). 

Tip If you want to know how L<sup>A</sup>TEX would hyphenate a list of words, place it in the argument <sup>of a</sup> \showhyphens <sup>command.</sup> 

## 3.5 Comments and footnotes

For instance, 

\showhyphens{summation reducible latticoid} 

The result, 

sum-ma-tion re-ducible lat-ti-coid 

<sup>is</sup> <sup>shown</sup> <sup>in</sup> <sup>the</sup> log <sup>file.</sup> 

Tip Some text editors wrap lines in a source file by breaking them at a hyphen, introducing errors in your typeset document. 

For instance, 

It follows from Theorem~\ref{T:M} that completesimple lattices are very large. 

is typeset by L<sup>A</sup>TEX as follows: 

It follows from Theorem 2 that complete- simple lattices are very large. 

As you can see, there is a space between the hyphen and the word simple. The text editor inserted an end-of-line character after the hyphen (by the second space rule, see Section 3.2.1). This end-of-line character was interpreted by L<sup>A</sup>TEX as a space. To correct the error, make sure that there is no such line break, or comment out (see Section 3.5.1) the end-of-line character: 

It follows from Theorem~\ref{T:M} that complete-% 

simple lattices are very large. 

Better yet, rearrange the two lines: 

```txt
It follows from Theorem~\ref{T:M} that complete-simple lattices are very large. 
```

Of course, L<sup>A</sup>TEX does not know everything about the complicated hyphenation rules of the English language. Consult The Chicago Manual of Style, 16th edition [11] and Lyn Dupré’s BUGS in Writing: A Guide to Debugging Your Prose, 2nd edition [13] for additional guidance. 

## 3.5 Comments andfootnotes

Various parts of your source file do not get typeset like most of the rest. The two primary examples are comments that do not get typeset at all and footnotes that get typeset at the bottom of the page. 

## 3.5.1 Comments

The % symbol tells L<sup>A</sup>TEX to ignore the rest of the line. A common use might be a comment to yourself in the source file: 

```txt
therefore, a reference to Theorem~1 % check this! 
```

```txt
The \% symbol has many uses. For instance, a document class command (see Section 9.5), 
```

```txt
\documentclass[twocolumn,twoside,legalpaper]{amsart} 
```

```latex
\documentclass[%  
twocolumn,% option for two-column pages  
twoside,% format for two-sided printing  
legalpaper% print on legal-size paper] {amsart} 
```

```latex
\documentclass[%  
twocolumn,% option for two-column pages  
twoside,% format for two-sided printing  
legalpaper% print on legal-size paper] {amsart} 
```

Notice that the first line is terminated with a % to comment out the end-of-line character. 

Tip Some command arguments do not allow any spaces. If you want to break a line within an argument list, you can terminate the line with a %, as shown in the previous example. 

See also the example at the end of Section 3.4.9. 

It is often useful to start a document with a comment line giving the file name and identifying the earliest version of L<sup>A</sup>TEX that must be used to typeset it. 

%This is article.tex \NeedsTeXFormat{LaTeX2e}[1994/12/01] 

The second line specifies the December 1, 1994 (or later) release of L<sup>A</sup>T X. You may need to use such a declaration if your document uses a feature that was not available in earlier releases. Since L<sup>A</sup>T X changes very little these days, this command is of limited use. (See, however, the discussion on page 293.) 

Other uses of % include marking parts of the article for your own reference. For instance, you may include comments to explain command definitions (as in 

Section 14.3). If something goes wrong inside a multiline math display (see Chapter 7), L<sup>A</sup>TEX does not tell you precisely where the error is. You can try commenting out all but one of the lines, until each line works separately. 

Note that % does not comment out lines in a BIBT<sub>E</sub>X database document (see Section 15.2.5). 

Tip Symbolic referencing With every \label command I add the commented out form of the symbolic reference, see Section 1.7.2. 

So if I start a new theorem, I type \the and my text expander inserts the following in the article: 

\end{theorem} 

And do remember: 

## Tip The 25% rule

If you want a % sign in text, make sure you type it as \%. Otherwise, % comments out the rest of the line. L<sup>A</sup>TEX does not produce a warning. 

Using % to comment out large blocks of text can be tedious even with block com-<sup>ment. The</sup> verbatim p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>e includes the</sup> comment <sup>environment:</sup> 

## Rule comment environments

1. \end{comment} <sup>must be on a line b</sup>y <sup>itself.</sup> 

2. <sup>There can be no</sup> comment <sup>within a</sup> comment<sup>.</sup> is not allowed. L<sup>A</sup>TEX may give one of several messages, depending on the circumstances. For instance, 

```latex
In other words,
\begin{comment}
    commented out text...
    \begin{comment}
    some more commented out text...
    \end{comment}
    and some more commented out text...
\end{comment} 
```

! LaTeX Error: \begin{document} ended by \end{comment}. 

l.175 \end{comment} 

## Tip Locating errors

<sup>The</sup> comment <sup>environment</sup> <sup>can</sup> <sup>be</sup> <sup>ver</sup>y <sup>useful</sup> <sup>in</sup> <sup>locatin</sup>g <sup>errors.</sup> 

Suppose you have unbalanced braces in your source file (see Section 3.3.2). Working with a copy of your source file, comment out the first half at a safe point (not within an environment!) and typeset. If you still get the same message, the error is in the second half. If there is no error message, the error is in the first half. Comment out the half that has no error. 

Now comment out half of the remaining text and typeset again. Check to see whether the error appears in the first half of the remaining text or the second. Continue applying this method until you narrow down the error to a paragraph that you can inspect visually. 

<sup>Since</sup> <sup>the</sup> comment <sup>environment</sup> <sup>re</sup>q<sup>uires</sup> <sup>the</sup> verbatim p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>e</sup>, y<sup>ou</sup> <sup>must</sup> <sup>include</sup> the line 

\usepackage{verbatim} 

in the preamble of the source file (see Sections 1.8, 10.3.1, and D.1). 

## 3.5.2 Footnotes

<sup>The text of a footnote is t</sup>yp<sup>ed as the ar</sup>g<sup>ument of a</sup> \footnote <sup>command. To illustrate</sup> the use of footnotes, I have placed one here.<sup>1</sup> This footnote is typed as 

\footnote{Footnotes are easy to place.} 

If you want to use symbols to designate the footnotes, instead of numbers, type the command 

\renewcommand{\thefootnote} {\ensuremath{\fnsymbol{footnote}}} 

before the first footnote; this provides up to nine symbols. In Section 14.1.1, we discuss the \ensuremath command. Section 3.2 of The L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X Companion, 2nd edition [56] describes how to further customize footnotes. 

<sup>In addition</sup>, <sup>there are title-</sup>p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>e footnotes</sup>, <sup>such as the</sup> \thanks <sup>and</sup> \date <sup>com-</sup> mands in the top matter. See page 4 for a typeset example of \date. See also Section 9.2 and the typeset title page footnotes on page 272. 

<sup>1</sup>Footnotes are easy to place. 

You can add a footnote marked by <sup>∗</sup> to the title of an article. For instance, type the title 

```txt
\title[Complete congruence lattices]% {Complete congruence lattices$~*$} 
```

and add the lines 

```latex
{\renewcommand{\thefootnote}{\fnsymbol{footnote}}
\setcounter{footnote}{1}
\footnotetext{Lecture delivered at the \AMS annual meeting in Brandon.}
\setcounter{footnote}{0}
} 
```

The footnote will appear as the first footnote on page 1 marked by <sup>∗</sup>. All the other footnotes are unmarked. 

## 3.6 Changingfont characteristics

Although a document class and its options determine how L<sup>A</sup>TEX typesets characters, there are occasions when you want control over the shape or size of the font used. 

## 3.6.1 Basicfont characteristics

You do not have to be a typesetting expert to recognize the following basic font attributes: 

```txt
Shape Normal text is typeset:
upright (or roman) as this text
slanted as this text
italic as this text
small caps AS THIS TEXT 
```

Monospaced and proportional Typewriters use monospaced fonts, that is, fonts all of whose characters are of the same width. Most text editors display text using a monospaced font. L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X calls monospaced fonts typewriter style. In this book, such a font is used to represent user input and L<sup>A</sup>TEX’s response, such as <sup>“</sup>typewriter style text<sup>”.</sup> <sup>Whereas</sup>, <sup>normal</sup> <sup>text</sup> <sup>is</sup> <sup>t</sup>yp<sup>eset</sup> <sup>in</sup> <sup>a</sup> proportional font, such as “proportional text with ii and mm”, in which ii is narrow and mm is wide: 

Monospaced and proportional Typewriters use monospaced fonts, 

```txt
mmmmmm
iiiiii
} monospaced
mmmmmm
iiiii
} proportional 
```

Serifs A serif is a small horizontal (sometimes vertical) stroke used to finish of a vertical stroke of a letter, as on the top and bottom of the letter M. L<sup>A</sup>TEX’s standard serif font is Computer Modern roman, such as “serif text”. Fonts without serifs are called sans serif, such as “sans serif text”. Sans serif fonts are often used for titles or for special emphasis. 

Series: weight and width The series is the combination of weight and width. A font’s weight is the thickness of the strokes and the width is how wide the characters are. 

Light, medium (or normal), and bold often describe weight. 

Narrow (or condensed), medium (or normal), and extended often describe width. 

The Computer Modern family includes bold fonts. Traditionally, when the user asks for bold CM fonts, L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X actually provides bold extended (a somewhat wider version). 

Size Most L<sup>A</sup>TEX articles are typeset with 10 point text unless otherwise instructed. Larger sizes are used for titles, section titles, and so on. Abstracts and footnotes are often set in 8-point type. 

Font family The collections of all sizes of a font is called afontfamily. 

## 3.6.2 Documentfontfamilies

In a document class, the style designer designates three document font families: 

1. Roman (upright and serifed) document font family 

2. Sans serif document font family 

3. Typewriter style document font family 

and picks one of these (for articles, as a rule, the roman document font family) as the documentfontfamily or normalfamily. In all the examples in this book, the document font family is the roman document font family except for presentations which use sans serif (see Section 1.11 and Chapter 12). When you use Computer Modern fonts in L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X, which is the default, the three document font families are Computer Modern roman, Computer Modern sans serif, and Computer Modern typewriter. The document font family is Computer Modern roman. 

In this book, the roman document font family is Times, the sans serif document font family is Helvetica, and the typewriter style document font family is Computer Modern typewriter. The document font family is the roman document font family Times. 

The document font family (normal family) is the default font. You can always switch back to it with 

\textnormal{...} 

or 

{\normalfont ...} 


Table 3.6 shows these two commands and three additional pairs of commands to help you switch among the three basic document font families. It also shows the command pairs for the basic font shapes.


<table><tr><td>Command with Argument</td><td>Command Declaration</td><td>Switches to the font family</td></tr><tr><td>\textnormal{...}</td><td>{\normalfont ...}</td><td>document</td></tr><tr><td>\emph{...}</td><td>{\em ...}</td><td>emphasis</td></tr><tr><td>\textrm{...}</td><td>{\rmfamily ...}</td><td>roman</td></tr><tr><td>\textsf{...}</td><td>{\sffamily ...}</td><td>sans serif</td></tr><tr><td>\texttt{...}</td><td>{\ttfamily ...}</td><td>typewriter style</td></tr><tr><td>\textup{...}</td><td>{\upshape ...}</td><td>upright shape</td></tr><tr><td>\textit{...}</td><td>{\itshape ...}</td><td>italic shape</td></tr><tr><td>\textsl{...}</td><td>{\slshape ...}</td><td>slanted shape</td></tr><tr><td>\textsc{...}</td><td>{\scshape ...}</td><td>SMALL CAPITALS</td></tr><tr><td>\textbf{...}</td><td>{\bfseries ...}</td><td>bold</td></tr><tr><td>\textmd{...}</td><td>{\mdseries ...}</td><td>normal weight and width</td></tr></table>


Table 3.6: Font family switching commands.


The font-changing commands of Table 3.6 come in two forms: 

<sup>A command with an ar</sup>g<sup>ument</sup>, <sup>such as</sup> \textrm{...}, <sup>chan</sup>g<sup>es its ar</sup>g<sup>ument. These</sup> <sup>are short commands</sup>, <sup>i.e.</sup>, <sup>the</sup>y <sup>cannot contain a blank line or a</sup> \par <sup>command.</sup> 

<sup>A command declaration</sup>, <sup>such as</sup> \rmfamily, <sup>carries out the font chan</sup>g<sup>e followin</sup>g the command and within its scope (see Section 3.3.2) 

You should always use commands with arguments for small changes within a paragraph. They have two advantages: 

You are less likely to forget to change back to the normal font. 

You do not have to worry about italic corrections (see Section 3.6.4). 

Note that MakeIndex requires you to use commands with arguments to change the font in which page numbers are typeset (see Section 16.1). 

For font changes involving more than one paragraph, use command declarations. These commands are preferred if you want to create custom commands and environments (see Chapter 14). 

## 3.6.3 Shape commands

There are five pairs of commands to change the font shape: 

\textup{...} <sup>or</sup> {\upshape ...} <sup>switch to the</sup> upright shape<sup>.</sup> 

\textit{...} <sup>or</sup> {\itshape ...} <sup>switch to the</sup> italic shape<sup>.</sup> 

\textsl{...} <sup>or</sup> {\slshape ...} <sup>switch</sup> <sup>to</sup> <sup>the</sup> <sup>slanted</sup> <sup>sha</sup>p<sup>e.</sup> 

\textsc{...} <sup>or</sup> {\scshape ...} <sup>switch to</sup> small capitals<sup>.</sup> 

\emph{...} or {\em ...} switch to emphasis. 

The document class specifies how emphasis is typeset. As a rule, it is italic or slanted unless the surrounding text is italic or slanted, in which case it is upright. For instance, 

\emph{Rubin space} 

in the statement of a theorem is typeset as 

the space satisfies all three conditions, a so-called Rubin space that ... L 

The emphasis changed the style of Rubin space from italic to upright. 

Tip Be careful not to interchange the command pairs. For instance, if by mistake you type {\textit serif}, <sup>the result is</sup> serif<sup>. Onl</sup>y <sup>the</sup> s <sup>is italicized since</sup> \textit <sup>takes</sup> s as its argument. 

## Rule Abbreviations and acronyms

For abbreviations and acronyms use small caps, except for two-letter geographical acronyms. 

So Submitted to tug should be typed as 

Submitted to \textsc{tug} 

<sup>Note that onl</sup>y <sup>the lowercase characters in the ar</sup>g<sup>ument of the</sup> \textsc <sup>command are</sup> printed as small caps. 

## 3.6.4 Italic corrections

The phrase 

when using a serif font 

may be typed as follows: 

when using a {\itshape serif\/} font 

The \/ command before the closing brace is called an italic correction. Notice that {\itshape M}M typesets as MM, w<sup>h</sup>ere t<sup>h</sup>e M <sup>i</sup>s <sup>l</sup>ean<sup>i</sup>ng <sup>i</sup>nto t<sup>h</sup>e M. 

## 3.6 Changing font characteristics

Type {\itshape M\/}M to get the correct spacing MM. Compare the typeset phrase from the previous example with and without an italic correction: 

when using a serif font 

when using a serif font 

The latter is not as pleasing to the eye. 

## Rule 1 Italic correction

If the emphasized text is followed by a period or comma, you should not type the italic correction. 

For example, 

Do not forget. My party is on Monday. 

should be typed as 

{\itshape Do not forget.} My party is on Monday. 

## Rule 2 Italic correction

The shape commands with arguments do not require italic correction. The corrections are provided automatically where needed. 

Thus you can type the phrase when using a serif font the easy way: 

when using a \textit{serif} font 

Whenever possible, let L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X take care of the italic correction. However, if L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X is adding an italic correction where you feel it is not needed, you can override the correc-<sup>tion with the</sup> \nocorr <sup>command. LAT X does not add an italic correction before a</sup> p<sup>eriod</sup> <sup>or a comma. These two</sup> p<sup>unctuation marks are stored in the</sup> \nocorrlist <sup>command.</sup> By redefining this command, you can modify L<sup>A</sup>TEX’s behavior. 

## Rule 3 Italic correction

<sup>The italic correction is re</sup>q<sup>uired with the commands</sup> \itshape, \slshape, \em<sup>.</sup> 

## 3.6.5 Series

These attributes play a very limited role with the Computer Modern fonts. There is only one important pair of commands, 

\textbf{...} {\bfseries ...} 

to change the font to bold (actually, bold extended). The commands 

\textmd{...} {\mdseries ...} 

which set both the weight and width to medium (normal) are seldom needed. 

## 3.6.6 Size changes

Standard L<sup>A</sup>TEX documents are typeset in 10 point type. The 11 point and 12 point type are often used for better readability and some journals require 12 point—if this is the case, use the 12pt document class option (see Sections 9.5, 10.1.2, and 17.1.3). The 8pt <sup>and</sup> 9pt <sup>document class o</sup>p<sup>tions are rarel</sup>y <sup>used. The sizes of titles</sup>, <sup>subscri</sup>p<sup>ts</sup>, <sup>and</sup> superscripts are automatically set by the document class, in accordance with the font size option. 

If you must change the font size for some text—it is seldom necessary to do so in an article—the following command declarations are provided (see Table 3.7): 

$$
\begin{array}{c}\text{\Tiny \tiny \SMALL \Small \small}\\ \text{\normalsize}\\ \text{\Large \ Large \ LARGE \ huge \ Huge}\end{array}
$$

<sup>The command</sup> \SMALL <sup>is also called</sup> \scriptsize <sup>and the command</sup> \Small <sup>is also</sup> <sup>called</sup> \footnotesize<sup>. The font size commands are listed in order of increasin</sup>g<sup>—to</sup> be more precise, nondecreasing—size.

Both commands take an o</sup>p<sup>tional ar</sup>g<sup>ument.</sup> <sup>For</sup> <sup>exam</sup>p<sup>le</sup>, \larger[2] <sup>moves</sup> <sup>u</sup>p <sup>2</sup> <sup>sizes.</sup> 

## 3.6.7 Orthogonality

You are now familiar with the commands that change the font family, shape, series, and size. Each of these commands afects one and only one font attribute. For example, if you change the series, then the font family, shape, and size do not change. These commands act independently. In L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X terminology, the commands are orthogonal. From the user’s point of view this behavior has an important consequence: The order in which these commands are given does not matter. Thus 

\Large \itshape \bfseries 

has the same efect as 

\bfseries \itshape \Large 

Note that L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X 2.09’s two-letter commands (see Section 3.6.8) are not orthogonal. 

Orthogonality also means that you can combine these font attributes in any way you like. For instance, the commands 

\sffamily \slshape \bfseries \Large 

instruct L<sup>A</sup>TEX to change the font family to sans serif, the shape to slanted, the series to <sup>bold</sup>, <sup>and the size to</sup> \Large<sup>. If the corres</sup>p<sup>ondin</sup>g <sup>font is not available</sup>, <sup>LAT</sup>E<sup>X uses a</sup> font that is available, and issues a warning. 

The font substitution algorithm (see Section 7.9.3 of The L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X Companion, 2nd edition [56] for details) may not provide the font you really want, so it is your responsibility to make sure that the necessary fonts are available. We discuss this topic further in Section 17.5. 

## 3.6.8 Obsolete two-letter commands

Users of L<sup>A</sup>TEX 2.09 and AMS-L<sup>A</sup>TEX version 1.1 are accustomed to using the two-letter <sup>commands</sup> \bf, \it, \rm, \sc, \sf, \sl, <sup>and</sup> \tt<sup>. These commands are not</sup> p<sup>art</sup> of L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X. They are, however, still defined in most document classes. The two-letter commands 

1. switch to the document font family, 

2. change to the requested shape. 

There are a number of reasons not to use them. The two-letter commands 

are not part of L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X, 

require manual italic corrections, 

are not orthogonal (see Section 3.6.7). 

\slshape \bfseries <sup>is the same as</sup> \bfseries \slshape (<sup>slanted bold</sup>), <sup>but</sup> \sl\bf <sup>is not the same as</sup> \bf\sl<sup>. Indeed</sup>, {\sl\bf sample} g<sup>ives</sup> sample <sup>and</sup> {\bf\sl sample} produces sample. 

## 3.6.9 Low-level commands

The font-characteristic changing commands we have discussed so far in this section are the high-level font commands. Each of these commands is implemented by L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X and the document class using low-level font commands. The low-level commands have been developed for document class and package writers. See Section 7.9 of The L<sup>A</sup>TEX Companion, 2nd edition [56]. 

There is one use of low-level commands you should keep in mind. When you choose a font size for your document or for some part thereof, you also determine the \baselineskip, <sup>the distance from the baseline of one line to the baseline of the next.</sup> <sup>T</sup>yp<sup>icall</sup>y, <sup>a 10-</sup>p<sup>oint font size uses a 12</sup> p<sup>oint</sup> \baselineskip<sup>. Occasionall</sup>y, y<sup>ou</sup> <sup>ma</sup>y <sup>want</sup> <sup>to</sup> <sup>chan</sup>g<sup>e</sup> <sup>the</sup> <sup>font</sup> <sup>size</sup> <sup>alon</sup>g <sup>with</sup> <sup>the</sup> \baselineskip<sup>.</sup> <sup>A</sup> <sup>command</sup> <sup>for</sup> accomplishing this is 

\fontsize{9pt}{11pt}\selectfont 

<sup>which chan</sup>g<sup>es the font size to 9</sup> p<sup>oint and the</sup> \baselineskip <sup>to 11</sup> p<sup>oint. To make</sup> this change for a single paragraph, you can type 

{%special paragraph 

\fontsize{9pt}{11pt}\selectfont 

text 

}%end special paragraph 

<sup>Observe the blank line that follows</sup> text <sup>and marks the end of the</sup> p<sup>ara</sup>g<sup>ra</sup>p<sup>h</sup>; \par would accomplish the same thing. 

## 3.7 Lines, paragraphs, andpages

When typesetting a document, L<sup>A</sup>TEX breaks the text into lines, paragraphs, and pages. Sometimes you may not like how L<sup>A</sup>TEX has chosen to lay out your text. There are ways to influence how LAT<sub>E</sub>X does its work and these are discussed in this section. 

## 3.7.1 Lines

L<sup>A</sup>T X typesets a document one paragraph at a time. It tries to split the paragraph into lines of equal width; for a preliminary discussion, see Section 1.4. If it fails to do so <sup>successfull</sup>y <sup>and a line is too wide</sup>, y<sup>ou</sup> g<sup>et an</sup> overfull \hbox <sup>messa</sup>g<sup>e. Here is a</sup> typical example: 

Overfull \hbox (15.38948pt too wide) in paragraph at lines 11--16 

[]\OT1/cmr/m/n/10 In sev-eral sec-tions of the course 

on ma-trix 

the-ory, the strange term ‘‘hamiltonian-

The log file records these messages. To place a visual warning in the typeset version <sup>of</sup> y<sup>our document as well</sup>, <sup>use the</sup> draft <sup>document class o</sup>p<sup>tion</sup> 

\documentclass[draft]{amsart} 

Lines that are too wide are be marked with a slug (a black box) in the margin. A slug <sup>is a vertical bar of width</sup> \overfullrule<sup>.</sup> 

Do not worry about such messages while writing the document. If you are prepar-<sup>in</sup>g <sup>the final version and receive a messa</sup>g<sup>e for an</sup> overfull \hbox, <sup>the first line of</sup> defense is to see whether optional hyphens would help (see Section 3.4.9). Read the warning message carefully to see which words L<sup>A</sup>TEX cannot hyphenate properly. If adding optional hyphens does not help, a simple rephrasing of the problem sentence often does the trick. 

Recall that there are 72.27 points in an inch (see Section 1.4). So if the message indicates a 1.55812 pt overflow, for instance, you can safely ignore it. 

Tip If you do not want the 1.55812pt overflow reported whenever the document is typeset, you can enclose the ofending paragraph (including the blank line indicating the end of the paragraph) between the lines 

{\setlength{\hfuzz}{2pt} 

and 

}% end of \hfuzz=2pt 

Choose an argument that is slightly more than the reported error (maybe 2pt). This does not afect the typeset output, but the warning message and the slug, if you are us<sup>i</sup>ng t<sup>h</sup>e draft opt<sup>i</sup>on, are suppressed. 

Alternatively, enclose the ofending paragraph including the blank line indicating <sup>the end of the</sup> p<sup>ara</sup>g<sup>ra</sup>p<sup>h in a</sup> setlength <sup>environment:</sup> 

\begin{setlength}{\hfuzz}{2pt} 

\end{setlength}

## Rule \\

<sup>Without o</sup>p<sup>tional ar</sup>g<sup>uments</sup>, <sup>the</sup> \\ <sup>command and the</sup> \newline <sup>command are the</sup> same in text, but not within environments or command arguments. 

<sup>You can</sup> q<sup>ualif</sup>y <sup>the</sup> \linebreak <sup>command with an o</sup>p<sup>tional ar</sup>g<sup>ument:</sup> 0 <sup>to</sup> 4<sup>. The</sup> higher the argument, the more it forces the occurrence of a line break. \linebreak[4] <sup>is the same as</sup> \linebreak, <sup>while</sup> \linebreak[0] <sup>allows the line</sup> break but does not force it. 

<sup>The</sup> \nolinebreak <sup>command</sup> p<sup>la</sup>y<sup>s the o</sup>pp<sup>osite role.</sup> \nolinebreak[0] <sup>=</sup> \linebreak[0], <sup>and</sup> \nolinebreak[4] <sup>=</sup> \nolinebreak<sup>.</sup> \nolinebreak <sup>is sel-</sup> dom used since the tie (˜) and the \text command (see Section 3.4.3) accomplish the same goal most of the time. 

## Double spacing

It is convenient to proofread documents double spaced. Sone journals even require submissions to be double spaced. 

To typeset a document double spaced, include the command 

\renewcommand{\baselinestretch}{1.5} 

in its preamble. <sup>Alternativel</sup>y, <sup>use Geor</sup>g<sup>e D. Greenwade’s</sup> setspace<sup>. Load this</sup> p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>e with a</sup> 

\usepackage{setspace} 

command in the preamble of the document and specify 

\doublespacing 

in the preamble. This changes not just the line spacing but a number of other parameters to make your article look good. 

See also Section 3.1.13 of The L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X Companion, 2nd edition [56]. 

## 3.7.2 Paragraphs

Paragraphs are separated by blank lines or by the \par command. L<sup>A</sup>TEX error messages always show paragraph breaks as \par. The \par form is also very useful in custom commands and environments (see Sections 14.1 and 14.2). 

In some document classes, the first line of a paragraph is automatically indented. <sup>Indentation can be</sup> p<sup>revented with the</sup> \noindent <sup>command and can be forced with the</sup> \indent <sup>command.</sup> 

Sometimes—for instance, in a schedule, glossary, or index—you may want a hanging indent, where the first line of a paragraph is not indented, and all the others are indented by a specified amount. 

Hanging indents are created by specifying the amount of indentation specified by \hangindent <sup>and set with the</sup> \setlength <sup>command:</sup> 

\setlength{\hangindent}{30pt} 

\noindent 

\textbf{sentence} a group of words terminated by 

a period, exclamation point, or question mark. 

\setlength{\hangindent}{30pt} 

\noindent 

\textbf{paragraph} a group of sentences terminated by a 

blank line or by the new paragraph command. 

produces 

sentence a group of words terminated by a period, exclamation point, or question mark. 

paragraph a group of sentences terminated by a blank line or by the new paragraph command. 

<sup>Notice</sup> <sup>that</sup> <sup>the</sup> \setlength <sup>command</sup> <sup>must</sup> <sup>be</sup> <sup>re</sup>p<sup>eated</sup> <sup>for</sup> <sup>each</sup> p<sup>ara</sup>g<sup>ra</sup>p<sup>h.</sup> 

<sup>Sometimes</sup> y<sup>ou ma</sup>y <sup>want to chan</sup>g<sup>e the value of</sup> \hangafter, <sup>the len</sup>g<sup>th com-</sup> mand that specifies the number of lines not to be indented. The default value is 1. To change it to 2, use the command 

\setlength{\hangafter}{2} 

<sup>For more about the</sup> \setlength <sup>command</sup>, <sup>see Section 14.5.2.</sup> The <sup>LAT X</sup> Companion, 2nd edition [56] discusses in Section 3.1.4 the style parameters of a paragraph. 

The preferred way to shape a paragraph or series of paragraphs is with a custom list environment (see Section 14.6). 

## 3.7.3 Pages

There are two page breaking commands: 

\newpage, <sup>which breaks the</sup> p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>e at the</sup> p<sup>oint of insertion but does not stretch the</sup> content 

\pagebreak, <sup>which breaks the</sup> p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>e at the</sup> p<sup>oint of insertion and stretches the</sup> p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>e’s</sup> content to normal length 

Text following either command starts at the beginning of the next page, indented. 

As you can see, the page breaking commands are analogous to the line breaking commands discussed in Section 3.7.1. This analogy continues with the optional argu-<sup>ment</sup>, 0 <sup>to</sup> 4<sup>:</sup> 

\pagebreak[0] <sup>to</sup> \pagebreak[4] 

\nopagebreak[0] <sup>to</sup> \nopagebreak[4] 

There are also special commands for allowing or forbidding page breaks in multiline math displays (see Section 7.9). 

When preparing the final version of a document (see Section 17.5), you may have to extend or shrink a page by a line or two to prevent it from breaking at an unsuitable <sup>line. You can do so with the</sup> \enlargethispage <sup>command. For instance</sup>, 

\enlargethispage{\baselineskip} 

adds one line to the page length. On the other hand, 

\enlargethispage{-\baselineskip} 

makes the page one line shorter. 

\enlargethispage{10000pt} 

makes the page very long. 

<sup>The</sup> *<sup>-ed version</sup>, \enlargethispage*, <sup>s</sup>q<sup>ueezes the</sup> p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>e as much as</sup> p<sup>ossible.</sup> 

<sup>There are two more variants of the</sup> \newpage <sup>command. The</sup> 

## \clearpage

<sup>command does a</sup> \newpage <sup>and t</sup>yp<sup>esets all the fi</sup>g<sup>ures and tables waitin</sup>g <sup>to be</sup> p<sup>ro-</sup> cessed (see Section 8.4.3). The variant 

## \cleardoublepage

<sup>is used with the</sup> twoside <sup>document class o</sup>p<sup>tion</sup> (<sup>see Sections 9.5 and 10.1.2</sup>)<sup>. It does</sup> <sup>a</sup> \clearpage <sup>and in addition makes the next</sup> p<sup>rinted</sup> p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>e a ri</sup>g<sup>ht-hand</sup>, <sup>that is</sup>, <sup>odd-</sup> numbered, page, by inserting a blank page if necessary. If for your document class this <sup>does not work</sup>, <sup>use the</sup> p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>e</sup> cleardoublepage.sty <sup>in the</sup> samples <sup>folder.</sup> 

Section 17.6 discusses the use of some of these commands in the final preparation of books. 

## 3.7.4 Multicolumn printing

<sup>Man</sup>y <sup>document</sup> <sup>classes</sup> p<sup>rovide</sup> <sup>the</sup> twocolumn <sup>o</sup>p<sup>tion</sup> <sup>for</sup> <sup>two-column</sup> <sup>t</sup>yp<sup>esettin</sup>g (<sup>see</sup> <sup>Sections 9.5 and 10.1.2</sup>)<sup>. In addition</sup>, <sup>there is a</sup> \twocolumn <sup>command which starts a</sup> <sup>new</sup> p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>e b</sup>y <sup>issuin</sup>g <sup>a</sup> \clearpage <sup>and then t</sup>yp<sup>esets in two columns. An o</sup>p<sup>tional</sup> <sup>ar</sup>g<sup>ument</sup> p<sup>rovides a two-column wide title. Use the</sup> \onecolumn <sup>command to switch</sup> back to a one-column format. 

<sup>Frank Mittelbach’s</sup> multicol p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>e</sup> (<sup>see Section 10.3.1</sup>) p<sup>rovides the much</sup> <sup>more so</sup>p<sup>histicated</sup> multicols <sup>environment</sup>, <sup>which can start in the middle of a</sup> p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>e</sup>, can handle more than two columns, and can be customized in a number of ways (see Section 3.5.3 of The L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X Companion, 2nd edition [56]). 

## 3.8 Spaces

The judicious use of horizontal and vertical space is an important part of the formatting of a document. Fortunately, most of the spacing decisions are made by the document class, but L<sup>A</sup>T X has a large number of commands that allow the user to insert horizontal and vertical spacing. 

Remember that L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X ignores excess spaces, tabs, and end-of-line characters. If you need to add horizontal or vertical space, then you must choose from the commands in this section. Use them sparingly (see Section 2.6). 

## 3.8.1 Horizontal spaces

In this section, we discuss fixed length horizontal space commands. Variable length horizontal space is discussed in Section 3.8.4. 

When typing text, there are three commands that are often used to create horizontal space, shown between the bars in the display below: 

$$
\begin{array}{c c} \backslash \sqcup & \sqcup \\ \backslash q u a d & \sqcup \\ \backslash q q u a d & \sqcup \end{array}
$$

<sup>The</sup> \quad <sup>command creates a 1 em s</sup>p<sup>ace and</sup> \qquad <sup>creates a 2 em s</sup>p<sup>ace</sup> (<sup>see Sec-</sup> tion 3.8.3). The interword space created by $\nu _ { \sf U }$ can both stretch and shrink. There are other commands that create smaller amounts of space. All the math spacing commands <sup>of Section 6.1.3—with the exce</sup>p<sup>tion of</sup> \mspace<sup>—can be used in ordinar</sup>y <sup>text</sup> (<sup>see</sup> <sup>Sections</sup> <sup>A.9</sup> <sup>and</sup> <sup>B.6</sup>), <sup>but</sup> <sup>the</sup> \hspace <sup>and</sup> \phantom <sup>commands</sup> <sup>ma</sup>y <sup>be</sup> <sup>more</sup> <sup>a</sup>pp<sup>ro-</sup> priate. 

T<sup>h</sup>e \hspace command ta<sup>k</sup>es a <sup>l</sup>engt<sup>h</sup> as a parameter. T<sup>h</sup>e <sup>l</sup>engt<sup>h</sup> may be negat<sup>i</sup>ve. For example, 

$$
\begin{array}{l l l} \text {   \text   } & \mid & \mid \\ \text {   \text   } & \mid & \mid \\ \text {   \text   } & \mid & \mid \\ \text {   \text   } & \mid & \mid \end{array}
$$

<sup>or</sup> \hspace{-40pt}<sup>. The command</sup> \hspace <sup>is often used with a ne</sup>g<sup>ative ar</sup>g<sup>ument</sup> when placing illustrations. 

```latex
And text \\
\hspace{20pt}And text \\
\hspace*{20pt}And text 
```

```txt

```

```latex
\textbar need space\textbar |need space|
\textbar\phantom{need space}\textbar | 
```

and

## \hphantom{argument }

creates a space with the horizontal dimension that would be occupied by its typeset argument <sup>and with zero hei</sup>g<sup>ht.</sup> 

For instance, the last two lines of the dedication of this book were typed as follows <sup>in the</sup> flushright <sup>environment:</sup>

## Horizontal space variant

When L<sup>A</sup>TEX typesets a line, it removes all spaces from the beginning of the line, in-<sup>cludin</sup>g <sup>the s</sup>p<sup>ace created b</sup>y \hspace, \quad, <sup>and other s</sup>p<sup>acin</sup>g <sup>commands. Usin</sup>g <sup>the</sup> *<sup>-ed variant of</sup> \hspace, \hspace*, p<sup>revents LAT</sup>E<sup>X from removin</sup>g <sup>the s</sup>p<sup>ace</sup> y<sup>ou</sup> have specified.

## Vertical space variants

L<sup>A</sup>TEX removes vertical space from the beginning and end of each page, including space p<sup>roduced b</sup>y \vspace<sup>. The s</sup>p<sup>ace created b</sup>y <sup>the variant</sup> \vspace* <sup>is not removed b</sup>y L<sup>A</sup>TEX under any circumstances. Use this command, for instance, to start the typeset text (say, of a letter) not at the top of the page. 

<sup>The</sup> \phantom <sup>command has also a vertical variant:</sup> \vphantom<sup>. The command</sup> \vphantom{argument } <sup>creates a vertical s</sup>p<sup>ace with the vertical dimension that would</sup> <sup>be occu</sup>p<sup>ied b</sup>y <sup>its t</sup>yp<sup>eset ar</sup>g<sup>ument</sup>, argument <sup>.</sup> 

## 3.8.3 Relative spaces

The length of a space is usually given in absolute units: 12pt (points), .5cm (centimeters), 1.5in (inches). Sometimes, relative units, em and ex, are more appropriate, units that are relative to the size of the letters in the current font. The unit 1 em is approximately the width of an M in the current font, while 1 ex is approximately the height of an x in the current font. These units are used in commands such as 

$$
\backslash h s p a c e \{1 2 e m \} \text { and } \backslash v s p a c e \{1 2 e x \}
$$

<sup>The</sup> \quad <sup>and</sup> \qquad <sup>commands</sup> (<sup>Section 3.8.1</sup>) p<sup>roduce 1 em and 2 em s</sup>p<sup>aces.</sup> 

## 3.8.4 Expanding spaces

## Horizontal spaces

<sup>The</sup> \hfill, \dotfill, <sup>and</sup> \hrulefill <sup>commands fill all available s</sup>p<sup>ace in the line</sup> with spaces, dots, or a horizontal line, respectively. If there are two of these commands on the same line, the space is divided equally between them. These commands can be used to center text, to fill lines with dots in a table of contents, and so on.
