<sup>Note that the ar</sup>g<sup>ument of</sup> alignat <sup>does not have to be</sup> p<sup>recise. If</sup> y<sup>ou want two</sup> columns, the argument can be 2, or 3, or any larger number. If you want to, you can simply type 10 and just ignore the argument. You may define a new environment (see Section 14.2.1) that does just that. 

## 7.5.5 Inserting text

<sup>The</sup> \intertext <sup>command</sup> p<sup>laces one or more lines of text in the middle of an ali</sup>g<sup>ned</sup> environment. For instance, to obtain 

$$
h (x) = \int \left(\frac {f (x) + g (x)}{1 + f ^ {2} (x)} + \frac {1 + f (x) g (x)}{\sqrt {1 - \sin x}}\right) d x
$$

The reader may find the following form easier to read: 

$= \int \frac{1 + f(x)}{1 + g(x)} dx - 2\arctan (x - 2)$ 

you would type 

```latex
\begin{align}\label{E:mm5}
    h(x) &= \int \left(
    \frac{ f(x) + g(x) }
    {1 + f^{-2}(x)} +
    \frac{1 + f(x)g(x)}
    { \sqrt{1 - \sin x} }
    \right) \, dx \\
\intertext{The reader may find the following form easier to read:}
&= \int \frac{1 + f(x)}
{1 + g(x)}
\, dx - 2 \arctan(x - 2) \notag
\end{align} 
```

Notice how the equal sign in the first formula is aligned with the equal sign in the second formula even though a line of text separates the two. 

<sup>Here is another exam</sup>p<sup>le</sup>, <sup>this one usin</sup>g align*<sup>:</sup> 

$f(x) = x + yz$ $g(x) = x + y + z$ 

The reader may also find the following polynomials useful: 

$h(x) = xy + xz + yz$ $k(x) = (x + y)(x + z)(y + z)$ is typed as
\begin{align*}
    f(x) &= x + yz & \qquad g(x) &= x + y + z \\
    \intertext{The reader may also find the following
    polynomials useful:}
    h(x) &= xy + xz + yz
    & \qquad k(x) &= (x + y)(x + z)(y + z)
\end{align*} 

<sup>The</sup> \intertext <sup>command must follow a line se</sup>p<sup>arator command</sup>, \\ <sup>or</sup> \\* (<sup>see</sup> Section 7.9). If you violate this rule, you get the message 

```txt
! Misplaced \noalign. \intertext #1->\noalign
{\penalty \postdisplaypenalty
\vskip ...} 
```

<sup>The text in</sup> \intertext <sup>can be centered usin</sup>g <sup>a</sup> center <sup>environment or with the</sup> \centering <sup>command</sup> (<sup>see Section 4.3</sup>)<sup>.</sup> 

## 7.6 Aligned subsidiary math environments

A subsidiary math environment is a math environment that can only be used inside another math environment. Think of it as creating a “large math symbol”. 

In this section, we discuss aligned subsidiary math environments. We discuss adj<sup>usted subsidiar</sup>y <sup>math environments</sup>, <sup>includin</sup>g cases, <sup>in Section 7.7.</sup> 

## 7.6.1 Subsidiary variants

<sup>The</sup> align, alignat, <sup>and</sup> gather <sup>environments</sup> (<sup>see Sections 7.5</sup>, <sup>7.5.4</sup>, <sup>and 7.2</sup>) <sup>have</sup> <sup>subsidiar</sup>y <sup>versions.</sup> <sup>The</sup>y <sup>are</sup> <sup>called</sup> aligned, alignedat, <sup>and</sup> gathered<sup>.</sup> <sup>To</sup> <sup>obtain</sup> 

$$
\begin{array}{l l} x = 3 + \mathbf {p} + \alpha & \mathbf {p} = 5 + a + \alpha \\ y = 4 + \mathbf {q} & \mathbf {q} = 1 2 \\ z = 5 + \mathbf {r} & \mathbf {r} = 1 3 \\ u = 6 + \mathbf {s} & \mathbf {s} = 1 1 + d \end{array}
$$

type 

```latex
\[\begin{aligned}
    x &= 3 + \mathbf{p} + \alpha \\
    y &= 4 + \mathbf{q} \\
    z &= 5 + \mathbf{r} \\
    u &= 6 + \mathbf{s}
\end{aligned}
\text{\qquad using\qquad}
\begin{gathered}
    \mathbf{p} = 5 + a + \alpha \\
    \mathbf{q} = 12 \\
    \mathbf{r} = 13 \\
    \mathbf{s} = 11 + d
\end{gathered}
\] 
```

Note how the list of aligned formulas 

$$
\begin{array}{l} {x = 3 + p + \alpha} \\ {y = 4 + {\bf q}} \\ {z = 5 + {\bf r}} \\ {u = 6 + {\bf s}} \end{array}
$$

and the list of centered formulas 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \mathbf {p} = 5 + a + \alpha \\ \mathbf {q} = 1 2 \\ \mathbf {r} = 1 3 \\ \mathbf {s} = 1 1 + d \end{array}
$$

are treated as individual large symbols. 

<sup>The</sup> aligned, alignedat, <sup>and</sup> gathered <sup>subsidiar</sup>y <sup>math environments follow</sup> <sup>the same rules as</sup> align <sup>and</sup> gather<sup>. The</sup> aligned <sup>subsidiar</sup>y <sup>math environment al-</sup> lows any number of columns, but you must specify the intercolumn spacing as in the alignat <sup>environment.</sup> 

<sup>You can use the</sup> aligned <sup>subsidiar</sup>y <sup>math environment to rewrite formula</sup> (<sup>4</sup>) from Section 1.7.3 so that the formula number is centered between the two lines: 

$$
\begin{array}{r} h (x) = \int \left(\frac {f (x) + g (x)}{1 + f ^ {2} (x)} + \frac {1 + f (x) g (x)}{\sqrt {1 - \sin x}}\right) d x \\ = \int \frac {1 + f (x)}{1 + g (x)} d x - 2 \arctan (x - 2) \end{array}\tag{21}
$$

this is typed as 

```latex
\begin{equation}\label{E:mm6}
\begin{aligned}
    h(x) &= \int \left(
    \frac{ f(x) + g(x) }
    { 1 + f^{-2}(x) } +
    \frac{ 1 + f(x)g(x) }
    { \sqrt{1 - \sin x} }
    \right) \, dx \\
    &= \int \frac{ 1 + f(x) }
    { 1 + g(x) } \, dx - 2 \arctan (x - 2)
\end{aligned}
\end{equation} 
```

See Section 7.6.2 for a better way to split a long formula. 

Symbols, as a rule, are vertically centrally aligned. This is not normally an issue with math symbols, but it may be important with large symbols created by sub-<sup>sidiar</sup>y <sup>math environments. The subsidiar</sup>y <sup>math environments</sup>, aligned, gathered, and array, take c, t, or b as optional arguments to force vertically centered, top, or bottom alignment, respectively. The default is c (centered). To obtain 

$\begin{array}{llll}x = 3 + \mathbf{p} + \alpha & & \mathbf{p} = 5 + a + \alpha \\ y = 4 + \mathbf{q} & & \mathbf{q} = 12\\ z = 5 + \mathbf{r} & & \mathbf{r} = 13\\ u = 6 + \mathbf{s} & \mathrm{using} & \mathbf{s} = 11 + d \end{array}$ 

for example, you would type 

```latex
\[\begin{aligned}[b]
    x &= 3 + \mathbf{p} + \alpha \\
    y &= 4 + \mathbf{q} \\
    z &= 5 + \mathbf{r} \\
    u &= 6 + \mathbf{s}
\end{aligned}
\text{\qquad using\qquad}
\begin{gathered}[b]
    \mathbf{p} = 5 + a + \alpha \\
    \mathbf{q} = 12 \\
    \mathbf{r} = 13 \\
    \mathbf{s} = 11 + d
\end{gathered}
\] 
```

There is no numbering or \tag-ing allowed in subsidiary math environments because L<sup>A</sup>T X does not number or tag what it considers to be a single symbol. 

## 7.6.2 Split

<sup>The</sup> split <sup>subsidiar</sup>y <sup>math environment is used to s</sup>p<sup>lit a lon</sup>g <sup>formula into ali</sup>g<sup>ned</sup> p<sup>arts. There are two ma</sup>j<sup>or advanta</sup>g<sup>es to use</sup> split<sup>:</sup> 

<sup>1. The math environment that contains it considers the</sup> split <sup>environment to be a</sup> single equation, so it generates only one number for it. 

<sup>2. If a</sup> split <sup>environment a</sup>pp<sup>ears inside an</sup> align <sup>environment</sup>, <sup>the ali</sup>g<sup>nment</sup> p<sup>oint</sup> <sup>of the</sup> split <sup>environment is reco</sup>g<sup>nized b</sup>y align <sup>and is used in ali</sup>g<sup>nin</sup>g <sup>all the</sup> <sup>formulas in the</sup> align <sup>environment.</sup> 

To illustrate the first advantage, consider 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {(x _ {1} x _ {2} x _ {3} x _ {4} x _ {5} x _ {6}) ^ {2}} \\ & {\qquad + (x _ {1} x _ {2} x _ {3} x _ {4} x _ {5} + x _ {1} x _ {3} x _ {4} x _ {5} x _ {6} + x _ {1} x _ {2} x _ {4} x _ {5} x _ {6} + x _ {1} x _ {2} x _ {3} x _ {5} x _ {6}) ^ {2}} \end{array}\tag{22}
$$

typed as 

```latex
\begin{equation}\label{E:mm7}
\begin{split}
(x_{1}x_{2}&x_{3}x_{4}x_{5}x_{6})^{2}\
&+ (x_{1}x_{2}x_{3}x_{4}x_{5}
+ x_{1}x_{3}x_{4}x_{5}x_{6}
+ x_{1}x_{2}x_{4}x_{5}x_{6}
+ x_{1}x_{2}x_{3}x_{5}x_{6})^{2}
\end{split}
\end{equation} 
```

<sup>See</sup> <sup>also</sup> <sup>the</sup> <sup>two</sup> <sup>exam</sup>p<sup>les</sup> <sup>of</sup> split <sup>in</sup> <sup>the</sup> secondarticle.tex <sup>sam</sup>p<sup>le</sup> <sup>article</sup> <sup>in</sup> <sup>Section</sup> <sup>9.3</sup> <sup>and</sup> <sup>in</sup> <sup>the</sup> samples <sup>folder</sup> (<sup>see</sup> p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>e</sup> <sup>5</sup>)<sup>.</sup> 

<sup>To illustrate the second advanta</sup>g<sup>e</sup>, <sup>here is an exam</sup>p<sup>le of a</sup> split <sup>subsidiar</sup>y <sup>math</sup> <sup>environment within an</sup> align <sup>environment:</sup> 

(23) 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {f = (x _ {1} x _ {2} x _ {3} x _ {4} x _ {5} x _ {6}) ^ {2}} \\ & {\quad = (x _ {1} x _ {2} x _ {3} x _ {4} x _ {5} + x _ {1} x _ {3} x _ {4} x _ {5} x _ {6} + x _ {1} x _ {2} x _ {4} x _ {5} x _ {6} + x _ {1} x _ {2} x _ {3} x _ {5} x _ {6}) ^ {2},} \\ & {g = y _ {1} y _ {2} y _ {3}.} \end{array}\tag{24}
$$

which is typed as 

$$
\begin{array}{l}\begin{align}\label{E:mm8}\begin{split}\(f \& = (x_{1} x_{2} x_{3} x_{4} x_{5} x_{6})^{2}\)\\&= (x_{1} x_{2} x_{3} x_{4} x_{5} \\+ x_{1} x_{3} x_{4} x_{5} x_{6}\\+ x_{1} x_{2} x_{4} x_{5} x_{6}\\+ x_{1} x_{2} x_{3} x_{5} x_{6})^{2},\\\end{split}\)\\\(g \& = y_{1} y_{2} y_{3}.\\label{E:mm9}\end{align}\end{align}
$$

<sup>Notice the</sup> \\ <sup>command followin</sup>g \end{split} <sup>to se</sup>p<sup>arate the lines for</sup> align<sup>.</sup> 

## Rule split subsidiary math environment

<sup>1.</sup> split <sup>can onl</sup>y <sup>be used inside another math environment</sup>, <sup>such as</sup> displaymath, equation, align, gather, flalign, gathered <sup>and their</sup> *<sup>-ed variants.</sup> 

2. A split formula has only one number, automatically generated by L<sup>A</sup>TEX, or one <sup>ta</sup>g <sup>from a</sup> \tag <sup>command. Use the</sup> \notag <sup>command to su</sup>pp<sup>ress numberin</sup>g<sup>.</sup> 

<sup>Here</sup> <sup>is</sup> <sup>an</sup> <sup>exam</sup>p<sup>le</sup> <sup>of</sup> split <sup>inside</sup> <sup>a</sup> gather <sup>environment:</sup> 

```latex
\begin{gather}\label{E:mm10}
\begin{split}
    f &= (x_{1} x_{2} x_{3} x_{4} x_{5} x_{6})^{2} \\
    &= (x_{1} x_{2} x_{3} x_{4} x_{5}
    + x_{1} x_{3} x_{4} x_{5} x_{6}
    + x_{1} x_{2} x_{4} x_{5} x_{6}
    + x_{1} x_{2} x_{3} x_{5} x_{6})^{2} \\
    &= (x_{1} x_{2} x_{3} x_{4}
    + x_{1} x_{2} x_{3} x_{5}
    + x_{1} x_{2} x_{4} x_{5}
    + x_{1} x_{3} x_{4} x_{5})^{2}
\end{split} \\
\begin{aligned}
    g &= y_{1} y_{2} y_{3} \\
    h &= z_{1}^{2} z_{2}^{2} z_{3}^{2} z_{4}^{2}
\end{aligned}
\end{gather} 
```

which produces 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {f = (x _ {1} x _ {2} x _ {3} x _ {4} x _ {5} x _ {6}) ^ {2}} \\ & {\quad = (x _ {1} x _ {2} x _ {3} x _ {4} x _ {5} + x _ {1} x _ {3} x _ {4} x _ {5} x _ {6} + x _ {1} x _ {2} x _ {4} x _ {5} x _ {6} + x _ {1} x _ {2} x _ {3} x _ {5} x _ {6}) ^ {2}} \\ & {\quad = (x _ {1} x _ {2} x _ {3} x _ {4} + x _ {1} x _ {2} x _ {3} x _ {5} + x _ {1} x _ {2} x _ {4} x _ {5} + x _ {1} x _ {3} x _ {4} x _ {5}) ^ {2}} \\ & {\qquad g = y _ {1} y _ {2} y _ {3}} \\ & {\qquad h = z _ {1} ^ {2} z _ {2} ^ {2} z _ {3} ^ {2} z _ {4} ^ {2}} \end{array}\tag{25}
$$

If you try to use split outside a displayed math environment, you get the message 

```txt
! Package amsmath Error: \begin{split} won't work here. 
```

<sup>You ma</sup>y <sup>want to read the discussion of the AMS document classes and</sup> amsmath package options in Section 9.5 that modify the placement of equation numbers. 

## 7.7 Adjusted columns

In an adjusted multiline math environment, the columns are adjusted so that they are displayed centered, flush left, or flush right, instead of aligned (as in Section 7.5). Since you have no control line by line over the alignment of the columns, & has only one role to play—it is the column separator. 

In Sections 7.2 and 7.3, we discussed two adjusted one-column math environments, gather <sup>and</sup> multline<sup>. All the other ad</sup>j<sup>usted constructs are subsidiar</sup>y <sup>math environ-</sup> <sup>ments. For exam</sup>p<sup>le</sup>, <sup>a</sup> matrix <sup>environment</sup> (<sup>see Section 7.7.1</sup>) p<sup>roduces a multicolumn</sup> 

centered display: 

$$
\left( \begin{array}{c c c c} a + b + c & u v & x - y & 2 7 \\ a + b & u + v & z & 1 3 4 0 \end{array} \right) = \left( \begin{array}{c c c c} 1 & 1 0 0 & 1 1 5 & 2 7 \\ 2 0 1 & 0 & 1 & 1 3 4 0 \end{array} \right)
$$

The array environment (see Section 7.7.2) produces a multicolumn adjusted display: 

$$
\left( \begin{array}{c c c c} a + b + c & u v & x - y & 2 7 \\ a + b & u + v & z & 1 3 4 0 \end{array} \right) = \left( \begin{array}{c c c c} 1 & 1 0 0 & 1 1 5 & 2 7 \\ 2 0 1 & 0 & 1 & 1 3 4 0 \end{array} \right)
$$

The columns are centered, flush left, or flush right. In this example, the first matrix has three centered columns and one flush right column, while the second matrix has four flush right columns. A variant, cases (see Sections 1.7.4 and 7.7.3), produces two columns set flush left: 

$$
f (x) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} - x ^ {2}, & \text { if } x <   0; \\ \alpha + x, & \text { if } 0 \leq x \leq 1; \\ x ^ {2}, & \text { otherwise }. \end{array} \right.\tag{26}
$$


which produces

## 7.7.3 Cases

<sup>The</sup> cases <sup>environment is also a subsidiar</sup>y <sup>math environment. Here is the exam</sup>p<sup>le</sup> from Section 1.7.4 and the introduction to this section: 

$$
f (x) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} - x ^ {2}, & \text {if} x <   0; \\ \alpha + x, & \text {if} 0 \leq x \leq 1; \\ x ^ {2}, & \text {otherwise.} \end{array} \right.
$$

It is typed as 

```latex
\begin{equation}
    f(x)= 
    \begin{cases}
    -x^{-2}, &\text{if $x < 0$;} \\
    \alpha + x, &\text{if $0 \leq x \leq 1$;} \\
    x^{-2}, &\text{otherwise.}
    \end{cases}
\end{equation} 
```

<sup>It would be eas</sup>y <sup>to code the</sup> cases <sup>environment as a s</sup>p<sup>ecial case of the</sup> array <sup>sub-</sup> sidiary math environment: 

```latex
\begin{equation}
    f(x) =
    \left\{
    \begin{array}{ll}
    -x^{2}, &\text{if $x < 0$;} \\
    \alpha + x, &\text{if $0 \leq x \leq 1$;} \\
    x^{2}, &\text{otherwise.}
    \end{array}
    \right.
\end{equation} 
```

<sup>or of the</sup> alignedat <sup>subsidiar</sup>y <sup>math environment:</sup> 

```latex
\begin{equation*}
    f(x) =
    \left\{
    \begin{alignedat}{2}
    &-x^{2}, &&\quad\text{if $x < 0$;} \\
    &\alpha + x, &&\quad\text{if $0 \leq x \leq 1$;} \\
    &x^{2}, &&\quad\text{otherwise.}
    \end{alignedat}
    \right.
\end{equation*} 
```

## 7.8 Commutative diagrams

The amscd package provides the CD subsidiary math environment for typesetting simple commutative diagrams. To use it, make sure that the command 

```latex
\usepackage{amscd} 
```

```txt
is in the preamble of the document.
For instance, to obtain 
```

<table><tr><td>A</td><td>→</td><td>B</td></tr><tr><td>↓</td><td></td><td>↓</td></tr><tr><td>C</td><td>——</td><td>D</td></tr></table>

```txt
type
\[ 
    \begin{CD}
    A    @>>>    B \\
    @VVV    @VVV \\
    C    @=    D
    \end{CD}
\] 
```

A commutative diagram is a matrix made up of two kinds of rows, horizontal rows, that is, rows with horizontal arrows; and vertical rows, rows with vertical arrows. For example, 

```txt
A @>>> B 
```

is a typical horizontal row. It defines two columns and a connecting horizontal arrow @>>><sup>. There ma</sup>y <sup>also be more than two columns</sup>, <sup>as in</sup> 

<table><tr><td>A</td><td>@&gt;&gt;&gt;</td><td>B</td><td>@&gt;&gt;&gt;</td><td>C</td><td>@=</td><td>D</td><td>@&lt;&lt;</td><td>E</td><td>@&lt;&lt;</td><td>F</td></tr></table>

The connecting pieces can be: 

<sup>Stretchable</sup> <sup>ri</sup>g<sup>ht</sup> <sup>arrows</sup>, @>>> 

Stretchable left arrows, $\textcircled { \scriptsize { 1 } } < < <$ 

Stretchable equal signs, @= 

<sup>Blanks</sup>, @. 

The label above a stretchable arrow should be typed between the first and second > or < symbols, whereas the label below should be typed between the second and third > or < symbo<sup>l</sup>s. You can <sup>h</sup>ave bot<sup>h</sup>. 

The following is a typical vertical row containing vertical arrows: 

@VVV @VVV @AAA 

The vertical pieces could be 

<sup>Stretchable down arrows</sup>, @VVV 

<sup>Stretchable u</sup>p <sup>arro</sup>w<sup>s</sup>, @AAA 

<sup>Double vertical lines</sup>, @| <sup>or</sup> @\vert 

<sup>Blanks</sup>, @. 

The vertical arrows are placed starting with the first column. 

The label to the left of a stretchable vertical arrow should be typed between the first and second V or A, whereas the label on the right should be typed between the second <sup>and third</sup> V <sup>or</sup> A <sup>s</sup>y<sup>mbols. You can ha</sup>v<sup>e both.</sup> 

These constructs are illustrated in 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \mathbb {C} \xrightarrow {H _ {1}} \mathbb {C} \xrightarrow {H _ {2}} \mathbb {C} \\ P _ {c, 3} \Big \downarrow \qquad P _ {\bar {c}, 3} \Big \downarrow \qquad \Big \downarrow P _ {- c, 3} \\ \mathbb {C} \xrightarrow {H _ {1}} \mathbb {C} \xrightarrow {H _ {2}} \mathbb {C} \end{array}
$$

typed as 

```latex
\[\begin{CD}
\mathbb{C} @>H_{1}>> \mathbb{C} @>H_{2}>>\mathbb{C}\
@VP_{c,3}VV @VP_{\bar{c},3}VV @VVP_{-c,3}V\
\mathbb{C} @>H_{1}>> \mathbb{C} @>H_{2}>> \mathbb{C}
\end{CD}
\] 
```

Here <sup>i</sup>s anot<sup>h</sup>er examp<sup>l</sup>e ut<sup>ili</sup>z<sup>i</sup>ng t<sup>h</sup>e \text command, <sup>f</sup>o<sup>ll</sup>owed by <sup>i</sup>ts source: 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/45f3cc63-7a26-418c-9a01-03dd91fad053/f3b6a12192ea7c40ab67e55c523dd910eb1cf8f98ef1c3732e5aecb349faf9ac.jpg)


```latex
\[\begin{CD}
A    @>\log>>    B    @>>\text{bottom}>    C
    @=    D    @<<   E
    @<<   F\\
@V\text{one-one}VV    @.    @AA\text{onto}A    @|\\
X    @=    Y    @>>>    Z
    @>>>    U\\
@A\beta AA    @AA\gamma A    @VVV    @VVV\\
D    @>\alpha>>    E    @>>>    H
    @.    I\\
\end{CD}
\] 
```

Diagrams requiring more advanced commands should be done with a drawing (or drafting) application or with specialized packages. The AMS recommends Kristofer H. Rose and Ross Moore<sup>’</sup>s xy-pic pac<sup>k</sup>age (see Sect<sup>i</sup>on D.<sup>1</sup>). I<sup>f</sup> you get <sup>f</sup>am<sup>ili</sup>ar w<sup>i</sup>t<sup>h</sup> t<sup>h</sup>e TikZ package in Chapter 13, then you should utilize the tikzcd package of Florêncio Neves to draw commutative diagrams, see Section 13.4. 

## 7.9 Adjusting the display

By default, the math environments described in this chapter do not allow page breaks. W<sup>hil</sup>e a page brea<sup>k i</sup>n a cases env<sup>i</sup>ronment <sup>i</sup>s obv<sup>i</sup>ous<sup>l</sup>y not des<sup>i</sup>rab<sup>l</sup>e, <sup>i</sup>t may be ac-<sup>ce</sup>p<sup>table in an</sup> align <sup>or</sup> gather <sup>environment. You can allow</sup> p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>e breaks b</sup>y <sup>usin</sup>g <sup>the</sup>

Document Structure 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/45f3cc63-7a26-418c-9a01-03dd91fad053/2f02f05482e911e6ec791224ae85f1643a23490d5df79f2682f984a03c5bc21d.jpg)


# Documents

In this chapter, we take up the organization of shorter documents. Longer documents and books are discussed in Part VI. 

If you are writing a simple article, start with a template (see Section 9.4), then you can safely ignore much of the material discussed in this chapter. In more complicated articles you may need the material discussed in this chapter. 

Section 8.1 discusses document structure in general, the preamble is presented in <sup>Section 8.2. Section 8.3 discusses the to</sup>p <sup>matter</sup>, <sup>in</sup> p<sup>articular</sup>, <sup>the</sup> abstract <sup>envi-</sup> ronment. Section 8.4 presents the main matter, including sectioning, cross-referencing, tables, and figures. Section 8.5 covers the back matter, including the bibliography and index. 

In Section 8.1–8.5 we discuss the logical design of a L<sup>A</sup>T X document. The visual design is largely left to the document class. In Section 8.6, however, we briefly discuss one frequently adjusted aspect of visual design, the page style. 

## 8.1 The structure of a document

The source file of a L<sup>A</sup>TEX document is divided into two main parts: the preamble and the body (see Figure 8.1). 

Preamble This is the portion of the source file before the 

\begin{document} 

command. It contains definitions and instructions that afect the entire document. 

Body <sup>This</sup> <sup>is</sup> <sup>the</sup> <sup>content</sup> <sup>of</sup> <sup>the</sup> document <sup>environment.</sup> <sup>It</sup> <sup>contains</sup> <sup>all</sup> <sup>the</sup> <sup>material</sup> <sup>to</sup> be typeset. 

These statements oversimplify the situation somewhat. For instance, you can define a command in the preamble to typeset some text that will appear wherever the command is used in the body, but the text is actually typed in the preamble. Nevertheless, I hope the division between the preamble and the body is clear. 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/45f3cc63-7a26-418c-9a01-03dd91fad053/56f698b9dc1f44b43e3cd8aee2763ae5ba37b2ebef1feb3963999b6c7b8c7d1f.jpg)



Figure 8.1: The structure of a L<sup>A</sup>TEX document.


The body is divided into three parts: 

Top matter This is the first part of the body. It is concluded with the \maketitle <sup>command. Traditionall</sup>y <sup>it included onl</sup>y <sup>the</sup> \title, <sup>the</sup> \author, <sup>and the</sup> \date <sup>commands. The to</sup>p <sup>matter is derived from these commands and from</sup> it the title page of an article was designed. This evolved to include a lot more information about the author(s), for instance, their e-mail addresses, academic afiliations, home pages, and about the article, for instance, research support, subject classification. The typeset top matter now is split into several locations, the top and bottom of the first page and the bottom of the last page. See page 4 and pages 272–275 for two examples and Section 17.1.2 for more components that can be used in longer documents and books. 

Main matter This is the main part of the document, including any appendices. 

Back matter This is the material that is typeset at the end of the document. For a typi cal shorter document, the back matter is just the bibliography. See Section 17.1.2 for more information about additional components—such as the index—that are often used in longer documents and books. 

## 8.2 The preamble

You were introduced to the preamble of a document in Section 1.8. Recall that the p<sup>reamble contains the crucial</sup> \documentclass <sup>line</sup>, <sup>s</sup>p<sup>ecif</sup>y<sup>in</sup>g <sup>the document class</sup> and the options that modify its behavior. For instance, 

\documentclass[draft,reqno]{amsart} 

<sup>loads the document class</sup> amsart <sup>with the</sup> draft <sup>o</sup>p<sup>tion</sup>, <sup>which</sup> p<sup>aints a slu</sup>g <sup>in the</sup> margin indicating lines that are too wide (see Section 3.7.1), and the reqno option, which places the equation numbers on the right (see Section 9.5). 

article <sup>is the most</sup> p<sup>o</sup>p<sup>ular le</sup>g<sup>ac</sup>y <sup>document class</sup> (<sup>see Section 10.1</sup>)<sup>. The com-</sup> mand 

\documentclass[titlepage,twoside]{article} 

<sup>loads the document class</sup> article <sup>with the</sup> titlepage <sup>o</sup>p<sup>tion</sup>, <sup>which creates a se</sup>p<sup>arate</sup> title page and places the abstract on a separate page, and the twoside option, which formats the typeset article for printing on both sides of the paper. 

<sup>The</sup> \documentclass <sup>command</sup> <sup>is</sup> <sup>usuall</sup>y <sup>followed</sup> <sup>b</sup>y <sup>the</sup> \usepackage <sup>com-</sup> mands, which load L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X enhancements called packages. For instance, 

\usepackage{latexsym} 

loads a package that defines some additional L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X symbol names (see Section 10.3), whereas 

\usepackage[demo]{graphicx} 

<sup>loads the</sup> graphicx p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>e</sup> (<sup>see Section 8.4.3</sup>) <sup>with the</sup> demo <sup>o</sup>p<sup>tion that inserts rect-</sup> angles in place of the illustrations. Document class options are also passed on to the packages as possible options, so 

\documentclass[demo]{amsart} 

\usepackage{graphicx} 

<sup>would also load the</sup> graphicx p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>e with the</sup> demo <sup>o</sup>p<sup>tion unless it is invoked with</sup> 

\usepackage[final]{graphicx} 

Any document class options that are not relevant for a package are ignored. 

\usepackage <sup>commands</sup> <sup>can</sup> <sup>also</sup> <sup>be</sup> <sup>combined:</sup> 

\usepackage{amssymb,latexsym} 

is the same as 

\usepackage{amssymb} 

\usepackage{latexsym} 

Document class files have a cls extension, whereas package files are designated <sup>b</sup>y <sup>the</sup> sty <sup>extension. The document class</sup> amsart <sup>is defined in the</sup> amsart.cls <sup>file</sup>, <sup>the</sup> graphicx p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>e is defined in the</sup> graphicx.sty <sup>file. You ma</sup>y <sup>define</sup> y<sup>our own</sup> p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>es</sup>, <sup>such as the</sup> newlattice p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>e described in Section 14.3.</sup> 

The preamble normally contains any custom commands (see Chapter 14) and the proclamation definitions (see Section 4.4). Some commands can only be in the p<sup>reamble.</sup> \DeclareMathOperator <sup>is such a command</sup> (<sup>see Section 14.1.6</sup>) <sup>and so is</sup> \numberwithin (<sup>see Section 5.3</sup>)<sup>. If</sup> y<sup>ou</sup> p<sup>ut such a command in the bod</sup>y, <sup>for exam</sup>p<sup>le</sup>, \DeclareMathOperator, y<sup>ou</sup> g<sup>et a messa</sup>g<sup>e:</sup> 

! LaTeX Error: Can be used only in preamble. 

l.103 \DeclareMathOperator 

There is one command that may only be placed before the 

\documentclass{...} 

line: 

\NeedsTeXFormat{LaTeX2e}[2005/12/01] 

This command checks the version of L<sup>A</sup>T X being used to typeset the document and issues a warning if it is older than December 1, 2005 or whatever date you specified. Use this optional date argument if your document contains a feature that was introduced on or after the date specified or if an earlier version had a bug that would materially afect the typesetting of your document. 

<sup>For instance</sup>, <sup>if</sup> y<sup>ou use the</sup> \textsubscript <sup>command</sup>, <sup>introduced in the</sup> <sup>December 1</sup>, <sup>2005 release</sup> (<sup>see</sup> p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>e 293</sup>), <sup>then</sup> y<sup>ou ma</sup>y <sup>use the</sup> \NeedsTeXFormat line shown above. L<sup>A</sup>TEX now hardly changes from year to year, so this command is rarely used except in document class files or package files. See, however, the discussion on page 293. 

## 8.3 Top matter

The top matter of an article is part of the article body and, as a rule, it contains the material used to create the “title page” and, optionally, an abstract. 

Discussion of the top matter should take place in the context of a particular doc-<sup>ument</sup> <sup>class.</sup> <sup>We</sup> <sup>discuss</sup> <sup>the</sup> <sup>to</sup>p <sup>matter</sup> <sup>of</sup> <sup>the</sup> amsart <sup>document</sup> <sup>class</sup> <sup>in</sup> <sup>Section</sup> <sup>1.8</sup>, and we continue discussing it in much more detail in Section 9.2. The top matter of the article <sup>document class is covered in Section 10.1.1.</sup> 

Long documents, such as books, have rather complicated top matter such as tables of contents (see Chapter 17). In this section, we only discuss the abstract. 

## 8.3.1 Abstract

Most standard document classes, except those for letters and books, make provision for <sup>an abstract</sup>, <sup>t</sup>yp<sup>ed in an</sup> abstract <sup>environment.</sup> 

The document class formats the heading as Abstract, or some variant, and, as a rule, typesets the text of the abstract in smaller type with wider margins. 

<sup>The</sup> amsart <sup>document class re</sup>q<sup>uires that</sup> y<sup>ou</sup> p<sup>lace the abstract environment</sup> before the \maketitle command (see Figure 8.1). See the abstract in the sample arti-<sup>cle</sup> firstarticle.tex <sup>on</sup> p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>e 4. If</sup> y<sup>ou for</sup>g<sup>et to</sup> p<sup>lace it there</sup>, y<sup>ou</sup> g<sup>et the warnin</sup>g 

Class amsart Warning: 

Abstract should precede \maketitle in AMS 

documentclasses; reported on input line 21. 

<sup>and the abstract is t</sup>yp<sup>eset wherever the</sup> abstract <sup>environment ha</sup>pp<sup>ens to be</sup> p<sup>laced</sup> 

<sup>In the</sup> article <sup>document class</sup> y<sup>ou</sup> p<sup>lace the abstract</sup> after <sup>the</sup> \maketitle <sup>com-</sup> <sup>mand. If</sup> y<sup>ou</sup> p<sup>lace the abstract before the</sup> \maketitle <sup>command</sup>, <sup>the abstract is</sup> p<sup>laced</sup> on page 1, and the article starts on page 2. 

If the abstract and the “footnotes” from the top matter fill the first page, the second p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>e has no runnin</sup>g <sup>head. To fix this</sup>, <sup>follow the</sup> \maketitle <sup>command with the</sup> \clearpage <sup>command</sup> (<sup>see Section 3.7.3</sup>)<sup>.</sup> 

## 8.4 Main matter

The main matter contains most of the essential parts of the document, including the appendices. 

We discuss now how to structure the main matter. We describe sectioning in Section 8.4.1, cross-referencing in Section 8.4.2, and tables and figures in Section 8.4.3. 

## 8.4.1 Sectioning

The main matter of a typical shorter document is divided into sections. We discuss sectioning of longer documents in Section 17.1.1. 

## Sections

<sup>LAT</sup>E<sup>X is instructed to start a section with the</sup> \section <sup>command</sup>, <sup>which takes the title</sup> of the section as its argument. This argument may also be used for the running head and it is also placed in the table of contents (see Section 17.2), which means that you need <sup>to</sup> p<sup>rotect fra</sup>g<sup>ile commands with the</sup> \protect <sup>command</sup> (<sup>see Section 3.3.3</sup>)<sup>. LAT</sup>E<sup>X</sup> automatically assigns a section number and typesets the section number followed by the section title. 

<sup>An</sup>y \section <sup>command ma</sup>y <sup>be followed b</sup>y <sup>a</sup> \label <sup>command</sup>, <sup>so that</sup> y<sup>ou</sup> can refer to the section number generated by L<sup>A</sup>TEX, as in 

\section{Introduction}\label{S:intro} 

<sup>The command</sup> \ref{S:intro} <sup>refers to the number of the section and the command</sup> \pageref{S:intro} <sup>refers to the number of the t</sup>yp<sup>eset</sup> p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>e where the section title</sup> appears. 

You save a lot of work if in the source file you type in the cross-reference: 

\section{Introduction}\label{S:intro} 

%Section~\ref{S:intro} 

## Other sectioning commands

A section may be subdivided into subsections, which may themselves be divided into subsubsections, paragraphs, and subparagraphs. Subsections are numbered within a section (in Section 1, they are numbered 1.1, 1.2, and so on). Here is the whole hierarchy: 

\section 

\subsection 

\subsubsection 

\paragraph 

\subparagraph 

It is important to understand that the five levels of sectioning are not just five diferent styles for typesetting section headers but they form a hierarchy. You should never have a subsection outside a section, a subsubsection outside a subsection, and so on. <sup>For instance</sup>, <sup>if the first sectionin</sup>g <sup>command in</sup> y<sup>our document is</sup> \subsection, <sup>the</sup> subsections are numbered 0.1, 0.2, . . . . Or if in the first section of your document the <sup>first sectionin</sup>g <sup>command is</sup> \subsubsection, <sup>the subsubsections are numbered</sup> 1.0.1, 1.0.2, . . . . Both are clearly undesirable. 

<sup>There</sup> <sup>are</sup> <sup>two</sup> <sup>additional</sup> <sup>sectionin</sup>g <sup>commands</sup> p<sup>rovided</sup> <sup>b</sup>y <sup>the</sup> report <sup>and</sup> <sup>b</sup>y <sup>the book document classes</sup> (book <sup>and</sup> amsbook)<sup>:</sup> \chapter <sup>and</sup> \part (<sup>discussed in</sup> Section 17.1.1). 

Any sectioning command may be followed by a \label command so that you can refer to the number (if any) generated by L<sup>A</sup>TEX and the page on which it appears (see Section 8.4.2). 

<sup>There is also the seldom used to</sup>p <sup>level</sup> \specialsection <sup>command. Articles do</sup> not have parts and chapters, but sometimes a long article may require further division <sup>usin</sup>g <sup>the</sup> \specialsection <sup>command.</sup> 

## Theform ofsectioning commands

All sectioning commands take one of the following three forms, illustrated below with <sup>the</sup> \section <sup>command:</sup> 

## Form 1 The simplest form is

\section{title } 

<sup>where</sup> title <sup>is the section title</sup>, <sup>of course. You need to</sup> p<sup>rotect an</sup>y <sup>fra</sup>g<sup>ile commands</sup> <sup>in</sup> title <sup>with the</sup> \protect <sup>command</sup> (<sup>see Section 3.3.3</sup>)<sup>.</sup> 

## Form 2 The sectioning command may have an optional argument

\section[short_title ]{title } 

<sup>The o</sup>p<sup>tional</sup> short_title <sup>ar</sup>g<sup>ument is used in the runnin</sup>g <sup>head. See Section 17.2 on</sup> <sup>what</sup> g<sup>oes into the table of contents. Protect an</sup>y <sup>fra</sup>g<sup>ile commands in</sup> short_title <sup>with the</sup> \protect <sup>command</sup> (<sup>see Section 3.3.3</sup>)<sup>.</sup> 

## Form 3 Finally, we consider the *-ed version

\section*{title } 

<sup>There are no section numbers</sup> p<sup>rinted and the</sup> title <sup>is not included in the runnin</sup>g head. Remember that if you * a section, all subsections, and so on, must also be *-ed to avoid having strange section numbers. 

## Sectioning commands typeset

Consider the following text: 

\section{Introduction}\label{S:Intro} 

We shall discuss the main contributors of this era. 

\subsection{Birkhoff’s contributions}\label{SS:contrib} 

\subsubsection{The years 1935--1945}\label{SSS:1935} 

Going to Oxford was a major step. 

\paragraph{The first paper} 

What should be the definition of a universal algebra? 

\subparagraph{The idea} 

One should read Whitehead very carefully. 

<sup>This is how it looks t</sup>yp<sup>eset in the</sup> amsart <sup>document class:</sup> 

## 1 Introduction

We shall discuss the main contributors of this era. 

## 1.1 Birkhof’s contributions

## 1.1.1 The years 1935–1945

Going to Oxford was a major step. 

The first paper What should be the definition of a universal algebra? 

The idea One should read Whitehead very carefully. 

Notice that paragraphs and subparagraphs are not displayed prominently by the AMS. 

<sup>B</sup>y <sup>contrast</sup>, <sup>look at the same text t</sup>yp<sup>eset in the le</sup>g<sup>ac</sup>y article <sup>document class:</sup> 

## 1. Introduction

We shall discuss the main contributors of this era. 

## 1.1. Birkhof’s contributions.

1.1.1. The years 1935–1945. Going to Oxford was a major step. 

The first paper. What should be the definition of a universal algebra? 

The idea. One should read Whitehead very carefully. 

This illustrates vividly one huge diference between the two document classes, the visual handling of sectioning. 

Section 14.5.1 discusses how you can change the format of the section numbers, and how to specify which sectioning levels are to be numbered. 

Section 2.2 of The L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X Companion, 2nd edition [56] explains how to change the layout of section headings, especially useful for document class designers. 

## Appendix

In the main matter, if the article contains appendices, mark the beginning of the appen-<sup>dices</sup> <sup>with</sup> <sup>the</sup> \appendix <sup>command.</sup> <sup>After</sup> <sup>the</sup> \appendix <sup>command</sup>, <sup>the</sup> \section command starts the appendices (for books, see Section 17.1.2): 

\appendix 

\section{A proof of the Main Theorem}\label{S:geom} 

<sup>This</sup> p<sup>roduces</sup> Appendix A <sup>with the</sup> g<sup>iven title</sup>, <sup>t</sup>yp<sup>eset</sup> j<sup>ust like a section.</sup> 

Note that appendices may be labeled and cross-referenced like any other section. In an appendix, subsections are numbered A.1, A.2, and so on, subsubsections within A.1 are numbered A.1.1, A.1.2, and so on. 

<sup>Let me re</sup>p<sup>eat</sup>, \appendix <sup>is not like</sup> \section<sup>. It is not a command with an</sup> argument. Append<sup>i</sup>ces are named by arguments o<sup>f</sup> t<sup>h</sup>e \section— commands (<sup>f</sup>or boo<sup>k</sup>s, by t<sup>h</sup>e \chapter—commands) placed after t<sup>h</sup>e \appendix command. 

## 8.4.2 Cross-referencing

There are three types of cross-referencing available in L<sup>A</sup>TEX: 

<sup>1. S</sup>y<sup>mbolic referencin</sup>g <sup>with</sup> \ref <sup>and</sup> \eqref <sup>for e</sup>q<sup>uations</sup> 

<sup>2. Pa</sup>g<sup>e referencin</sup>g <sup>with</sup> \pageref 

3. B<sup>i</sup>b<sup>li</sup>ograp<sup>hi</sup>c re<sup>f</sup>erenc<sup>i</sup>ng w<sup>i</sup>t<sup>h</sup> \cite 

In this section, we discuss the first two, while bibliographies are discussed in Section 8.5.1 and in Chapter 15. 

## Symbolic referencing

Wherever L<sup>A</sup>TEX can automatically generate a number in your document, you can place <sup>a</sup> \label <sup>command</sup> 

\label{symbol } 

Then, at any place in your document, you can use the \ref command 

\ref{symbol } 

to place that number in the document. We call symbol the label. You can use labels for sectioning units, equations, figures, tables, items in an enumerated list environment (see Section 4.2.1), as well as for theorems and other proclamations. 

<sup>If the e</sup>q<sup>uation labeled</sup> E:int <sup>is the fifth e</sup>q<sup>uation in an article</sup>, <sup>then LAT</sup>E<sup>X stores</sup> <sup>the number</sup> 5 <sup>for the label</sup> E:int, <sup>so</sup> \ref{E:int} p<sup>roduces the number</sup> 5<sup>. If e</sup>q<sup>uations</sup> are numbered within sections (see Section 5.3), and an equation is the third equation <sup>in Section 2</sup>, <sup>then LAT</sup>E<sup>X stores the number</sup> 2.3 <sup>for the label</sup> E:int, <sup>so the reference</sup> \ref{E:int} p<sup>roduces the number</sup> 2.3<sup>.</sup> 

Example 1 The present section starts with the command 

\section{Main matter}\label{S:MainMatter} 

<sup>So</sup> \ref{S:MainMatter} p<sup>roduces the number</sup> 8.4 <sup>and we</sup> g<sup>et the number of the t</sup>yp<sup>e-</sup> <sup>set</sup> p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>e where the section title a</sup>pp<sup>ears with</sup> \pageref{S:MainMatter}, <sup>which is</sup> 234<sup>.</sup> 

```latex
Tip Type
    \section{Main matter}\label{S:MainMatter}
    %Section~\ref{S:MainMatter}
    to make cross-referencing quicker.

Example 2
    \begin{equation}\label{E:int}
    \int_{0}^{-\pi} \sin x \, dx = 2.
    \end{equation}
In this case, \ref{E:int} produces the number of the equation, \eqref{E:int} produces the number of the equation in parentheses.

    \begin{equation}\label{E:int}%\eqref{E:int}
    \int_{0}^{-\pi} \sin x \, dx = 2.
    \end{equation}
to make cross-referencing quicker. 
```


It is dificult to overemphasize how useful automatic cross-referencing can be when writing a document. 

Tip Make your labels meaningful to yourself, so they are easy to remember. Systematize your labels. For example, start the label for a section with S:, theorem with T:, lemma <sup>with</sup> L:, <sup>and so on.</sup> 

When you are cross-referencing, even if you follow these tips, it may not be easy <sup>to remember a label. David Carlisle’s</sup> showkeys p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>e ma</sup>y <sup>hel</sup>p y<sup>ou out. It is</sup> p<sup>art</sup> of the tools distribution (see Section 10.3.1 and Section D.1). Include the line 

\usepackage{showkeys} 

<sup>in the</sup> p<sup>reamble of</sup> y<sup>our document. The</sup> showkeys p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>e shows all s</sup>y<sup>mbolic refer-</sup> ences in the margin of the typeset document. With the notcite option, my preference, 

\usepackage[notcite]{showkeys} 

showkeys <sup>does not show the labels for biblio</sup>g<sup>ra</sup>p<sup>hic references. When the document</sup> is ready for final typesetting, then comment out this line. 

Section 2.4 ofThe L<sup>A</sup>T X Companion, 2nd edition [56] describes varioref, a pack age which extends the power of \ref, and xr, a package for referencing external documents. 

## Absolute referencing

There are two forms of absolute referencing. 

1. Equations can be tagged. The \tag{name } command attaches a name to the formula. The tag replaces the equation number. 

<sup>2. Items in an</sup> itemize <sup>environment can be ta</sup>gg<sup>ed with the</sup> \item[name ] <sup>construct.</sup> The tag replaces the item number. 

Our first example is the equation 

$$
\int_ {0} ^ {\pi} \sin x d x = 2\tag{Int}
$$

```latex
is typed as
\begin{equation}
    \int_{0}^{-\pi} \sin x \, dx = 2 \tag{Int}
\end{equation}

Our second example is the numbered list:
This space has the following properties:
(a) Grade 2 Cantor;
(b) Half-smooth Hausdorff;
(c) Metrizably smooth.

Typed as
\noindent This space has the following properties:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item[(a)] Grade 2 Cantor\label{Cantor};
    \item[(b)] Half-smooth Hausdorff\label{Hausdorff};
    \item[(c)] Metrizably smooth\label{smooth}.
\end{enumerate}

Tags are absolute. This equation is always referred to as (Int). Equation numbers, on the other hand, are relative, they may change when the file is edited.

p Do not label absolute references. It may lead to problems that are hard to explain.

Page referencing
The command
\pageref{symbol}
produces the number of the typeset page corresponding to the location of the command
\label{symbol}. For example, if the following text is typeset on page 5,
There may be three types of problems with the construction of such lattices.\label{problem}
and you type
Because of the problems associated with
the construction (see page~\pageref{problem}) 
```

anywhere in the document, L<sup>A</sup>TEX produces 

Because of the problems associated with the construction (see page 5) 

Because of the way L<sup>A</sup>TEX typesets a page, page references may be of by one. See the discussion in Section 17.6 on how to guarantee that the page number is correct. 

## 8.4.3 Floating tables and illustrations

Many documents contain tables and illustrations. These must be treated in a special way since they cannot be broken across pages. If necessary, L<sup>A</sup>TEX moves—floats—a table or an illustration to the top or bottom of the current or the next page if possible and further away if not. 

<sup>LAT</sup>E<sup>X</sup> p<sup>rovides</sup> <sup>the</sup> table <sup>and</sup> <sup>the</sup> figure <sup>environments</sup> <sup>for</sup> <sup>t</sup>yp<sup>esettin</sup>g <sup>floats.</sup> <sup>The</sup> two are essentially identical except that the figure environments are named Figure 1, Figure 2, and so on, whereas the table environments are numbered as Table 1, Table 2, and so on. 

## Tables

<sup>A</sup> table <sup>environment</sup> <sup>is</sup> <sup>set</sup> <sup>u</sup>p <sup>as</sup> <sup>follows:</sup> 

```latex
\begin{table}
    Place the table here
    \caption{title}\label{Ta:xxx}
\end{table} 
```

<sup>The</sup> \caption <sup>command is o</sup>p<sup>tional and ma</sup>y <sup>also</sup> p<sup>recede the table. The o</sup>p<sup>tional</sup> \label <sup>command must be</sup> p<sup>laced between the command</sup> \caption <sup>and the command</sup> \end{table}<sup>. The label is used to reference the table’s number. A</sup> table <sup>environment</sup> can have more than one table, each with its own caption. 

```latex
Tip Type
\begin{table}
    Place the table here
    \caption{title}\label{Ta:xxx}%Table~\ref{Ta:xxx}
\end{table}
to make cross-referencing quicker. 
```

<sup>The</sup> table <sup>environment is</sup> p<sup>rimaril</sup>y <sup>used for tables made with the</sup> tabular <sup>or</sup> similar environments (see Section 4.6). There are many examples of tables in this book, for instance, Section 3.4 has four. 

<sup>If</sup> y<sup>our document uses the</sup> twocolumn <sup>document class o</sup>p<sup>tion</sup>, <sup>the</sup> table <sup>environ-</sup> <sup>ment</sup> p<sup>roduces tables that s</sup>p<sup>an onl</sup>y <sup>one column and the</sup> table* <sup>environment</sup> p<sup>roduces</sup> tables that span both columns. Such tables can be placed only at the top of a page. 

## Figures

Illustrations, also called graphics or figures, include drawings, scanned images, digi-<sup>tized</sup> p<sup>hotos</sup>, <sup>and so on. These can be inserted with a</sup> figure <sup>environment:</sup> 

```latex
\begin{figure}
    Place the graphics here
    \caption{title}\label{Fi:xxx}
\end{figure} 
```

The above discussion of captions and labels for tables also applies to figures. Like <sup>the</sup> table <sup>environment</sup>, <sup>if</sup> y<sup>our document uses the</sup> twocolumn <sup>document class o</sup>p<sup>tion</sup>, <sup>the</sup> figure <sup>environment</sup> p<sup>roduces</sup> <sup>fi</sup>g<sup>ures</sup> <sup>that</sup> <sup>s</sup>p<sup>an</sup> <sup>onl</sup>y <sup>one</sup> <sup>column</sup>, <sup>but</sup> <sup>the</sup> figure* environment produces figures that span both columns. However, these figures can be placed only at the top of a page. 

```latex
Tip Type
\begin{figure}
    Place the table here
    \caption{title}\label{Fi:xxx}%Table~\ref{Fi:xxx}
\end{figure}
to make cross-referencing quicker. 
```

The standard way of including a graphics file is with the commands provided by the graphicx p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>e b</sup>y <sup>David Carlisle and Sebastian Rahtz</sup>, <sup>which is</sup> p<sup>art of the LAT</sup>E<sup>X</sup> distribution (see Section 10.3). Save your graphics in PDF (Portable Document Format) format—as a rule. 

<sup>Your</sup> g<sup>ra</sup>p<sup>hics can also be made within a</sup> picture <sup>environment</sup>, <sup>an a</sup>pp<sup>roach that</sup> is neither encouraged nor discussed in this book. To draw within L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X, use TikZ, see Chapter 13. 

<sup>Usin</sup>g <sup>the</sup> graphicx p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>e</sup>, <sup>a t</sup>yp<sup>ical</sup> figure <sup>is s</sup>p<sup>ecified as follows:</sup> 

```latex
\begin{figure}
\centering\includegraphics{file}
\caption{title}\label{Fi:xxx}
\end{figure} 
```

<sup>The illustration</sup> circle.pdf <sup>is included with the command</sup> 

```txt
\includegraphics{circle} 
```

<sup>without the extension! LAT</sup>E<sup>X and the</sup> graphicx p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>e assumes the</sup> pdf <sup>extension.</sup> 

If you have to scale the graphics image, say to 68% of its original size, use the command 

```txt
\includegraphics[scale=.68]{file} 
```

For instance, the figure on page 32 is included with the commands 

```latex
\begin{figure}
    \centering\includegraphics[scale=.8]{StrucLaT}
    \caption{The structure of \protect\la.}
    \label{Fi:StrucLaT}
\end{figure} 
```

<sup>For another use of the</sup> graphicx p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>e</sup>, <sup>see Section 6.2.1.</sup> 

## Float control

<sup>The</sup> table <sup>and</sup> figure <sup>environments ma</sup>y <sup>have an o</sup>p<sup>tional ar</sup>g<sup>ument</sup>, <sup>with which</sup> y<sup>ou</sup> can influence L<sup>A</sup>TEX’s placement of the typeset table. The optional argument consists of one to four letters: 

b, the bottom of the page 

h, here (where the environment appears in the text) 

t, the top of the page 

p, a separate page 

For instance, 

\begin{table}[ht] 

requests L<sup>A</sup>TEX to place the table “here” or at the “top” of a page. The default is [tbp] and the order of the optional arguments is immaterial, for example, [th] is the same as [ht]. I<sup>f</sup> h <sup>i</sup>s spec<sup>ifi</sup>ed, <sup>i</sup>t ta<sup>k</sup>es precedence, <sup>f</sup>o<sup>ll</sup>owed by t and b. 

L<sup>A</sup>T X has more than a dozen internal parameters that control a complicated algorithm to determine the placement of tables and figures. If you want to override these parameters for one table or figure only, add an exclamation mark (!) to the optional argument. For instance, [!h] requests that this table or figure be placed where it is in the source file even if this placement violates the algorithm. For a detailed discussion of the float mechanism, see Chapter 6 of The L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X Companion, 2nd edition [56]. 

<sup>The</sup> \suppressfloats <sup>command sto</sup>p<sup>s LAT</sup>E<sup>X from</sup> p<sup>lacin</sup>g <sup>an</sup>y <sup>more tables or</sup> figures on the page it appears on. An optional argument t or b (but not both) prohibits placement of floats at the top or bottom of the current page. The table or figure that is suppressed appears on the next page or later in the document, if necessary. 

Your demands and L<sup>A</sup>TEX’s float mechanism may conflict with one another with the result that L<sup>A</sup>TEX may not place material where you want it. The default values of the float placement parameters are good only for documents with a small number of floating objects. Combining two tables or illustrations into one sometimes helps. <sup>The</sup> \clearpage <sup>command</sup> <sup>not</sup> <sup>onl</sup>y <sup>starts</sup> <sup>a</sup> <sup>new</sup> p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>e</sup> <sup>with</sup> <sup>the</sup> \newpage <sup>command</sup>, but also forces L<sup>A</sup>TEX to print all the tables and figures it has accumulated but not yet placed in the typeset document. See also some related commands discussed in Section 3.7.3. 

For more information on graphics, see Chapter 10 of The L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X Companion, 2nd edition [56] and Chapter 2.4 of The L<sup>A</sup>T X Graphics Companion [17]. See also the <sup>documentation for the</sup> graphicx p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>e in the LAT</sup>E<sup>X distribution</sup> (<sup>see Section 10.3</sup>)<sup>.</sup> 

## 8.5 Back matter

The back matter of an article is very simple, as a rule. It is either empty or consists of only a bibliography. A long document, such as a book, may have more complicated back matter (see Chapter 17). In this section, we discuss only the bibliography and a very simple index.

## 8.5.2 Simple indexes

<sup>Usin</sup>g <sup>the</sup> \label <sup>and</sup> \pageref <sup>commands</sup> (<sup>see Section 8.4.2</sup>), <sup>it is</sup> q<sup>uite sim</sup>p<sup>le to</sup> p<sup>roduce a small index in a</sup> theindex <sup>environment. At each</sup> p<sup>oint in the text that</sup> y<sup>ou</sup> want to re<sup>f</sup>erence <sup>i</sup>n t<sup>h</sup>e <sup>i</sup>ndex, p<sup>l</sup>ace a \label command. T<sup>h</sup>e correspond<sup>i</sup>ng entry <sup>i</sup>n <sup>the index t</sup>yp<sup>esets the</sup> p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>e number with the</sup> \pageref <sup>command.</sup> 

<sup>The</sup> \item, \subitem, <sup>and</sup> \subsubitem <sup>commands create an entr</sup>y, <sup>subentr</sup>y, and subsubentry, respectively. If you need additional vertical spacing when the first letter changes, for instance, between the “h” entries and the “i” entries, you can use the \indexspace <sup>command. Here are some exam</sup>p<sup>les of index entries:</sup> 

\begin{theindex} \item Lakser, H., \pageref{Lakser} \item Lattice, \pageref{Lattice_intro}, \textbf{\pageref{Lattice}} \subitem distributive, \pageref{Lattice_distributive} \subitem modular, \pageref{Lattice_distributive}, 

```latex
\textbf{\pageref{Lattice_distributive2}}
\item Linear subspace, \pageref{Linear_subspace}
\end{theindex} 
```

And here is the typeset index: 

INDEX 

Lakser, H., 2 Lattice, 14, 25 distributive, 18 modular, 19, 37 Linear subspace, 38 

For a larger index, you should use the MakeIndex application (see Chapter 16). 

## 8.6 Visual design

In this chapter, we have discussed the logical design of a L<sup>A</sup>TEX document. The visual design is largely left to the document class. But there is one small aspect of the visual design we have to discuss, the page style. 

To get a visual representation of the page style of your document, use layout package of Kent McPherson. Load the package with 

## \usepackage{layout}

<sup>and</sup> p<sup>lace the</sup> \layout <sup>command somewhere in the bod</sup>y <sup>of</sup> y<sup>our article. LAT</sup>E<sup>X</sup> p<sup>ro-</sup> duces a graphical representation of the page layout. Figure 8.4 shows the page layout <sup>for odd</sup> p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>es for the</sup> amsart <sup>document class with no o</sup>p<sup>tions.</sup> 

A typeset page has three parts, the running head or header, the body, and the footer. As a rule, the document class takes care of the contents and formatting of all three parts. For the running head and footer, however, you can override the page design of the document class with the command 

\pagestyle{style } 

<sup>where the ar</sup>g<sup>ument</sup> style <sup>is one of the followin</sup>g<sup>:</sup> 

plain The running head is empty and the footer contains only the page number 

empty <sup>Both the runnin</sup>g <sup>head and the footer are blank</sup> 

headings <sup>The runnin</sup>g <sup>head contains the information</sup> p<sup>rovided b</sup>y <sup>the document class</sup> and the footer is empty 

myheadings <sup>The runnin</sup>g <sup>head contains the information</sup> p<sup>rovided b</sup>y <sup>the commands</sup> \markboth <sup>and</sup> \markright, <sup>the footer is em</sup>p<sup>t</sup>y 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/45f3cc63-7a26-418c-9a01-03dd91fad053/4d319f3f39a5a34ba12fde69f8446a69ca221b77ef277a136db3954f38029b11.jpg)



<sup>Fi</sup>g<sup>ure 8.4: Pa</sup>g<sup>e la</sup>y<sup>out for the</sup> amsart <sup>document class.</sup>


<sup>The</sup> \markright <sup>command</sup> <sup>takes</sup> <sup>onl</sup>y <sup>one</sup> <sup>ar</sup>g<sup>ument.</sup> <sup>The</sup> <sup>last</sup> \markright <sup>on</sup> <sup>a</sup> p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>e</sup> p<sup>rovides the runnin</sup>g <sup>head information for that</sup> p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>e. The</sup> \markboth <sup>command has</sup> two arguments. The first provides the running head information for a left-hand page, the second provides the running head information for a right-hand page. The AMS <sup>document classes also have a</sup> \markleft <sup>command for the runnin</sup>g <sup>head information</sup> for a left-hand page. 

<sup>The</sup> \thispagestyle <sup>command</sup> <sup>is</sup> <sup>the</sup> <sup>same</sup> <sup>as</sup> \pagestyle <sup>exce</sup>p<sup>t</sup> <sup>that</sup> <sup>it</sup> <sup>afects</sup> only the current page. 

For instance, if the current page is a full-page graphic, you might want to issue the command 

\thispagestyle{empty} 

<sup>The</sup> \maketitle <sup>command automaticall</sup>y <sup>issues a</sup> 

\thispagestyle{plain} 

command, so if you want to suppress the page number on the first page of a document, you have to put 

\thispagestyle{empty} 

<sup>immediatel</sup>y <sup>after the</sup> \maketitle <sup>command.</sup> 

The commands listed in Figure 8.4 are length commands (see Section 14.5.2) and can be changed with the commands introduced in that section. As a rule, you do not have to worry about these settings, they are chosen by the document class for you. Sometimes, however, you have a job that requires such changes. I once had to submit a research plan on a form with a 7.5 inch by 5 inch box. To be able to cut and paste the <sup>t</sup>yp<sup>eset re</sup>p<sup>ort</sup>, <sup>I had to</sup> p<sup>roduce the text with a</sup> \textwidth <sup>of 7 inches. If I sim</sup>p<sup>l</sup>y <sup>set</sup> 

\setlength{\textwidth}{7in} 

the text would overflow the printed page and the last few characters of each line would be missing. So I had to change the margins by starting the document with 

\documentclass[12pt]{report} 

\setlength{\textwidth}{7in} 

\setlength{\oddsidemargin}{0pt} 

All ofChapter 4 ofThe L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X Companion, 2nd edition [56] deals with page layouts. <sup>There</sup> y<sup>ou can find a descri</sup>p<sup>tion of the</sup> geometry p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>e of Hideo Umeki</sup>, <sup>which</sup> computes all the parameters from the ones you supply. Also you find there a discussion <sup>of Piet van Oostrum’s excellent</sup> p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>e</sup>, fancyhdr, <sup>which allows</sup> y<sup>ou to create</sup> y<sup>our</sup> own page style (see also [24]). 

However, if you submit an article to a journal, do not change the type size, page dimensions, headers. Use the document class and the article templates the journal provides (if any). This will make your submission easier for you and the journal. See also Section 2.6. 

# The AMS article document class

<sup>In this cha</sup>p<sup>ter</sup>, <sup>we discuss</sup> amsart, <sup>the main AMS document class for</sup> j<sup>ournal articles.</sup> The AMS book document class is discussed in Chapter 17. 

In Section 9.1, I argue that there are good reasons why you should write your arti-<sup>cles</sup> <sup>for</sup> p<sup>ublication</sup> <sup>in</sup> amsart<sup>.</sup> <sup>Section</sup> <sup>9.2</sup> <sup>introduces</sup> <sup>the</sup> <sup>rules</sup> g<sup>overnin</sup>g <sup>the</sup> <sup>to</sup>p <sup>mat-</sup> <sup>ter in the</sup> amsart <sup>document class. The</sup> amsart <sup>sam</sup>p<sup>le article</sup> secondarticle.tex <sup>is</sup> presented in Section 9.3. In Section 9.4, you are guided through the process for creating detailed templates. 

A document class is finely tuned by its options. In Section 9.5, we discuss the <sup>o</sup>p<sup>tions of</sup> amsart<sup>. Section 9.6 briefl</sup>y <sup>describes the various</sup> p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>es in the AMS</sup> distribution and their interdependencies. 

## 9.1 Why amsart?

## 9.1.1 Submitting an article to the AMS

<sup>You want to submit an article written with the</sup> amsart <sup>document class to the Proceed</sup> ings of the American Mathematical Society. 

For general information on the AMS journals, go to the AMS Web site 

```txt
http://www.ams.org/ 
```

<sup>and start discoverin</sup>g <sup>the wealth of relevant information for</sup> Author, <sup>in the</sup> Author Resource Center<sup>.</sup> 

<sup>To</sup> <sup>find</sup> <sup>the</sup> <sup>class</sup> <sup>file</sup> <sup>for</sup> <sup>the</sup> <sup>Proceedin</sup>g<sup>s</sup> <sup>at</sup> <sup>the</sup> http://www.ams.org/ <sup>site</sup>, <sup>t</sup>yp<sup>e</sup> <sup>in the search field:</sup> proc_amslatex<sup>. Click on</sup> Proceedings of the AMS, <sup>choose</sup> <sup>the</sup> TeX package AMS-LaTeX, <sup>and finall</sup>y, <sup>choose</sup> proc-l.cls <sup>to download it.</sup> 

Now, in the preamble of your article, replace the line 

\documentclass{amsart} 

with 

\documentclass{proc-l} 

Typeset the article and you are done. Your article is formatted as it will appear in the Proceedings. 

## 9.1.2 Submitting an article to Algebra Universalis

<sup>There are man</sup>y j<sup>ournals whose document classes are based on</sup> amsart<sup>. For instance</sup>, 

http://www.algebrauniversalis.com 

takes you to the home page of the journal Algebra Universalis. To find the document <sup>class</sup>, <sup>click on</sup> Instructions for Authors <sup>and in Section D</sup>, <sup>click on</sup> au.cls<sup>. Now</sup> in your article make the replacement 

\documentclass{au} 

and your article typesets in the format appropriate for this journal. 

## 9.1.3 Submitting to otherjournals

<sup>A lar</sup>g<sup>e number of</sup> j<sup>ournals use document classes based on</sup> amsart<sup>. Not all are as</sup> friendly as Algebra Universalis, but as a rule a small number of changes in the article sufice. 

All of them share the attribute that the top matter is given as the arguments of <sup>several commands. In the introductor</sup>y <sup>sam</sup>p<sup>le article</sup>, firstarticle.tex, <sup>on</sup> p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>e 4</sup>, <sup>there were onl</sup>y <sup>four</sup>, <sup>but in the sam</sup>p<sup>le article</sup> secondarticle.tex <sup>in Section 9.3</sup>, <sup>there are nine—there could be more. Contrast this with the le</sup>g<sup>ac</sup>y article <sup>class</sup> (<sup>see</sup> Section 10.1.1). As a result, this document class is able to shape the top matter as the journal requires. Even if the names of some of these commands are diferent (e.g., affiliation <sup>for</sup> address), <sup>the</sup> p<sup>rinci</sup>p<sup>les</sup> y<sup>ou learn from the</sup> amsart <sup>document class</sup> apply. 

Many journals insist that you use their own document classes. For these, you may have to add the AMS packages (see Section 9.6) to continue using the enhancements of the AMS. 

A shrinking number ofjournals use document classes incompatible with the AMS packages. If you can, avoid these journals. 

## 9.1.4 Submitting to conference proceedings

The AMS also has a document class for articles for book-form proceedings of meetings. <sup>The diferences in the rules for the</sup> amsart <sup>and</sup> amsproc <sup>document classes are minor</sup>, <sup>for instance</sup>, amsproc <sup>does not access</sup> \date<sup>.</sup> 

## 9.2 The top matter

<sup>See</sup> <sup>the</sup> <sup>t</sup>yp<sup>eset</sup> <sup>to</sup>p <sup>matter</sup> <sup>of</sup> <sup>the</sup> secondarticle.tex <sup>article</sup> <sup>on</sup> p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>es</sup> <sup>272</sup> <sup>and</sup> <sup>275</sup> <sup>for</sup> a fairly representative example. As you may recall from Section 1.8, part of the author information is moved to the end of the typeset article—see page 275. 

Title page information is provided as arguments of several commands. For your convenience, I divide them into three groups: information about the article, information about the author, and AMS related information. 

There is only one general rule. 

## Rule Top matter commands

All top matter commands are short. 

This means that there can be no blank line (or \par command) in the argument of any of these commands (see Section 3.3.3). 

## 9.2.1 Article information

You have to supply five pieces of information about the article. 

Rule Title 

<sup>Command:</sup> \title 

Separate lines with \\ 

Optional argument: Short title for running head 

Do not put a period at the end of a title 

Do not use custom commands in the title 

The typeset title is placed on the front page of the typeset article. 

Many titles are too long to be typeset on a single line. If the way L<sup>A</sup>TEX breaks the title is not satisfactory, you can indicate where the title should be broken with the \\ command. Alternatively, you may nudge L<sup>A</sup>TEX in the right direction with ~ (see Section 3.4.3). For instance, the title: 

The \texttt{amsart} document class 

<sup>is broken b</sup>y <sup>LAT</sup>E<sup>X between</sup> document <sup>and</sup> class<sup>. So either add</sup> \\<sup>:</sup> 

The \texttt{amsart}\\ document class 

<sup>or re</sup>p<sup>lace</sup> document class <sup>with</sup> document~class<sup>:</sup> 

The \texttt{amsart} document~class 

The running head (see Section 8.6) is the title on odd-numbered pages, set in capital letters. If the title is more than a few words long, use an optional argument to specify a short title for the running head. Do not use \\ in the short title. 

Example of a title: 

\title{A construction of distributive lattices} 

A title with a short title: 

\title[Complete-simple distributive lattices] 

{A construction of\\ complete-simple 

distributive lattices} 

Note the AMS rules about short titles and the table of contents in Section 17.2.1. 

## Rule Translator

<sup>Command:</sup> \translator 

Do not put a period at the end of the argument. 

<sup>The t</sup>yp<sup>eset</sup> \translator <sup>is</sup> p<sup>laced on the last</sup> p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>e of the t</sup>yp<sup>eset article</sup>, <sup>before the ad-</sup> dress(es). There can be more than one translator. Each should be given as the argument <sup>of a se</sup>p<sup>arate</sup> \translator <sup>command.</sup> 

Example: 

\translator{Harry~M. Goldstein} 

## Rule Dedication

<sup>Command:</sup> \dedicatory 

Separate lines with \\ 

The typeset dedication is placed under the author(s). 

Example: 

\dedicatory{To the memory of my esteemed friend and teacher,\\ Harry~M. Goldstein} 

## Rule Date

<sup>Command:</sup> \date 

Example: 

\date{January 22, 2015} 

The typeset \date is placed on the front page of the typeset article as a footnote. Do not use this when you submit an article; specify the submission date. 

<sup>To su</sup>pp<sup>ress the date</sup>, <sup>use</sup> \date{} <sup>or omit the</sup> \date <sup>command entirel</sup>y<sup>.</sup> 

## 9.2.2 Author information

There are seven pieces of information about yourself. 

## Rule Author

<sup>Command:</sup> \author 

Optional argument: Short form of the name for the running head 

The typeset author is placed on the front page of the typeset article. Examples: 

\author{George~A. Menuhin} 

With a short form of the name for the running head: 

\author[G.\,A. Menuhin]{George~A. Menuhin} 

Section 9.2.4 discusses how to specify multiple authors. 

## Rule Contributor

<sup>Command:</sup> \contrib 

Optional argument: Describing the contribution 

The typeset contributor’s name is placed on the front page of the typeset article. 

Examples: 

A contributor authoring an appendix: 

\contrib[with an appendix by]{John Blaise} 

If this appendix has two authors: 

\contrib[with an appendix by]{J. Blaise} \contrib[]{W. Brock} 

This typesets (with author G. A. Menuhin) the author line as 

G.A. MENUHIN, WITH AN APPENDIX BY J. BLAISE AND W. Brock 

Contributors can have addresses, current addresses, etc., just like authors. 

## Rule Address

<sup>Command:</sup> \address 

Separate lines with \\ 

Optional argument: Name of author 

The typeset address is placed at the end of the typeset article. Example: 

DEPARTMENT OF APPLIED MATHEMATICS, UNIVERSITY OF WINNEBAGO, WINNEBAGO, MN 53714 

which is typed as 

\address{Department of Applied Mathematics\\ University of Winnebago\\ Winnebago, MN 53714} 

Notice that L<sup>A</sup>T X replaces the \\ line separators with commas. 

If there are several authors, you can use the author’s name as an optional argument of \address to avoid ambiguity. See Example 4 in Section 9.2.5 (page 267) for a complete example. 

## Rule Current address

<sup>Command:</sup> \curraddr 

Separate lines with \\ 

Optional argument: name of author 

The typeset current address is placed at the end of the typeset article. Example: 

Current address: Department of Mathematics, University of York, Heslington, York, England 

is typed as 

\curraddr{Department of Mathematics\\ University of York\\ Heslington, York, England} 

If there are several authors, you can use the author’s name as an optional argument <sup>of</sup> \curraddr <sup>to avoid ambi</sup>g<sup>uit</sup>y; <sup>for some exam</sup>p<sup>les</sup>, <sup>see Section 9.2.5.</sup> 

## Rule E-mail address

<sup>Command:</sup> \email 

Optional argument: Name of author 

The typeset e-mail address is placed at the end of the typeset article. Example: 

\email{gmen@ccw.uwinnebago.edu} 

Example: 

\email{George\_Gratzer@umanitoba.ca} 

type \% to get % (see Section 3.4.4). 

Example: 

\email{h1175moy\%ella@relay.eu.net} 

Rule Web (home) page (URL) 

<sup>Command:</sup> \urladdr 

Optional argument: Name of author 

The typeset Web (home) page is placed at the end of the typeset article. Example: 

\urladdr{http://www.maths.umanitoba.ca/homepages/gratzer/} 

Tip Many Internet addresses contain the tilde (˜), indicating the home directory of the user. Type ˜ to get ˜ and not \~, as recommended in Section 3.4.4. $\sim$ is also unacceptable. 

Example: 

\urladdr{http://kahuna.math.hawaii.edu/~ralph/} 

Rule Research support or other acknowledgments 

<sup>Command:</sup> \thanks 

Do not specify linebreaks. 

Terminate the sentence with a period. 

The typeset research support or other acknowledgments is placed on the front page of the typeset article as an unmarked footnote. 

Example: 

\thanks{Supported in part by NSF grant PAL-90-2466.} 

A \thanks{} command is ignored in typesetting. 

## 9.2.3 AMS information

The AMS requires that you supply two more pieces of information about the article. The following are collected at the bottom of the first page as unmarked footnotes <sup>alon</sup>g <sup>with the ar</sup>g<sup>uments of the</sup> \thanks <sup>and</sup> \date <sup>commands.</sup> 

## Rule AMS subject classifications

<sup>Command:</sup> \subjclass 

<sup>O</sup>p<sup>tional ar</sup>g<sup>ument:</sup> 2010<sup>—the default is 1991.</sup> 

amsart supplies the phrase 1991 Mathematics Subject Classification and a period at t<sup>h</sup>e end o<sup>f</sup> t<sup>h</sup>e subject c<sup>l</sup>ass<sup>ifi</sup>cat<sup>i</sup>on—w<sup>i</sup>t<sup>h</sup> t<sup>h</sup>e opt<sup>i</sup>ona<sup>l</sup> argument 2010, t<sup>h</sup>e p<sup>h</sup>rase is 2010 Mathematics Subject Classification 

<sup>The ar</sup>g<sup>ument should be either a five-character code or the</sup> p<sup>hrase</sup> Primary: <sup>followed</sup> <sup>b</sup>y <sup>a five-character code</sup>, <sup>a semicolon</sup>, <sup>the</sup> p<sup>hrase</sup> Secondary: <sup>and one or more ad-</sup> ditional five-character codes. 

The typeset AMS subject classifications is placed at the bottom of the front page of the typeset article as a footnote. 

Examples: 

\subjclass[2010]{06B10} 

\subjclass[2010]{Primary: 06B10; Secondary: 06D05} 

The current subject classification scheme for mathematics was adopted in 2010, <sup>makin</sup>g <sup>the 1991 classification scheme obsolete. Thus</sup>, 2010 <sup>should be considered as a</sup> compulsory optional argument—maybe the only one in all of L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X. 

The current subject classification scheme, MSC 2010, is available from the AMS Web site 

http://www.ams.org/ 

<sup>Search for</sup> MSC<sup>. Or in the</sup> Author Resource Center <sup>click on</sup> MSC<sup>.</sup> 

## Rule Keywords

<sup>Command:</sup> \keywords 

Do not indicate line breaks. 

amsart supplies the phrase Key words and phrases. and a period at the end of the list of keywords. 

The typeset keywords are placed on the front page of the typeset article as a footnote. Example: 

\keywords{Complete lattice, distributive lattice, complete congruence, congruence lattice} 

Keywords are optional for many journals. 

Further footnotes An additional \thanks command creates an unmarked footnote. Examples: 

\thanks{This is a preliminary version of this article, prepared for the Second Annual Meeting of the Statistical Association of Winnebago.} 

\thanks{This article is in final form, and no version of it will be submitted elsewhere.} 

## 9.2.4 Multiple authors

If an article has several authors, repeat the author information commands for each one. Take care that the e-mail address follows the address. 

<sup>If two authors share the same address</sup>, <sup>omit the</sup> \address <sup>command for the second</sup> author, who can still have a diferent e-mail address and Web home page. An additional \thanks <sup>command for the first author should</sup> p<sup>recede an</sup>y \thanks <sup>commands for</sup> <sup>the second author. Since the footnotes are not marked</sup>, <sup>the ar</sup>g<sup>ument of the</sup> \thanks command for research support should contain a reference to the author: 

\thanks{The research of the first author was supported in part by NSF grant PAL-90-2466.} 

\thanks{The research of the second author was supported by the Hungarian National Foundation for Scientific Research, under Grant No.~9901.} 

Finally, if an article has more than two authors, supply the author information <sup>for each author as usual</sup>, <sup>but ex</sup>p<sup>licitl</sup>y <sup>s</sup>p<sup>ecif</sup>y <sup>the runnin</sup>g <sup>heads with the</sup> \markleft command: 

```latex
\markleft{FIRST AUTHOR ET AL.} 
```

<sup>where</sup> FIRST AUTHOR <sup>must be all ca</sup>p<sup>itals.</sup> 

If there are multiple authors, sometimes it may not be clear whose address, current address, e-mail address, or Web home page is being given. In such cases, give the name of the authors as optional arguments for these commands. For example, 

Email address, Ernest T. Moynahan: emoy@ccw.uwinnebago.edu. 

is typed as 

\email[Ernest~T. Moynahan]{emoy@ccw.uwinnebago.edu} 

See also Example 4 in Section 9.2.5. 

## 9.2.5 Examples

The following examples show typical top matter commands and can be found in the topmat.tpl <sup>file in the</sup> samples <sup>folder</sup> (<sup>see</sup> p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>e 5</sup>)<sup>.</sup> 

Example 1 One author. 

```latex
%Article information
\title[Complete-simple distributive lattices]
    {A construction of complete-simple\
    distributive lattices}
\date{\today}

%Author information
\author{George~A. Menuhin}
\address{Computer Science Department\
    University of Winnebago\
    Winnebago, MN 53714}
\email{gmen@ccw.uwinnebago.edu}
\urladdr{http://math.uwinnebago.edu/homepages/menuhin/}
\thanks{This research was supported by
    the NSF under grant number 23466.}

%AMS information
\keywords{Complete lattice, distributive lattice,
    complete congruence, congruence lattice}
\subjclass[2010]{Primary: 06B10; Secondary: 06D05} 
```

In the \title command, supplying the optional argument for the running head is the rule, not the exception. The only required item is \title. If it is missing, you get the strange message: 

! Undefined control sequence. 

<argument> \shorttitle 

## l.49 \maketitle

```latex
\thanks{The research of the second author
    was supported by the Hungarian
    National Foundation for Scientific Research,
    under Grant No. 9901.} 
```

```latex
\email[George~A. Menuhin]{gmen@ccw.uwinnebago.edu}

```

Moynahan]{emoy@ccw.uwinnebago.edu} \thanks{The research of the second author was supported by the Hungarian National Foundation for Scientific Research, under Grant No. 9901.} 

<sup>Note that the second author has no</sup> \address<sup>.</sup>
