# A CONSTRUCTION OF COMPLETE-SIMPLE DISTRIBUTIVE LATTICES

GEORGE A. MENUHIN 

ABSTRACT. In this note we prove that there exist complete-simple distributive lattices, that is, complete distributive lattices in which there are only two complete congruences. 

## 1. INTRODUCTION

In this note we prove the following result; 

Main Theorem. There exists an infinite complete distributive lattice K with only the two trivial complete congruence relations. 

## 2. THE $D ^ { \langle 2 \rangle }$ CONSTRUCTION

For the basic notation in lattice theory and universal algebra, see Ferenc R. Richardson [5] and George A. Menuhin [2]. We start with some definitions: 

Definition 1. Let V be a complete lattice, and let ${ \mathfrak { p } } = [ u , v ]$ be an interval of V. Then p is called complete-prime if the following three conditions are satisfied: 

(1) u is meet-irreducible but u is not completely meet-irreducible; 

(2) v is join-irreducible but v is not completely join-irreducible; 

(3) $[ u , v ]$ is a complete-simple lattice 

Now we prove the following result: 

Lemma 1. Let D be a complete distributive lattice satisfying conditions (1) and (2). Then $D ^ { \langle 2 \rangle }$ is a sublattice of $D ^ { 2 }$ ; hence $D ^ { \langle 2 \rangle }$ is a lattice, and $D ^ { \langle 2 \rangle }$ is a complete distributive lattice satisfying conditions (1) and (2) 

Proof. By conditions (1) and (2), $D ^ { \langle 2 \rangle }$ is a sublattice of $D ^ { 2 }$ . Hence, $D ^ { \langle 2 \rangle }$ is a lattice. Since $D ^ { \langle 2 \rangle }$ is a sublattice of a distributive lattice, $D ^ { \langle 2 \rangle }$ is a distributive lattice Using the characterization of standard ideals in Ernest T. Moynahan [3], $D ^ { \langle 2 \rangle }$ has a zero and a unit element, namely, (0, 0) and $\langle 1 , 1 \rangle$ . To show that $D ^ { \langle 2 \rangle }$ is complete. let $\varnothing \neq A \subseteq D ^ { \langle 2 \rangle }$ , and let $a = \vee A$ in $D ^ { 2 }$ . If $a \in D ^ { \langle 2 \rangle }$ , then $a = \vee A$ in $D ^ { \langle 2 \rangle }$ • otherwise, a is of the form $\langle b , 1 \rangle$ for some $b \in D$ with $b < 1$ . Now $\vee A = \left. 1 , 1 \right.$ in $D ^ { 2 }$ and the dual argument shows that $\Lambda A$ also exists in $D ^ { 2 }$ . Hence D is complete. Conditions (1) and (2) are obvious for $\dot { D } ^ { \langle 2 \rangle }$ □ 

Corollary 1. If D is complete-prime, then so is $D ^ { \langle 2 \rangle }$ 

## GEORGE A. MENUHIN

The motivation for the following result comes from Soo-Key Foo [1]. 

Lemma 2. Let Θ be a complete congruence relation of $D ^ { \langle 2 \rangle }$ such that 

$$
\langle 1, d \rangle \equiv \langle 1, 1 \rangle \pmod {\Theta},\tag{2.1}
$$

for some $d \in D$ with $d < 1$ . Then $\Theta = \iota$ 

Proof. Let Θ be a complete congruence relation of $D ^ { \langle 2 \rangle }$ satisfying (2.1). Then $\Theta = \iota$ □ 

## 3. THE II* CONSTRUCTION

The following construction is crucial to our proof of the Main Theorem: 

Definition 2. Let $D _ { i }$ , for $i \in I$ , be complete distributive lattices satisfying condition (2). Their I* product is defined as follows: 

$$
\Pi^ {*} (D _ {i} \mid i \in I) = \Pi (D _ {i} ^ {-} \mid i \in I) + 1;
$$

that is, $\Pi ^ { * } ( D _ { i } \mid i \in I )$ is $\Pi ( D _ { i } ^ { - } \mid i \in I )$ with a new unit element 

Notation. If $i \in I$ and $d \in D _ { i } ^ { - }$ , then 

$$
\langle \dots , 0, \dots , d, \dots , 0, \dots \rangle
$$

is the element of $\Pi ^ { * } ( D _ { i } \ | \ i \in I )$ whose i-th component is d and all the other components are 0 

See also Ernest T. Moynahan [4]. Next we verify: 

Theorem 1. Let $D _ { i } , f o r \ i \in I$ , be complete distributive lattices satisfying condition (2). Let Θ be a complete congruence relation on $\Pi ^ { * } ( D _ { i } \mid i \in I )$ . If there exist $i \in I$ and $d \in D _ { i }$ with $d < 1 _ { i }$ such that for all $d \leq c < 1 _ { i }$ 2 

$$
\langle \dots , 0, \dots , d, \dots , 0, \dots \rangle \equiv \langle \dots , 0, \dots , c, \dots , 0, \dots \rangle \pmod {\Theta},\tag{3.1}
$$

then $\Theta = \iota$ 

Proof. Since 

$$
\langle \dots , 0, \dots , \stackrel {i} {d}, \dots , 0, \dots \rangle \equiv \langle \dots , 0, \dots , \stackrel {i} {c}, \dots , 0, \dots \rangle \pmod {\Theta},\tag{3.2}
$$

and Θ is a complete congruence relation, it follows from condition (3) that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \langle \ldots , d, \ldots , 0, \ldots \rangle \\ \equiv \bigvee (\langle \ldots , 0, \ldots , c, \ldots , 0, \ldots \rangle \mid d \leq c <   1) \equiv 1 \pmod {\Theta}. \end{array}\tag{3.3}
$$

Let $j \in I$ for $j \neq i ,$ and let $a \in D _ { j } ^ { - }$ . Meeting both sides of the congruence (3.2) with $\langle \dots , 0 , \dots , { \overset { j } { a } } , \dots , 0 , \dots \rangle$ , we obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{l} 0 = \langle \ldots , 0, \ldots , d, \ldots , 0, \ldots \rangle \wedge \langle \ldots , 0, \ldots , a, \ldots , 0, \ldots \rangle \\ \equiv \langle \ldots , 0, \ldots , a, \ldots , 0, \ldots \rangle \pmod {\Theta}. \end{array}\tag{3.4}
$$

Using the completeness of Θ and (3.4), we get 

$$
0 \equiv \bigvee (\langle \dots , 0, \dots , a ^ {j}, \dots , 0, \dots \rangle \mid a \in D _ {j} ^ {-}) = 1 \pmod {\Theta},
$$

hence $\Theta = \iota$ 

Theorem 2. Let $D _ { i } ~ f o r ~ i \in I$ be complete distributive lattices satisfying conditions (2) and (3). Then $\Pi ^ { * } ( D _ { i } \mid i \in I )$ also satisfies conditions (2) and (3) 

Proof. Let Θ be a complete congruence on $\Pi ^ { * } ( D _ { i } \mid i \in I )$ ). Let $i \in I .$ . Define 

$$
\widehat {D} _ {i} = \{\langle \dots , 0, \dots , d, \dots , 0, \dots \rangle \mid d \in D _ {i} ^ {-} \} \cup \{1 \}.
$$

Then $\widehat { D } _ { i }$ is a complete sublattice of $\Pi ^ { * } ( D _ { i } \mid i \in I )$ ), and $\widehat { D } _ { i }$ is isomorphic to $D _ { i }$ Let $\Theta _ { i }$ be the restriction of Θ to $\widehat { D } _ { i }$ 

Since $D _ { i }$ is complete-simple, so is $\widehat { D } _ { i } ,$ , and hence $\Theta _ { i }$ is $\omega$ or t. If $\Theta _ { i } = \rho$ for all $i \in I .$ , then $\Theta = \omega$ . If there is an $i \in I$ , such that $\Theta _ { i } = \iota ,$ , then $0 \equiv 1$ (mod Θ), hence $\Theta = \iota ,$ □ 

The Main Theorem follows easily from Theorems 1 and 2

## Equations and equation numbers

A number of options deal with the placement of equations and equation numbers. 

Options: leqno default reqno 

By default, equation numbers are placed on the left, the default leqno option. The reqno <sup>o</sup>p<sup>tion</sup> p<sup>laces the e</sup>q<sup>uation numbers on the ri</sup>g<sup>ht.</sup> 

Option: fleqn 

This option positions equations a fixed distance from the left margin rather than cen-<sup>terin</sup>g <sup>them. The</sup> fleqn <sup>o</sup>p<sup>tion is t</sup>yp<sup>icall</sup>y <sup>used in con</sup>j<sup>unction with the</sup> reqno <sup>o</sup>p<sup>tion.</sup> <sup>Here is how an e</sup>q<sup>uation looks with the</sup> fleqn <sup>and</sup> reqno <sup>o</sup>p<sup>tions:</sup> 

$\int_0^\pi \sin x dx = 2$ 

(1) 

typed as 

```latex
\begin{equation}\label{E:firstInt}
\int_{0}~{\pi} \sin x \, dx = 2
\end{equation} 
```

```txt
Options: tbtags
centertags default 
```

The tbtags option uses top-or-bottom tags for a split environment, that is, it places the equation number level with the last line if numbers are on the right, or level with the first line if the numbers are on the left: 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & f = (x _ {1} x _ {2} x _ {3} x _ {4} x _ {5} x _ {6}) ^ {2} \\ & \quad = (x _ {1} x _ {2} x _ {3} x _ {4} x _ {5} + x _ {1} x _ {3} x _ {4} x _ {5} x _ {6} + x _ {1} x _ {2} x _ {4} x _ {5} x _ {6} + x _ {1} x _ {2} x _ {3} x _ {5} x _ {6}) ^ {2} \\ & \quad = (x _ {1} x _ {2} x _ {3} x _ {4} + x _ {1} x _ {2} x _ {3} x _ {5} + x _ {1} x _ {2} x _ {4} x _ {5} + x _ {1} x _ {3} x _ {4} x _ {5}) ^ {2} \end{array}\tag{1}
$$

## 9.6 The AMS packages

If you follow the recommendation of this book and begin each article with 

\documentclass{amsart} 

\usepackage{amssymb,latexsym} 

then you can safely ignore most of the information in this section. There are two minor <sup>exce</sup>p<sup>tions</sup>, <sup>the</sup> p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>es</sup> amsxtra <sup>and</sup> upref<sup>.</sup> 

However, if you use a document class that does not load the same packages that amsart loads, then you have to load the packages needed for your work. Typically, you have 

\usepackage{amsmath,amsfonts,amsthm} 

\usepackage{amssymb,latexsym} 

as a minimum. 

The AMS distribution contains many packages that can be loaded together or by themselves. 

## Math enhancements

amsmath The primary math enhancement package, which loads the four packages, amsgen, amsbsy, amsopn, <sup>and</sup> amstext<sup>.</sup> 

amsbsy <sup>Provides two commands for the use of bold math s</sup>y<sup>mbols</sup>, \boldsymbol <sup>and</sup> \pmb (see Section 6.4.3). 

amscd Commands <sup>f</sup>or creat<sup>i</sup>ng s<sup>i</sup>mp<sup>l</sup>e commutat<sup>i</sup>ve d<sup>i</sup>agrams (see Sect<sup>i</sup>on 7.8). 

amsgen <sup>An auxiliar</sup>y p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>e that is never invoked directl</sup>y<sup>. It is loaded b</sup>y <sup>all the AMS</sup> mat<sup>h</sup> pac<sup>k</sup>ages (except <sup>f</sup>or upref). 

amsopn <sup>Provides o</sup>p<sup>erator names and also the</sup> \DeclareMathOperator <sup>command for</sup> defining new ones (see Section 5.6). 

amstext <sup>Defines the</sup> \text <sup>command and redefines commands such as</sup> \textrm <sup>and</sup> \textbf <sup>to behave like the</sup> \text <sup>command</sup> (<sup>see Section 5.4.6</sup>)<sup>.</sup> 

amsxtra <sup>Provides the “s</sup>p<sup>” math accents</sup> (<sup>see Sections 5.7 and A.8</sup>) <sup>and loads the</sup> amsmath p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>e.</sup> 

upref <sup>Ensures that the</sup> \ref <sup>command alwa</sup>y<sup>s</sup> p<sup>roduces u</sup>p<sup>ri</sup>g<sup>ht numbers.</sup> 

## AMSFonts

amsfonts <sup>Contains the basic commands needed to utilize the AMSFonts. It also de-</sup> <sup>fines the</sup> \mathfrak <sup>command which makes the Euler Fraktur math al</sup>p<sup>habet</sup> available (see Section 6.4.2). If you use the PostScript AMSFonts font set, you should load this package with the option

In addition, if you want to use the 12pt document class option, then you must <sup>also load the</sup> exscale p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>e</sup> (<sup>see Section 10.3</sup>)<sup>:</sup>

amssymb <sup>Defines the s</sup>y<sup>mbol names for</sup> amsfonts<sup>. It loads</sup> amsfonts<sup>.</sup> 

eucal Replaces the calligraphic math alphabet with the Euler Script math alphabet (<sup>see Section 6.4.2</sup>)<sup>. If</sup> y<sup>ou load it with the o</sup>p<sup>tion</sup> mathscr, <sup>as in</sup>

<sup>then both the</sup> \mathscr <sup>and the</sup> \mathcal <sup>commands are available</sup>, <sup>so</sup> y<sup>ou can</sup> have both CE and CE, typed as

eufrak <sup>Defines the Euler Fraktur math al</sup>p<sup>habet</sup> (<sup>see Section 6.4.2</sup>)<sup>.</sup> 

## Loading packages

amsart <sup>contains code to</sup> p<sup>rovide more flexible formattin</sup>g <sup>of</sup> p<sup>roclamations and the</sup> proof <sup>environment</sup> (<sup>see Sections 4.4.2 and 4.5</sup>)<sup>. B</sup>y <sup>loadin</sup>g <sup>the</sup> amsthm p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>e</sup> y<sup>ou</sup> <sup>can add this functionalit</sup>y <sup>to a non-AMS document class. A typ<sup>i</sup>ca<sup>l</sup> art<sup>i</sup>c<sup>l</sup>e us<sup>i</sup>ng t<sup>h</sup>e <sup>l</sup>egacy article document c<sup>l</sup>ass (see Sect<sup>i</sup>on <sup>1</sup>0.<sup>1</sup>) and the AMS enhancements would normally have

# Legacy documents

<sup>Even thou</sup>g<sup>h the AMS s</sup>p<sup>ent a few decades refinin</sup>g <sup>the</sup> amsart <sup>document class</sup>, <sup>some</sup> of the legacy document classes of L<sup>A</sup>TEX are still around. If you want to whip up a quick <sup>re</sup>p<sup>ort</sup> <sup>or</sup> <sup>write</sup> <sup>u</sup>p <sup>a</sup> <sup>research</sup> <sup>note</sup>, <sup>the</sup> <sup>le</sup>g<sup>ac</sup>y article <sup>or</sup> report <sup>document</sup> <sup>classes</sup> may serve you well. 

In this chapter, we discuss some of the legacy L<sup>A</sup>TEX document classes. We take <sup>u</sup>p <sup>the</sup> book <sup>document class in Cha</sup>p<sup>ter 17. We do not discuss the</sup> slides <sup>document</sup> <sup>class for</sup> p<sup>re</sup>p<sup>arin</sup>g <sup>slides. It is now considered obsolete. Use instead the</sup> beamer <sup>class</sup> which we discuss in Chapter 12. 

We conclude this chapter with a description of the components of the standard LAT<sub>E</sub>X distribution.

## 10.1.1 Top matter

For a detailed discussion of the top matter, refer to Chapter 8, in particular Sections 8.1 and 8.3—see also Figure 8.1. Here is the top matter of the legacy article: 

```latex
\title{A construction of complete-simple\\
    distributive lattices}
\author{George~A. Menuhin\thanks{Research supported
    by the NSF under grant number 23466.}\\
    Computer Science Department\\
    Winnebago, MN 23714\\\

\date{March 15, 2010}
\maketitle
There are four commands for the top matter: \title, \author, \thanks, and

```

## Rule Top matter for the article document class

1. If necessary, break the title into separate lines with \\. Do not put a \\ at the end of the last line. 

<sup>2.</sup> \thanks p<sup>laces a footnote at the bottom of the first</sup> p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>e. If it is not needed</sup>, <sup>omit it.</sup> 

3. Separate the lines of the address with \\. Do not put a \\ at the end of the last line. 

4. Multiple authors are separated by \and. 

5. There is only one \author command, and it contains all the information—name, address, support—about all the authors. There is no \\ command before the \and command. 

6. I<sup>f</sup> t<sup>h</sup>ere <sup>i</sup>s no \date command, L<sup>A</sup>TEX w<sup>ill i</sup>nsert t<sup>h</sup>e date on w<sup>hi</sup>c<sup>h</sup> you typeset the file (\date{\today} will produce the same result). If you do not want any date to appear, type \date{}. For a specific date, such as February 21, 2007, type \date{February 21, 2007}<sup>.</sup> 

<sup>7. The</sup> \title <sup>command is the onl</sup>y <sup>re</sup>q<sup>uired command. The others are o</sup>p<sup>tional.</sup> 

# A construction of complete-simple distributive lattices

George A. Menuhin∗ Computer Science Department Winnebago, MN 23714 menuhin@cc.uwinnebago.edu 

March 15, 2006 

## Abstract

In this note, we prove that there exist complete-simple distributive lattices, that is, complete distributive lattices in which there are only two complete congruences. 

## 1 Introduction

In this note, we prove the following result: 

Theorem 1 There exists an infinite complete distributive lattice K with only the two trivial complete congruence relations. 

## 2 The $\Pi ^ { * }$ construction

The following construction is crucial in the proof of our Theorem: 

Definition 1 Let $D _ { i } , f o r i \in I$ , be complete distributive lattices satisfying condition (J). Their Π∗ product is defined as follows: 

$$
\Pi^ {*} (D _ {i} \mid i \in I) = \Pi (D _ {i} ^ {-} \mid i \in I) + 1;
$$

that is, $\Pi ^ { * } ( D _ { i } \mid i \in I )$ is $\Pi ( D _ { i } ^ { - } \mid i \in I )$ with a new unit element. 

Notation 1 $I f i \in I$ and $d \in D _ { i } ^ { - }$ , then 

$$
\langle \dots , 0, \dots , d, \dots , 0, \dots \rangle
$$

is the element of $\Pi ^ { * } ( D _ { i } \mid i \in I )$ whose $_ { i - t h }$ component is d and all the other components are 0. 

As you see, t<sup>h</sup>e ru<sup>l</sup>es <sup>f</sup>or t<sup>h</sup>e \date command <sup>h</sup>ere d<sup>if</sup>er s<sup>li</sup>g<sup>h</sup>t<sup>l</sup>y <sup>f</sup>rom t<sup>h</sup>e ru<sup>l</sup>es <sup>for the</sup> \date <sup>command in the</sup> amsart <sup>document class. However</sup>, <sup>the rules for the</sup> command \author here are very diferent from the rules for the \author command in <sup>the</sup> amsart <sup>document class.</sup> 

For two authors use the following template: 

```latex
\author{name1\thanks{support1}\
    address1line1\
    address1line2\
    address1line3
    \and
    name2\thanks{support2}\
    address2line1\
    address2line2\
    address2line3} 
```

<sup>Note the use of the</sup> \and <sup>command</sup>, <sup>which se</sup>p<sup>arates the two authors.</sup> 

<sup>One more diference to kee</sup>p <sup>in mind. Place the abstract</sup> after <sup>the</sup> \maketitle command.

# The PDF file format

## 11.1 PostScript and PDF

## 11.1.1 PostScript

PostScript is the preeminent platform and device independent page-description and programming language, introduced by Adobe Systems Inc. in 1982. It describes the placement and shapes of all the elements in the document, including the fonts. Documents placed on the Web in PostScript format can be downloaded to any computer and print identically on all PostScript printers. Until the appearance of PDF, PostScript was the format of choice for sharing L<sup>A</sup>TEX articles with diagrams or complex forms. 

There are a number of disadvantages to using PostScript files on the Web: 

The files tend to be very large. 

They cannot be viewed until the whole file has been downloaded 

If a PostScript file does not include a particular font used in the document and you do not have that font installed on your computer, then another font—usually Courier— is substituted causing graphically unacceptable rendering. 

## 11.1.2 PDF

All of these concerns have been addressed by Adobe’s Portable Document Format (PDF). See Adobe Systems’ PDF Reference, Version 1.7, 1st edition [2] for a complete description of this file format. PDF is based on the PostScript language, with some important diferences: 

PDF is much more concise than PostScript. A PDF file is normally about 10 percent of the size of the corresponding PostScript file. 

Missing fonts are usually substituted by fonts with the same metrics, so that the size of the substituted text is the same as that of the original. In particular, there are no incorrect line breaks caused by the substitution. 

PDF files allow partial inclusion offonts. As a result, it is much easier to obtain permission to include proprietary fonts in PDF documents. 

PDF files can be downloaded and viewed in a Web browser one page at a time, without having to wait for the whole file to download first. 

Most L<sup>A</sup>TEX implementations produce PDF files. 

PDF files and Adobe Acrobat Professional ofer many nice features, including: 

Eficient navigational tools 

Searching and indexing capability for documents and even for collections of documents 

Bookmarks 

Thumbnails of pages 

Limited editing 

Annotations (notes, text, and voice) and markups 

Hyperlinks to the same document or to another document or Web site (see Section 11.1.3) 

The inclusion of programs, particularly JavaScript 

The creation of interactive features 

The inclusion of multimedia objects such as video and sound files 

PDF files can also be used to make legacy documents available on the Internet. For instance, if you go to my home page, 

http://www.maths.umanitoba.ca/homepages/gratzer/ <sup>and click on</sup> Mathematical articles, <sup>then</sup> 1980-89, <sup>in the bottom frame</sup> y<sup>ou will</sup> find entry 102, which links to a PDF file. I created that PDF file by scanning the pages of the original article, converting them to PDF files, and finally stringing them together into a single document. The scanned pages totalled 32 MB, the PDF file is 320 KB. The printed version of the PDF file is somewhat lower in quality than the original, but it is still quite satisfactory. See my article [33] on some practical pointers about scanning and PDF files. 

## 11.1.3 Hyperlinks

With Adobe Acrobat Professional you can place hyperlinks in PDF documents. Clicking on a hyperlink, you jump to another location in the same document, to an electronic document, or to a Web site. For instance, in the table of contents, you can put a hyperlink to Chapter 3, so that clicking on it takes you to Chapter 3. Adobe Acrobat’s help system has ample information on how to set up links. 

## 11.2 Hyperlinks for LAT<sub>E</sub>X

It is tedious to set hyperlinks one at a time in your PDF file. Would it not be nice if hyperlinks corresponding to cross-references were set automatically? For instance, clicking on Lemma 6 in 

This follows from Lemma 6 and the relevant definitions. 

would cause the display to jump to the page containing Lemma 6. 

<sup>Sebastian Rahtz’s</sup> hyperref p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>e</sup> (<sup>maintained now b</sup>y <sup>Heiko Oberdiek</sup>) <sup>doe</sup> just that.

## 11.2.3 Bookmarks

An important navigational feature of Acrobat is the ability to set and use bookmarks. <sup>If</sup> y<sup>ou</sup> <sup>choose</sup> View>Navigation Tabs>Bookmarks <sup>in</sup> <sup>Adobe</sup> <sup>Reader</sup>, <sup>the</sup> <sup>navi</sup>g<sup>ation</sup> pane opens up showing the bookmarks. 

<sup>The</sup> hyperref p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>e o</sup>p<sup>tion</sup> bookmarks=true <sup>makes bookmarks from the sec-</sup> tioning commands of the L<sup>A</sup>TEX document, thereby producing a table of contents even if the document had none. You can invoke all these options together:

\BOOKMARK [1][-]{section*.2}{References}{} 

Once you have produced the final version of your document, you should edit this file to make sure that it contains no LAT X code. Math formulas in titles create havoc. So do <sup>accented characters.</sup> hyperref <sup>does its best to convert internal encodin</sup>g<sup>s for accented</sup> characters to the encoding used by Acrobat Reader, but it is still best to avoid them. Once this file has been edited, add the line

## Preventing links

<sup>If</sup> y<sup>ou</sup> <sup>do</sup> <sup>not</sup> <sup>want</sup> <sup>a</sup> \ref <sup>or</sup> \pageref <sup>command</sup> <sup>to</sup> <sup>a</sup>pp<sup>ear</sup> <sup>as</sup> <sup>a</sup> <sup>link</sup>, y<sup>ou</sup> <sup>can</sup> <sup>use</sup> <sup>their</sup> *<sup>-ed</sup> <sup>forms</sup>, \ref* <sup>and</sup> \pageref*<sup>.</sup> 

## Long links

An often heard complaint is that in the link Theorem 6, only the 6 can be clicked to <sup>activate the link</sup>, <sup>and it is too short.</sup> hyperref p<sup>rovides the</sup> \autoref <sup>command to</sup> help out. Instead of 

Theorem~\ref{T:new} 

you can simply type 

\autoref{T:new} 

and hyperref will provide the word Theorem so that the link becomes Theorem 6. <sup>The names su</sup>pp<sup>orted b</sup>y <sup>the</sup> \autoref <sup>command are listed in Table 11.1.</sup> 

For my own use, I redefine: 

\renewcommand{\chaptername}{Chapter} 

\renewcommand{\sectionname}{Section} 

\renewcommand{\subsectionname}{Section} 

\renewcommand{\subsubsectionname}{Section} 

## External links

External links can be links to websites or other files that are located on the Internet. Use the

# Presentations

In Section 1.11, we describe how a presentation is a PDF file that you open with Adobe <sup>Reader. You can</sup> p<sup>ut it in full screen mode1</sup> (View>Full screen), <sup>and then</sup> p<sup>ro</sup>j<sup>ect</sup> the presentation one page at a time by pressing the space bar or the arrow keys. 

Remember overhead transparencies? If we want to see half of what is on the transparency, we cover up the bottom part so that only the top part is projected. This way we have control over what the audience sees and when. We sometimes used overlays: placing another transparency on top of the projected one to modify it by adding text or graphics. 

In t<sup>hi</sup>s c<sup>h</sup>apter, we d<sup>i</sup>scuss T<sup>ill</sup> Tantau<sup>’</sup>s beamer pac<sup>k</sup>age <sup>i</sup>n more deta<sup>il</sup> to <sup>h</sup>e<sup>l</sup>p you p<sup>re</sup>p<sup>are</sup> p<sup>resentations with overla</sup>y<sup>s and with stunnin</sup>g <sup>visual efects.</sup> beamer <sup>relies on</sup> <sup>other</sup> p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>es such as the</sup> hyperref p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>e</sup> (<sup>see Section 11.2</sup>) <sup>to establish links</sup>, <sup>Till</sup> Tantau’s Portable Graphics Format package for creating graphics, Uwe Kern’s xcolor package for coloring, the AMS packages for formatting math formulas and defining declarations, and some others. 

The documentation for these packages runs to about a thousand pages. The good <sup>news is that</sup> y<sup>ou can use</sup> beamer <sup>“out of the box”. You onl</sup>y <sup>have to learn about</sup> 20 commands—this is more than the four new command we had to learn in Section 1.11 but still an easily manageable task. 

<sup>So</sup> <sup>we</sup> <sup>set</sup> <sup>ourselves</sup> <sup>in</sup> <sup>this</sup> <sup>cha</sup>p<sup>ter</sup> <sup>a</sup> <sup>modest</sup> g<sup>oal</sup>, <sup>usin</sup>g beamer <sup>“out</sup> <sup>of</sup> <sup>the</sup> <sup>box”.</sup> It is amazing how much you can achieve with a small investment of your time. 

<sup>Chances are</sup> beamer <sup>is alread</sup>y <sup>installed for</sup> y<sup>ou. If not</sup>, <sup>consult Section D.1 on</sup> how to get it.

## 12.2.1 Overlays

<sup>The outline frame of the</sup> quickbeamer2 p<sup>resentation created five</sup> p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>es in the</sup> PDF <sup>file.</sup> Observe how each page, from the second on, completely overlaps the previous one, making it appear that the previous one stayed put and an additional line is displayed “on top of it”. In beamer terminology these pages are overlays or slides. The five overlays will be referenced as overlay 1, . . . , overlay 5. A single frame may create one or many overlays. The subsequent sections discuss many more variants. 

beamer <sup>has man</sup>y <sup>commands creatin</sup>g <sup>overla</sup>y<sup>s. We start with some exam</sup>p<sup>les of</sup> \pause, <sup>then</sup> \only, <sup>and</sup> \onslide<sup>.</sup> 

<sup>We</sup> <sup>introduce</sup> <sup>overla</sup>y<sup>s</sup> <sup>with</sup> <sup>some</sup> p<sup>resentations.</sup> <sup>The</sup> <sup>first</sup>, babybeamer1, <sup>intro-</sup> <sup>duces</sup> <sup>the</sup> \pause <sup>command</sup> <sup>to</sup> <sup>create</sup> <sup>overla</sup>y<sup>s.</sup> 

%babybeamer1 presentation 

\documentclass{beamer} 

\begin{document} 

\begin{frame} 

\frametitle{Some background} 

We start our discussion with some concepts. 

\pause 

The first concept we introduce originates with Erd\H os. 

\end{document} 

produces the presentation of Figure 12.5. 

## Rule The \pause command

1. A <sup>f</sup>rame may <sup>h</sup>ave many \pause commands. 

2. <sup>The</sup> \pause <sup>command cannot be</sup> g<sup>iven in an AMS multiline math environment.</sup> 

You move past a \pause command the same way as you get to the next frame, by pressing the space bar or the forward arrow key. 

Using the \pause commands you can create many overlays, each containing a little more material on the overlays. If this is all you need, skip to Section 12.2.7, you do not need the more detailed discussion of overlays in the next few pages. 

<sup>We could have coded the same</sup> p<sup>resentation with the</sup> \only <sup>command:</sup> 

%babybeamer2 presentation 

\documentclass{beamer} 

```latex
\begin{document}
\begin{frame}
\frametitle{Some background}
\only<1,2>{We start our discussion with some concepts.}
\only<2>{The first concept we introduce originates with Erd\H os.}
\end{frame}
\end{document} 
```

<sup>Fi</sup>g<sup>ure 12.5:</sup> babybeamer1 p<sup>resentation.</sup>


<sup>This</sup> p<sup>resentation is sli</sup>g<sup>htl</sup>y <sup>diferent from</sup> babybeamer1<sup>. Overla</sup>y <sup>1 i</sup>g<sup>nores the</sup> second \only command and displays the line as appropriate to display one line. Overlay 2 displays the two lines as appropriate to display two lines. As a result, the first line moves slightly up when passing from overlay 1 to overlay 2. The argument of the \only command is typeset only on the overlays specified. On the other overlays, it is ignored. 

```txt
This is a very important concept. To start the definition ... 
```

<sup>If</sup> <sup>instead</sup> <sup>of</sup> <sup>the</sup> \only <sup>command</sup> y<sup>ou</sup> <sup>use</sup> <sup>the</sup> \onslide <sup>command</sup> (<sup>on</sup> <sup>slide</sup>, g<sup>et</sup> it?), as in 

```txt
\onslide<1,2>{We start our discussion with some concepts.}
```


then the first line of overlay 2 completely overlaps the first line of overlay 1, so the <sup>first line seems to sta</sup>y p<sup>ut. The ar</sup>g<sup>ument of the</sup> \onslide <sup>command is t</sup>yp<sup>eset on</sup> the overlays specified and on the other overlays it is typeset but invisible. This is the behavior you would want most often, but you may find that sometimes you prefer \only. 

## 12.2.2 Understanding overlays

We introduced overlays in Section 12.2.1—probably the most important new concept for presentations. L<sup>A</sup>TEX typesets the content of a frame and the typeset material 

appears on all overlays for the parts of the source (maybe all) not modified by any command with an overlay specification; 

appears only on the overlays specified and is ignored on the other overlays for the <sup>ar</sup>g<sup>uments</sup> <sup>of</sup> <sup>the</sup> \only <sup>commands</sup>; 

appears on the overlays specified and is typeset but made invisible on the other over-<sup>la</sup>y<sup>s for the ar</sup>g<sup>uments of the</sup> \onslide <sup>commands.</sup> 

More on overlay specifications at the end of this section. Here are some illustrations. 

## Example 1

```latex
This is a very \only<1>{very, very} important concept.  
\only<1,2>{To start the definition \dots} 
```

will typeset overlay 1 as 

This is a very very, very important concept. To start the definition . . . 

and will typeset overlay 2 as 

## Example 2

What is $2+2$? It is \onslide<2>{$4$}. 

\onslide<2>{I hope you all got it right.} 

will typeset overlay 1 as 

What is 2 + 2? It is . Can you figure it out? 

and will typeset overlay 2 as 

What is $2 + 2?$ It is 4. I hope you all got it right. 

Note that there is room in overlay 1 for the number 4. 

## Example 3

```txt
Example 3
What is $2+2$?
\onslide<2>{It is { $4$ }.}
Can you figure it out?
will typeset overlay 1 as
What is 2 + 2?
Can you figure it out?
and will typeset overlay 2 as
What is 2 + 2?
It is 4.
Can you figure it out?
Note that there is room in overlay 1 for the “missing” second line. 
```

## Overlay specifications

The angle brackets contain the overlay specification. Here are some more examples: 

<1-2,4-> <sup>means all overla</sup>y<sup>s from 1 to 2</sup>, <sup>and all overla</sup>y<sup>s from 4 onwards.</sup> 

<-3> means all overlays up to 3. 

<2,4,6> means overlays 2, 4, and 6. 

<sup>We have two overla</sup>y <sup>s</sup>p<sup>ecifications in the</sup> p<sup>resentation</sup> babybeamer2<sup>:</sup> <1,2> <sup>and</sup> <2><sup>.</sup> <sup>Ma</sup>y<sup>be</sup>, <1-> <sup>and</sup> <2-> <sup>would</sup> <sup>be</sup> <sup>better</sup>, <sup>so</sup> <sup>that</sup> <sup>if</sup> y<sup>ou</sup> <sup>add</sup> <sup>a</sup> <sup>third</sup> <sup>overla</sup>y y<sup>ou</sup> <sup>do</sup> not have to change these. 

T<sup>h</sup>e command \pause can on<sup>l</sup>y ta<sup>k</sup>e t<sup>h</sup>e s<sup>i</sup>mp<sup>l</sup>est over<sup>l</sup>ay spec<sup>ifi</sup>cat<sup>i</sup>on, a number. \pause<3> <sup>takes</sup> <sup>efect</sup> <sup>from</sup> <sup>overla</sup>y 3 <sup>on.</sup> 

Note that overlay specifications are attached to commands but the overlays created are overlays of the frame in which the commands appear. 

## 12.2.3 More on the \only and \onslide commands

<sup>The</sup> \only <sup>and</sup> \onslide <sup>commands</sup> <sup>can</sup> <sup>accom</sup>p<sup>lish</sup> <sup>ever</sup>y<sup>thin</sup>g <sup>the</sup> \pause <sup>command</sup> can and a lot more. 

## The basic syntax

<sup>The</sup> <sup>s</sup>y<sup>ntax</sup> <sup>of</sup> \only <sup>is</sup> 

\only<overlay spec >{source } 

<sup>where</sup> overlay spec <sup>is the overla</sup>y <sup>s</sup>p<sup>ecification and</sup> source <sup>is the code t</sup>yp<sup>eset</sup> by L<sup>A</sup>TEX. 

<sup>A</sup> (p<sup>artial</sup>) <sup>s</sup>y<sup>ntax</sup> <sup>of</sup> \onslide <sup>is</sup> 

\onslide<overlay spec >{source } 

With the same syntax you can give overlay specifications to many commands, in-<sup>cludin</sup>g \textbf, \textit, \alert<sup>—</sup>beamer<sup>’s alternative to the</sup> \emph <sup>command—</sup> and then the command is in efect only on the overlays specified. 

%babybeamer3 presentation 

\documentclass{beamer} 

\begin{document} 

\begin{frame} 

\frametitle{Some background} 

\textbf<1>{We start our discussion with some concepts.} 

\textbf<2>{The first concept we introduce originates with Erd\H os.} 

\end{frame} 

\end{document} 

<sup>So the</sup> babybeamer3 p<sup>resentation</sup> (<sup>see Fi</sup>g<sup>ure 12.6</sup>) <sup>has two overla</sup>y<sup>s</sup>, <sup>each with</sup> two lines of text. On overlay 1 the first line is bold, on overlay 2 the second line is bold. 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/45f3cc63-7a26-418c-9a01-03dd91fad053/4f767815d2ac7aa3b8c626206e1fcd18c9515af9f614e3f254101838bbaf59bf.jpg)



<sup>Fi</sup>g<sup>ure</sup> <sup>12.6:</sup> babybeamer3 p<sup>resentation.</sup>


## A diferent syntax

<sup>The command</sup> \only <sup>has an alternate s</sup>y<sup>ntax:</sup> 

\only{source }<overlay spec > 

So 

\only<1>{Can you figure it out?} 

and 

\only{Can you figure it out?}<1> 

accomplish the same. 

With this syntax, you can define your own commands that allow overlay specifica-<sup>tions. For instance</sup>, <sup>usin</sup>g <sup>the command</sup> \color{blue} <sup>defined in Section 12.2.9</sup>, y<sup>ou</sup> can define the command 

\newcommand{\myblue}{\only{\color{blue}}} 

Then 

\myblue<2>{Some more text} 

will color the text blue on overlay 2 only. 

## 12.2.4 Lists as overlays

<sup>Lists ma</sup>y <sup>be</sup> p<sup>resented one item at a time</sup>, <sup>for exam</sup>p<sup>le the</sup> babybeamer4 p<sup>resentation in</sup> <sup>Fi</sup>g<sup>ure</sup> <sup>12.7</sup> (<sup>in</sup> <sup>the</sup> samples <sup>folder</sup>) <sup>shows</sup> <sup>the</sup> <sup>four</sup> <sup>overla</sup>y<sup>s</sup> <sup>of</sup> <sup>a</sup> <sup>list.</sup> <sup>R.</sup> <sup>Padmanabhan</sup> appears on the first, R. Padmanabhan and Brian Davey appear on the second, and so on. This is accomplished simply by adding the overlay specification <1-> to the item for R. Padmanabhan, the overlay specification <2-> to the item for Brian Davey, and so on. 

%babybeamer4 presentation 

\documentclass{beamer} 

\begin{document} 

\begin{frame} 

\frametitle{Overlaying lists} 

We introduce our guests: 

\begin{itemize} 

\end{itemize} 

<sup>Such an overla</sup>y <sup>structure is used so often that</sup> beamer <sup>has a shorthand for it</sup>, [<+->]<sup>. Here it is in</sup> babybeamer5<sup>.</sup> 

%babybeamer5 presentation 

\documentclass{beamer} 

\begin{document} 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/45f3cc63-7a26-418c-9a01-03dd91fad053/51f725ea3fa2900bec68b41870e7b51752d23cec4e8c50dd3384ef4f8dd33cf8.jpg)



<sup>Fi</sup>g<sup>ure 12.7:</sup> babybeamer4 p<sup>resentation.</sup>


```latex
\begin{frame}
\frametitle{Overlaying lists}

We introduce our guests:
\begin{itemize}[<+->]
\item R. Padmanabhan
\item Brian Davey
\item Harry Lakser
\item Dick Koch
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}
\end{document} 
```

This shorthand allows adding and reordering items without having to change overlay specifications. Of course, if you do not want the items to appear in sequence, you have to use overlay specifications. 

## 12.2.5 Out of sequence overlays

We now present an example of “out of sequence overlays”. Look at Figure 12.8. I want to make this part of my presentation. First, I want to show the theorem, then illustrate it with the diagram at the bottom. Finally, I present the proof in the middle. So I need three overlays. 

Theorem 

Every finite distributive lattice can be embedded in a boolean lattice. 

Proof. 

Use join-irreducible elements. 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/45f3cc63-7a26-418c-9a01-03dd91fad053/68e66a06d387dd026ae3902481c0cd7bc9f7a0da82dbae724cc3c1c32c358519.jpg)



Figure 12.8: The slide to represent.


The theorem is on all three overlays, 1, 2, 3. Its illustration is on overlays 2 and 3, leaving room for the proof that appears only on overlay 3, This is an example of “out of <sup>se</sup>q<sup>uence overla</sup>y<sup>s”. We code this in</sup> babybeamer6 (<sup>in the</sup> samples <sup>folder</sup>)<sup>.</sup> 

<sup>Since declarations</sup>, p<sup>roofs</sup>, <sup>and the</sup> \includegraphics <sup>command ma</sup>y <sup>all have</sup> overlay specifications, this seems easy to accomplish. 

```latex
%babybeamer6 presentation, first try
\documentclass{beamer}
\begin{document}

\begin{frame}
\frametitle{Overlaying declarations and graphics}
\begin{theorem}<1->
Every finite distributive lattice can be embedded in a boolean lattice.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}<3->
Use join-irreducible elements.
\end{proof}
\includegraphics<2,->{cube}
\end{frame}
\end{document} 
```

This does not work too well. On overlay 1 the theorem appears in the middle and then it jumps up to make room for the illustration. This is the same problem we <sup>encountered in the</sup> babybeamer2 p<sup>resentation in Section 12.2.1 and the solution is also</sup> <sup>the same</sup>, <sup>the use of the</sup> \onslide <sup>command. Re</sup>p<sup>lace the line</sup> 

\includegraphics<2,->{cube} 

with 

```txt
\onslide<2->{{\includegraphics{cube}} 
```

## 12.2.6 Blocks and overlays

<sup>You can think of a theorem in</sup> beamer <sup>as the contents of the</sup> theorem <sup>environment</sup> with a heading and, optionally, with an overlay specification, and with most themes— see Section 12.5—colorful visual highlighting, see Figures 12.3 and 12.4. 

beamer p<sup>rovides the</sup> block <sup>environment that works the same wa</sup>y <sup>exce</sup>p<sup>t that</sup> y<sup>ou</sup> <sup>name the block. The</sup> (p<sup>artial</sup>) <sup>s</sup>y<sup>ntax of the</sup> block <sup>environment is</sup> 

```latex
\begin{block}<overlay spec>{title}
source
\end{block} 
```

Blocks are shaped as theorems. If there is no title, you still need the braces. The overlay specification is optional. 

<sup>As an exam</sup>p<sup>le</sup>, <sup>save</sup> babybeamer6.tex <sup>as</sup> babybeamer6block.tex <sup>in the</sup> work <sup>folder</sup> (<sup>also in the</sup> samples <sup>folder alon</sup>g <sup>with the</sup> PDF <sup>file</sup>) <sup>and re</sup>p<sup>lace the</sup> theorem environment with 

\begin{block}<1->{Theorem} 

Every finite distributive lattice can be embedded 

in a boolean lattice. 

\end{block} 

If you want a block of L<sup>A</sup>TEX code with an overlay specification but with no title <sup>and no visual hi</sup>g<sup>hli</sup>g<sup>htin</sup>g, <sup>use one of the commands</sup>, \onslide <sup>and</sup> \only<sup>.</sup> 

## 12.2.7 Links

A presentation is a PDF file, so it is not surprising that you can set links of various types <sup>in</sup> <sup>a</sup> beamer p<sup>resentation.</sup> <sup>Just</sup> <sup>as</sup> <sup>the</sup> hyperref p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>e</sup> <sup>hel</sup>p<sup>s</sup> <sup>us</sup> <sup>with</sup> <sup>h</sup>yp<sup>erlinks</sup> <sup>in</sup> <sup>a</sup> PDF <sup>fil</sup>e (see Sect<sup>i</sup>on <sup>11</sup>.<sup>2</sup>), t<sup>h</sup>e beamer pac<sup>k</sup>age a<sup>ll</sup>ows us to conven<sup>i</sup>ent<sup>l</sup>y set <sup>li</sup>n<sup>k</sup>s <sup>i</sup>n a presentation. 

Some links are automatically provided. If you look closer at Figures 12.1 and 12.2, you see that the section titles are shown in the sidebar. In fact, the sidebar is a navigation bar. First, it shows which section you are in. Second, clicking on a section title takes you to that section. 

Creating a link is a two-step process. 

1. Name the place you want to link to. 

2. Create a button with the property that clicking on it jumps you to the designated place. 

<sup>To illustrate this</sup> p<sup>rocess</sup>, <sup>we modif</sup>y <sup>the</sup> p<sup>resentation</sup> babybeamer4<sup>. O</sup>p<sup>en the</sup> <sup>file</sup> babybeamer4.tex <sup>and save it as</sup> babybeamer7.tex <sup>in the</sup> work <sup>folder</sup> (<sup>the edited</sup> <sup>version is in the</sup> samples <sup>folder alon</sup>g <sup>with the</sup> PDF <sup>file</sup>)<sup>.</sup> 

<sup>1. Name the frame</sup> y<sup>ou want to link to b</sup>y <sup>addin</sup>g <sup>a label to the</sup> \begin{frame} <sup>line.</sup> <sup>In</sup> babybeamer7, <sup>add a label to the frame</sup> fourguests<sup>:</sup> 

\begin{frame}[label=fourguests] 

Labels of frames are also useful for selective typesetting of your presentation, see Section 12.6. 

<sup>2. Add the followin</sup>g <sup>line to</sup> babybeamer7<sup>:</sup> 

\hyperlink{fourguests<3>}% {\beamergotobutton{Jump to third guest}} <sup>This creates a link to the third overla</sup>y <sup>of the frame named</sup> fourguests, <sup>and creates</sup> <sup>a button</sup>, <sup>with the text</sup> Jump to third guest<sup>. Clickin</sup>g <sup>on this button will</sup> j<sup>um</sup>p <sup>to the third overla</sup>y <sup>of the frame</sup> fourguests<sup>.</sup> 

## 3. To add variety to linking, include a new first frame:

<sup>which</sup> <sup>has</sup> <sup>a</sup> <sup>button</sup> <sup>for</sup> j<sup>um</sup>p<sup>in</sup>g <sup>to</sup> <sup>the</sup> <sup>third</sup> <sup>overla</sup>y <sup>of</sup> <sup>the</sup> fourguests <sup>frame.</sup> 

## 4. We also add a new third frame.

<sup>with a button</sup>, <sup>with the text</sup> Jump to guest list<sup>. Clickin</sup>g <sup>on this button will</sup> jump to the second frame, overlay not specified (defaults to 1). 

## 5. Add a fourth frame,

\begin{frame} \frametitle{Hidden link} \hyperlink{fourguests}{Jumping to the guest list} \end{frame} 

stance, you may want to link the use of a concept to its earlier definition, where you also need a button for the return jump. 

<sup>Here is</sup> babybeamer7<sup>:</sup> 

%babybeamer7 presentation \documentclass{beamer} \begin{document} \begin{frame} \frametitle{First frame with a button} Button example Jumping to an overlay of a different frame \bigskip \hyperlink{fourguests<3>}% {\beamergotobutton{Jump to third guest}} \end{frame} \begin{frame}[label=fourguests] \frametitle{Overlaying lists} We introduce our guests: \begin{itemize} \item<1-> R. Padmanabhan \item<2-> Brian Davey \item<3-> Harry Lakser \item<4-> Dick Koch \end{itemize} \hyperlink{fourguests<3>}% {\beamergotobutton{Jump to third guest}} \end{frame} \begin{frame} \frametitle{Third frame with a button} Button example Jumping to another frame \bigskip 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/45f3cc63-7a26-418c-9a01-03dd91fad053/75b71233de4afb2c897efb42656fef170e61a8051d1f1bd028f49280869c366b.jpg)



<sup>Fi</sup>g<sup>ure 12.9:</sup> babybeamer7 p<sup>resentation.</sup>


```latex
\hyperlink{fourguests}%
{\beamergotobutton{Jump to guest list}}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}
\frametitle{Hidden link}

\hyperlink{fourguests}{Jumping to the guest list}
\end{frame}
\end{document} 
```

Figure 12.9 shows all these buttons. We do not show overlays 3 and 4 of frame 2 and frame 4, where the button is invisible. 

## 12.2.8 Columns

Often, it is useful to put the display into columns. A simple illustration is given in babybeamer8<sup>:</sup> 

```latex
%babybeamer8 presentation
\documentclass{beamer}
\begin{document}

\begin{frame}
\frametitle{Columns, top alignment}

\begin{columns}[t]
\begin{column}{2in}
Is it true that there is no new result
on the Congruence Lattice Characterization Problem?
\end{column}
\begin{column}{2in}
F. Wehrung found a distributive algebraic lattice that
cannot be represented as the congruence lattice
of a lattice.
\end{column}
\end{columns}
\end{frame}
\end{document} 
```

<sup>The environment is</sup> columns<sup>. It has an o</sup>p<sup>tional ar</sup>g<sup>ument for ali</sup>g<sup>nment</sup>, t <sup>for to</sup>p, c <sup>for center</sup>, <sup>and</sup> b <sup>for bottom. The columns</sup>, <sup>usuall</sup>y <sup>two</sup>, <sup>are both in the</sup> column <sup>envi-</sup> ronment; the width of the column is in the argument; it can be given as a measurement— 2in <sup>in the exam</sup>p<sup>le—or relative to the width of the whole frame as</sup> 0.4\textwidth<sup>.</sup> 


<sup>Fi</sup>g<sup>ure</sup> <sup>12.10</sup> <sup>shows</sup> <sup>the</sup> babybeamer8 p<sup>resentation.</sup>


![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/45f3cc63-7a26-418c-9a01-03dd91fad053/cbb6d46e283201b4a09ccdb4471daceeea2ab584d1d44811763da5a28afa6649.jpg)



<sup>Fi</sup>g<sup>ure</sup> <sup>12.10:</sup> babybeamer8 p<sup>resentation.</sup>


## 12.2.9 Coloring

L<sup>A</sup>TEX’s job is to produce articles and books that contain text, math formulas, and graphics. Such publications—with the exception of textbooks—cannot aford color printing. Presentations are diferent. If you prepare a color presentation, it will project in color. 

Nevertheless, the color commands are of limited use even for presentations. You probably use the color scheme of the chosen theme (see Section 12.5), and have limited opportunity to color things yourself. If you do, be very careful, too much color distracts from the presentation but judicious use of color—say, for highlighting a word or phrase—may be very efective. 

beamer <sup>uses the so</sup>p<sup>histicated</sup> xcolor p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>e of Uwe Kern. It colors b</sup>y <sup>s</sup>p<sup>ecif</sup>y<sup>-</sup> ing the color model: rgb (red, green, blue), or cmyk (cyan, magenta, yellow, black), or gray (<sup>black and white</sup>)<sup>—there are man</sup>y <sup>more models to choose from—and how much</sup> of each color you want to mix. 

<sup>So</sup> \color[rgb]{0,1,0} p<sup>aints ever</sup>y<sup>thin</sup>g<sup>—within its sco</sup>p<sup>e—</sup>g<sup>reen. You can</sup> color some text green with the command 

\textcolor[rgb]{0,1,0}{This text is green.} 

There are seventeen predefined colors: red, green, blue, cyan, magenta, yellow, orange, violet, purple, brown, pink, olive, black, darkgray, gray, lightgray, and white. With the proper options, there are hundreds more. So the previous command could also be given as 

\textcolor{green}{This text is green.} 

or as 

{\color{green}This text is green.} 

<sup>To</sup> p<sup>rett</sup>y <sup>thin</sup>g<sup>s</sup> <sup>u</sup>p, y<sup>ou</sup> <sup>can</sup> <sup>use</sup> \colorbox{green}{Green box}, <sup>which</sup> p<sup>uts</sup> <sup>the ar</sup>g<sup>ument in a</sup> g<sup>reen box and</sup> \fcolorbox{red}{green}{Green box}, <sup>which also</sup> adds a red frame. 

xcolor <sup>is automaticall</sup>y <sup>loaded b</sup>y beamer<sup>. To make sure that</sup> xcolor <sup>is loaded</sup> with the options desired, you have to include these options in the preamble in the 

\documentclass{beamer} 

<sup>line.</sup> <sup>For</sup> <sup>instance</sup>, <sup>to</sup> <sup>have</sup> <sup>the</sup> dvipsnam <sup>o</sup>p<sup>tion</sup> <sup>for</sup> xcolor, <sup>invoke</sup> beamer <sup>with</sup> 

\documentclass[xcolor=dvipsnam]{beamer} 

You can also mix predefined colors: 

{\color{green!40!yellow} This text is of what color?} 

which sets the text 40% green and 60% yellow. 

There are commands for defining colors and color sets, as well as for coloring the background, frames, and hyperlinks (see Uwe Kern, Extending L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X’s colorfacilities: the xcolorpackage [46]). 

Here is a simple illustration: 

%babybeamer9 presentation 

\documentclass{beamer} 

\begin{document} 

\setbeamercolor{normal text}{bg=yellow!15} 

\begin{frame} 

\frametitle{Colors} 

\begin{columns}[t] \begin{column}{2in} {\color{red}Is it true that there is no new result on the Congruence Lattice Characterization Problem?} \end{column} \begin{column}{2in} {\color{green}F. Wehrung found a distributive algebraic lattice that cannot be represented as the congruence lattice of a lattice.} \end{column} \end{columns} \end{frame} \setbeamercolor{normal text}{bg=green!15} 

\begin{frame} 

\frametitle{Colors fading out} 

The command 

\setbeamercolor{normal text}{bg=yellow!15} 

sets the background color to light (15%) yellow. In the first column, the text is red, in t<sup>h</sup>e second, green. Set t<sup>h</sup>e <sup>f</sup>oreground w<sup>i</sup>t<sup>h</sup> fg=. 

The background of the second frame is light green. The four participants are in lighter and lighter shades of red. 

<sup>Fi</sup>g<sup>ure 12.11 shows the frames of the</sup> babybeamer9 p<sup>resentation—unfortunatel</sup>y, not in color (unless you have the PDF of the book). 

## 12.3 The structure of a presentation

The structure of your presentation is, by and large, determined by the sectioning com-<sup>mands:</sup> \section <sup>and</sup> \subsection<sup>. For a ver</sup>y <sup>lon</sup>g <sup>lecture there ma</sup>y <sup>also be</sup> \part commands. The argument of any of these commands may have a short version for the navigational side bar (see Section 12.1.4). 

<sup>The sectionin</sup>g <sup>commands used in a</sup> beamer p<sup>resentation look the same as the</sup>y do for articles and books, but they play a diferent role. They do not display a section title, but they add an entry to the table of contents. They also act as place markers in the sense that if you click on the title of a section in a navigation bar, then you will jump to theframefollowing the section command. 

## Rule Sectioning commands

1. Sectioning commands can only be placed between frames. 

2. There must be a frame following the last sectioning command. 

3. <sup>For a lon</sup>g (<sup>sub</sup>)<sup>section title</sup>, <sup>use</sup> \breakhere <sup>to break a line.</sup> 

4. The optional short versions are for the navigation bar. 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/45f3cc63-7a26-418c-9a01-03dd91fad053/6db98dab8b4c44ea89caf0a125abb32f93b11c9d0097d7998d545debbc82d688.jpg)



<sup>Fi</sup>g<sup>ure 12.11:</sup> babybeamer9 p<sup>resentation.</sup>


<sup>These are illustrated with</sup> beamerstructure1, <sup>see Fi</sup>g<sup>ure 12.12. The line</sup> 

\tableofcontents[pausesections, pausesubsections] 

causes the table of contents to appear a line at a time. This command may also be used <sup>without an o</sup>p<sup>tion or onl</sup>y <sup>with one</sup>, pausesections<sup>.</sup> 

The second page shown in Figure 12.12 is the table of contents. The page is about half filled with only five listed items, so no more than 10 sections and subsections would fit. There should be fewer. 

%beamerstructure1 presentation 

\documentclass{beamer} 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/45f3cc63-7a26-418c-9a01-03dd91fad053/4f0a137d98f6acf5d07945c99874dee83e1a3aa8640c4d2c29ab94576212a302.jpg)



<sup>Fi</sup>g<sup>ure 12.12:</sup> beamerstructure1 p<sup>resentation</sup>, p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>es 3 and 5.</sup>


\tableofcontents[pausesections, pausesubsections] \end{frame} \section[Sec1]{Section 1} \begin{frame} \frametitle{Section 1} Text of Section 1 \end{frame} \subsection[Sec1 Subsec1]{Section 1 -- Subsection 1} \begin{frame} \frametitle{Section 1\\Subsection 1} Text of Section 1. Subsection 1 \ { } \subsection[Sec1 Subsec2]{Section 1 -- Subsection 2} \begin{frame} \frametitle{Section 1\\Subsection 2} Text of Section 1, Subsection 2 \end{frame} \subsection[Sec1 Subsec3]{Section 1 -- Subsection 3} \begin{frame} \frametitle{Section 1\\Subsection 3} Text of Section 1, Subsection 3 \end{frame} \section[Sec2]{Section 2} \begin{frame} \frametitle{Section 2} Text of Section 2 \end{frame} 

\end{document} 

## 12.3.1 Longer presentations

Longer presentations may need parts and a more complicated table of contents. I will <sup>not discuss these to</sup>p<sup>ics</sup>, <sup>but the</sup> p<sup>resentation</sup> beamerstructure2 (<sup>in the</sup> samples folder) illustrates the use of parts and some other features. I added some comments to point these out. See Figure 12.13 for two sample pages of this presentation. 

## 12.3.2 Navigation symbols

The more structure you have in a presentation, the more you may appreciate the navigation icons shown by default on each page in the last line on the right. The icons are: 

the slide 

the frame 

the section 

the presentation icons 

each surrounded by a left and a right arrow 

the appendix 

the back and forward icons (circular arrows) 

the search icon (a magnifying glass) 

<sup>If</sup> y<sup>ou decide not to have them</sup>, <sup>as in the</sup> p<sup>resentation</sup> beamerstructure2, <sup>then</sup> g<sup>ive</sup> the following command in the preamble: 

\setbeamertemplate{navigation symbols}{} 

## 12.4 Notes

You can place notes in your presentation to remind yourself of what you want to say in addition to what is being projected. A note is placed in the presentation as the argument <sup>of the</sup> \note <sup>command</sup>, <sup>as in</sup> 

\note{This is really difficult to compute.} 

<sup>B</sup>y <sup>default</sup>, <sup>notes are not shown in the</sup> p<sup>resentation. If</sup> y<sup>ou invoke</sup> beamer <sup>with</sup> 

\documentclass[notes=show]{beamer} 

then the notes pages are included. The command 

\documentclass[notes=show, trans]{beamer} 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/45f3cc63-7a26-418c-9a01-03dd91fad053/ac1ee62a71cbb81785df0a932e3f88d9d56bc47acc6992b8a90836dcb5e5ac47.jpg)


# Sectionally complemented chopped lattices

George Gr¨atzer<sup>1</sup> Harry Lakser<sup>1</sup> Michael Roddy<sup>2</sup> 

<sup>1</sup>University of Manitoba 

<sup>2</sup>Brandon University 

Conference on Lattice Theory, 2006 

George Gr¨atzer, Harry Lakser, Michael Roddy 

Sectionally complemented chopped lattices 

Chopped lattices Ideals and congruences 

1 Chopped lattices 

2 Ideals and congruences 

George Gr¨atzer, Harry Lakser, Michael Roddy 

Sectionally complemented chopped lattices 

<sup>Fi</sup>g<sup>ure 12.13:</sup> beamerstructure2 p<sup>resentation</sup>, p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>es 1 and 10.</sup> 

produces transparencies with notes, and 

\documentclass[notes=only]{beamer} 

produces only the note pages, one note page for every overlay of a frame with a note. To avoid this, print the output of 

\documentclass[trans, notes=only]{beamer} 

In addition to these examples, all the notes placed in a single frame are collected together on one note page. And a note between frames becomes a page on its own. 

beamer does an excellent job of producing notes pages, for example, see Fig ure 12.14. In the upper-left corner, it displays precisely where we are in the structure of the presentation. The upper-right corner shows a small picture of the page to which the notes are attached. 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/45f3cc63-7a26-418c-9a01-03dd91fad053/8bcb7db43a9715fe2fe6026e384d93db8984e37bb05211438bab37138492f2c6.jpg)



Figure 12.14: A note page.


## 12.5 Themes

If you look carefully at Figures 12.1, 12.2, and 12.13 (even better, if you look at the PDF files of these presentations), you see how every little detail of the presentation is prov<sup>i</sup>ded by beamer. F<sup>i</sup>gures 12.1 and 12.2 s<sup>h</sup>ow a presentat<sup>i</sup>on sty<sup>l</sup>e dom<sup>i</sup>nated by a dark blue headline and left sidebar, a complete navigation bar in the left sidebar, the name of the author(s) and the title repeated in every overlay, section numbers in colored squares, and so on. 

The presentation in Figure 12.13 has no sidebars, section numbers are in colored circles, the navigation elements are in the headline. The display of lists and theorems (and other similar elements of a presentation) also vary a great deal. 

You can achieve such detailed control over your presentation by defining all these <sup>elements</sup> y<sup>ourself.</sup> beamer p<sup>laces dozens of commands at</sup> y<sup>our dis</sup>p<sup>osal to make this</sup> possible. Or you can use a presentation theme that will do the job for you. 

<sup>The command to name a</sup> p<sup>resentation theme is</sup> \usetheme{}<sup>. The</sup> p<sup>resentation</sup> beamerstructure2 <sup>uses the theme</sup> Warsaw (<sup>see Fi</sup>g<sup>ure 12.13</sup>), <sup>so followin</sup>g <sup>the doc-</sup> ument class line type the command 

\usetheme{Warsaw} 

quickbeamer1 <sup>uses the theme</sup> Berkeley (<sup>see Fi</sup>g<sup>ures 12.1 and 12.2</sup>) <sup>and so does</sup> beamerstructure1 (<sup>see Fi</sup>g<sup>ure 12.12</sup>)<sup>.</sup> 

<sup>The</sup> p<sup>resentation themes are in the</sup> theme <sup>subfolder ofthe</sup> themes <sup>folder of</sup> beamer<sup>.</sup> As of this writing, there are 26 of them, named after cities: 

## Presentation Themes

Without Navigation Bars default, Bergen, Boadilla, Madrid, AnnArbor, CambridgeUS, Pittsburgh, Rochester 

With a Navigation Bar Antibes, JuanLesPins, Montpellier 

With a table of contents Sidebar Berkeley, PaloAlto, Goettingen, Marburg, Hannover 

With Mini Frame Navigation Berlin, Ilmenau, Dresden, Darmstadt, Frankfurt, Singapore, Szeged 

With Section and Subsection Table Copenhagen, Luebeck, Malmoe, Warsaw 

How do you choose a presentation theme? After the presentation is finished, try out the various themes. Ask yourself: 

Do sidebars take too much room away from my illustrations? 

Do stronger colors add to the presentation or do they distract? 

Do I want to use a navigation bar? 

Answering these questions will narrow your choice. 

The presentation theme defines all the colors, but you can alter them with the <sup>command</sup> \usecolortheme{}<sup>. You have a choice of</sup> albatross, beetle, crane, fly, <sup>and</sup> seagull<sup>.</sup> 

For instance, 

\usetheme{Warsaw} 

\usecolortheme{seagull} 

is a gray version of the Warsaw theme, appropriate for printing in black-and-white. In addition, you can further modify the “inner elements”, such as blocks, with 

\usecolortheme{lily} 

<sup>or</sup> orchid, <sup>or</sup> rose<sup>. You can modif</sup>y <sup>the “outer elements”</sup>, <sup>such as headlines and side-</sup> bars, with 

\usecolortheme{whale} 

<sup>or</sup> seahorse, <sup>or</sup> dolphin<sup>.</sup> <sup>So</sup> y<sup>ou</sup> <sup>can</sup> <sup>have</sup>, <sup>for</sup> <sup>instance</sup>, 

\usetheme{Warsaw} 

\usecolortheme{lily} 

\usecolortheme{whale} 

This gives you 45 “out of the box” color schemes. 

Similarly, font themes can also be specified, modifying the presentation theme, <sup>with the command</sup> \usefonttheme{}<sup>. You have the default and the followin</sup>g <sup>o</sup>p<sup>tions:</sup> professionalfonts structurebold structureitalicserif structuresmallcapserif<sup>.</sup> 

## 12.6 Planning your presentation

Step 1 As a rule, your presentation is based on one or more of your articles. Collect them in one folder. Resolve naming conventions as necessary. There should be <sup>onl</sup>y <sup>one</sup> Fig1<sup>!</sup> 

Step 2 Rewrite the article(s) to sketch out your presentation. The pages correspond to frames. A page should not have too many words, say, no more than 40. Replace your numbered theorems with named theorems. Never reference another page. Have few sections and subsections. Add a table of contents, which is a readable overview of the new article. 

Step 3 Base the new presentation on a presentation in the samples folder, a sample p<sup>resentation in</sup> beamer<sup>’s</sup> solution <sup>folder</sup>, <sup>or on one of</sup> y<sup>our own or of a collea</sup>g<sup>ue’s</sup> older presentations. Turn the pages into frames. 

Step 4 Design your frames and add frame titles. Completely disregard what we wrote in Section 2.3 (the idea behind L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X is that you should concentrate on what you have to say and let L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X take care ofthe visual design). The new principle is: You are completely responsible for the visual appearance of every frame and overlay. 

This is, of course, in addition to brevity and readability. Do not let L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X break your lines. Do it with the \\ command and keep words that belong together on the same line. 

Step 5 Write notes to remind yourself what you want to say in your lecture that is not on the slides. Print the notes for your lecture. 

Step 6 Build in flexibility. For instance, if you have four examples to illustrate a definition, put each one on a diferent frame or overlay, and add a link to each that skips the rest of the examples. Depending on your audience’s understanding, show an example or two, and skip the rest. The same way, you may skip proof ideas and even topics. 

Step 7 Prepare for the worst—the computer system may fail, but projectors seldom do—so print a set of transparencies for your lecture as a backup by invoking the option trans <sup>of the documentclass</sup> 

\documentclass[trans]{beamer} 

To print a handout, use the handout option 

\documentclass[handout]{beamer} 

<sup>O</sup>p<sup>en the</sup> p<sup>resentation in Acrobat Reader. In</sup> Printer/Page Setup... <sup>set landsca</sup>p<sup>e</sup> <sup>and</sup> 140<sup>%</sup> <sup>ma</sup>g<sup>nification.</sup> <sup>In</sup> <sup>the</sup> Print <sup>dialo</sup>g<sup>ue</sup> <sup>box</sup> <sup>in</sup> Layout <sup>choose</sup> <sup>two</sup> p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>es</sup> p<sup>er</sup> sheet and print—assuming, of course, that you have a printer ofering these options. 

## 12.7 What did I leave out?

<sup>Since the</sup> beamer <sup>reference manual is 245</sup> p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>es lon</sup>g, <sup>it is clear that this cha</sup>p<sup>ter covers</sup> maybe 10% of it. 

For most presentations, you won’t even need most of what I have included. If you read Sections 12.1, 12.2.1 and maybe Section 12.3, you should have enough for most math presentations. 

If you are in other fields, or if you are more ambitious, you may need more. For <sup>exam</sup>p<sup>le</sup>, <sup>a com</sup>p<sup>uter scientist will want</sup> p<sup>ro</sup>g<sup>ram listin</sup>g<sup>s in a</sup> verbatim <sup>environment.</sup> This is easy. Start your frame with 

\begin{frame}{fragile} 

<sup>and then</sup> y<sup>ou can use the</sup> verbatim <sup>environment.</sup> 

If you want to include sounds or movies in your presentation, consult Till Tantau’s User’s Guide to the Beamer Class [69]. 

You can do very simple animation with what we have covered here. This is illus-<sup>trated with the</sup> babybeamer10 p<sup>resentation</sup> (<sup>in the</sup> samples <sup>folder</sup>)<sup>.</sup> 

babybeamer10 presentation 

\documentclass{beamer} 

\begin{document} 

\begin{frame} 

\includegraphics<1>{basem3-1} 

\includegraphics<2>{basem3-2} 

\includegraphics<3>{basem3-3} 

\includegraphics<4>{basem3-4} 

\end{frame} 

\end{document} 

The congruence generated by the dashed red line, see Figure 12.15, spreads in three steps, illustrating an interesting result. The animation is quite efective and instructive. 

If you want to place such changing pictures lower in a frame, put them in the overprint <sup>environment.</sup> 

I would recommend that you read Section 5 of Till Tantau, User’s Guide, which has many good pointers about creating presentations.

<sup>Fi</sup>g<sup>ure 12.15: The four</sup> p<sup>ictures of</sup> babybeamer10<sup>.</sup>

## Illustrations

Most illustrations in math are “vector graphics” such as the following example: 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/45f3cc63-7a26-418c-9a01-03dd91fad053/4e10131d9db1ca3b246827aa631d9519b0c3769ee6ab1964f502c5342597fa0d.jpg)


There are lots of circles, connecting lines, arrows, and so on. And the annotations are in L<sup>A</sup>T X! Many mathematician used Adobe Illustrator or special purpose software to 

© Springer International Publishing AG 2016 G. Grätzer, More Math Into L<sup>A</sup>T X, DOI 10.1007/978-3-319-23796-1_13 create such diagrams; see Sections 7.8 and 13.4 for commutative diagrams. Since there is no more academic pricing to buy Adobe Illustrator (you have to subscribe to Creative Cloud), some turn to Till Tantau’s TikZ package. 

We introduce TikZ in this chapter with a few commands. We hope they will serve your needs. 

This chapter is based on Jacques Crémer’s A very minimal introduction to TikZ, with his permission, and Michael Doob’s detailed suggestions. 

## 13.1 Your first picture

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/45f3cc63-7a26-418c-9a01-03dd91fad053/b6e96982d9c264336a1d89e219700482a92101f97f5566afcd426a602d98920c.jpg)



Figure 13.1: Our first TikZ illustration



Step 1: Draw the grid


![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/45f3cc63-7a26-418c-9a01-03dd91fad053/b62743fcaec21537377d77fb0a64869d99be008b5e030ee980fab9107a75a4f7.jpg)


## 13.1 Your first picture

Note the semicolon terminating the line. If you forget, you get the helpful reminder: 

Package tikz Error: Giving up on this path. 

Did you forget a semicolon? 

Step 2: Draw the four edges 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/45f3cc63-7a26-418c-9a01-03dd91fad053/2dca01d9b2866309404c7f4978d658f8cd1315b16f75f21d78ef60341c140cc1.jpg)


The command is \draw; the argument is a series of grid points connected by two <sup>dashes</sup>, --<sup>.</sup> 

{\centering\begin{tikzpicture} 

```sql
\draw[help lines] (0,0) grid (2,2); 
```

\draw (1,0)--(2,1)--(1,2)--(0,1)--(1,0); 

```latex
\end{tikzpicture} 
```

Again, note the semicolon terminating the line. It has to terminate all TikZ lines!!! No more warnings. 

Let me specify the conventions used in my field for such a diagram (note that 1 inch is 2.54 cm and 1 cm is 28.35 points): We use a grid with lines 1 cm apart; the circles have radius 1.8 mm and line width 1 pt; the lines have line width 0.7 pt. 

<sup>So the</sup> \draw <sup>command we would use for the illustration is</sup> 

```javascript
\draw[line width=0.7pt] (1,0)--(2,1)--(1,2)--(0,1)--(1,0); 
```

to make the lines a little thicker. More about line width soon. 

## Step 3: Draw the circles

<sup>We add a circle with the</sup> \draw <sup>command</sup> 

\draw (1,0) circle[radius=1.8mm]; 

By the conventions (above), we want the line width to be 1pt: 

```javascript
\draw[line width=1pt] (1,0) circle(radius=1.8mm]; 
```

<sup>We add four circles at</sup> (1,0), (2,1), (1,2), (0,1)<sup>:</sup> 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/45f3cc63-7a26-418c-9a01-03dd91fad053/f71b103337ac3541747b98b57dd1f97d23ba2fc04b3b59e7749c2aecd4d21605.jpg)


## Step 4: Fill the circles

This looks ugly. We should not be seeing the line segments in the circles. Easy to help. <sup>Fill the circles with white b</sup>y <sup>addin</sup>g <sup>the</sup> fill=white <sup>o</sup>p<sup>tion to</sup> \draw<sup>. So we</sup> g<sup>et the</sup> illustration of Figure 13.1 with the grid. We comment out the line producing the grid: 

```latex
{\centering\begin{tikzpicture}
\draw[help lines] (0,0) grid (2,2);
\draw[line width=0.7pt](1,0)--(2,1)--(1,2)--(0,1)--(1,0);
\draw[fill=white, line width=1pt] (1,0) circle(radius=1.8mm);
\draw[fill=white, line width=1pt] (2,1) circle(radius=1.8mm);
\draw[fill=white, line width=1pt] (1,2) circle(radius=1.8mm);
\draw[fill=white, line width=1pt] (0,1) circle(radius=1.8mm);
\end{tikzpicture}} 
```

and this produces the illustration of Figure 13.1 except for the labels. 

## Step 5: Add the labels

<sup>We add the labels with the</sup> \node at <sup>command. To add the label</sup> � <sup>to the circle with</sup> center at (2,1): 

```txt
\node at (2.5,1) {$y$}; 
```

You get 2.5 by 2.5 = 2 + 0.18 + a little nudge. Experiment until you like the result. Then proceed to the other circles: 

```latex
\begin{figure}[h!]
{\centering\begin{tikzpicture}
\draw[help lines] (0,0) grid (2,2);
\draw[line width=0.7pt] (1,0)--(2,1)--(1,2)--(0,1)--(1,0);
\draw[fill=white, line width=1pt] (1,0) circle(radius=1.8mm);
\draw[fill=white, line width=1pt] (2,1) circle(radius=1.8mm);
\node at (2.5,1){$y$};
\draw[fill=white, line width=1pt] (1,2) circle(radius=1.8mm);
\node at (1,2.5){$x \vee y$};
\draw[fill=white, line width=1pt] (0,1) circle(radius=1.8mm);
\node at (-0.5,1){$x$};
\end{tikzpicture}}
\caption{Our first \tikzname illustration}\label{Fi:firsttikz}
\end{figure}

producing the illustration of Figure 13.1! 
```

## Step 6: Remember, this is LAT X

Section 14.1 introduces custom commands. Let’s get a little ahead of ourselves, and define 

```txt
\newcommand{\mycircle}[1]
{\draw[fill=white,line width=1pt] (#1) circle(radius=1.8mm]} 
```

Even better. TikZ allows us to set default values. The command 

```latex
\tikzset{every picture/.style={line width=0.7pt}} 
```

sets the default value of line width to 0.7pt. Now the code for Figure 13.1 becomes easier to read (and write): 

```latex
{\centering\begin{tikzpicture}
\draw[help lines] (0,0) grid (2,2);
\draw (1,0)--(2,1)--(1,2)--(0,1)--(1,0);
\mycircle{1,0};
\mycircle{2,1};
\node at (2.5,1){$y$};
\mycircle{1,2};
\node at (1,2.5){$x \vee y$};
\mycircle{0,1};
\node at (-0.5,1){$x$};
\end{tikzpicture} 
```

## 13.2 The building blocks ofan illustration

An illustration is built from components. We discuss some of them: line segments, circles, dots (or vertices), ellipses, rectangles, arcs, smooth curves (Bézier curves), and labels. 

Line segments A path drawn with the command \draw $( 1 , 0 ) \mathrm { - - } ( 2 , 2 ) \mathrm { - - } ( 4 , 1 )$ ; 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/45f3cc63-7a26-418c-9a01-03dd91fad053/bdb9413fbb65cef8fc54c031755fc33f627e5de8f299a65237da238cf64328c4.jpg)


Circles <sup>A circle drawn usin</sup>g \draw (2,2) circle[radius=1]; 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/45f3cc63-7a26-418c-9a01-03dd91fad053/8b292fde3882c359964c453dcc6fa5a435c7a66512bf676c82563e3bd0c5b6c6.jpg)


Dots (or vertices) <sup>The command</sup> \draw[fill] (2,2) circle[radius=1pt]; draws a dot (or vertex): 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/45f3cc63-7a26-418c-9a01-03dd91fad053/8c860cab6a91ca36b38d24845e546f639ccbf28638a3f20bd9c2eef80964bc52.jpg)


Ellipses <sup>Drawn b</sup>y \draw (2,2) ellipse[x radius=2, y radius=1]; 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/45f3cc63-7a26-418c-9a01-03dd91fad053/1d3f64dce425f98574d2aa8f6c92d0d7615e339e0023cde0442fa921ee4667e3.jpg)


Rectangles <sup>A</sup> <sup>rectan</sup>g<sup>le</sup> <sup>drawn</sup> <sup>with</sup> \draw (1,1) rectangle (2,3); 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/45f3cc63-7a26-418c-9a01-03dd91fad053/790f52c123f6a6e57699623762d1e8c6199342cbb1de90e131ed0999e18319a3.jpg)


Arcs \draw (2,1) arc[start angle=0, end angle=90, radius=1]; draws an arc of a circle: 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/45f3cc63-7a26-418c-9a01-03dd91fad053/be131b35b2ba30d0bca75ac8478cba1259715e2b0899fddbbf5d9e66ee711a27.jpg)


Surprise! The point is not the center of the circle. 

Finally, an arc of an ellipse is drawn with the command 

\draw (2,0) arc[x radius=1cm, y radius=5mm, start angle=0, end angle=120]; 

which typesets as 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/45f3cc63-7a26-418c-9a01-03dd91fad053/59c9f07ca72f7ff2f6e2a7770d9a15033d8c74a968ea6f18485629f4ebeed9af.jpg)


Smooth curves (Bézier curves) Nice curves can be drawn with a single control point (quadratic), as in 

\draw (2,0)..controls (2,3)..(0,2); 

\draw (2,0)..controls (4,2)..(0,2); 

or with two control points (cubic): 

\draw[dotted] (2,0)..controls (4,2) and (2,3)..(0,2); 

These three curves typeset as 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/45f3cc63-7a26-418c-9a01-03dd91fad053/d0124a27c03d874337a0543d0208acd57547e812fbf2f7d75d62435d69bebec3.jpg)


Alternatively, draw the curve defined by two points, A and B, the start and the end, and by the direction it leaves A and the direction it arrives at B with the command: \draw[very thick] (0,0) to[out=90,in=195] (2,1.5); <sup>This draws a</sup> curve <sup>f</sup>rom (0,0) to (2,1) w<sup>hi</sup>c<sup>h</sup> “<sup>l</sup>eaves” at an ang<sup>l</sup>e o<sup>f</sup> 90<sup>◦</sup> and “arr<sup>i</sup>ves” at an an<sub>g</sub>le of 195<sup>◦</sup>: 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/45f3cc63-7a26-418c-9a01-03dd91fad053/45caee8d759fbfcfd7a056590ffebb0caff09210bfdf76cfca499cf5379dbc43.jpg)


Labels We p<sup>l</sup>ace text or <sup>f</sup>ormu<sup>l</sup>a <sup>i</sup>n a p<sup>i</sup>cture w<sup>i</sup>t<sup>h</sup> \node at (1,1) {yes}; 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/45f3cc63-7a26-418c-9a01-03dd91fad053/97e84d1f2f2deab562b87d846c26118051d4b90591c7e443a156fbfb0a43e9c9.jpg)


Notice how the “yes” is positioned relative to (1,1). 

To place a label below a point, use the option below: 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/45f3cc63-7a26-418c-9a01-03dd91fad053/41ad798ea0bf04d01f2be31182cdf4704031a6c93effd334c461f47d136a81d9.jpg)


<sup>with the command</sup> \node[below] at (1,1) {below};<sup>. You can also use</sup> above, left, <sup>and</sup> right, <sup>and their combinations</sup>, <sup>for instance</sup>, above left<sup>.</sup> 

If the text is several lines long, break it with \\ and tell TikZ how to align it: 

```latex
\begin{mypicture}[xscale=1.3]
\draw[thick] (0,0)--(3,0);
\draw (0,-.2)--(0,.2);
\draw (3,-.2)--(3,.2);
\node[align=left, below] at (1.5,-.5)% {This text\\ is left justified};
\end{mypicture} 
```

which typesets as 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/45f3cc63-7a26-418c-9a01-03dd91fad053/45d9143caf1e6fa3e4c112167b872dc6d62abda80e53e27909703308375fe634.jpg)



This text is left justified


Text could be 

<sup>left</sup> j<sup>ustified</sup>, <sup>o</sup>p<sup>tion:</sup> align=left; 

<sup>ri</sup>g<sup>ht</sup> j<sup>ustified</sup>, <sup>o</sup>p<sup>tion:</sup> align=right; 

<sup>centered</sup>, <sup>o</sup>p<sup>tion:</sup> align=center; 

## 13.3 Transformations

We can rotate, translate, and scale the illustrations. 

```txt
Rotations The command
\draw[rotate=30] (1,1) rectangle (2,3);
rotates the rectangle by 30° (around the origin) and
\draw (2,2) ellipse[x radius=2, y radius=1, rotate=60];
rotates an ellipse by 60° (around its center): 
```

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/45f3cc63-7a26-418c-9a01-03dd91fad053/9d5d343fc691d905d78ba2c21ae515dbfd4e91bb8a6be9e884f50439bb6fc8ff.jpg)



Translations \draw[shift={(3,1)}] (1,1) rectangle (2,3); <sup>shifts the</sup> rectangle:


![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/45f3cc63-7a26-418c-9a01-03dd91fad053/57d6f3e6edb4849327ac02ec580b570f2b465bb8ee2ebe8d80bf6ee6c2bae846.jpg)


Scaling <sup>The command</sup> \draw[scale=0.3] (1,1) rectangle (2,3); <sup>scales the</sup> rectangle by 0.3 from the origin and \draw[scale around={0.5:(4.5,2)}] (4,1) rectangle (5,3); scales the rectangle by 2.5 using around the center of the rectangle, that is, around (4.5, 2):

## 13.4 Path attributes

A \draw command draws a pat<sup>h</sup>, w<sup>i</sup>t<sup>h</sup> a start po<sup>i</sup>nt and an end po<sup>i</sup>nt. T<sup>h</sup>e start and end p<sup>oints of</sup> \draw $( 1 , 0 ) \dots ( 2 , 1 ) \dots ( 1 , 2 ) \dots ( 0 , 1 )$ ; <sup>are</sup> (1,0) <sup>and</sup> (0,1); <sup>of</sup> \draw (2,2) circle[radius=1.5]; <sup>are</sup> (2,2) <sup>and</sup> (2,2)<sup>.</sup> 

We consider now some of the common attributes. 

Line width <sup>We have alread</sup>y <sup>seen the</sup> line width=1pt <sup>o</sup>p<sup>tion of</sup> \draw<sup>. Ti</sup>k<sup>Z comes</sup> <sup>with</sup> <sup>seven</sup> <sup>additional</sup> <sup>built</sup> <sup>in</sup> <sup>widths:</sup> ultra thin, very thin, thin, semithick, thick, very thick, <sup>and</sup> ultra thick<sup>.</sup> 

Dashes and dots You can also make dotted and dashed lines. The commands 

\draw[dashed] (0,0.5)--(2,0.5); 

\draw[dotted, thick] (0,0)--(2,0); 

make two thick lines, one dashed and one dotted: 

Colors Articles, as a rule, are printed black and white. But illustrations in PDF files and in presentations are shown in full color. 

<sup>Ti</sup>k<sup>Z comes with the followin</sup>g <sup>colors read</sup>y <sup>to use:</sup> red, green, blue, cyan, magenta, yellow, black, gray, darkgray, lightgray, brown, lime, olive, orange, pink, purple, <sup>and</sup> teal<sup>.</sup> 

<sup>The</sup> <sup>followin</sup>g <sup>exam</sup>p<sup>le</sup> <sup>uses</sup> white, lightgray, <sup>and</sup> gray<sup>.</sup> 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/45f3cc63-7a26-418c-9a01-03dd91fad053/f997ac9577d5db47bb731440d9ca0fcecc4a80862652ea79d16e5f5dff17368c.jpg)


Arrows We can put arrows or bars on one or both ends of a path:

coded as 

```latex
\begin{tikzpicture}
\draw[->, lightgray] (0,0)--(3,0)--(3,-1);
\draw[<--] (0,-0.5)--(2,-0.5);
\draw[|->, dashed] (0,-1)--(2,-1);
\draw[very thick, <->] (0,-3) to[out=90,in=195] (3,-1.5);
```
