
TikZ provides you with dozens of arrows. You get them by invoking the arrows <sup>librar</sup>y <sup>with</sup> \usepgflibrary{arrows} <sup>in the</sup> p<sup>reamble. Even better</sup>, <sup>use the</sup> tikzcd p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>e b</sup>y <sup>Florêncio Neves invoked b</sup>y \usepackage{tikz-cd}<sup>. It</sup> is designed to code commutative diagrams and it provides arrows very close to the L<sup>A</sup>T X style, see Figure 13.2. It comes with an excellent (and short) manual tikz-cd-doc.pdf<sup>.</sup> 

<sup>In the</sup> tikzcd <sup>environment</sup>, <sup>the command</sup> \arrow p<sup>roduces an arrow. It takes</sup> one argument, a character r, l, u, or d, for right, left, up and down. A label is placed on an arrow as the second argument. 

<sup>Here are two exam</sup>p<sup>les of commutative dia</sup>g<sup>rams from the</sup> tikz-cd <sup>manual.</sup>

## 13.5 Coding the example

To code the example on page 343, at the start of your article, following the 

\usepackage{tikz} 

line, define: 

```latex
\tikzset{every picture/.style={line width=0.7pt}}
\newcommand{\mycircle}[1]
{\draw[fill=white,line width=1pt] (#1) circle(radius=1.0mm]} 
```

Then the following code will produce the diagram: 

```latex
\begin{figure}[hbt]
\centerline{\begin{tikzpicture}
%\draw[help lines] (0,0) grid (6,6);
\draw (2,0)--(0,3)--(4,5)--(6,2)--(2,0);
\draw (1.325,1)--(4.325,2.5);
\draw (6,2)--(4.325,2.5)--(4.66,4);
\mycircle{2,0};
\node at (2-.4,0){$0_I$};
\mycircle{6,2};
\node at (6+.4,2){$0_J$};
\mycircle{0,3}; 
```

```latex
\node at (0-.4,3) {$1_I$};
\mycircle{4,5};
\node at (4+.4,5) {$1_J$};
\mycircle{1.325,1};
\node at (1.325-.4,1) {$u$};
\mycircle{5.325,3};
\mycircle{4.325,2.5};
\mycircle{4.46,3};
\mycircle{4.67,4};
\node at (6,3.5) {$J$};
\node at (0,1.5) {$I$};
\node at (3.7,2.66) {$u \vee 0_J$};
\end{tikzpicture}}
\end{figure} 
```

## 13.6 What did I leave out?

The TikZ manual is 726 pages, so this chapter covers maybe 2% of it. For most math illustrations, this chapter will do. (I still use Adobe Illustrator for my lattice diagrams. I use maybe 2% of Illustrator’s power for my work.) 

TikZ can plot. It can graph many built in functions, has a small programming language, has libraries, for instance, for circuits. 

There is an excellent book on TikZ: Gérard Tisseau and Jacques Duma’s TikZ pur l’impatient [70]. Although the book is in French, the TikZ code is in English; this book should be easy enough to read. 

Customization 

## Commands and environments

In Section C.1.2, we discuss how Donald E. Knuth designed TEX as a platform on which convenient work environments could be built. One such work environment, L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X, predominates today, and it is indeed convenient. 

Nevertheless, L<sup>A</sup>TEX is designed for all of us, so it is not surprising that we could improve on it for our personal use. There are many reasons to customize L<sup>A</sup>TEX: 

Goal 1 to enhance the readability of the source file 

Goal 2 to make notational and terminological changes easier 

Goal 3 to redefine names used by L<sup>A</sup>TEX 

Goal 4 to introduce consistent layouts 

There are many techniques to accomplish these. 

Technique 1 Define commands and environments in order to enhance L<sup>A</sup>TEX to meet your particular needs (see Sections 14.1, 14.1.7, and 14.2). 

Technique 2 Utilize delimited commands to write L<sup>A</sup>TEX documents in a more readable fashion (see Section 14.1.9). 

Technique 3 Collect your frequently used commands into a command file (see Section 14.3). 

Technique 4 Manipulate counters, integers—for instance, equation numbers and section numbers—and length commands, distance measurements—the \voffset command is an example (see Section 14.5). 

Technique 5 Create customized list environments with the list environment (see Section 14.6). 

Of course, there are many more reasons to customize and many more techniques to employ. We cover them in detail in this chapter. 

We dedicate the last section to the pitfalls of customization (see Section 14.7). While the benefits of customization are great, there are many practices to avoid. 

## 14.1 Custom commands

L<sup>A</sup>TEX provides hundreds of commands. Chances are good, however, that you still have specific needs that are not directly addressed by these commands. Byjudiciously adding custom commands (or macros) you can make your work more productive. 

Custom commands follow the same rules as regular L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X commands (see Section 3.3.1). 

## 14.1.1 Examples and rules

## Commands to enhance readability

Let us start with a few examples of custom commands as shorthand for longer command(s) or text in order to enhance readability of the source file (Goal 1). 

<sup>1. If</sup> y<sup>ou use the</sup> \leftarrow <sup>command a lot</sup>, y<sup>ou could define</sup> 

\newcommand{\larr}{\leftarrow} 

Then you would only have to type \larr to obtain a left arrow. 

## 2. Instead of

\widetilde{a} 

you could simply type \wtilda after defining 

\newcommand{\wtilda}{\widetilde{a}} 

I show you how to define a generalized version of such a command in Section 14.1.2. 

3. If you want to suppress the ligature in iff (see Section 3.4.6), you would normally have to type 

if\textcompwordmark f 

By de<sup>fi</sup>n<sup>i</sup>ng a command \Iff, 

\newcommand{\Iff}{if\textcompwordmark f} 

you can type \Iff to get iff. We name this command \Iff because \iff is the symbol ⟺ (see Section A.4). 

4. If you use the construct $D ^ { [ 2 ] } \times D ^ { [ 3 ] }$ o<sup>f</sup>ten, you cou<sup>l</sup>d <sup>i</sup>ntroduce t<sup>h</sup>e \DxD (� t<sup>i</sup>mes �) command, 

\newcommand{\DxD}{D^{[2]}\times D^{[3]}} 

and then type \DxD instead of the longer, and hard to read, version throughout your document—serves also Goal 2. 

5. If you want to get a backslash in typewriter style, you would normally have to type (see Section 3.4.4) 

\texttt{\symbol{92}} 

<sup>Instead</sup>, y<sup>ou can introduce the</sup> \bsl <sup>command</sup>, 

\newcommand{\bsl}{\texttt{\symbol{92}}} 

and \bsl typesets as \. 

6. You can also use commands as a shorthand for text. For instance, if you use the p<sup>hrase</sup> subdirectly irreducible <sup>man</sup>y <sup>times in</sup> y<sup>our document</sup>, y<sup>ou could de-</sup> fine 

\newcommand{\subdirr}{subdirectly irreducible} 

\subdirr <sup>is now shorthand for</sup> subdirectly irreducible, <sup>which t</sup>yp<sup>esets as</sup> subdirectly irreducible. 

letters are entered to match the first entry in the completion dictionary. Hitting escape again cycles through all possible completions. To make this feature useful, you have to customize the completion dictionary. Note that command completion minimizes the number of characters you have to type, but it does not improve the readability of the source. 

## Rule Custom commands

<sup>1. Issue the</sup> \newcommand <sup>command.</sup> 

<sup>2. In braces</sup>, <sup>t</sup>yp<sup>e the name of</sup> y<sup>our new command</sup>, <sup>for exam</sup>p<sup>le</sup>, \subdirr, <sup>includin</sup>g the backslash (\). 

<sup>3.</sup> <sup>In</sup> <sup>a</sup> <sup>second</sup> p<sup>air</sup> <sup>of</sup> <sup>braces</sup>, <sup>define</sup> <sup>the</sup> <sup>command</sup>, <sup>in</sup> <sup>this</sup> <sup>exam</sup>p<sup>le</sup>, subdirectly irreducible<sup>.</sup> 

<sup>4.</sup> <sup>Use</sup> <sup>the</sup> <sup>command</sup> <sup>as</sup> \subdirr\␣ <sup>or</sup> \subdirr{} <sup>before</sup> <sup>a</sup> <sup>s</sup>p<sup>ace</sup>, <sup>before</sup> <sup>an</sup> <sup>al</sup>p<sup>ha-</sup> <sup>betical character as</sup> \subdirr{}, <sup>and</sup> \subdirr <sup>otherwise.</sup> 

Examples for Rule 4. For subdirectly irreducible lattice type 

\subdirr{} lattice 

or 

\subdirr\ lattice 

<sup>and not</sup> \subdirr lattice<sup>. Indeed</sup>, <sup>t</sup>yp<sup>esettin</sup>g \subdirr lattice <sup>results in</sup> subdirectly irreduciblelattice. By the first spacing rule, \subdirr␣lattice is not any better (see Section 3.2.1). If you want subdirectly irreducibles, you must use the \subdirr{} form. Indeed, \subdirr{}s typesets as subdirectly irreducibles. 

## Using new commands

It is good practice to place custom commands in the preamble of your document or in <sup>a command</sup> (<sup>st</sup>y<sup>le</sup>) <sup>file</sup> y<sup>ou load with a</sup> \usepackage <sup>command</sup> (<sup>see Section 14.3</sup>)<sup>—</sup> provided that you do not submit to a journal that does not allow this. Then you always know where to look for the command definitions. An exception is a custom command that you want to restrict to a part of the document. Delimit the segment with braces and define the custom command within those braces (see Section 3.3.2). Instead of <sup>a</sup> p<sup>air of braces</sup>, y<sup>ou can use</sup> \begingroup <sup>and</sup> \endgroup, <sup>which is easier to see.</sup> Section 14.2.5 recommends yet another approach. 

Tip 

If errors occur, isolate the problem. Comment out the custom commands and reintroduce them one at a time. 

L<sup>A</sup>TEX only checks whether the braces match in the command definition. Other mistakes are found only when the command is used. 

For instance, if you define a command with a spelling error 

\newcommand{\bfA}{\textf{A}} 

then at the first use of \bfA you get the message 

```txt
! Undefined control sequence.
\bfA ->\textf
{A} 
```

<sup>Note that LAT</sup>E<sup>X is not com</sup>p<sup>lainin</sup>g <sup>about</sup> \bfA <sup>but about the miss</sup>p<sup>elled</sup> \textbf <sup>com-</sup> <sup>mand in the definition of</sup> \bfA<sup>.</sup> 

Be careful not to define a custom command with a name that is already in use. If you do, you get a message such as 

! LaTeX Error: Command \larr already defined. 

To correct the error, replace the command name with a new one. On the other hand, if you need to replace an existing command, you have to redefine it. See Section 14.1.5 for how to do so. 

Tip Use spaces to make your source files more readable, but avoid them in definitions. 

For example, you may type 

$D^{ \langle 2 \rangle } + 2 = x^{ \mathbf{a} }$ 

This may help you see how the braces match, easily identify relations and operations, and so on. Do not add these spaces in command definitions because it may result in unwanted spaces in your typeset document. You may start a new line to increase the readability of a command definition, provided that you terminate the previous line with %. For instance, borrowing an example from page 370: 

\newcommand{\Xquotphi}[2]{% \dfrac{\varphi \cdot X_{n, #1}}% {\varphi_{#2}\times \varepsilon_{#1}}} 

Tip In the definition of a new command, command declarations need an extra pair of braces (see Section 3.3.3). 

Say you want to define a command that typesets the warning: Do not redefine this variable! It is very easy to make the following mistake: 

\newcommand{\Warn}{\em Do not redefine this variable!} 

\Warn typesets the warning emphasized, but everything that follows the warning is also emphasized (more precisely, until the end of the \Warn command’s scope). Indeed, \Warn <sup>is</sup> <sup>re</sup>p<sup>laced</sup> <sup>b</sup>y \em Do not redefine this variable! <sup>so</sup> <sup>the</sup> <sup>efect</sup> <sup>of</sup> \em goes beyond the sentence to the next closing brace. 

The correct definition is 

\newcommand{\Warn}{{\em Do not redefine this variable!}} 

Even simpler, you could use a command with an argument 

\newcommand{\Warn}{\emph{Do not redefine this variable!}} 

Tip There are limits as to what can be done with custom commands. For instance, you <sup>cannot introduce</sup> \bal <sup>for</sup> \begin{align} <sup>and</sup> \eal <sup>for</sup> \end{align}<sup>. So if</sup> y<sup>ou</sup> want to introduce a new type of custom command, do just one and try it out. 

The xspacepackage 

Rule 4 (on page 364) is the source ofmany annoying problems in L<sup>A</sup>TEX. David Carlisle’s xspace package (see Section 10.3.1) helps eliminate such problems. In the preamble, load the package with 

\usepackage{xspace} 

<sup>Whenever</sup> y<sup>ou define a command that ma</sup>y <sup>have such</sup> p<sup>roblems</sup>, <sup>add the</sup> \xspace <sup>com-</sup> <sup>mand to the definition. For instance</sup>, <sup>define</sup> \subdirr <sup>as</sup> 

\newcommand{\subdirr}{subdirectly irreducible\xspace} 

<sup>Then all the followin</sup>g <sup>t</sup>yp<sup>esets</sup> subdirectly irreducible lattice <sup>correctl</sup>y<sup>:</sup> 

\subdirr\␣lattice 

\subdirr{}␣lattice 

\subdirr␣lattice 

<sup>Note</sup> <sup>that</sup> \xspace <sup>does</sup> <sup>not</sup> <sup>add</sup> <sup>s</sup>p<sup>ace</sup> <sup>if</sup> <sup>followed</sup> <sup>b</sup>y <sup>a</sup> p<sup>unctuation</sup> <sup>mark</sup>, <sup>so</sup> <sup>to</sup> g<sup>et</sup>厂the lattice is subdirectly irreducible.Ltypethe lattice is \subdirr.

For instance, if you define\newcommand{\tex}{\TeX\xspace}\newcommand{\bibtex}{\textsc{Bib}\kern-.1em\tex\xspace}% Bad!!!then\bibtex, followed by a commatypesets as厂BibT X , followed by a commaLThe correct definitions are\newcommand{\tex}{\TeX\xspace}\newcommand{\bibtex}{\textsc{Bib}\kern-.1em\TeX\xspace}% Correct!<sup>Of course</sup>, <sup>if</sup> y<sup>ou want to</sup> g<sup>et T</sup>E<sup>Xbook</sup>, y<sup>ou cannot use the</sup> \xspace <sup>variant definition:</sup>\tex<sup>.</sup>

## Ensuring math

<sup>The</sup> \ensuremath <sup>command is useful for definin</sup>g <sup>commands for both text and math</sup> mode. Suppose you want to define a command for �⟨<sup>2</sup>⟩. If you define it as \newcommand{\Dsq}{D^{\langle2\rangle}} then you can use the command in math mode, but not in text mode. If you define it as \newcommand{\Dsq}{$D^{\langle2\rangle}$} then it works in text mode, but not in math mode. Instead, define this command as \newcommand{\Dsq}{\ensuremath{D^{\langle2\rangle}}} <sup>Then</sup> \Dsq <sup>works correctl</sup>y <sup>in both contexts.</sup> 

This example also shows the editorial advantages of custom commands. Suppose the referee suggests that you change the notation to $D ^ { [ 2 ] }$ . To carry out the change you only have to change one line: 

\newcommand{\Dsq}{\ensuremath $\{ \mathsf { D } ^ { \sim } \{ [ 2 ] \} \} \}$ 

It is hard to overemphasize the importance of this example. You may want to change notation because: 

you found a better notation; 

your coauthor insists; 

your article appears in a conference proceedings, and the editor wants to unify the notation; 

you are reusing the code from this article in another one or in a book, where the notation is diferent. 

<sup>See also the discussion of the</sup> \TextOrMath <sup>command on</sup> p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>e 293.</sup> 

## 14.1.2 Arguments

Arguments of custom commands work the same way as for L<sup>A</sup>TEX commands (see page 52). Define 

$$
\backslash \text {newcommand} \{\backslash \text {fsqAB} \} \{(f ^ {\wedge} 2) ^ {\wedge} \{[ [ \backslash \text {frac} \{A ^ {\wedge} 2 \} \{B - 1 \} ] ] \} \}
$$

<sup>Then</sup> \fsqAB <sup>t</sup>yp<sup>esets as</sup> $( f ^ { 2 } ) ^ { [ [ \frac { A ^ { 2 } } { B - 1 } ] ] }$ <sup>in a math formula. If</sup> y<sup>ou want to use</sup> \fsqAB <sup>in</sup> <sup>math and also b</sup>y <sup>itself in text</sup>, <sup>define it with</sup> \ensuremath, <sup>as</sup> 

\newcommand{\fsqAB}{\ensuremath{(f^2)^ 

$$
\{[ [ \backslash \text { frac } \{A ^ {2} \} \{B - 1 \} ] ] \} \}
$$

However, if you use this construct for many functions �, then you may need a generalized command, such as 

\newcommand{\sqAB}[1]{\ensuremath{(#1^2)^ 

$$
\{\left[ \left[ \left[ \text { frac } \{A ^ {2} \} \{B - 1 \} \right] \right] \right\} \}
$$

Now $\scriptstyle \mathtt { \backslash s q A B \{ g \} }$ typesets $( g ^ { 2 } ) ^ { [ [ \frac { A ^ { 2 } } { B - 1 } ] ] }$ <sup>. The form of this</sup> \newcommand <sup>is the same as</sup> before, except that after the name of the command in braces, {\sqAB}, we specify the number of arguments in brackets (in this example, [1]). Then we can use #1 in the definition of the command. When the command is invoked, the argument you provide replaces #1 in the definition. Typing $\$ 123,456,78$ results in the formula $( q ^ { 2 } ) ^ { [ [ \frac { A ^ { 2 } } { B - 1 } ] ] }$ while $\sqAB{r}$ gives $( r ^ { 2 } ) ^ { [ [ \frac { A ^ { 2 } } { B - 1 } ] ] }$ 

Notice how these examples disrupt the normal spacing between lines—a practice to avoid! 

A custom command may have up to nine arguments, numbered 1–9. 

The simplest examples just allow you to invoke an existing command under a <sup>new name. For instance</sup>, <sup>the</sup> \eqref <sup>command introduced in Section 5.3 to refer-</sup> ence equations (the equation number upright, enclosed in parentheses), would also be <sup>useful to reference items for the custom list environment</sup> enumeratei <sup>introduced in</sup> <sup>Section 14.2.1—see Exam</sup>p<sup>le 3. So if the first item has label First, we could reference it with \eqref{First}, which typesets as (i). But \eqref{First} <sup>seems awkward and ina</sup>pp<sup>ro</sup>p<sup>riate</sup>; <sup>we are referencin</sup>g <sup>an item not an</sup> equation. 

So define 

\newcommand{\itemref}[1]{\eqref{#1}} 

and now we can reference the first item with \itemref{First}, which typesets as (i).

## 14.1.3 Short arguments

There are three ways of defining new commands: 

```txt
\newcommand \renewcommand \providecommand 
```

We take up the last two in Section 14.1.5. They define commands that can take any number of paragraphs as arguments. The *-ed versions of these commands define short commands (see Section 3.3.3) that take a block of text that contains no paragraph break as an argument. For instance, 

```latex
\newcommand{\bigbold}[1]{{\large\bfseries#1}} 
```

makes its argument large and bold. So 

\bigbold{First paragraph. 

Second paragraph. 

} 

prints 

## First paragraph. Second paragraph.

as expected. On the other hand, if you define 

\newcommand*{\bigbold}[1]{{\large\bfseries#1}} 

and then attempt to typeset the previous example, you get the message 

Paragraph ended before \bigbold was complete. <to be read again> \par \par \par 

Short commands are often preferable because of their improved error checking.

\newcommand{\BetterSum}[1][n]{a_{1}+a_{2}+\dots+a_{#1}} 

$\BetterSum$ <sup>still</sup> p<sup>roduces</sup> $a _ { 1 } + a _ { 2 } + \cdots + a _ { n } .$ , <sup>but</sup> $\BetterSum[m]$ <sup>t</sup>yp<sup>esets as</sup> $a _ { 1 } + a _ { 2 } + \cdots + a _ { m } .$ 

A \newcommand may have up to nine arguments, but only the first may be optional. The following command has two arguments, one optional: 

\newcommand{\BestSum}[2][n]{#2_{1}+#2_{2}+\dots+#2_{#1}}

## 14.1.7 Redefining names

A number of names, such as Table, List of Tables, Abstract, and so on, are typeset in your document by L<sup>A</sup>TEX. You can easily change these names. 

For instance, if you are preparing your manuscript for the proceedings of a meeting, and Abstract has to be changed to Summary, you can do so with 

\renewcommand{\abstractname}{Summary} 

Table 14.1 lists the commands that define such names in various document classes, along with their default definitions and the major document classes using the commands. It is easy to check whether your document class defines such a command, simply open the appropriate cls file and search for the command. 

If your document has photographs rather than figures, you could redefine 

\renewcommand{\figurename}{Photograph} 

\renewcommand{\listfigurename}{List of Photographs}

## 14.1.9 Delimited commands

You can define new commands in TEX using characters and symbols to delimit arguments. Such delimited commands provide a way to write more readable source documents. 

First we have to learn how to define a command using TEX’s \def command. Type \def, followed by the new command name (not in braces), then the definition in braces. For example, the first command defined in Section 14.1.1, 

\newcommand{\larr}{\leftarrow} 

could be typed 

\def\larr{\leftarrow} 

<sup>T X’s</sup> \def <sup>command does not check whether a new command name is alread</sup>y <sup>in use</sup>, <sup>so</sup> \def <sup>behaves diferentl</sup>y <sup>from the LAT X’s</sup> \newcommand, \renewcommand, <sup>and</sup> \providecommand (<sup>see Section 14.1.5</sup>)<sup>. If the</sup> \larr <sup>command was defined</sup> p<sup>re-</sup> viously, the original definition is overwritten. 

Tip It is your responsibility to ensure that your command name is unique when you define a command using \def. L<sup>A</sup>TEX provides no protection. Use the techniques introduced <sup>in Section 14.1.8 to check a name before</sup> y<sup>ou define a command with</sup> \def<sup>.</sup> 

Now we can start discussing delimited commands with a simple example, defining a command for vectors: 

\def\vect<#1>{\langle#1\rangle} 

<sup>Note</sup> <sup>that</sup> \vect <sup>is</sup> <sup>a</sup> <sup>command</sup> <sup>with</sup> <sup>one</sup> <sup>ar</sup>g<sup>ument</sup>, #1<sup>.</sup> <sup>When</sup> <sup>invoked</sup>, <sup>it</sup> <sup>t</sup>yp<sup>esets</sup> , <sup>the</sup> argument, and then . 

<sup>In</sup> <sup>the</sup> <sup>definition</sup> <sup>of</sup> \vect, <sup>the</sup> <sup>ar</sup>g<sup>ument</sup> #1 <sup>is</sup> <sup>delimited</sup> <sup>b</sup>y < <sup>and</sup> ><sup>.</sup> <sup>When</sup> <sup>the</sup> command is invoked, the argument must be delimited the same way. So to typeset the <sup>vector</sup> �, <sup>�</sup> , <sup>we invoke</sup> \vect <sup>with</sup> 

\vect<a,b> 

<sup>This looks somewhat like a vector</sup>, <sup>and the name</sup> \vect <sup>serves as a reminder.</sup> 

You have to be careful with delimited commands because the math spacing rules (see Section 5.2) do not hold in either the definition or the invocation. So if there is a <sup>s</sup>p<sup>ace</sup> <sup>before</sup> #1, <sup>in</sup> <sup>the</sup> <sup>definition</sup> <sup>of</sup> \vect,

<sup>then</sup> $\vect<a,b>$ <sup>results in the messa</sup>g<sup>e</sup> 

! Use of \vect doesn’t match its definition. 

l.12 $\vect<a 

which is clear enough. If the space is on the other side of the #1, as in

Runaway argument? a,b>$ ! Paragraph ended before \vect was complete. <to be read again> \par

## 14.2 Custom environments

Most custom commands are new commands. Custom environments, as a rule, are built on existing environments. We start with such custom environments (Section 14.2.1) and then proceed to investigate 

arguments (Section 14.2.2) 

optional arguments (Section 14.2.3) 

short arguments (Section 14.2.4) 

Finally, we discuss how to define brand-new environments (Section 14.2.5). 

## 14.2.1 Modifying existing environments

```latex
If you do not like the name of the proof environment and would prefer to use the name demo, define
\newenvironment{demo}
{\begin{proof}}
{\end{proof}}
Note that this does not change how the environment is typeset, only the way it is invoked.
To modify an existing environment, oldenv, type
\newenvironment{name}
{begin_text}
{end_text}
where begin_text contains the command \begin{oldenv} and end_text contains the command \end{oldenv}. 
```

```latex
For instance, if you define
\newenvironment{parbox}
    {...}
    {...}
you get the message
! LaTeX Error: Command \parbox already defined.
If there is an error in such a custom environment, the message generated refers to the environment that was modified, not to your environment. For instance, if you misspell proof as prof when you define
\newenvironment{demo}
    {\begin{prof}}
    {\end{proof}}
then at the first use of the demo environment you get the message
! LaTeX Error: Environment prof undefined.
1.13 \begin{demo} 
```

## If you define

\newenvironment{demo} {\begin{proof}\em} {\end{prof}} 

<sup>at the first use of</sup> demo y<sup>ou</sup> g<sup>et the messa</sup>g<sup>e</sup> 

! LaTeX Error: \begin{proof} on input line 5 ended by \end{prof}. 

## l.14 \end{demo}

Here are four more examples of modified environments. 

1. The command 

\newenvironment{demo} 

{\begin{proof}\em} 

{\end{proof}}+ 

defines a demo environment that typesets an emphasized proof. Note that the scope <sup>of</sup> \em <sup>is the</sup> demo <sup>environment.</sup> 

2. The following example defines a very useful environment. It takes an argument to be typeset as the name of a theorem: 

```latex
\newtheorem {*namedtheorem}{theoremname}
\newcommand{\theoremname}{testing}
\newenvironment{named}[1){
\renewcommand{\theoremname}{#1}
\begin{namedtheorem}}
{\end{namedtheorem}} 
```

For example, 

\begin{named}{Name of the theorem} 

Body of theorem. 

\end{named} 

## produces

Name of the theorem. Body oftheorem. 

<sup>in the st</sup>y<sup>le a</sup>pp<sup>ro</sup>p<sup>riate for the</sup> \newtheorem* <sup>declaration. This t</sup>yp<sup>e of environment</sup> is often used to produce an unnumbered Main Theorem (see Section 14.4) or when typesetting an article or book in which the theorem numbering is already fixed, for instance, when publishing a book in L<sup>A</sup>TEX that was originally typeset by another typesetting system. 

<!-- === Source: MinerU_markdown_More_Math_Into_LaTeX,_5ed,_G._Gratzer,_Springer,_2016_(1)_401_2122706526345998339.md (Page 401) === -->

<sup>3. In Sections 4.2.4 and 10.3.1</sup>, <sup>we came across the</sup> enumerate p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>e</sup>, <sup>which allows</sup> y<sup>ou to customize the</sup> enumerate <sup>environment. If the</sup> enumerate p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>e is loaded</sup>, y<sup>ou can invoke the</sup> enumerate <sup>environment with an o</sup>p<sup>tional ar</sup>g<sup>ument s</sup>p<sup>ecif</sup>y<sup>in</sup>g <sup>h</sup>ow t<sup>h</sup>e counter s<sup>h</sup>ou<sup>l</sup>d be typeset, <sup>f</sup>or <sup>i</sup>nstance, w<sup>i</sup>t<sup>h</sup> t<sup>h</sup>e opt<sup>i</sup>on [\upshape (i)], 

\begin{enumerate}[\upshape (i)] \item First item\label{First} \end{enumerate} 

items are numbered (i), (ii), and so on. So now we define 

\newenvironment{enumeratei}{\begin{enumerate}% [\upshape (i)]}% {\end{enumerate}} 

and we can invoke the new environment with (see Sections 14.3 and 14.4) 

\begin{enumeratei} \item \label{ } \end{enumeratei} 

<sup>Reference items in the</sup> enumeratei <sup>environment with the</sup> \itemref <sup>command</sup> introduced in Section 14.1.2. 

4. If you want to define an environment for displaying text that is numbered as an equation, you might try 

```latex
\newenvironment{texteqn}
{\begin{equation} \begin{minipage}{0.9\linewidth}}
{\end{minipage} \end{equation}} 
```

But there is a problem. If you use this environment in the middle of a paragraph, an interword space appears at the beginning of the first line after the environment. <sup>To remove this unwanted s</sup>p<sup>ace</sup>, <sup>use the</sup> \ignorespacesafterend <sup>command</sup>, <sup>as in</sup> 

\newenvironment{texteqn} {\begin{equation} \begin{minipage}{0.9\linewidth}} {\end{minipage} \end{equation} \ignorespacesafterend} 

<sup>Exam</sup>p<sup>les 2 and 3 are included in the</sup> newlattice.sty <sup>command file</sup> (<sup>see Sec-</sup> <sup>tion 14.3</sup>)<sup>. See the sam</sup>p<sup>le article</sup>, secondarticleccom.tex <sup>in Section 14.4</sup>, <sup>for some</sup> instances of their use. 

See Section 14.6.3 for custom lists as custom environments. 

<sup>Redefine an existin</sup>g <sup>environment with the</sup> \renewenvironment <sup>command. It is</sup> <sup>similar to the</sup> \renewcommand <sup>command</sup> (<sup>see Section 14.1.5</sup>)<sup>.</sup> 

<sup>There are some environments</sup> y<sup>ou cannot redefine</sup>; <sup>for instance</sup>, verbatim <sup>and all</sup> the AMS multiline math environments. 

## 14.2.2 Arguments

<sup>An environment defined b</sup>y <sup>the</sup> \newenvironment <sup>command can take ar</sup>g<sup>uments</sup> (<sup>see</sup> <sup>Exam</sup>p<sup>le 2 in Section 14.2.1</sup>), <sup>but the</sup>y <sup>can onl</sup>y <sup>be used in the</sup> begin_text <sup>ar</sup>g<sup>ument</sup> <sup>of the</sup> \newenvironment <sup>command. Here is a sim</sup>p<sup>le exam</sup>p<sup>le. Define a</sup> theorem proclamation in the preamble (see Section 4.4), and then define a theorem that can be referenced: 

\newenvironment{theoremRef}[1] 

{\begin{theorem}\label{T:#1}} 

{\end{theorem}} 

This is invoked with 

```latex
\begin{theoremRef}{label} 
```

<sup>The</sup> theoremRef <sup>environment is a modified environment. It is a</sup> theorem <sup>that can</sup> <sup>be referenced</sup> (<sup>with the</sup> \ref <sup>and</sup> \pageref <sup>commands</sup>, <sup>of course</sup>) <sup>and it invokes the</sup> theorem <sup>environment when it defines</sup> T:label <sup>to be the label for cross-referencin</sup>g<sup>.</sup> 

## 14.2.3 Optional arguments with default values

<sup>The first ar</sup>g<sup>ument of an environment created with the</sup> \newenvironment <sup>command</sup> may be an optional argument with a default value. For example, 

```latex
\newenvironment{narrow}[1][3in]
{\noindent\begin{minipage}{#1}}
{\end{minipage}} 
```

<sup>creates a</sup> narrow <sup>environment. B</sup>y <sup>default</sup>, <sup>it sets the bod</sup>y <sup>of the environment in a</sup> 3-inch wide box, with no indentation. So 

```latex
\begin{narrow}
This text was typeset in a \texttt{narrow}
environment, in a 3-inch wide box, with no indentation.
\end{narrow} 
```

typesets as 

This text was typeset in a narrow environment, in 

a 3-inch wide box, with no indentation. 

You can also give an optional argument to specify the width. For example, 

```latex
\begin{narrow}[3.5in]
This text was typeset in a \texttt{narrow} environment,
in a 3-inch wide box, with no indentation.
\end{narrow} 
```

```latex
\newenvironment{exception}
{\relax}
{\relax}
and then
\begin{exception}
    new commands
    body
\end{exception} 
```

which produces the following false statement: 

```txt
This text was typeset in a narrow environment, in a 3-inch wide box, with no indentation. 
```

## 14.2.4 Short contents

We have discussed two commands that define new environments, 

```txt
\newenvironment and \renewenvironment 
```

<sup>These commands allow</sup> y<sup>ou to define environments whose contents</sup> (begin_text <sup>and</sup> end_text ; <sup>see</sup> p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>e 380</sup>) <sup>can include an</sup>y <sup>number of</sup> p<sup>ara</sup>g<sup>ra</sup>p<sup>hs. The</sup> *<sup>-ed versions of</sup> these commands define short environments whose contents cannot contain a paragraph break (a blank line or a \par command). 

## 14.2.5 Brand-new environments

Some custom environments are not modifications of existing environments. Here are two examples: 

1. A command remains efective only within its scope (see Section 3.3.2). Now suppose that you want to make a change, say redefining a counter, for only a few paragraphs. You could simply place braces around these paragraphs, but they are hard to see. So define 

The environment stands out better than a pair of braces, reminding you later about <sup>the s</sup>p<sup>ecial circumstances. The</sup> \relax <sup>command does nothin</sup>g, <sup>but it is customar</sup>y <sup>to include a</sup> \relax <sup>command in such a definition to make it more readable.</sup> 

2. In this example, we define a new environment that centers its body vertically on a new page: 

```latex
\newenvironment{vcenterpage}
{\newpage\vspace*{\fill}}
{\vspace*{\fill}\par\pagebreak} 
```

<sup>For</sup> \vspace, <sup>see Section 3.8.2 and for</sup> \fill, <sup>see the last subsection in</sup> Section 14.5. 

## 14.3 A custom commandfile

Custom commands, of course, are a matter of individual need and taste. I have collected <sup>some commands for writin</sup>g p<sup>a</sup>p<sup>ers in lattice theor</sup>y <sup>in the</sup> newlattice.sty <sup>file</sup>, <sup>which</sup> you can find in the samples folder (see page 5). I hope that this model helps you to develop a command file of your own. Please remember that everything we discuss in this section is a reflection of my work habits. Many experts disagree with one or another aspect of the way I define the commands, so take whatever suits your needs. And keep in mind the dangers of customization discussed in Section 14.7. 

Tip Some journals do not permit the submission of a separate custom command file. For such journals, just copy the needed custom commands into the preamble of the article. 

<sup>This file is named</sup> newlattice.sty<sup>. It can be loaded with</sup> \usepackage<sup>. This</sup> has a number of advantages. 

Your command names should be mnemonic. If you cannot easily remember a command’s name, rename it. The implication here is that your command file should not be very large unless you have an unusual ability to recall abbreviations. 

<sup>Here are the first few lines of the</sup> newlattice.sty <sup>command file:</sup> 

```latex
% newlattice.sty
% New command file for lattice papers
\NeedsTeXFormat{LaTeX2e}[2011/01/30]
\ProvidesPackage{newlattice}[2015/03/15 v1.6 Commands for lattices based on LTF]
\RequirePackage{amsmath}
\RequirePackage{amssymb}
\RequirePackage{latexsym}
\RequirePackage[mathscr]{eucal}
\RequirePackage{verbatim}
\RequirePackage{enumerate}
\RequirePackage{xspace} 
```

The line 

\NeedsTeXFormat{LaTeX2e}[2005/12/01] 

g<sup>ives a messa</sup>g<sup>e if a document loadin</sup>g <sup>the</sup> newlattice p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>e is t</sup>yp<sup>eset with LAT</sup>E<sup>X</sup> 2.09 or with an older version of the standard L<sup>A</sup>T X. The next line provides information <sup>that is written in</sup> y<sup>our</sup> log <sup>file.</sup> 

The next seven lines declare what packages are required. If some of these packages have not yet been loaded, then the missing packages are loaded. A package already <sup>loaded is not read in a</sup>g<sup>ain b</sup>y \RequirePackage<sup>.</sup> 

Being able to specify the packages we need is one of the great advantages of command files. When I write a document, the packages are there if I need them. 

You may want some justification for the inclusion of two of these packages in this <sup>list. The</sup> verbatim p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>e is on the list so that I can use the</sup> comment <sup>environment</sup> to comment out large blocks of text (see Section 3.5.1), which is useful for finding errors and typesetting only parts of a longer document—but do not forget to remove y<sup>our comments before submission. The</sup> enumerate p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>e is on the list because the</sup> enumeratei <sup>and</sup> enumeratea <sup>environments</sup>, <sup>defined in</sup> newlattice.sty, <sup>re</sup>q<sup>uire it.</sup> 

If you start your article with 

\documentclass{amsart} 

\usepackage{newlattice} 

<sup>then</sup> <sup>the</sup> \listfiles <sup>command</sup> (<sup>see</sup> <sup>Section</sup> <sup>C.2.4</sup>) p<sup>roduces</sup> <sup>the</sup> <sup>followin</sup>g <sup>list</sup> <sup>when</sup> your document is typeset:

```latex
\section{Introduction}\label{S:intro}
In this note we prove the following result:
\begin{name}/{Main Theorem}
    There exists an infinite complete distributive lattice $K$ with only the two trivial complete congruence relations.
\end{name}
\section{The $Dsq$ construction}\label{S:Ds}
For the basic notation in lattice theory and universal algebra, 
```

see Ferenc~R. Richardson~\cite{fR82} and George~A.
Menuhin~\cite{gM68}. We start with some definitions:

\begin{definition}\label{D:prime}
Let $V$ be a complete lattice, and let $Frak{p} = [u, v]$ be an interval of $V$ . Then $Frak{p}$ is called
\emph{complete-prime} if the following three conditions are satisfied:
\begin{enumeratei}
\item $u$ is meet-irreducible but $u$ is \emph{not}
completely meet-irreducible;\label{m-i}
\item $v$ is join-irreducible but $v$ is \emph{not}
completely join-irreducible;\label{j-i}
\item $[u, v]$ is a complete-simple lattice.\label{c-s}
\end{enumeratei}
\end{definition}

Now we prove the following result:

\begin{lemma}\label{L:Dsq}
Let $D$ be a complete distributive lattice satisfying conditions \itemref{m-i} and~\itemref{j-i}.
Then $Dsq$ is a sublattice of $D^{-2}$ ; hence $Dsq$ is a lattice, and $Dsq$ is a complete distributive lattice satisfying conditions \itemref{m-i} and~\itemref{j-i}.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
By conditions~\itemref{m-i} and \itemref{j-i}, $Dsq$ is a sublattice of $D^{-2}$ . Hence, $Dsq$ is a lattice.

Since $Dsq$ is a sublattice of a distributive lattice, $Dsq$ is a distributive lattice. Using the characterization of standard ideals in Ernest~T. Moynahan~\cite{eM57}, $Dsq$ has a zero and a unit element, namely, $vect<0, 0>$ and $vect<1, 1>$ . To show that $Dsq$ is complete, let $empset \ne A \contd Dsq$ , and let $a = JJ A$ in $D^{-2}$ . If $a \in Dsq$ , then $a = JJ A$ in $Dsq$ ; otherwise, $a$ is of the form $vect<b, 1>$ for some $b \in D$ with $b < 1$ . Now $JJ A = \vect<1, 1>$ in $D^{-2}$ , and
the dual argument shows that $MM A$ also exists in 

$D^{2}$. Hence \(D$ is complete. Conditions \itemref{m-i} and~\itemref{j-i} are obvious for $Dsq$ .
\end{proof}
\begin{corollary}\label{C:prime} If $D$ is complete-prime, then so is $Dsq$ .
\end{corollary}

The motivation for the following result comes from Soo-Key Foo~\cite{sF90}{.

\begin{lemma}\label{L:ccr} Let $gQ$ be a complete congruence relation of $Dsq$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{E:rigid} 
\congr \vect<1, d>=\vect<1, 1>(\gQ), 
\end{equation} for some $d$ in D$ with $d < 1$ . Then $gQ = gi$ .
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof} Let $gQ$ be a complete congruence relation of $Dsq$ satisfying \itemref{E:rigid}. Then $gQ = gi$ .
\end{proof}

\section{The $gp^{*}$ construction}\label{S:P*} The following construction is crucial to our proof of the Main~Theorem:

\begin{definition}\label{D:P*} Let $D_{i}$ , for $i$ in I$, be complete distributive lattices satisfying condition~\itemref{j-i}. Their $gp^{*}$ product is defined as follows:
\[ 
\Prodsm{ D_{i}} {i \in I} = \Prodsm{ D_{i}^{-}- } {i \in I}+1; 
\] that is, $Prodsm{ D_{i}} {i \in I}$ is $Prodsm{ D_{i}^{-}- } {i \in I}$ with a new unit element.
\end{definition}

\begin{notation} If $i$ in I$ and $d$ in D_{i}^{-}-\), then 

```latex
\[
    \vectsup{i}{d}
\]
is the element of \(Prodsm{ D_{i} }{i \in I\} whose
\(i\)-th component is \(d\) and all the other
components are \(0\).

\end{notation}

See also Ernest~T. Moynahan~\cite{eM57a}. Next we verify:

\begin{theorem}\label{T:P*}
Let \(D_{i}\), for \(i \in I\), be complete distributive
lattices satisfying condition~\itemref{j-i}. Let \(gQ\)
be a complete congruence relation on
\(Prodsm{ D_{i} }{i \in I\} . If there exist
\(i \in I\) and \(d \in D_{i}\) with \(d < 1_{i}\) such
that for all \(d \leq c < 1_{i}\),
\begin{equation}\label{E:cong1}
    \congr\vectsup{i}{d}=\vectsup{i}{c}(\gQ),
\end{equation}
then \(gQ = gi\).

\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Since
\begin{equation}\label{E:cong2}
    \congr\vectsup{i}{d}=\vectsup{i}{c}(\gQ),
\end{equation}
and \(gQ\) is a complete congruence relation, it follows
from condition~\itemref{c-s} that
\begin{equation}\label{E:cong}
\begin{split}
    &\langle \dots, \overset{i}{d}, \dots, 0,
    \dots \rangle \\
    &\equiv \bigvee (\ \langle \dots, 0, \dots,
    \overset{i}{c}, \dots, 0, \dots \rangle \mid d \leq c < 1)
    \equiv 1 \pmod{\Theta}.
\end{split}
\end{equation}

Let \(j \in I\), for \(j \neq i\), and let
\(a \in D_{j}^{--}\). Meeting both sides of the congruence 
```

```latex
\itemref{E:cong} with \( \textsup{j}{a} \), we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{E:comp}
\begin{split}
0 &= \textsup{i}{d} \mm \textsup{j}{a} \\
&\equiv \textsup{j}{a}\pod{\gQ}.
\end{split}
\end{equation}
Using the completeness of \( \textsup{gQ} \) and \itemref{E:comp}, we get:
\begin{equation}\label{E:cong3}
\congr{0=\JJm{\textsup{j}{a}}{ a \in D_{j}^{-}- }}={1}(\gQ),
\end{equation}
hence \( \textsup{gQ} = \textsup{gi}. \)
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}\label{T:P*a}
Let \( D_{i} \), for \( i \) in I$, be complete distributive
lattices satisfying
conditions \itemref{j-i} and~\itemref{c-s}. Then
\( \textsup{D_{i}} \) {i \in I}$ also satisfies
conditions~\itemref{j-i} and \itemref{c-s}.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let \( \textsup{gQ} \) be a complete congruence on
\( \textsup{D_{i}} \) {i \in I}$. Let \( i \) in I$. Define
\begin{equation}\label{E:dihat}
\widehat{D}_{i} = \textsup{vectsup{i}{d}} { d \in D_{i}^{-}- } \)
\uu \set{1}.
\end{equation}
Then \( \textsup{widehat{D}_{i}} \) is a complete sublattice of
\( \textsup{D_{i}} \) {i \in I}$, and \( \textsup{widehat{D}_{i}} \) 
is isomorphic to \( D_{i} \). Let \( \textsup{gQ_{i}} \) be the
restriction of \( \textsup{gQ} \) to \( \textsup{widehat{D}_{i}} \). Since
\( D_{i} \) is complete-simple, so is \( \textsup{widehat{D}_{i}} \), 
hence \( \textsup{gQ_{i}} \) is \( \textsup{go} \) or \( \textsup{gi}. \) If \( \textsup{gQ_{i}} = \textsup{go} \)
for all \( i \) in I$, then \( \textsup{gQ} = \textsup{go}. \)
If there is an \( i \) in I$, such that \( \textsup{gQ_{i}} = \textsup{gi}. \)
then \( \textsup{congr0=1(\textsup{gQ})} \), and hence \( \textsup{gQ} = \textsup{gi}. \)
\end{proof}

The Main Theorem follows easily from Theorems~\ref{T:P*} and
\ref{T:P*a}.
```

## 14.5 Numbering and measuring

L<sup>A</sup>TEX stores integers in counters. For example, the section counter contains the current section number. Distance measurements are saved in length commands. For in-<sup>stance</sup>, <sup>the</sup> \textwidth <sup>command contains the width of the text. For this book</sup>, <sup>the</sup> <sup>len</sup>g<sup>th command</sup> \textwidth <sup>is set to 345.0</sup> p<sup>oints.</sup> 

In this section, we take a closer look at counters and length commands. 

## 14.5.1 Counters

Counters may be defined by L<sup>A</sup>TEX, by document classes, by packages, or by the user. 

## Standard L<sup>A</sup>T X counters

L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X automatically generates numbers for equations, sections, theorems, and so on. Each such number is stored in a counter. Table 14.2 shows the standard L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X counters. Their names are more or less self-explanatory. In addition, for every proclamation name, <sup>there is a matchin</sup>g <sup>counter called</sup> name (<sup>see Section 4.4</sup>)<sup>.</sup> 

## Setting counters

<sup>The command for settin</sup>g <sup>a counter’s value is</sup> \setcounter<sup>. When LAT</sup>E<sup>X</sup> g<sup>enerates a</sup> number, it first increments the appropriate counter, so if you want the next chapter to <sup>be numbered</sup> 3, y<sup>ou should set the</sup> chapter <sup>counter to</sup> 2 <sup>b</sup>y <sup>t</sup>yp<sup>in</sup>g 

\setcounter{chapter}{2} 

<sup>before</sup> <sup>the</sup> \chapter <sup>command.</sup> <sup>The</sup> <sup>onl</sup>y <sup>exce</sup>p<sup>tion</sup> <sup>to</sup> <sup>this</sup> <sup>rule</sup> <sup>is</sup> <sup>the</sup> p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>e</sup> <sup>number</sup>, which is first used to number the current page, and then incremented. If you wanted to set the current page number to 63, you would include the command 

\setcounter{page}{63} 

somewhere in the page. 

L<sup>A</sup>TEX initializes and increments its standard counters automatically. Sometimes y<sup>ou ma</sup>y <sup>want to mani</sup>p<sup>ulate them</sup> y<sup>ourself. To t</sup>yp<sup>eset onl</sup>y chapter3.tex, <sup>the third</sup> chapter of your book, start with 

\setcounter{chapter}{2} 

\include{chapter3} 

<sup>and</sup> <sup>when</sup> chapter3.tex <sup>is</sup> <sup>t</sup>yp<sup>eset</sup>, <sup>the</sup> <sup>cha</sup>p<sup>ter</sup> <sup>is</sup> p<sup>ro</sup>p<sup>erl</sup>y <sup>numbered.</sup> <sup>You</sup> <sup>can</sup> <sup>also</sup> type 

\setcounter{page}{63} 

if the first page of this chapter is supposed to be 63. Of course, the preferred way <sup>to t</sup>yp<sup>eset</sup> p<sup>arts of a lar</sup>g<sup>er document is with the</sup> \includeonly <sup>command</sup> (<sup>see Sec-</sup> tion 17.3.2). 

日 Tip If you need to manipulate counters, always look for solutions in which L<sup>A</sup>TEX does thework for you.

You can define your own counters. For example,

<sup>makes</sup> mycounter <sup>a new counter. In the definition</sup>, y<sup>ou can use an o</sup>p<sup>tional ar</sup>g<sup>ument</sup>, the name of another counter:

This com-</sup> mand has the same form as the command L<sup>A</sup>TEX uses internally for tasks such as numbering theorems and subsections within sections.

## Rule New counters

New counters should be defined in the preamble of the document. They should not be <sup>defined in a file read in with an</sup> \include <sup>command</sup> (<sup>see Section 17.3.2</sup>)<sup>.</sup> 

<sup>Let us su</sup>pp<sup>ose that</sup> y<sup>ou define a new counter</sup>, mycounter, <sup>in</sup> chapter5.tex, <sup>which</sup> <sup>is made</sup> p<sup>art of</sup> y<sup>our whole document with an</sup> \include <sup>command. When</sup> y<sup>ou t</sup>yp<sup>eset</sup> y<sup>our</sup> <sup>document</sup> <sup>with</sup> \includeonly <sup>commands</sup> <sup>not</sup> <sup>includin</sup>g chapter5.tex, y<sup>ou</sup> g<sup>et</sup> a message, such as

Counter styles

\thecounter 

## 14.5 Numbering and measuring

I<sup>f</sup> you want to c<sup>h</sup>ange t<sup>h</sup>e counter<sup>’</sup>s appearance w<sup>h</sup>en typeset, <sup>i</sup>ssue t<sup>h</sup>e command 

\renewcommand{\thecounter}{new_style } 

<sup>where</sup> new_style <sup>s</sup>p<sup>ecifies the</sup> counter <sup>modified as shown in Table 14.3. The default</sup> style is arabic. For instance, if you give the command 

\renewcommand{\thetheorem}{\Alph{theorem}} 

then the theorems appear as Theorem A, Theorem B, . . . 

Here is a more complicated example for a book: 

\renewcommand{\thechapter}{\arabic{chapter}}

\renewcommand{\thesubsection} 

{\thechapter-\arabic{section}.\arabic{subsection}} 

With these definitions, Section 1 of Chapter 3 is numbered in the form 3-1 and Subsection 2 of Section 1 of Chapter 3 is numbered in the form 3-1.2. 

<sup>The</sup> \pagenumbering <sup>command is a shorthand method for settin</sup>g <sup>the</sup> p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>e num-</sup> <sup>berin</sup>g <sup>in a</sup> g<sup>iven st</sup>y<sup>le. For instance</sup>, \pagenumbering{roman} <sup>numbers</sup> p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>es as</sup> i, ii, and so on. 

<sup>The</sup> subequations <sup>environment</sup> (<sup>see</sup> <sup>Section</sup> <sup>6.6</sup>) <sup>uses</sup> parentequation <sup>as</sup> <sup>the</sup> <sup>counter for the whole e</sup>q<sup>uation</sup> g<sup>rou</sup>p <sup>and it uses</sup> equation <sup>as the counter for the sube-</sup> quations. To change the default format of the equation numbers from (2a), (2b), and so forth, to (2i), (2ii), and so on, type the following line inside the subequations environment

{\theparentequation\roman{equation}} 

If you want equation numbers like (2.i), (2.ii), and so on, type

## Counter arithmetic

<sup>The</sup> \stepcounter{counter} <sup>command increments</sup> counter <sup>and sets all the coun-</sup> <sup>ters that were defined with the o</sup>p<sup>tional ar</sup>g<sup>ument</sup> counter <sup>to</sup> 0<sup>. The variant</sup> 

\refstepcounter{counter} 

<sup>does the same</sup>, <sup>and also sets the value for the next</sup> \label <sup>command.</sup> 

You can do some arithmetic with the command 

\addtocounter{counter}{n } 

where n is an integer. For example, 

\setcounter{counter}{5} 

\addtocounter{counter}{2} 

<sup>sets</sup> counter <sup>to</sup> 7<sup>.</sup> 

<sup>The value stored in a counter can be accessed usin</sup>g <sup>the</sup> \value <sup>command</sup>, <sup>which</sup> <sup>is mostl</sup>y <sup>used with the</sup> \setcounter <sup>or</sup> \addtocounter <sup>commands. For instance</sup>, y<sup>ou can set</sup> counter <sup>to e</sup>q<sup>ual the value of another counter</sup>, oldcounter, <sup>b</sup>y <sup>t</sup>yp<sup>in</sup>g 

\setcounter{counter}{\value{oldcounter}} 

Here is a typical example of counter manipulation. You have a theorem (invoked <sup>in a</sup> theorem <sup>environment</sup>) <sup>and</sup> y<sup>ou want it followed b</sup>y <sup>several corollaries</sup> (<sup>each in</sup> a corollary environment) starting with Corollary 1. In other words, Theorem 1 should be followed by Corollary 1, Corollary 2, and so forth and so should Theorem 3. By default, L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X numbers the next corollary as Corollary 3, even if it follows another theorem. To tell L<sup>A</sup>TEX to start numbering the corollaries from 1 again, issue the command 

\setcounter{corollary}{0} 

after each theorem. But such a process is error-prone, and goes against the spirit of L<sup>A</sup>TEX. 

Instead, follow my advice on page 401, and let L<sup>A</sup>TEX do the work for you. In the preamble, type the proclamations 

\newtheorem{theorem}{Theorem} 

\newtheorem{corollary}{Corollary}[theorem] 

We are almost there. Theorem 1 now is followed by Corollary 1.1, Corollary 1.2 and Theorem 3 by Corollary 3.1. If we redefine \thecorollary, 

\renewcommand{\thecorollary}{\arabic{corollary}} 

then Theorem 1 is followed by Corollary 1 and Corollary 2, and Theorem 3 is also followed by Corollary 1. 

If you need to perform more complicated arithmetic with counters, use Kresten K. Thorup and Frank Jensen’s calc package (see Section 10.3.1). This package is discussed in Section A.3.1 of The L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X Companion, 2nd edition [56]. 

## Two special counters

<sup>The</sup> secnumdepth <sup>and</sup> tocdepth <sup>counters control which sectional units are numbered</sup> and which are listed in the table of contents, respectively. For example, 

\setcounter{secnumdepth}{2} 

<sup>sets</sup> secnumdepth <sup>to</sup> 2<sup>. As a result</sup>, <sup>cha</sup>p<sup>ters—if the</sup>y <sup>are</sup> p<sup>resent in the document</sup> class—sections, and subsections are numbered, but subsubsections are not. This com-<sup>mand must be</sup> p<sup>laced in the</sup> p<sup>reamble of the document.</sup> tocdepth <sup>is similar.</sup> 

## 14.5.2 Length commands

While a counter contains integers, a length command contains a real number and a dimensional unit. 

L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X recognizes many diferent dimensional units. We list five absolute units: 

cm <sup>centimeter</sup> 

in <sup>inch</sup> 

pc p<sup>ica</sup> (1 pc = 12 pt) 

tip p<sup>oint</sup> (1 in = 72.27 pt) 

mm <sup>millimeter</sup> 

and two relative units: 

em, approximately the width of the letter M in the current font 

ex, approximately the height of the letter x in the current font 

L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X defines many length commands. For instance, Section 4.1 of The L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X Companion, 2nd edition [56] lists 17 length commands for page layout alone. You can find some of them in Figure 8.4. A list environment sets about a dozen additional length commands (see Figure 14.2). Length commands are defined for almost every aspect of L<sup>A</sup>TEX’s work, including displayed math environments—a complete list would probably contain a few hundred. Many are listed in Leslie Lamport’s L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X: A Document Preparation System, 2nd edition [53] and in The L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X Companion, 2nd edition [56]. Many <sup>more are hidden in</sup> p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>es such as</sup> amsmath<sup>.</sup> 

The most common length commands are: 

\parindent, <sup>the</sup> <sup>amount</sup> <sup>of</sup> <sup>indentation</sup> <sup>at</sup> <sup>the</sup> <sup>be</sup>g<sup>innin</sup>g <sup>of</sup> <sup>a</sup> p<sup>ara</sup>g<sup>ra</sup>p<sup>h</sup> 

\parskip, <sup>the extra vertical s</sup>p<sup>ace inserted between</sup> p<sup>ara</sup>g<sup>ra</sup>p<sup>hs</sup> 

\textwidth, <sup>the width of the text on a</sup> p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>e</sup> 

<sup>A more esoteric exam</sup>p<sup>le is</sup> \marginparpush, <sup>the minimum vertical s</sup>p<sup>ace between two</sup> marginal notes. Luckily, you do not have to be familiar with many length commands because L<sup>A</sup>TEX and the document class set them for you. 

## Defining new length commands

You can define your own length commands. For example, 

\newlength{\mylength} 

<sup>makes</sup> \mylength <sup>a new len</sup>g<sup>th command with a value of 0</sup> p<sup>oints. Note that while</sup> you have to type 

\newcounter{counter} 

to get a new counter, typing 

\newlength{mylength} 

results in a message such as 

! Missing control sequence inserted. 

<inserted text> 

l.3 \newlength{mylength} 

## Setting length

<sup>The</sup> \setlength <sup>command sets or resets the value of a len</sup>g<sup>th command. So</sup> 

\setlength{\textwidth}{3in} 

<sup>creates a ver</sup>y <sup>narrow</sup> p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>e. The first ar</sup>g<sup>ument of</sup> \setlength <sup>must be a len</sup>g<sup>th com-</sup> mand, not simply the command name, that is 

\setlength{textwidth}{3in} % Bad 

<sup>is incorrect. The second ar</sup>g<sup>ument of</sup> \setlength <sup>must be a real number with a di-</sup> mensional unit, for instance, 3in, and not simply a real number. In other words, 

\setlength{\textwidth}{3} % Bad 

<sup>is also incorrect. You can also use</sup> \setlength <sup>as an environment</sup>, <sup>as in Section 7.3.</sup> 

Tip A common mistake is to type a command such as 

\setlength{\marginpar}{0} 

Instead, type 

\setlength{\marginpar}{0pt} 

Always be sure to include a dimensional unit. 

<sup>The</sup> \addtolength <sup>command adds a</sup> q<sup>uantit</sup>y <sup>to the value of a len</sup>g<sup>th command.</sup> For instance, 

\addtolength{\textwidth}{-10pt} 

narrows the page width by 10 points. 

If you define 

\newlength{\shorterlength} 

\setlength{\shorterlength}{\mylength} 

\addtolength{\shorterlength}{-.5in} 

<sup>then</sup> \parbox{\shorterlength}{...} <sup>alwa</sup>y<sup>s</sup> <sup>t</sup>yp<sup>esets</sup> <sup>its</sup> <sup>second</sup> <sup>ar</sup>g<sup>ument</sup> <sup>in</sup> <sup>a</sup> <sup>box</sup> <sup>1/2</sup> <sup>inch</sup> <sup>narrower</sup> <sup>than</sup> <sup>the</sup> p<sup>arboxes</sup> <sup>set</sup> <sup>to</sup> <sup>be</sup> <sup>of</sup> <sup>width</sup> \mylength<sup>.</sup> 

When L<sup>A</sup>TEX typesets some text or math, it creates a box. Three measurements are used to describe the size of the box: 

the width 

the height, from the baseline to the top 

the depth, from the baseline to the bottom 

as illustrated in Figure 14.1. For instance, the box typesetting “aa” has a width of 10.00003 pt, a height of 4.30554 pt, and a depth of 0 pt. The box typesetting “ag” has the same width and height, but a depth of 1.94444 pt. The box “Ag” (see Figure 14.1) has a width of 12.50003 pt, a height of 6.83331 pt, and a depth of 1.94444 pt. 

The commands 

\settowidth 

\settoheight 

\settodepth 

each take two arguments. The first argument is a length command, the second is text (or math) to be measured by L<sup>A</sup>TEX. The corresponding measurement of the box in which the second argument is typeset is assigned to the length command in the first argument. <sup>For</sup> <sup>exam</sup>p<sup>le</sup>, <sup>if</sup> \mylength <sup>is</sup> <sup>a</sup> <sup>len</sup>g<sup>th</sup> <sup>command</sup>, <sup>then</sup> 

\settowidth{\mylength}{Ag} 

<sup>assi</sup>g<sup>ns 12.50003</sup> p<sup>t to</sup> \mylength<sup>. It should be clear from this exam</sup>p<sup>le how the</sup> \phantom <sup>and</sup> \hphantom <sup>commands</sup> (<sup>see Section 3.8.1</sup>) <sup>are related to this command.</sup> 

To per<sup>f</sup>orm more comp<sup>li</sup>cated ar<sup>i</sup>t<sup>h</sup>met<sup>i</sup>c w<sup>i</sup>t<sup>h l</sup>engt<sup>h</sup> commands, use t<sup>h</sup>e calc package.

Figure 14.1: The measurements of a box.


## Rubber lengths

In addition to rigid lengths, such as 3in, L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X can also set rubber lengths, that is, lengths that are allowed to stretch and shrink. Here is an example: 

\setlength{\stretchspace}{3in plus 10pt minus 8pt} 

<sup>Assumin</sup>g <sup>that</sup> \stretchspace <sup>is a len</sup>g<sup>th command</sup>, <sup>this command assi</sup>g<sup>ns it a value</sup> of 3 inches that can stretch by 10 points or shrink by 8 points, if necessary. So a box of <sup>width</sup> \stretchspace <sup>is 3 inches wide</sup>, p<sup>lus u</sup>p <sup>to 10</sup> p<sup>oints</sup>, <sup>or minus u</sup>p <sup>to 8</sup> p<sup>oints.</sup> 

Stretchable vertical spaces are often used before and after displayed text environments. L<sup>A</sup>TEX adjusts these spaces to make the page look balanced. An example can be <sup>found in Section 14.1.8.</sup> \medskipamount <sup>is defined as</sup> 

6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0pt 

See Section 14.6.3 for more examples. 

T<sup>h</sup>e \fill command <sup>i</sup>s a spec<sup>i</sup>a<sup>l</sup> rubber <sup>l</sup>engt<sup>h</sup> t<sup>h</sup>at can stretc<sup>h</sup> any amount. T<sup>h</sup>e stretc<sup>hi</sup>ng <sup>i</sup>s done even<sup>l</sup>y <sup>if</sup> t<sup>h</sup>ere <sup>i</sup>s more t<sup>h</sup>an one \fill present. See t<sup>h</sup>e second example of brand-new environments in Section 14.2.5. 

## 14.6 Custom lists

Although there are three ready-made list environments provided by L<sup>A</sup>TEX (see Section 4.2), it is often necessary to create one of your own using L<sup>A</sup>TEX’s list environ-<sup>ment.</sup> <sup>In</sup> <sup>fact</sup>, <sup>LAT</sup>E<sup>X</sup> <sup>itself</sup> <sup>uses</sup> <sup>the</sup> list <sup>environment</sup> <sup>to</sup> <sup>define</sup> <sup>man</sup>y <sup>of</sup> <sup>its</sup> <sup>standard</sup> environments, including: 

The three list environments (Section 4.2) 

<sup>The</sup> quote, quotation, <sup>and</sup> verse <sup>environments</sup> (<sup>Section 4.8</sup>) 

Proclamations (Section 4.4) 

<sup>The st</sup>y<sup>le environments</sup> center, flushleft, <sup>and</sup> flushright (<sup>Section 4.3</sup>) 

<sup>The</sup> thebibliography <sup>environment</sup> (<sup>Section 8.5.1</sup>) 

<sup>The</sup> theindex <sup>environment</sup> (<sup>Section 8.5.2</sup>) 

## 14.6.1 Length commandsfor the list environment

The general layout of a list is shown in Figure 14.2. It uses six horizontal measurements and three vertical measurements. I now list these length commands.

Figure 14.2: The layout of a custom list.


## Vertical length commands

\topsep <sup>is</sup> <sup>most</sup> <sup>of</sup> <sup>the</sup> <sup>vertical</sup> <sup>s</sup>p<sup>ace</sup> <sup>between</sup> <sup>the</sup> <sup>first</sup> <sup>item</sup> <sup>and</sup> <sup>the</sup> p<sup>recedin</sup>g <sup>text</sup>, and also between the last item and the following text. This space also includes \parskip, t<sup>h</sup>e extra vert<sup>i</sup>ca<sup>l</sup> space <sup>i</sup>nserted between paragrap<sup>h</sup>s, and opt<sup>i</sup>ona<sup>ll</sup>y, \partopsep, p<sup>rovided that the list environment starts a new</sup> p<sup>ara</sup>g<sup>ra</sup>p<sup>h.</sup> 

\parsep <sup>is</sup> <sup>the</sup> <sup>s</sup>p<sup>ace</sup> <sup>between</sup> p<sup>ara</sup>g<sup>ra</sup>p<sup>hs</sup> <sup>of</sup> <sup>the</sup> <sup>same</sup> <sup>item.</sup> 

\itemsep <sup>is the s</sup>p<sup>ace between items. Like</sup> \topsep, <sup>the actual</sup> g<sup>a</sup>p <sup>is the sum of</sup> \itemsep <sup>and</sup> \parsep<sup>.</sup> 

All of these vertical length commands are rubber lengths (see Section 14.5.2). 

## Horizontal length commands

By de<sup>f</sup>au<sup>l</sup>t, t<sup>h</sup>e marg<sup>i</sup>ns o<sup>f</sup> a list env<sup>i</sup>ronment are t<sup>h</sup>e same as t<sup>h</sup>e marg<sup>i</sup>ns o<sup>f</sup> t<sup>h</sup>e surrounding text. If the list is nested within a list, the margins are wider and so the text is narrower. 

<sup>The</sup> \leftmargin <sup>and</sup> \rightmargin <sup>len</sup>g<sup>th commands s</sup>p<sup>ecif</sup>y <sup>the distance</sup> between the edge of the item box and the left and right margins of the page. 

<sup>The</sup> label <sup>is the text</sup> p<sup>rovided b</sup>y <sup>the o</sup>p<sup>tional ar</sup>g<sup>ument of an</sup> \item <sup>command</sup> or provided as a default in the definition of the list environment. It is typeset in a box of <sup>width</sup> \labelwidth, <sup>which is indented</sup> \itemindent <sup>units from the left mar</sup>g<sup>in</sup>, <sup>and</sup> <sup>se</sup>p<sup>arated b</sup>y <sup>a s</sup>p<sup>ace of</sup> \labelsep <sup>units from the text box. If the label is too wide to</sup> fit in the box, it is typeset at its full natural width, and the first line in the text box is indented. 

The second and subsequent paragraphs of an item are typeset with their first lines <sup>indented b</sup>y \listparindent <sup>units.</sup> 

## 14.6.2 The list environment

<sup>Custom lists are created with the</sup> list <sup>environment</sup>, <sup>which is invoked as follows:</sup> 

```latex
\begin{list}{default_label}{declarations}
    \item item1
    \item item2
...
\end{list} 
```

The arguments are 

default_label, <sup>the label for an</sup>y <sup>items that do not s</sup>p<sup>ecif</sup>y <sup>their own</sup>, <sup>similar to the</sup> <sup>o</sup>p<sup>tional ar</sup>g<sup>ument of the</sup> \item <sup>command</sup> 

declarations, <sup>the vertical and horizontal len</sup>g<sup>th commands and an</sup>y <sup>other re</sup>q<sup>uired</sup> parameters for the list 

Here is a very simple example: 

Here are the most important L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X rules about spaces in text, sentences, and paragraphs: 

♢ Rule 1: Two or more spaces in text are the same as one. 

♢ Rule 2: A blank line (that is, two end-of-line characters separated only by blanks and tabs) indicates the end of a paragraph. 

Rules 1 and 2 make typing and copying very convenient. 

I have used the ♢ math symbol ($\diamondsuit$) as a default label, and I set the item box 0.5 inch from either margin. So this example is typed as follows: 

```latex
\noindent Here are the most important \la\ rules about spaces in text, sentences, and paragraphs:
\begin{list}{\(diamondsuit${setlength{\leftmargin}\%{.5in}\setlength{\rightmargin}{.5in}\}
\item \textbf{Rule 1:} Two or more spaces in text are the same as one.
\item \textbf{Rule 2:} A blank line (that is, two end-of-line characters separated only by blanks and tabs) indicates the end of a paragraph.
\end{list}
Rules 1 and~2 make typing and copying very convenient. 
```

Here is a second variant: 

Here are the most important L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X rules about spaces in text, sentences, and paragraphs: 

Rule 1: Two or more consecutive spaces in text are the same as one. 

Rule 2: A blank line (that is, two end-of-line characters separated only by blanks and tabs) indicates the end of a paragraph. 

Rules 1 and 2 make typing and copying very convenient. 

In this example, I dropped the optional default_label and typed Rule 1: and Rule 2: as (optional) arguments of the \item commands: 

\noindent Here are the most important \la\ rules about spaces in text, sentences, and paragraphs: \begin{list}{}{\setlength{\leftmargin}{.5in}% \setlength{\rightmargin}{.5in}} 

```latex
\newcounter{spacerule} 
```

```latex
\item[\textbf{Rule 1:}] Two or more consecutive spaces in text are the same as one.
\item[\textbf{Rule 2:}] A blank line (that is, two end-of-line characters separated only by blanks and tabs) indicates the end of a paragraph.
\end{list}
Rules 1 and~2 make typing and copying very convenient. 
```

For further simple examples, you can look at various document class files to see how <sup>standard environments such as</sup> verse, quote, <sup>and so on</sup>, <sup>are defined.</sup> 

## Using counters

It is not very L<sup>A</sup>TEX-like to provide the numbers for the rules in the examples above. It would be more logical for L<sup>A</sup>TEX to do the numbering. The following is a more L<sup>A</sup>TEXlike coding of the second example: 

```latex
\noindent Here are the most important \la\ rules about
spaces in text, sentences, and paragraphs:
\newcounter{spacerule}
\begin{list}{\textbf{Rule \arabic{spacerule}:}}
{\setlength{\leftmargin}{.5in}
\setlength{\rightmargin}{.5in}
\usecounter{spacerule}}
\item Two or more consecutive spaces in text are the
same as one.\label{Li:Twoor}
\item A blank line (that is, two end-of-line
characters separated only by blanks and tabs)
indicates the end of a paragraph. \label{Li:blankline}
\end{list}
Rules \ref{Li:Twoor} and~\ref{Li:blankline} make typing
and copying very convenient. 
```

## Note that

<sup>1. I declared the counter before the</sup> list <sup>environment with the line</sup> 

<sup>2. I defined the</sup> default_label <sup>as</sup> 

```latex
\textbf{Rule \arabic{spacerule}:} 
```

```latex
3. In the declarations, I specified that the list should use the spacerule counter with the command
\usecounter{spacerule} 
```

## 14.6.3 Two complete examples

<sup>In the</sup> p<sup>revious exam</sup>p<sup>les</sup>, <sup>I set the values of</sup> \leftmargin <sup>and</sup> \rightmargin<sup>. The</sup> other length commands were not redefined, so their values remained the values set by the document class. In the following examples, I set the values of many more length commands. 

Example 1 To get the following list, 

Here are the most important L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X rules about spaces in text, sentences, and paragraphs: 

Rule 1: Two or more consecutive spaces in text are the same as one. 

Rule 2: A blank line—that is, two end-of-line characters separated only by blanks and tabs— indicates the end of a paragraph. 

Rules 1 and 2 make typing and copying very convenient. 

## we type

```latex
\noindent Here are the most important \la\ rules about spaces in text, sentences, and paragraphs:
\newcounter{spacerule}
\begin{list}{\upshape\bfseries Rule \arabic{spacerule}:}
{\setlength{\leftmargin}{1.5in}
\setlength{\rightmargin}{0.6in}
\setlength{\labelwidth}{1.0in}
\setlength{\labelsep}{0.2in}
\setlength{\parsep}{0.5ex plus 0.2ex minus 0.1ex}
\setlength{\itemsep}{0ex plus 0.2ex minus 0ex}
\usecounter{spacerule}
\itshape}
\item Two or more consecutive spaces in text are the same as one.\label{Li:Twoor}
\item A blank line---that is, two end-of-line characters separated only by blanks and tabs---indicates
the end of a paragraph.\label{Li:blankline}
\end{list}
Rules \ref{Li:Twoor} and~\ref{Li:blankline} make typing and copying very convenient. 
```

Note that 

1. I declared the counter as in the previous example. 

<sup>2. The last item in</sup> declarations <sup>is</sup> \itshape, <sup>which t</sup>yp<sup>esets the entire list in italics.</sup> 

<sup>3. The</sup> default_label <sup>is defined as</sup> 

\upshape\bfseries Rule \arabic{spacerule} 

My first attempt was to define it as 

\bfseries Rule \arabic{spacerule} 

w<sup>hi</sup>c<sup>h</sup> typesets Rule <sup>i</sup>n bo<sup>l</sup>d <sup>i</sup>ta<sup>li</sup>cs (because <sup>i</sup>n Step <sup>2</sup> we set t<sup>h</sup>e w<sup>h</sup>o<sup>l</sup>e <sup>li</sup>st <sup>i</sup>n <sup>i</sup>ta<sup>l</sup>- <sup>ics</sup>)<sup>.</sup> <sup>To</sup> <sup>force</sup> <sup>the</sup> <sup>label</sup> <sup>to</sup> <sup>be</sup> <sup>t</sup>yp<sup>eset</sup> <sup>u</sup>p<sup>ri</sup>g<sup>ht</sup>, <sup>I</sup> <sup>start</sup> <sup>the</sup> default_label <sup>with</sup> <sup>the</sup> \upshape <sup>command.</sup> 

4. The left margin is set to 1.5 inches and the right margin to 0.6 inches: 

\setlength{\leftmargin}{1.5in} \setlength{\rightmargin}{0.6in} 

5. Next I set the width of the label to 1 inch, and the space between the label and the item to 0.2 inches: 

\setlength{\labelwidth}{1.0in} \setlength{\labelsep}{0.2in} 

6. Finally, I set the paragraph separation to 0.5 ex, allowing stretching by 0.2 ex and shrinking by 0.1 ex, and the item separation to 0 ex, allowing stretching by 0.2 ex and no shrinking, by 

\setlength{\parsep}{0.5ex plus 0.2ex minus 0.1ex} \setlength{\itemsep}{0ex plus 0.2ex minus 0ex} 

The actual amount of item separation is calculated by adding the values specified for \parsep <sup>and</sup> \itemsep<sup>.</sup> 

A complicated list such as this should be defined as a new environment. For ex-<sup>am</sup>p<sup>le</sup>, y<sup>ou could define a</sup> myrules <sup>environment:</sup> 

```latex
\newenvironment{myrules}
{\begin{list}
{\upshape \bfseries Rule \arabic{spacerule}:}
{\setlength{\leftmargin}{1.5in}
\setlength{\rightmargin}{0.6in}
\setlength{\labelwidth}{1.0in}
\setlength{\labelsep}{0.2in}
\setlength{\parsep}{0.5ex plus 0.2ex minus 0.1ex} 
```

```latex
\setlength{\itemsep}{0ex plus 0.2ex minus 0ex}
\usecounter{spacerule}
\itshape} }
{\end{list}} 
```

and then use it anywhere, as in 

```latex
\begin{myrules}
    \item Two or more consecutive spaces in text are the same as one.\label{Li:Twoor}
    \item A blank line---that is, two end-of-line characters separated only by blanks and tabs---indicates the end of a paragraph.
    \label{Li:blankline}
Rules \ref{Li:Twoor} and~\ref{Li:blankline} make typing \end{myrules}
and copying very convenient. 
```

which typesets as the first example shown on page 413. 

Example 2 In Section 3.7.2, we discussed the formatting of the following type of glossary: 

sentence a group of words terminated by a period, exclamation point, or question mark. 

paragraph a group of sentences terminated by a blank line or by the new paragraph command. 

Now we can create the glossary as a custom list: 

```latex
\begin{list}{}  
{\setlength{\leftmargin}{30pt}  
    \setlength{\rightmargin}{0pt}  
    \setlength{\itemindent}{14pt}  
    \setlength{\labelwidth}{40pt}  
    \setlength{\labelsep}{5pt}  
    \setlength{\parsep}{0.5ex plus 0.2ex minus 0.1ex}  
    \setlength{\itemsep}{0ex plus 0.2ex minus 0ex}}  
    \item[\textbf{sentence}\hfill] is a group of words terminated by a period, exclamation point, or question mark.  
    \item[\textbf{paragraph}\hfill] is a group of sentences terminated by a blank line or by the \com{par} command.  
\end{list} 
```

T<sup>h</sup>ere <sup>i</sup>s not<sup>hi</sup>ng new <sup>i</sup>n t<sup>hi</sup>s examp<sup>l</sup>e except t<sup>h</sup>e \hfill commands <sup>i</sup>n t<sup>h</sup>e opt<sup>i</sup>ona<sup>l</sup> arguments to left adjust the labels. With the long words in the example this adjustment is not necessary, but it would be needed for shorter words. 

See Section 3.3 of The L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X Companion, 2nd edition [56] on how to customize the three standard list environments and also for more complicated custom lists. 

## 14.6.4 The trivlist environment

<sup>LAT</sup>E<sup>X also</sup> p<sup>rovides a</sup> trivlist <sup>environment</sup>, <sup>meant more for</sup> p<sup>ro</sup>g<sup>rammers than users.</sup> The environment is invoked in the form 

```latex
\begin{trivlist}
    body
\end{trivlist} 
```

## 14.7 The dangers of customization

We can customize L<sup>A</sup>TEX in so many ways. We can add packages to expand its power and define new commands that better suit our work habits. These enhance LAT<sub>E</sub>X and make it easier to work with. But they also introduce dificulties. Let us start with the obvious. 

<sup>Whoever introduced the command</sup> \textcompwordmark <sup>knew that—even if we</sup> use command completion—we are not going to type 

## if\textcompwordmark f

to avoid having a ligature (see Section 3.4.6). It is a lot of typing, and the source file <sup>becomes hard to read. This cries out for a custom command</sup>, <sup>sa</sup>y, \Iff, <sup>which is short</sup> and readable (see Section 14.1.1). 

When introducing custom commands, watch out for the following traps. 

Trap 1 Redefining a command that is a necessary part of LAT<sub>E</sub>X. 

This is easy to avoid. As discussed in Section 14.1.8, you can easily find out whether a command is already in use. If it is, do not redefine it unless you really know what you are doing. 

Trap 2 Defining too many commands. 

This creates two problems. Your editor has a hard time making changes in your source file. And a few years later, when you want to reuse the material, you have a dificult time understanding all those clever commands. 

Trap 3 Your contribution appears in a volume with many other authors and your custom commands create conflicts. 

As your article appears in a publication, some parts of it are used for the whole volume. The title and maybe even the section titles are used in the table of contents. The abstracts may be collected for the whole volume or there may be a joint bibliography. 

With the advent of the internet, there are now collections of thousands of math articles; PlanetMath.org is one example. Write your articles so that even the editors of PlanetMath.org can use it. 

Rule 1 Do not use your own commands in the title of the article, in the abstract, in section titles, in the bibliography, or in captions of figures and tables. 

Trap 4 You submit the article to a journal that does not permit a separate custom command file. 

For such journals, just copy the needed custom commands into the preamble of your article. Go through the list and delete those custom commands that are not used in this article. This helps the editor to look up your commands from a shorter list. 

Rule 2 Introduce judiciously custom commands with very short names. 

Introducing one-letter commands—for instance, using \C for the complex field— is dangerous because many one-letter commands are reserved by L<sup>A</sup>TEX. 

Two-letter custom commands are not quite this bad. Of the 2,500 or so possibil ities only a few dozen are used by L<sup>A</sup>TEX. The danger here is, of course, conflict with other authors and confusion for the editor. My command file has about 15 two-letter <sup>commands. For instance</sup> \jj, p<sup>art of the</sup> \jj, \JJ, \JJm <sup>famil</sup>y<sup>. Also</sup> \Id, <sup>because</sup> Id is the standard notation for ideal lattices. Some editors may think that this is 15 too many. 

Rule 3 Do not use \def to define your commands, with the exception of a very few delimited commands. 

Using \def means giving up L<sup>A</sup>TEX’s built in defense. In the editorial ofice of my journal, about half the submitted articles that we cannot typeset violate this rule. 

Rule 4 Do not redefine length commands, especially, if you do not know what other length commands are computed based on the ones you change. 

The page layout diagram, Figure 8.4, should provide examples. Even simpler, Do not redefine length commands. Let the document class define them for your article. 

Rule 5 Make sure that the packages you use are compatible. 

<sup>For instance</sup>, <sup>the</sup> p<sup>o</sup>p<sup>ular</sup> psfrag <sup>and</sup> epsfig p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>es cause</sup> p<sup>roblems if used</sup> with the AMS packages. 

Be cautious when you use packages that redefine a lot of L<sup>A</sup>TEX commands, such <sup>as</sup> hyperref (<sup>see Section 11.2</sup>)<sup>.</sup> 

You can read more about the plight of authors in the hands of incompetent editors in my article [32] and the dificult job of editors with articles violating the above rules in Enrico Gregorio [16]. 

# Long Documents

# BIBT<sub>E</sub>X

The BIBTEX application, written by Oren Patashnik, assists L<sup>A</sup>TEX users in compiling bibliographies, especially long ones. Short bibliographies can easily be placed in the document directly (see Section 8.5.1). 

It takes a little efort to learn BIBTEX. But in the long run, the advantages of building bibliographic databases that can be reused and shared outweigh the disadvantage of a somewhat steep learning curve. The bibliographic database files, the bib files, contain the bibliographic entries. We discuss the format of these entries in Section 15.1, and then describe how to use BIBTEX to create bibliographies in Section 15.2. 

BIBT<sub>E</sub>X uses a style, called a bibliographic style, or bst file, to format entries. <sup>On</sup> <sup>the</sup> <sup>next</sup> <sup>two</sup> p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>es</sup> <sup>we</sup> <sup>show</sup> <sup>the</sup> <sup>biblio</sup>g<sup>ra</sup>p<sup>h</sup>y <sup>of</sup> <sup>the</sup> secondarticleb.tex <sup>sam</sup>p<sup>le</sup> article typeset with six diferent style files. 

To simplify our discussion, in the rest of this chapter I discuss only one style, <sup>the AMS</sup> p<sup>lain st</sup>y<sup>le</sup>, amsplain.bst, <sup>version 2.0. All of the exam</sup>p<sup>les shown are in</sup> this style, and several of the comments I make are true only for the AMS plain style. If you choose to use a diferent style, you should check its documentation for special rules.
