## ieeetr.bst

## 15.1 The database

A BIBTEX database is a text file containing bibliographic entries. To use BIBTEX, you first have to learn how to assemble a database. This section explains how to do that. 

There may be special tools available for your computer system that assist you in building and maintaining your bibliographic data. Such tools make compiling the data easier and may minimize formatting errors. 

<sup>You can find all the exam</sup>p<sup>les in this section in the</sup> template.bib <sup>file in the</sup> samples <sup>folder</sup> (<sup>see</sup> p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>e 5</sup>)<sup>.</sup> 

## 15.1.1 Entry types

A bibliographic entry is given in pieces called fields. The style (see Section 15.2.2) specifies how these fields are typeset. Here are two typical entries: 

@BOOK{gM68, 

```lua
author = "George A. Menuhin",
title = "Universal Algebra",
publisher = "D.~Van Nostrand",
address = "Princeton",
year = 1968,
} 
```

```bib
@ARTICLE{eM57,
author = "Ernest T. Moynahan",
title = "On a Problem of {M. Stone}", 
```

```txt
journal = "Acta Math. Acad. Sci. Hungar.", pages = "455-460", volume = 8, year = 1957, } 
```

The start of an entry is indicated with an at sign (@) followed by the entry type. In the <sup>first exam</sup>p<sup>le</sup>, <sup>the entr</sup>y <sup>t</sup>yp<sup>e is</sup> BOOK, w<sup>hile in the second</sup>, <sup>it is</sup> ARTICLE<sup>. The entr</sup>y <sup>t</sup>yp<sup>e</sup> is followed by a left brace ({). The matching right brace (}) indicates the end of the entry. BIBTEX also allows you to use parentheses as delimiters for an entry. In this book, however, we use braces to enclose an entry. 

T<sup>h</sup>e str<sup>i</sup>ng @BOOK{ <sup>i</sup>s <sup>f</sup>o<sup>ll</sup>owed by a label, gM68, w<sup>hi</sup>c<sup>h</sup> des<sup>i</sup>gnates t<sup>h</sup>e name o<sup>f</sup> t<sup>h</sup>e <sup>entr</sup>y<sup>. Refer to this entr</sup>y <sup>in</sup> y<sup>our document with</sup> \cite{gM68}<sup>. The label is followed</sup> <sup>b</sup>y <sup>a comma and a series of fields. In this exam</sup>p<sup>le</sup>, <sup>there are five fields</sup>, author, title, publisher, address, <sup>and</sup> year<sup>.</sup> <sup>Each</sup> <sup>field</sup> <sup>starts</sup> <sup>with</sup> <sup>the</sup> <sup>field</sup> <sup>name</sup>, <sup>followed</sup> <sup>b</sup>y = and the value of the field enclosed in double quotes ("). Be sure to use " and not L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X double quotes ( “ or ” ). Alternatively, BIBT<sub>E</sub>X also allows you to use braces to enclose the field value. In this book, we use double quotes to enclose a field. 

Numeric field values, that is, fields consisting entirely of digits, do not need to be <sup>enclosed in double</sup> q<sup>uotes or braces</sup>, <sup>for instance</sup>, year <sup>in the exam</sup>p<sup>les above</sup>, volume <sup>i</sup>n t<sup>h</sup>e second examp<sup>l</sup>e, and number <sup>i</sup>n some o<sup>f</sup> t<sup>h</sup>e examp<sup>l</sup>es t<sup>h</sup>at <sup>f</sup>o<sup>ll</sup>ow. Page ranges, <sup>such as</sup> 455-460, <sup>are not numeric field</sup> v<sup>alues since the</sup>y <sup>contain</sup> -, <sup>so the</sup>y <sup>must be</sup> enclosed in double quotes or braces. 

There must be a comma before each field. The comma before the first field is placed after the label. 

There are many standard entry types, including 

ARTICLE <sup>an article in a</sup> j<sup>ournal or ma</sup>g<sup>azine</sup> 

BOOK <sup>a</sup> <sup>book</sup> <sup>with</sup> <sup>an</sup> <sup>author</sup> (<sup>or</sup> <sup>editor</sup>) <sup>and</sup> <sup>a</sup> p<sup>ublisher</sup> 

BOOKLET <sup>a</sup> p<sup>rinted</sup> <sup>work</sup> <sup>without</sup> <sup>a</sup> p<sup>ublisher</sup> 

INBOOK a part of a book, such as a chapter or a page range that, in general, is not titled or authored separately 

INCOLLECTION <sup>a</sup> p<sup>art of a book with its own title and</sup> p<sup>erha</sup>p<sup>s author</sup> 

INPROCEEDINGS <sup>an article in a conference</sup> p<sup>roceedin</sup>g<sup>s with its own title and</sup> author 

MANUAL <sup>technical documentation</sup> 

MASTERSTHESIS <sup>a master’s thesis</sup> 

MISC an entry t<sup>h</sup>at does not <sup>fi</sup>t <sup>i</sup>n any ot<sup>h</sup>er category 

PHDTHESIS <sup>a Ph.D. thesis</sup> 

PROCEEDINGS <sup>the</sup> p<sup>roceedin</sup>g<sup>s of a conference</sup> 

TECHREPORT <sup>a re</sup>p<sup>ort</sup> p<sup>ublished b</sup>y <sup>a school or institution</sup> 

UNPUBLISHED <sup>an</sup> <sup>un</sup>p<sup>ublished</sup> p<sup>a</sup>p<sup>er</sup> 

Each entry includes a number offields from the following list: 

<table><tr><td>address</td><td>institution</td><td>pages</td></tr><tr><td>author</td><td>journal</td><td>publisher</td></tr><tr><td>booktitle</td><td>key</td><td>school</td></tr><tr><td>chapter</td><td>language</td><td>series</td></tr><tr><td>crossref</td><td>month</td><td>title</td></tr><tr><td>edition</td><td>note</td><td>type</td></tr><tr><td>editor</td><td>number</td><td>volume</td></tr><tr><td>howpublished</td><td>organization</td><td>year</td></tr></table>

The style you choose determines which of the fields within an entry are actually used. All the others are ignored. You may also add fields for your own use. For example, you <sup>ma</sup>y <sup>want to add a</sup> mycomments <sup>field for</sup> p<sup>ersonal comments. Such fields are i</sup>g<sup>nored</sup> unless you have a bibliography style that uses them. 

<sup>Commonl</sup>y <sup>used exam</sup>p<sup>les of new field names include</sup> URL, abstract, ISBN, keywords, mrnumber, <sup>and so on. The</sup> language <sup>field is used b</sup>y <sup>the AMS st</sup>y<sup>les but</sup> not by any of the other styles mentioned in this chapter. 

## Tip

1. BIBT X does not care whether you use uppercase or lowercase letters (or mixed) for the names of entry types and fields. In this book, the entry types are shown in uppercase and field names in lowercase. 

2. Placing a comma after the last field is optional. I recommend that you put it there so that when you append a new field to the entry, the required comma separating the fields is present. 

For each entry type there are both required and optional fields. Later in this section, I give two examples of each entry type. The first example of an entry type uses a small set of fields, while the second example is a maximal one, showing a large number of optional fields. 

## 15.1.2 Typing fields

Make sure you type the field names correctly. If you misspell one, BIBTEX ignores the <sup>field. B</sup>IB<sup>T</sup>E<sup>X also warns</sup> y<sup>ou if a re</sup>q<sup>uired field is missin</sup>g<sup>. The</sup> author <sup>and</sup> editor fields require a name. 

## Rule Names

<sup>1. Most names can be t</sup>yp<sup>ed as usual</sup>, "Ernest T. Moynahan" <sup>or</sup> "Moynahan, Ernest T.", <sup>with one comma se</sup>p<sup>aratin</sup>g <sup>the famil</sup>y <sup>name from the</sup> g<sup>iven names.</sup> 

2. Type two or more names separated by and. For instance, 

author= "George Blue and Ernest Brown and Soo-Key Foo", 

3. The family name of Miguel Lopez Fernandez is Lopez Fernandez, so type it as "Lopez Fernandez, Miguel"<sup>.</sup> <sup>This</sup> <sup>informs</sup> <sup>B</sup>IB<sup>T</sup>E<sup>X</sup> <sup>that</sup> <sup>Lo</sup>p<sup>ez</sup> <sup>is</sup> <sup>not</sup> <sup>a</sup> <sup>middle</sup> name. 

<sup>4. T</sup>yp<sup>e Orrin Frink</sup>, <sup>Jr. as</sup> "Frink, Jr., Orrin"<sup>.</sup> 

Rules 3 and 4 are seldom needed. In a bibliography of about 1,500 items, I found fewer than 10 names that could not be typed as usual. Note that you can type John <sup>von Neumann as</sup> "John von Neumann" <sup>or</sup> "von Neumann, John"<sup>. Because B</sup>IB<sup>T</sup>E<sup>X</sup> knows about von, it handles the name properly. 

<sup>There are a few rules concernin</sup>g <sup>the</sup> title <sup>field.</sup> 

## Rule Title

1. You should not put a period at the end of a title. The style supplies the appropriate punctuation. 

2. Many styles, including the AMS styles, convert titles, except for the first letter of the title, to lowercase for all entry types. If you want a letter to appear in uppercase, p<sup>ut it—or the entire word—in braces. The same rule a</sup>pp<sup>lies to the</sup> edition <sup>field.</sup> Some other styles only do this conversion for the titles of non-book-like entries. 

3. To maximize the portability of your database, you should type titles with each important word capitalized: 

title = "On a Problem of {M. Stone}", 

<sup>The st</sup>y<sup>le used in this book</sup>, amsplain.bst, <sup>converts</sup> Problem <sup>to</sup> problem, <sup>so it</sup> makes no diference, but some styles do not. To be on the safe side, you should capitalize all words that may have to be capitalized. 

For the record, here are the complete rules for titles: 

## Rule Capitalize:

1. the first word; 

2. the first word in a subtitle (BIBT<sub>E</sub>X assumes that a subtitle follows a colon, so it capitalizes the first word after a colon—a colon not introducing a subtitle should be typed in braces); 

3. all other words except articles, unstressed conjunctions, and unstressed prepositions. 

Words that should never be converted to lowercase, for example proper names such <sup>as</sup> Hilbert, <sup>should be enclosed in braces to</sup> p<sup>revent them from bein</sup>g <sup>converted to</sup> lowercase. In the example above, two letters in the title should not be converted to <sup>lowercase</sup>, <sup>so we enclosed</sup> M. Stone <sup>in braces. We could also have t</sup>yp<sup>ed</sup> 

{M. S}tone+ or \verb+{M.} {S}tone 

BIBTEX and the style automatically handle a number of things for you that you would have to handle yourself when typing text. 

1. You do not have to mark periods in abbreviations, as .\␣ in the names of journals (see Section 3.2.2). So 

journal = "Acta Math. Acad. Sci. Hungar.", 

typesets correctly. 

2. You can type a single hyphen for a page range instead of the usual -- in the pages field (see Section 3.4.2). So 

pages = "455-460", 

typesets correctly with an en dash. 

<sup>3. You do not have to t</sup>yp<sup>e nonbreakable s</sup>p<sup>aces with</sup> ˜ <sup>in the</sup> author <sup>or</sup> editor <sup>fields</sup> (see Section 3.4.3): 

author = "George A. Menuhin", 

<sup>is correct. Normall</sup>y y<sup>ou would t</sup>yp<sup>e</sup> George˜A. Menuhin<sup>.</sup> 

Finally, we state a rule about accented characters. 

## Rule Accents

Put accented characters in braces: {\"{a}}. 

This rule means that 

```txt
author = "Paul Erd\H{o}s", 
```

is not recommended. Instead, type 

```javascript
author = "Paul Erd{\H{o}}s", 
```

<sup>This rule is</sup>, <sup>a</sup>g<sup>ain</sup>, <sup>about</sup> p<sup>ortabilit</sup>y<sup>. Some st</sup>y<sup>les</sup>, <sup>e.</sup>g<sup>.</sup>, alpha <sup>and</sup> amsalpha, <sup>create a</sup> citation for an article from the first three letters of the name and the last two digits of the year. 

```txt
author = "Kurt G{\\"{o}}del",
year = 1931, 
```

creates the citation: [Göd31]. The accent is used only if the accents rule has been followed. 

The downside of this rule is that the braces suppress kerning. 

## 15.1.3 Articles

Entry type ARTICLE Required fields author, title, journal, year, pages Optional fields volume, number, language, note 

Examples: 

1. Ernest T. Moynahan, On a problem of M. Stone, Acta Math. Acad. Sci. Hungar. 8 (1957), 455–460. 

2. Ernest T. Moynahan, On a problem of M. Stone, Acta Math. Acad. Sci. Hungar. 8 (1957), no. 5, 455–460 (English), Russian translation available. 

typed as 

```bib
@ARTICLE{eM57,
author = "Ernest T. Moynahan",
title = "On a Problem of {M. Stone}",
journal = "Acta Math. Acad. Sci. Hungar.",
pages = "455-460",
volume = 8,
year = 1957,
} 
```

```bib
@ARTICLE{eM57a,
author = "Ernest T. Moynahan",
title = "On a Problem of {M. Stone}",
journal = "Acta Math. Acad. Sci. Hungar.",
pages = "455-460", 
```

```txt
volume = 8,
number = 5,
year = 1957,
note = "Russian translation available",
language = "English",
} 
```

## 15.1.4 Books

Entry type BOOK Required fields author (<sup>or</sup> editor), title, publisher, year Optional fields edition, series, volume, number, address, month, language, note 

Examples: 

1. George A. Menuhin, Universal algebra, D. Van Nostrand, Princeton, 1968. 2. George A. Menuhin, Universal algebra, second ed., University Series in Higher Mathematics, vol. 58, D. Van Nostrand, Princeton, March 1968 (English), no Russian translation. 

```bib
typed as
@BOOK{gM68,
    author = "George A. Menuhin",
    title = "Universal Algebra",
    publisher = "D.~Van Nostrand",
    address = "Princeton",
    year = 1968,
    }

@BOOK{gM68a,
    author = "George A. Menuhin",
    title = "Universal Algebra",
    publisher = "D.~Van Nostrand",
    address = "Princeton",
    year = 1968,
    month = mar,
    series = "University Series in Higher Mathematics",
    volume = 58,
    edition = "Second",
    note = "no Russian translation",
    language = "English",
}

Abbreviations, such as mar, are discussed in Section 15.1.9. 
```

```bib
15. Robert S. Prescott (ed.), Universal algebra, D. Van Nostrand, Princeton, 1968.
typed as
@BOOK{rP68,
editor = "Robert S. Prescott",
title = "Universal Algebra",
publisher = "D.~Van Nostrand",
address = "Princeton",
year = 1968,
} 
```

<sup>A second variant of book has an</sup> editor <sup>instead of an</sup> author<sup>:</sup> 

## 15.1.5 Conference proceedings and collections

```txt
Entry type INPROCEEDINGS
Required fields author, title, booktitle, year
Optional fields address, editor, series, volume, number,
organization, publisher, month, note, pages, language 
```

Examples: 

7. Peter A. Konig, Composition of functions. Proceedings of the Conference on Universal Algebra, 1970. 

8. Peter A. Konig, Composition of functions. Proceedings of the Conference on Universal Algebra (Kingston, ON) (G. H. Birnbaum, ed.), vol. 7, Canadian Mathematical Society, Queen’s Univ., December 1970, available from the Montreal ofice, pp. 1–106 (English). 

typed as 

```bib
@INPROCEEDINGS{pK69,
```

## Cross-referencing

If your database has several articles from the same conference proceedings and collections, you may prefer to make an entry for the entire volume, and cross-reference individual articles to that entry. For instance, 

```bib
@PROCEEDINGS{UA69,
    title = "Proceedings of the Conference on,
    Universal Algebra",
    booktitle = "Proceedings of the Conference on
    Universal Algebra",
    address = "Kingston, ON",
    publisher = "Canadian Mathematical Society",
    editor = "G. H. Birnbaum",
    volume = 7,
    year = 1970,
} 
```

may be the entry for the proceedings volume as a whole, and 

```bib
@INPROCEEDINGS{pK69a,
author = "Peter A. Konig",
title = "Composition of Functions",
booktitle = "Proceedings of the Conference on Universal Algebra",
pages = "1-106",
crossref = "UA69",
} 
```

is the cross-referencing entry for a specific article. These two entries produce the following: 

```txt
1. G. H. Birnbaum (ed.), Proceedings of the conference on universal algebra, vol. 7, Kingston, ON, Canadian Mathematical Society, 1970. 
```

2. Peter A. Konig, Composition of functions, in Birnbaum [1], pp. 1–106. 

## Rule Cross-references

1. All the required fields of the cross-referencing entry must appear in either that entry or in the cross-referenced entry. 

<sup>2. The cross-referenced entr</sup>y <sup>should have both a</sup> title <sup>and a</sup> booktitle <sup>field.</sup> 

3. The cross-referenced entry must appear in the bib file later than any entry that crossreferences it.

```lua
Entry type BOOKLET
Required field title

Entry type INBOOK

Entry type MANUAL
Required field title
Optional fields author, organization, address, edition, month, year, note
Entry type MISC
Required field at least one of the optional fields must be present
Optional fields author, title, howpublished, month, year, note, pages
Entry type PROCEEDINGS
Required fields title, year
Optional fields editor, series, volume, number, address, organization, publisher, month, note 
```

## 15.1.9 Abbreviations

<sup>You ma</sup>y <sup>have noticed the field</sup> month = dec <sup>in some of the exam</sup>p<sup>les. This field uses</sup> an abbreviation. Most BIBTEX styles, including the AMS styles, include abbreviations <sup>for the months of the</sup> y<sup>ear:</sup> jan, feb, <sup>. . .</sup> , dec<sup>. When an abbreviation is used</sup>, <sup>it is not</sup> enclosed in quotes (") or braces ({ }). The style defines what is actually to be typeset. Most styles typeset dec as either Dec. or December. 

T<sup>h</sup>e name o<sup>f</sup> t<sup>h</sup>e abbrev<sup>i</sup>at<sup>i</sup>on, suc<sup>h</sup> as dec, <sup>i</sup>s a str<sup>i</sup>ng o<sup>f</sup> c<sup>h</sup>aracters t<sup>h</sup>at starts w<sup>i</sup>t<sup>h</sup> a letter, does not contain a space, an equal sign (=), a comma, or any of the special characters listed in Section 3.4.4. 

<sup>You</sup> <sup>ma</sup>y <sup>define</sup> y<sup>our</sup> <sup>own</sup> <sup>abbreviations</sup> <sup>usin</sup>g <sup>the</sup> <sup>command</sup> @STRING<sup>.</sup> <sup>For</sup> example, 

$$
@ \text { STRING } \{\text { au } = \text {"Algebra Universalis"} \}
$$

A string definition can be placed anywhere in a bib file, as long as it precedes the first use of the abbreviation in an entry. 

<sup>The AMS su</sup>pp<sup>lies the</sup> mrabbrev.bib <sup>file containin</sup>g <sup>the standard abbreviations</sup> <sup>for man</sup>y <sup>mathematical</sup> j<sup>ournals. Find it at</sup> ams.org, <sup>under</sup> Reference Tools, <sup>click</sup> <sup>on</sup> MR Serials Abbreviations for BibTeX<sup>. Based on this file</sup>, y<sup>ou can make</sup> y<sup>our</sup> <sup>own</sup> abbrev.bib <sup>file containin</sup>g <sup>entries for all the</sup> j<sup>ournals</sup> y<sup>ou reference with whatever</sup> abbreviations you find easiest to remember. 

If you use this scheme, the command you use to specify the bib files may look like 

\bibliography{abbrev,... } 

<sup>Section 15.2.1 ex</sup>p<sup>lains the</sup> \bibliography <sup>command.</sup>

## 15.2.2 Setup

Before you start BIBTEX, make sure that everything is set up properly as described in this section. 

To <sup>li</sup>st database entr<sup>i</sup>es <sup>i</sup>n t<sup>h</sup>e b<sup>i</sup>b<sup>li</sup>ograp<sup>h</sup>y, use t<sup>h</sup>e \cite command. Re<sup>f</sup>er to Section 8.5.1 for details on how to use citations. If you want to have a reference listed in <sup>the biblio</sup>g<sup>ra</sup>p<sup>h</sup>y <sup>without a citation in the text</sup>, <sup>then use the</sup> \nocite <sup>command. For ex-</sup> ample, 

```txt
\cite{pK57} 
```

includes the reference in the bibliography and cites the entry with label pK57, whereas 

```latex
\nocite{pK57} 
```

includes the reference in the bibliography but does not cite the entry. In either case, one <sup>of the</sup> bib <sup>files s</sup>p<sup>ecified in the ar</sup>g<sup>ument of the</sup> \bibliography <sup>command must con-</sup> <sup>tain an entr</sup>y <sup>with the label</sup> pK57<sup>. The</sup> \nocite{*} <sup>command includes</sup> all <sup>the entries</sup> from the bibliographic databases you’ve specified. 

Your document must specify the bibliography style and must name the bib files <sup>to be used. For instance</sup>, <sup>the</sup> secondarticleb.tex <sup>sam</sup>p<sup>le article contains the lines</sup> 

```latex
\bibliographystyle{amsplain}
\bibliography{secondarticleb} 
```

<sup>The</sup> \bibliographystyle <sup>command s</sup>p<sup>ecifies</sup> amsplain.bst <sup>as the st</sup>y<sup>le and the</sup> \bibliography <sup>command s</sup>p<sup>ecifies the database file</sup> secondarticleb.bib<sup>. To use</sup> several database files, separate them with commas, as in

where

gg.bib <sup>contains</sup> p<sup>ersonal articles</sup> 

lattice.bib <sup>contains lattice theor</sup>y <sup>articles b</sup>y <sup>other authors</sup> 

secondarticleb.bib <sup>contains additional references needed</sup> 

<sup>It is im</sup>p<sup>ortant to make sure that the</sup> bst <sup>file</sup>, <sup>the</sup> bib <sup>file</sup>(<sup>s</sup>), <sup>and the LAT</sup>E<sup>X docu-</sup> ment(s) are in folders where BIBTEX can find them. If you are just starting out, you can simply copy all of them into one folder. Later, you may want to look for a more per-<sup>manent solution b</sup>y <sup>kee</sup>p<sup>in</sup>g <sup>the files</sup> abbrev.bib <sup>and</sup> lattice.bib <sup>in one “central”</sup> <sup>location</sup>, <sup>while</sup> p<sup>lacin</sup>g secondarticleb.bib <sup>in</sup> <sup>the</sup> <sup>same</sup> <sup>folder</sup> <sup>as</sup> <sup>its</sup> <sup>corres</sup>p<sup>ondin</sup>g LAT<sub>E</sub>X document.

## 15.2.5 BIBT X rules and messages

Rule BIBT X and % You cannot comment out a field with an %. 

```bib
For example, the entry
@ARTICLE{eM57,
    author = "Ernest T. Moynahan",
    title = "On a Problem of {M. Stone}",
    journal = "Acta Math. Acad. Sci. Hungar.",
    % pages = "455-460",
    volume = 8,
    year = 1957,
} 
```

causes BIBTEX to generate the message 

Recall that BIBTEX ignores field names it cannot recognize. So changing the field name pages, <sup>for exam</sup>p<sup>le to</sup> pages-comment, <sup>does not</sup> g<sup>ive a messa</sup>g<sup>e. However</sup>, <sup>doin</sup>g <sup>so</sup> removes a required field, so you get the warning message 

```txt
Warning--missing pages in eM57 
```

## Rule BIBT X field names Do not abbreviate field names.

```bib
For instance, if you abbreviate volume to vol, as in
@ARTICLE{eM57,
author = "Ernest T. Moynahan",
title = "On a Problem of {M. Stone}",
journal = "Acta Math. Acad. Sci. Hungar.",
pages = "455-460",
vol = 8,
year = 1957,
} 
```

```txt
Rule ■ BIBTEX field terminations
Make sure that every field of an entry, except possibly the last, is terminated with a comma. 
```

If you drop a comma before a field, you get a message such as 

```txt
I was expecting a ‘,’ or a ‘）
    line 6 of file secondarticleb.bib
:
: year = 1968,
(ay have been on previous line)
I'm skipping whatever remains of this entry
Warning--missing year in gM68+ 
```

## Rule BIBT X field value terminations Make sure that the field value is properly terminated.

You should be careful not to drop a double quote or brace. If you drop the closing quote <sup>on line 11 of the</sup> bib <sup>file</sup>, 

```txt
title = "General Lattice Theory
you get the message
I was expecting a ',' or a '}"
    line 12 of file secondarticleb.bib
: edition = "+\\
: Expanded and Revised",
I'm skipping whatever remains of this entry
Warning--missing publisher in fR82
Warning--missing year in fR82

I was expecting a ',' or a '}"
    line 12 of file secondarticleb.bib
: edition = "
: Expanded and Revised",
I'm skipping whatever remains of this entry
Warning--missing publisher in fR82
Warning--missing year in fR82

If, instead, you drop the opening double quote in the same line, you get the message
Warning--string name "general" is undefined
--line 11 of file secondarticleb.bib
I was expecting a ',' or a '} 
```

```txt
line 11 of file secondarticleb.bib
:    title = general
:    Lattice Theory",
I'm skipping whatever remains of this entry
Warning--missing title in fR82
Warning--missing publisher in fR82
Warning--missing year in fR82
(There was 1 message)+ 
```

<sup>B</sup>IB<sup>T</sup>E<sup>X assumed that</sup> general <sup>was an abbreviation</sup>, <sup>since it was not</sup> p<sup>receded b</sup>y <sup>a</sup> "<sup>.</sup> 

The obvious conclusion is that you have to be very careful about typing your bibliographic entries for BIBTEX. If you have access to special tools for maintaining your <sup>biblio</sup>g<sup>ra</sup>p<sup>hic data</sup>, <sup>use them. Otherwise</sup>, <sup>refer to the</sup> template.bib <sup>file that contains</sup> templates of often-used entry types. 

## 15.2.6 Submitting an article

If you submit an article to a journal that provides you with a BIBTEX style file, then you can submit the article and the BIBT<sub>E</sub>X database file, pared down of course. If this is not <sup>the case</sup>, <sup>create the</sup> bbl <sup>file with</sup> amsplain.bst <sup>and co</sup>py <sup>and</sup> p<sup>aste the content into</sup> <sup>the</sup> thebibliography <sup>environment in the article. Then the</sup> j<sup>ournal’s editor can edit</sup> the bibliography. 

## 15.3 Concluding comments

There is a lot more to BIBTEX than what has been covered in this chapter. For example, BIBTEX’s algorithm to alphabetize names is fairly complicated. Some names create additional dificulties. Where should John von Neumann be placed, under the “v”-s or the “N”-s? It depends on the style. How do we handle names where the first word is the family name, as in Ho Chi Minh or Grätzer György? Again, it depends on the style. 

Oren Patashnik’s BIBT Xing [62] has many helpful hints. It includes a clever hack to order entries correctly even when the style does not do so. Chapter 13 of The L<sup>A</sup>TEX Companion, 2nd edition [56] has a long discussion of BIBT<sub>E</sub>X. It also contains a long list of styles. 

There are many tools to make BIBT<sub>E</sub>Xing easier. BibDesk for the Mac is an excellent graphical BIBT<sub>E</sub>X-bibliography manager. For Windows, there is BibTexMng. For UNIX, there is pybibliographer and if you are an Emacs user, there is Ebib. Written in Java, so available on most platforms, is JBibtexManager. There are many BIBT<sub>E</sub>X databases. The largest one may be “The Collection of Computer Science Bibliographies” with more than two million references. 

You can easily build your own mathematical databases with MathSciNet from the AMS. Do a search. When the result page comes up, go to the pull down menu next <sup>to</sup> Batch Download <sup>and select</sup> Citations (BibTeX)<sup>. Now</sup> y<sup>ou can check mark the</sup> <sup>items</sup> y<sup>ou want b</sup>y <sup>clickin</sup>g <sup>on the little s</sup>q<sup>uares and then click on</sup> Retrieve Marked <sup>next to the</sup> p<sup>ull down menu or click on</sup> Retrieve First 50<sup>. For the latter to work</sup> <sup>well</sup>, <sup>before</sup> y<sup>our search</sup>, <sup>click on the</sup> Preferences <sup>button and click on the circle next</sup> <sup>to</sup> 50, <sup>so</sup> y<sup>ou</sup> g<sup>et at most 50 items</sup> p<sup>er result</sup> p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>e. Then</sup> Retrieve First 50 <sup>retrieves</sup> them all. 

F<sup>i</sup>na<sup>ll</sup>y, a<sup>f</sup>ter many years o<sup>f</sup> deve<sup>l</sup>opment, t<sup>h</sup>e AMS re<sup>l</sup>eased amsrefs, t<sup>h</sup>e <sup>ki</sup>d brother of BIBTEX, at its annual meeting in January 2002. The presentation was made by Michael Downes, who designed and coded the package. I was very excited to hear his lecture—bibliographic management was the last block needed to complete the re-<sup>buildin</sup>g <sup>of LAT</sup>E<sup>X. It turned out that</sup> amsrefs <sup>is not sim</sup>p<sup>l</sup>y <sup>a B</sup>IB<sup>T</sup>E<sup>X re</sup>p<sup>lacement.</sup> It has a number of very important new features. 

<sup>1.</sup> <sup>You</sup> <sup>can</sup>, <sup>with</sup> amsrefs, <sup>enter</sup> <sup>the</sup> <sup>marked</sup> <sup>u</sup>p <sup>biblio</sup>g<sup>ra</sup>p<sup>hic</sup> <sup>entries</sup> <sup>into</sup> <sup>the</sup> <sup>docu-</sup> ment. This means that the document class of the journal publishing the paper can format your bibliography. 

<sup>2.</sup> amsrefs <sup>is a LAT</sup>E<sup>X</sup> p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>e. Therefore</sup>, y<sup>ou do not have to learn</sup> (<sup>another</sup>) <sup>esoteric</sup> language to control the formatting of your bibliography. Developing a format for a journal is very easy. 

3. The bibliographic data files are also L<sup>A</sup>TEX files, so you can print them within L<sup>A</sup>TEX, making it easy to maintain them. 

After Michael Downes passed away, David Jones took over the project, and released version 2.0 in June of 2004. 

<sup>Unfortunatel</sup>y, <sup>unlike the B</sup>IB<sup>T</sup>E<sup>X and its</sup> bbl <sup>file</sup>, amsrefs <sup>directl</sup>y <sup>creates the</sup> typeset file. So if the journal you want to submit your article to does not have an amsrefs <sup>st</sup>y<sup>le file—and toda</sup>y <sup>onl</sup>y <sup>the AMS</sup> j<sup>ournals have them—then</sup> y<sup>ou have to</sup> <sup>manuall</sup>y <sup>convert the</sup> amsrefs <sup>entries into the format the</sup> j<sup>ournal would acce</sup>p<sup>t. There</sup> <sup>is no o</sup>p<sup>tion to set in</sup> amsrefs <sup>to</sup> p<sup>roduce a LAT X source file for the biblio</sup>g<sup>ra</sup>p<sup>hic en-</sup> tries. Therefore, unless you know that you intend to submit to an AMS journal—and y<sup>ou know that it will acce</sup>p<sup>t</sup> y<sup>our article for</sup> p<sup>ublication—</sup>y<sup>ou should not use</sup> amsrefs<sup>.</sup> 

<sup>There is a second obstacle. There is no BibDesk or BibTexMn</sup>g <sup>for</sup> amsrefs<sup>. But</sup> <sup>I believe that if</sup> amsrefs <sup>overcomes the first obstacle</sup>, <sup>then the second obstacle would</sup> resolve itself fast. 

<sup>Phili</sup>pp <sup>Lehman’s</sup> biblatex p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>e shares some of Michael Downes’</sup> g<sup>oals. It</sup> works with (some) BIBTEX databases and uses L<sup>A</sup>TEX to format the bibliography. 

# MakeIndex

Pehong Chen’s MakeIndex application, described in Pehong Chen and Michael A. Harrison’s Index preparation and processing [10], helps L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X users create long indexes. For short indexes, you can easily do without it (see Section 8.5.2). 

In Section 16.1, we show you by an example how to prepare an article for indexing. We introduce formally the index commands in Section 16.2. In Section 16.3, we describe how L<sup>A</sup>T X and MakeIndex process the index entries. The rules are stated in Section 16.4. 

Multiple indexes are almost as easy as single indexes. They are described in Section 16.5. We conclude with glossaries in Section 16.6. 

Indexing is a dificult task. For an extensive discussion on how to create a useful index, consult The Chicago Manual ofStyle, 15th edition [11]. 

## 16.1 Preparing the document

<sup>LAT X</sup> p<sup>rovides the</sup> theindex <sup>environment</sup> (<sup>see Section 8.5.2</sup>)<sup>. Within this environ-</sup> <sup>ment</sup>, <sup>it</sup> p<sup>rovides the</sup> \item, \subitem, <sup>and</sup> \subsubitem <sup>commands to t</sup>yp<sup>eset entries</sup>, <sup>subentries</sup>, <sup>and subsubentries</sup>, <sup>res</sup>p<sup>ectivel</sup>y, <sup>and the</sup> \indexspace <sup>command for addin</sup>g vertical space between alphabetical blocks, see Figure 16.1 for an example. 

<sup>The</sup> makeidx p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>e</sup> p<sup>rovides</sup> <sup>the</sup> \index <sup>command</sup> <sup>for</sup> <sup>s</sup>p<sup>ecif</sup>y<sup>in</sup>g <sup>the</sup> <sup>index</sup> entry at a particular point in the document, which becomes a page reference for the entry in the typeset index. 

Making an index entry with MakeIndex is easy. You simply place the index commands in your source file, and then let L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X and MakeIndex do the work of gathering the entries and the page numbers for the entries, sorting them, and formatting the typeset index. 

There are three steps: 

1. In the preamble of your L<sup>A</sup>TEX document, include the line 

\makeindex 

If you do not use an AMS document class, include the two lines 

\usepackage{makeidx} 

\makeindex 

2. Type the line 

\printindex 

at the point in your document where you want the index to appear, usually as part of the back matter (see Section 8.5). 

<sup>3. Mark all entries in</sup> y<sup>our document with</sup> \index <sup>commands.</sup> 

<sup>We illustrate this</sup> p<sup>rocedure with the</sup> firstarticlei.tex <sup>article</sup>, <sup>which modifies</sup> <sup>the article</sup> firstarticle.tex <sup>b</sup>y <sup>insertin</sup>g <sup>a number of index entries</sup> (<sup>both these files</sup> <sup>are in the</sup> samples <sup>folder</sup>; <sup>see</sup> p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>e 5</sup>)<sup>.</sup> 

<sup>We now add a dozen</sup> \index <sup>commands to</sup> firstarticle.tex<sup>.</sup> 

Command 1 

Retype the line 

\begin{theorem} 

to read 

\begin{theorem}\index{Main Theorem} 

Commands 2 and 3 

Type the commands 

\index{pistar@$\Pi^{*}$ construction}% \index{Main Theorem!exposition|(}% 

after the line 

\section{The $\Pi^{*}$ construction}\label{S:P*} 

## Command 4

Retype the line 

See also Ernest~T. Moynahan~\cite{eM57a}. 

as follows: 

See also Ernest~T. \index{Moynahan, Ernest~T.}% Moynahan~\cite{eM57a}. 

## Commands 5 to 7

Type the three index items 

\index{lattice|textbf}% \index{lattice!distributive}% \index{lattice!distributive!complete}% 

before the line 

\begin{theorem}\label{T:P*} 

## Command 8

Type 

\index{Main Theorem!exposition|)} 

after the line 

hence $\Theta = \iota$. 

Command 9 

Retype the line 

\bibitem{sF90} 

as follows: 

\bibitem{sF90}\index{Foo, Soo-Key}% 

Command 10 

Retype the line 

\bibitem{gM68} 

as follows: 

\bibitem{gM68}\index{Menuhin, George~A.}% 

## Command 11

Retype the line 

\bibitem{eM57} 

as follows: 

\bibitem{eM57}\index{Moynahan, Ernest~T.}% 

Command 12 

Retype the line 

\bibitem{eM57a} 

as follows: 

\bibitem{eM57a}\index{Moynahan, Ernest~T.}% 

<sup>These</sup> \index <sup>commands</sup> p<sup>roduce the index for the</sup> firstarticlei.tex <sup>article shown</sup> in Figure 16.1. Notice that although you typed 12 index commands, only 11 entries appear in the index. The last two entries for Moynahan (commands 11 and 12) occur on the same typeset page, so only one page number shows up in the index. 

INDEX

lattice, 1 distributive, 1 complete, 1 

Menuhin, George A., 2 

Moynahan, Ernest T., 1, 2 

I* construction, 1

## 16.2 Index commands

<sup>There are a few ma</sup>j<sup>or forms of</sup> \index <sup>commands. The</sup>y <sup>are discussed in this section</sup>, illustrated by the commands shown in Section 16.1. 

```latex
Simple \index commands
The index entry
Foo, Soo-Key, 2
was created by command 9,
\index{Foo, Soo-Key}
This entry is an example of the simplest form of an index command:
\index{entry}
The entry
lattice, 2
was created as command 5,
\index{lattice|textbf}
Ignore, for the time being, the |textbf part. This entry has a subentry,
lattice, 2
distributive, 2
which was created by command 6,
\index{lattice!distributive} 
```

There is also a subsubentry,厂lattice, 2distributive, 2complete, 21

which was created by command 7, 

\index{lattice!distributive!complete} 

<sup>The form of the</sup> \index <sup>command for subentries is</sup> 

\index{entry !subentry } 

and for subsubentries it is 

\index{entry !subentry !subsubentry } 

## Modifiers

## Command 5

\index{lattice|textbf} 

produces a bold page number in the entry lattice. 

The command whose name follows the symbol | (in this case, the command name is textbf) is applied to the page number. For instance, if you want a large bold page <sup>number</sup>, <sup>then define the command</sup> \LargeBold <sup>as</sup> 

\newcommand{\LargeBoldB}[1]{\textbf{\Large #1}} 

<sup>and t</sup>yp<sup>e the</sup> \index <sup>command as</sup> 

\index{entry |LargeBold} 

You can also modify \index commands to indicate page ranges: 

Main Theorem, 1 exposition, 1–2 

The latter index entry has a page range. It was created with commands 3 and 8: 

\index{Main Theorem!exposition|(} \index{Main Theorem!exposition|)} 

Separate an entry from its modifier with |, open the page range with (, and close it with ). 

Modifiers can also be combined. The index commands 

\index{Main Theorem!exposition|(textbf} \index{Main Theorem!exposition|)textbf} 

produce a bold page range. 

Sorting control 

<sup>Observe the</sup> \index <sup>command</sup> 

\index{pistar@$\Pi^{*}$ construction} 

This produces the entry 

Π<sup>∗</sup> construction, 1 

To place this entry in the correct place in the index, use a sort key. The general form of <sup>an</sup> \index <sup>command</sup> <sup>with</sup> <sup>a</sup> <sup>sort</sup> <sup>ke</sup>y <sup>is</sup> 

\index{sortkey @entry } 

<sup>In this exam</sup>p<sup>le</sup>, <sup>the sortke</sup>y <sup>is</sup> pistar<sup>. When the entries are sorted</sup>, <sup>the</sup> sortkey <sup>is</sup> used to sort the entry. A few typical examples follow: 

Example 1 An \index command for G.I. Žitomirski˘ı, 

\index{Zitomirskii@\v{Z}itomirski\u{\i}, G.I.} 

sorts Žitomirski˘ı with the Z entries. 

If you used the command 

\index{\v{Z}itomirski\u{\i}, G.I.} 

Žitomirski˘ı would be sorted with the v’s. 

Example 2 An \index command for the Őrmester lemma, 

\index{Ormester@\H{O}rmester lemma} 

would sort Őrmester lemma with the O entries. 

If you used the command 

\index{\H{O}rmester lemma} 

Őrmester lemma would be sorted with the H’s. 

Example 3 An \index command for truncated lattice, 

\index{truncated lattice@\emph{truncated} lattice} 

sorts truncated lattice with the t entries. 

If you use the command 

\index{\emph{truncated} lattice} 

this would sort truncated lattice with the e’s. 

Example 4 We want to place the symbol Truncat �, typed as \Trunc f (see Sec tion 14.1.6) in the index, sorted as Trunc. 

\index{$\Trunc f$} 

would place Truncat � near the beginning of the index, sorted with the $ symbol. If you use the command 

\index{Trunc@$\Trunc f$} 

this would sort Truncat � with the T’s. 

## Sorting control and subentries

If you want to place a subentry under an entry with a sort key, you must include the sort key part of the entry as well: 

\index{sortkey @entry !subentry } 

For instance, 

\index{Zitomirskii@\v{Z}itomirski\u{\i}, G.I.!education} 

You can also use a sort key for subentries (and subsubentries), such as 

\index{lattice!weakly distributive@ \emph{weakly} distributive} 

or, a more complicated example, 

\index{Zitomirskii@\v{Z}itomirski\u{\i}, G.I.!elementary education@\textbf{elementary} education} 

## Special characters

<sup>Since the</sup> !, @, <sup>and</sup> | <sup>characters have s</sup>p<sup>ecial meanin</sup>g<sup>s within an</sup> \index <sup>command</sup>, y<sup>ou</sup> need to quote those characters if you want them to appear as themselves. MakeIndex uses t<sup>h</sup>e doub<sup>l</sup>e quote c<sup>h</sup>aracter (") <sup>f</sup>or t<sup>hi</sup>s purpose: "!, "@, and "|. 

Because this usage makes the double quote a special character itself, it also has to <sup>be</sup> q<sup>uoted if</sup> y<sup>ou need to use it in an</sup> \index <sup>command:</sup> ""<sup>.</sup> 

Example 1 To produce the entry Start here!, type the \index command as 

\index{Start here"!} 

Example 2 To produce the entry @ symbol, type the \index command as 

\index{"@ symbol} 

Example 3 To produce the entry � , type the \index command as 

\index{"|A"|@$"|A"|$} 

## 16.2 Index commands

## Cross-references

It is easy to make a cross-reference to another index entry. For instance, to list distribu tive lattice by cross-referencing it to lattice, distributive, the command is 

\index{distributive lattice|seeonly{lattice, 

distributive}} 

which produces the entry 

distributive lattice, see lattice, distributive 

<sup>For</sup> <sup>non-AMS</sup> <sup>document</sup> <sup>classes</sup>, seeonly <sup>should</sup> <sup>be</sup> see<sup>.</sup> 

A command of this form can be placed anywhere in the document.

Let $L$ be a distributive lattice
\index{lattice}% 
\index{distributive lattice}% 
that is strongly complete. 

Read also Section 17.5 on page breaks and index entries. 

Listing theforms ofthe \index command 

We have discussed the following forms: 

```latex
\index{entry}
\index{entry!subentry}
\index{entry!subentry!subsubentry}
\index{entry|modifier}
\index{entry|open/close modifier}
\index{sortkey@entry}
\index{sortkey@entry!subentry}
\index{sortkey@entry!subsortkey@subentry} 
```

Of course, more combinations are possible; the following may be the longest form: 

```latex
\index{sortkey@entry!subsortkey@subentry
!subsubsortkey@subsubentry|open/close modifier} 
```

## 16.3 Processing the index entries

<sup>Once</sup> y<sup>ou are satisfied with the</sup> \index <sup>commands</sup>, <sup>the index is read</sup>y <sup>to be created.</sup> 

Step 1 <sup>T</sup>yp<sup>eset</sup> firstarticlei.tex (<sup>see Fi</sup>g<sup>ure 16.3</sup>)<sup>.</sup> 

Step 2 Run the MakeIndex application on firstarticlei.idx (see Figure 16.4). 

Step 3 <sup>T</sup>yp<sup>eset</sup> firstarticlei.tex <sup>a</sup>g<sup>ain.</sup> 

You find the index on page 3 of the typeset document. 

Let us look at this process in detail. In step 1 (see Figure 16.3), L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X creates the firstarticlei.idx <sup>file:</sup> 

\indexentry{Main Theorem}{1}
\indexentry{pistar@ $\Pi^{*}$ construction}{1}
\indexentry{Main Theorem!exposition|({1}
\indexentry{Moynahan, Ernest~T.}{1}
\indexentry{lattice|textbf}{1}
\indexentry{lattice!distributive}{1}
\indexentry{lattice!distributive!complete}{1}
\indexentry{Main Theorem!exposition|}{2}
\indexentry{Foo, Soo-Key}{2}

<sup>In ste</sup>p <sup>2</sup> (<sup>see Fi</sup>g<sup>ure 16.4</sup>), MakeIndex p<sup>rocesses</sup> firstarticlei.idx <sup>and cre-</sup> <sup>ates the index file</sup> firstarticlei.ind, <sup>which contains a</sup> theindex <sup>environment with</sup> all the index entries: 

begin{theindex}
\item Foo, Soo-Key, 2
\indexspace

```latex
\end{theindex} 
```

<sup>The</sup> \printindex <sup>command reads</sup> firstarticlei.ind <sup>durin</sup>g <sup>the next t</sup>yp<sup>esettin</sup>g cycle. 

MakeIndex <sup>also</sup> p<sup>roduces the index</sup> log <sup>file</sup> firstarticlei.ilg<sup>:</sup> 

```txt
This is makeindex, version 2.14 [02-Oct-2002] (kpathsea + Thai support).
Scanning input file firstarticlei.idx....done (12 entries accepted, 0 rejected).
Sorting entries....done (43 comparisons).
Generating output file firstarticlei.ind....done (22 lines written, 0 warnings).
Output written in firstarticlei.ind.

```

It is important to understand that in step 1, L<sup>A</sup>TEX does not process the index ent-<sup>ries</sup>, <sup>it sim</sup>p<sup>l</sup>y <sup>writes the ar</sup>g<sup>uments of the</sup> \index <sup>commands in the source file to the</sup> idx <sup>file as ar</sup>g<sup>uments of</sup> \indexentry <sup>commands verbatim</sup> (<sup>that is</sup>, <sup>with no chan</sup>g<sup>e</sup>)<sup>.</sup> MakeIndex then processes the idx file by removing the double quote marks for the special characters, sorting the entries, and collating the page numbers. The resulting ind file is a normal L<sup>A</sup>T X source file (you can edit it, if necessary) that is included in <sup>the ori</sup>g<sup>inal document b</sup>y <sup>the</sup> \printindex <sup>command the next time</sup> y<sup>ou run LAT X.</sup> 

<sup>In Ste</sup>p <sup>2</sup>, <sup>we run the</sup> MakeIndex <sup>a</sup>pp<sup>lication on</sup> firstarticlei.idx<sup>. How we</sup> do this depends on the L<sup>A</sup>TEX installation you have. In UNIX installations, you type 

MakeIndex firstarticlei 

at the command line. In newer user interfaces, MakeIndex is represented by an icon, <sup>and</sup> y<sup>ou dro</sup>p firstarticlei.idx <sup>into it. In modern installations</sup>, y<sup>our editor also</sup> runs MakeIndex. 

## 16.4 Rules

There are some simple rules to keep in mind when entering index items. 

<table><tr><td>Rule ■ Spaces in \indexDo not leave unnecessary spaces in the argument of an \index command.\index{item},\index{Item},and\index{Item}produces three different entries.There are options that instruct MakeIndex to ignore such spaces, but you are better off typing the \index commands correctly in the first place.</td></tr><tr><td>Rule ■ Spacing rules for MakeIndexLATEX&#x27;s text spacing rules (Section 3.2.1) do not apply.MakeIndex does not follow these rules when it sorts the index items. While LATEX ignores spaces,MakeIndex does not.</td></tr><tr><td>Rule ■ Sort keysIn \index{sortkey@item},the sortkey is both space and case sensitive.For instance,\index{alpha@\$ \alpha\$}\index{Alpha@\$ \alpha\$}\index{ALPHA@\$ \alpha\$}represent three different items.</td></tr><tr><td>Rule ■ BracesIn every entry, the braces must be balanced.</td></tr></table>

Normally, balancing braces is not a problem. The braces within a math formula or a T X <sup>ex</sup>p<sup>ression should alwa</sup>y<sup>s be balanced. However</sup>, <sup>the</sup> \index <sup>command that creates the</sup> <sup>entr</sup>y <sup>for</sup> { <sup>with the sort ke</sup>y leftbrace <sup>cannot be t</sup>yp<sup>ed as</sup> 

\index{@\{} 

because L<sup>A</sup>TEX would give the error message 

```txt
Runaway argument?
{leftbrace@\{}}
! Paragraph ended before \@wrindex was complete. 
```

T<sup>h</sup>ere are many ways to correct t<sup>hi</sup>s \index command. Per<sup>h</sup>aps t<sup>h</sup>e s<sup>i</sup>mp<sup>l</sup>est <sup>i</sup>s to de<sup>fi</sup>ne 

\newcommand{\printleftbrace}{\{} 

<sup>and rewrite the</sup> \index <sup>command</sup> 

\index{@\printleftbrace} 

This produces the entry 

There is, of course, a lot more to MakeIndex than what we have discussed in this short introduction, but what we have covered here should do for most documents. See Pehong Chen and Michael A. Harrison’s Index preparation and processing [10] for more detail. Chapter 12 of The L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X Companion, 2nd edition [56] covers MakeIndex in great detail, including the customization of indexes. 

## 16.5 Multiple indexes

<sup>We do multi</sup>p<sup>le indexes with Enrico Gre</sup>g<sup>orio’s</sup> imakeidx p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>e.</sup> 

As an example, we split the index file into two parts, Subject Index and Author Index. We include the following three lines in the preamble: 

```latex
\usepackage{imakeidx}
\makeindex[title=Subject Index]
\makeindex[name=author, title=Author Index] 
```

Now enter each index command for authors in the following form: 

\index{author}{Moynahan, Ernest~T.} 

The other index commands are entered as usual. 

Where you want the two indexes to appear in the typeset document, enter the commands 

\printindex[author] 

\printindex 

These two commands are usually, but not necessarily, adjacent. 

<sup>If</sup> y<sup>ou want to t</sup>yp<sup>eset the indexes in the st</sup>y<sup>le</sup> p<sup>rovided b</sup>y <sup>the</sup> theindex <sup>environ-</sup> ment in your document class, invoke with 

\usepackage[original]{imakeidx} 

<sup>Also</sup> <sup>note</sup> <sup>the</sup> <sup>ver</sup>y <sup>useful</sup> \indexprologue <sup>command.</sup> <sup>It</sup> p<sup>rovides</sup> <sup>text</sup> (<sup>the</sup> <sup>ar</sup>g<sup>ument</sup> of the command) to be typeset between the index header and the entries. 

<sup>The</sup> imakeidx p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>e has lots of nice features</sup>; <sup>see the excellent documentation.</sup> 

## 16.6 Glossary

Using the glossary commands is very similar to using the corresponding index commands. 

Instead of the 

index makeindex 

commands, use the 

glossary makeglossary 

commands, respectively. Glossary entries are written in the glo file, which corresponds to the idx file. L<sup>A</sup>TEX gives you no further assistance in making a glossary file. There <sup>is</sup> <sup>no</sup> \printglossary <sup>command</sup>, theglossary <sup>environment</sup>, <sup>or</sup> MakeGlossary <sup>a</sup>pp<sup>-</sup> <sup>lication. There is</sup>, <sup>however</sup>, <sup>Thomas Henlich’s</sup> makeglos p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>e</sup> (<sup>see Section D.1</sup>)<sup>.</sup> 

## 16.7 Concluding comments

Style files are available in a very limited form also for MakeIndex. Google 

makeindex style 

for an up-to-date listing. 

Indexing is a very complex process, so it is not surprising that there are many <sup>index</sup> p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>es available. CTAN lists a number of them in the</sup> index <sup>director</sup>y<sup>. The</sup> best known is xindy, described in detail in The L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X Companion, 2nd edition [56].

# Books in LAT<sub>E</sub>X

Since the introduction of L<sup>A</sup>T X, the visual quality of articles published in mathematical journals has improved dramatically. Unfortunately, the same cannot be said of books published using L<sup>A</sup>TEX. A record number of very ugly books have appeared. 

<sup>It is eas</sup>y <sup>to understand wh</sup>y<sup>. While</sup> amsart <sup>has been desi</sup>g<sup>ned to</sup> p<sup>roduce hi</sup>g<sup>h-</sup> quality printed output, the standard book document classes do not produce attractive books without additional work. 

<sup>LAT</sup>E<sup>X</sup> p<sup>rovides the</sup> book <sup>and the</sup> amsbook <sup>document classes to serve as founda-</sup> tions for well-designed books. Better quality books have to use document classes designed by professionals. We briefly discuss logical and visual design in Section 2.3. 

So this chapter is not about how to produce a finished book using L<sup>A</sup>TEX. Our goal is much more modest, how to prepare a book manuscript for your publisher. In <sup>Section 17.1 we describe the book document classes</sup> book <sup>and</sup> amsbook<sup>. The table of</sup> contents and lists of figures and tables are discussed in Section 17.2. 

Typesetting a book involves dozens of files. Section 17.3.3 gives some tips on how to organize them. Section 17.4 covers logical design. Section 17.5 deals with the final preparation of your edited manuscript for your publisher. Finally, Section 17.6 suggests a few more things to do if you typeset your book yourself. 

## 17.1 Book document classes

<sup>In this section</sup>, <sup>we briefl</sup>y <sup>discuss the wa</sup>y <sup>in which</sup> book <sup>and</sup> amsbook, <sup>the two standard</sup> book document classes, difer from the corresponding article document classes. 

## 17.1.1 Sectioning

Book document classes have chapters, invoked with the \chapter command andparts, <sup>i</sup>nvo<sup>k</sup>ed w<sup>i</sup>t<sup>h</sup> \part. T<sup>h</sup>e \part command <sup>i</sup>s genera<sup>ll</sup>y used to group c<sup>h</sup>apters <sup>i</sup>n <sup>l</sup>onger documents, for instance in this book. Parts have no efect on the numbering of chapters, sections, and so on, so Chapter 1 of Part I is not numbered as I.1 but as 1. 

<sup>Both</sup> \chapter <sup>and</sup> \part <sup>take</sup> <sup>a</sup> <sup>title</sup> <sup>as</sup> <sup>an</sup> <sup>ar</sup>g<sup>ument</sup>, <sup>but</sup> <sup>the</sup> \chapter <sup>com-</sup> mand also has an optional argument: 

\chapter[short_title ]{title } 

<sup>The o</sup>p<sup>tional</sup> short_title <sup>ar</sup>g<sup>ument is used in the runnin</sup>g <sup>head. You ma</sup>y <sup>need to</sup> p<sup>rotect an</sup>y <sup>fra</sup>g<sup>ile commands in</sup> title <sup>and</sup> short_title <sup>with the</sup> \protect <sup>com-</sup> mand (see Section 3.3.3). 

Here is the whole hierarchy: 

\part 

\chapter 

\section 

\subsection 

\subsubsection 

\paragraph 

\subparagraph 

Book document classes, as a rule, do not number subsubsections or any of the sectioning divisions below that level. 

## Equations in chapters

By default, equations are numbered from 1 within chapters. So in Chapter 1 as well as in Chapter 3, the equations are numbered (1), (2), and so forth. If you have the 

\numberwithin{equation}{chapter} 

command in the preamble, then equations in Chapter 2 are numbered as (2.1), (2.2), and so on. 

## 17.1.2 Division of the body

The book document classes formalize the division of the body into three parts. 

Front matter The material that appears in the front of the document, including the title pages (normally four), table of contents, preface, introduction, and so on. L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X numbers these pages using roman numerals. The front matter is introduced with <sup>the</sup> \frontmatter <sup>command.</sup> 

Main matter The main part of the book, including the appendices if any. Page numbering starts from 1 using arabic numerals. The main matter is introduced with <sup>the</sup> \mainmatter <sup>command.</sup> 

Back matter Material that appears in the back of the book, including the bibliography, index, and various other sections, such as the colophon, afterword, and so on. The <sup>back matter is introduced with the</sup> \backmatter <sup>command.</sup> 

<sup>For the</sup> book <sup>document class—and the document classes built on it—in the front</sup> <sup>and back matter</sup>, <sup>the</sup> \chapter <sup>command does not</sup> p<sup>roduce a cha</sup>p<sup>ter number but the</sup> title is listed in the table of contents. So you can start your introduction with 

\chapter{Introduction} 

Within such a chapter, you should use the *-ed forms of the sectioning commands \section, \subsection, <sup>and so on</sup>, <sup>otherwise</sup> y<sup>ou have sections with numbers such</sup> as 0.1. 

<sup>In the main matter</sup>, <sup>the</sup> \appendix <sup>command marks the be</sup>g<sup>innin</sup>g <sup>of the a</sup>pp<sup>en-</sup> dices. Each subsequent chapter becomes a new appendix. For example, 

\appendix 

\chapter{A proof of the Main Theorem}\label{A:Mainproof} 

produces an appendix with the given title. 

Note that appendices may be labeled and cross-referenced. In Appendix A, sections are numbered A.1, A.2, and so on, subsections in A.1 are numbered A.1.1, A.1.2, and so on. The precise form these numbers take depends, of course, on the document class, packages, and user-specific changes (see Section 14.5.1). 

See Section 17.3.1 for a detailed example. 

<sup>The</sup> \chapter <sup>and</sup> \chapter* <sup>commands alwa</sup>y<sup>s</sup> p<sup>roduce a title listed in the table</sup> <sup>of contents for the</sup> amsbook <sup>document class</sup>, <sup>and the document classes built on it.</sup> 

The following two questions are frequently asked: 

My book has only one appendix. How can I get it to be called just “Appendix”, not “Appendix A”? 

The single appendix in my book is being labeled “Appendix A”. How can I change this to just “Appendix”? This appendix has a title, so the answer to the preceding question doesn’t apply. These questions are answered in the author FAQ of the AMS, go to 

http://www.ams.org/authors/author-faq.html 

## 17.1.3 Document class options

The options and defaults for the book document classes are the same as those of other document classes (see Sections 9.5 and 10.1.2) with a few exceptions. 

## Two-sided printing

Options: twoside default oneside 

<sup>The</sup> twoside <sup>o</sup>p<sup>tion</sup> <sup>formats</sup> <sup>the</sup> <sup>out</sup>p<sup>ut</sup> <sup>for</sup> p<sup>rintin</sup>g <sup>on</sup> <sup>both</sup> <sup>sides</sup> <sup>of</sup> <sup>a</sup> p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>e.</sup> 

Titlepage 

Options: titlepage default notitlepage 

<sup>The</sup> titlepage <sup>o</sup>p<sup>tion</sup> <sup>creates</sup> <sup>a</sup> <sup>se</sup>p<sup>arate</sup> <sup>title</sup> p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>e.</sup> <sup>The</sup> notitlepage <sup>o</sup>p<sup>tion</sup> <sup>creates</sup> no separate pages. 

## Chapter start

Options: openright default openany 

A c<sup>h</sup>apter a<sup>l</sup>ways starts on a new page. T<sup>h</sup>e book document c<sup>l</sup>ass—and t<sup>h</sup>e doc-<sup>ument classes built on it—uses the o</sup>p<sup>tion</sup> openright <sup>to start each cha</sup>p<sup>ter on an odd</sup> page, w<sup>hil</sup>e t<sup>h</sup>e opt<sup>i</sup>on openany starts eac<sup>h</sup> c<sup>h</sup>apter on t<sup>h</sup>e <sup>fi</sup>rst ava<sup>il</sup>ab<sup>l</sup>e new page. I<sup>f</sup> you use the default option, end each chapter with the command 

## \cleardoublepage

Then if a chapter ends on an odd page, a blank page is added with no header or page <sup>number. The</sup> \cleardoublepage <sup>command is correctl</sup>y <sup>coded if</sup> y<sup>ou use</sup> amsbook<sup>.</sup> <sup>Otherwise</sup>, <sup>use the</sup> p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>e</sup> cleardoublepage.sty (<sup>in the</sup> samples <sup>folder</sup>)<sup>.</sup> 

<sup>The</sup> amsbook <sup>document class—and the document classes built on it—automatic-</sup> ally clears to a right-hand page and leaves a totally blank page if needed. 

## 17.1.4 Title pages

<sup>The</sup> book <sup>document class su</sup>pp<sup>orts the commands:</sup> \title, \author, \date, <sup>and</sup> \maketitle (<sup>see Section 10.1.1</sup>)<sup>. The</sup> amsbook <sup>document class su</sup>pp<sup>orts the same</sup> <sup>commands as</sup> amsart (<sup>see Section 9.2</sup>), <sup>exce</sup>p<sup>t for</sup> \date<sup>.</sup> 

<sup>You can desi</sup>g<sup>n</sup> y<sup>our own title</sup> p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>e within the</sup> titlepage <sup>environment</sup>, <sup>which</sup> <sup>does not re</sup>q<sup>uire the use of the</sup> \maketitle <sup>command. Title</sup> p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>es for books</sup>, <sup>of course</sup>, should be created by a book designer for the publisher. 

## 17.2 Tables of contents, lists of tables and figures

A long document, as a rule, has a table of contents. It may also include a list of figures and a list of tables. 

## 17.2.1 Tables of contents

What goes into the table of contents? 

<sup>For the</sup> amsbook <sup>document class—and the document classes built on it—all titles</sup>, not the short titles, of the sectioning commands, whether *-ed or not, subject only to the <sup>value of the</sup> tocdepth <sup>counter</sup>, <sup>as described in the last subsection of Section 14.5.1.</sup> <sup>For instance</sup>, <sup>if</sup> tocdepth <sup>is set to</sup> 2, <sup>the default</sup>, <sup>then the titles of cha</sup>p<sup>ters</sup>, <sup>sections</sup>, and subsections are included in the table of contents, and subsubsections are excluded. 

This leaves us with the problem, what do we do if the title is too long? You cannot break the line with \\, because this would the appear in table of contents. The AMS coded the following solution: enter the line break in the form 

\except{toc}{\linebreak} 

<sup>For the</sup> book <sup>document class—and the document classes built on it—the title or</sup> <sup>o</sup>p<sup>tional ar</sup>g<sup>ument of the sectionin</sup>g <sup>commands</sup>, <sup>sub</sup>j<sup>ect to the value of the</sup> tocdepth counter, with the following exceptions: 

In Section 8.4.1 we discuss the *-ed versions of sectioning commands. They are excluded from the table of contents. 

If the sectioning command has a short title, then it is the short title that is utilized. The example in Section 9.2 shows why this is important. If you have \\ in the title, you must have a short title without it, otherwise the linebreak would show up in the running head and the table of contents. 

When you typeset your document with a table of contents, L<sup>A</sup>TEX creates a file with <sup>the</sup> toc <sup>extension. The next time the document is t</sup>yp<sup>eset</sup>, <sup>the</sup> toc <sup>file is t</sup>yp<sup>eset too</sup> and included in your typeset document at the point where the command 

## \tableofcontents

appears in the source file, normally in the front matter. If your source file is named myart.tex, <sup>the</sup> toc <sup>file is named</sup> myart.toc<sup>. This file lists all the sectionin</sup>g <sup>units as</sup> well as their titles and page numbers. 

<sup>If</sup> y<sup>ou alread</sup>y <sup>have a</sup> toc <sup>file</sup>, <sup>the</sup> \tableofcontents <sup>command t</sup>yp<sup>esets a table</sup> <sup>of contents usin</sup>g <sup>the</sup> p<sup>reviousl</sup>y <sup>created</sup> toc <sup>file and creates a new</sup> toc <sup>file.</sup> 

L<sup>A</sup>T X adds a line to the table of contents, formatted like a section title, if you include the command 

\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{text_to_be_added } 

in your source file. There are three arguments: 

1. The first argument informs L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X that a line, the third argument, should be added to <sup>the</sup> toc <sup>file.</sup> 

2. The second argument specifies how the line should be formatted in the table of con-<sup>tents. In our exam</sup>p<sup>le</sup>, <sup>the second ar</sup>g<sup>ument is</sup> section, <sup>so the line is formatted as</sup> a section title in the table of contents. The second argument must be the name of a sectioning command. 

3. The third argument is the text to be added. 

You can add an unformatted line to the table of contents with the command 

```latex
\addtocontents{toc}{text_to_be_added} 
```

Such a command can also be used to add vertical spaces into the table of contents. For instance, if you want to add some vertical space before a part, you should insert the following line before the sectioning command for the part: 

\addtocontents{toc}{\protect\vspace{10pt}} 

Tip <sup>If</sup> y<sup>ou have a</sup> \addcontentsline <sup>or</sup> \addtocontents <sup>command in a file that is</sup> \include<sup>-ed</sup>, <sup>then</sup> p<sup>lace it as a first line of this file.</sup> 

The toc file is easy to read. The following are typical lines from the table of <sup>contents file for a document usin</sup>g <sup>the</sup> book <sup>document class:</sup> 

```latex
\contentsline{section}{\numberline {5-4.}Top matter}{119}
\contentsline{subsection}{\numberline {5-4.1.}
Article info}{119}
\contentsline {subsection}{\numberline {5-4.2.}
Author info}{121} 
```

Section 14.5.1 explains how you can specify which levels of sectioning appear in the table of contents. Section 2.3 of The L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X Companion, 2nd edition [56] lists the style p<sup>arameters for the table of contents. It also shows</sup> y<sup>ou how to define new</sup> toc<sup>-like files</sup> and use multiple tables of contents in a single document, for instance, adding a mini table of contents for each chapter. 

Tip You may have to typeset the document three times to create the table of contents and set the numbering of the rest of the document right. 

1. T<sup>h</sup>e <sup>fi</sup>rst typesett<sup>i</sup>ng creates t<sup>h</sup>e toc <sup>fil</sup>e. 

2. The second inserts the table of contents with the old page numbers into the typeset document, re-records in the aux file the page numbers, which may have changed as a resu<sup>l</sup>t o<sup>f</sup> t<sup>h</sup>e <sup>i</sup>nsert<sup>i</sup>on, and cross-re<sup>f</sup>erences <sup>i</sup>n t<sup>h</sup>e aux <sup>fil</sup>e, and generates a new toc <sup>file with the correct</sup> p<sup>a</sup>g<sup>e numbers.</sup> 

<sup>3. The third t</sup>yp<sup>esettin</sup>g <sup>uses these new</sup> aux <sup>and</sup> toc <sup>files to t</sup>yp<sup>eset the document cor-</sup> <sup>rectl</sup>y <sup>and creates a new</sup> toc <sup>file.</sup> 

Fragile commands in a movable argument, such as a section (short) title, must be \protect<sup>-ed</sup> (<sup>see Section 3.3.3</sup>)<sup>. Here is a sim</sup>p<sup>le exam</sup>p<sup>le usin</sup>g <sup>the table of contents.</sup> <sup>If the document contains the</sup> \section <sup>command</sup> 

\section{The function $f(x^{2})$ } 

<sup>the section title is stored in the</sup> toc <sup>file as</sup> 

```latex
\contentsline {section}{\numberline
{1}The function\relax $ f(x^{2}) \relax \GenericError { }
{LaTeX Error: Bad math environment delimiter}{Your command was ignored.\MessageBreak Type I <command>
<return> to replace it with another command,\MessageBreak or <return> to continue without it.}}{1} 
```

<sup>and the</sup> log <sup>file contains the messa</sup>g<sup>e</sup> 

! LaTeX Error: Bad math environment delimiter. 

```txt
1.1 ...continue without it.}}{1} 
```

Error messages usually refer to a line in the source file, but in this case the error message <sup>refers to a line in the</sup> toc <sup>file.</sup> 

The correct form for this section title is 

```latex
\section{The function \protect\ ( f(x^{2}) \protect\)} 
```

or, even simpler, 

\verb+\section{The function $f(x^{2})$ } 

Note that this example is merely an illustration of unprotected fragile commands in movable arguments. As a rule, avoid using formulas in (sectioning) titles. 

## 17.2.2 Lists of tables and figures

<sup>If</sup> y<sup>ou</sup> p<sup>lace a</sup> \listoftables <sup>command in the document</sup>, <sup>LAT</sup>E<sup>X stores information for</sup> <sup>the list of tables in a</sup> lot <sup>file. The list of tables is inserted into the bod</sup>y <sup>of</sup> y<sup>our document</sup> at the point where the command appears, normally in the front matter, following the table of contents. 

A list of figures, similar to a list of tables, can be compiled with the command \listoffigures<sup>.</sup> <sup>This</sup> <sup>command</sup> <sup>creates</sup> <sup>an</sup> <sup>auxiliar</sup>y <sup>file</sup> <sup>with</sup> <sup>the</sup> <sup>extension</sup> lof<sup>.</sup> 

<sup>An o</sup>p<sup>tional ar</sup>g<sup>ument of the</sup> \caption <sup>commands in</sup> y<sup>our tables and fi</sup>g<sup>ures can</sup> replace the argument in the list of tables and figures. Typically, the optional argument is used to specify a shorter caption for the list of tables or list of figures. There are other uses. For instance, you may notice that, as a rule, captions should be terminated by periods. If in the list of tables or list of figures, your book style fills the space between the text and the page number with dots, the extra period looks bad. This problem goes <sup>awa</sup>y <sup>if</sup> y<sup>ou</sup> <sup>use</sup> <sup>the</sup> <sup>followin</sup>g <sup>form</sup> <sup>of</sup> <sup>the</sup> \caption <sup>command:</sup> 

```txt

```

There are analogs of the table of contents commands for use with tables and figures. The command

<sup>adds a line to the list of tables or to the list of fi</sup>g<sup>ures with the first ar</sup>g<sup>ument</sup> lof<sup>.</sup> 

## 17.2.3 Exercises

<sup>For exercises</sup>, amsbook p<sup>rovides the</sup> xcb <sup>environment. It is used for a series of exercises</sup> at the end of a section or chapter. The argument of the environment specifies the phrase (<sup>such as</sup> Exercises) <sup>to be</sup>g<sup>in the list:</sup> 

```latex
\begin{xcb}{Exercises}
\begin{enumerate}
\item A finite lattice $L$ is modular if{f} it does not contain a pentagon.\label{E:pent}
\item Can the numbers of covering pairs in\label{E:incr}
Exercise~\ref{E:pent} be increased?\label{E:incr}+
\end{enumerate}
\end{xcb} 
```

which typesets as 

Exercises 

(1) A finite lattice L is modular iff it does not contain a pentagon. 

(2) Can the numbers of covering pairs in Exercise 1 be increased? 

## 17.3 Organizing the files for a book

An article is typically one tex file and maybe some PDF files for the illustrations. On the other hand, a book, like this one, is composed of hundreds of files. In this section, I describe how the files for a book like this may be organized. 

There are three commands that help with the organization: 

\include \includeonly \graphicspath 

We discuss these commands in this section. 

## 17.3.1 Thefolders and the master document

<sup>All the files for this book are in a folder</sup> MiL5 <sup>and in this folder the most im</sup>p<sup>ortant</sup> document is MiL5.tex, the master document. 

<sup>The master document</sup>, MiL5.tex <sup>reads</sup>, <sup>in a somewhat sim</sup>p<sup>lified form</sup>, <sup>as follows:</sup> 

```latex
%MiL5 master document
\documentclass[leqno]{book}
\usepackage{MiL5}
\usepackage{makeidx}
\makeindex
\usepackage{cleardoublepage}
\includeonly{
%frontmatter,
%intro,
%Chapter1,% terminology
...
Chapter17,% books
%appA,% Math symbol tables
...
}
\begin{document}
\frontmatter
\include{frontmatter}
\tableofcontents
\listoftables\listoffigures
\include{intro}%Intro
\mainmatter
\include{Chapter1}%Mission Impossible
...
\include{Chapter17}% Books

\appendix+\\
\include{AppendixA}%Math symbol tables+\\
... +\\ 
```

\backmatter+\\ 

\printindex+\\ 

\end{document}+\\[8pt] 

Some parts of the master file deserve comment, for example, the third line, 

\usepackage{MiL5} 

loads the command file 

MiL5.sty 

which contains all the commands defined for the book and the code for the book style. <sup>Since the book st</sup>y<sup>le is based on</sup> book.cls, <sup>in line 5</sup>, <sup>we load the</sup> makeidx p<sup>acka</sup>g<sup>e</sup> <sup>and</sup> p<sup>rint the index with</sup> \printindex (<sup>see Section 16.1</sup>)<sup>.</sup> 

Line 7 states 

\usepackage{cleardoublepage} 

This creates blank pages after chapters that end on an odd page number (see <sup>Section 17.1.3</sup>)<sup>. For the three</sup> ...matter <sup>commands</sup>, <sup>see Section 17.1.2.</sup>

<sup>This book is</sup> p<sup>ieced to</sup>g<sup>ether b</sup>y <sup>the</sup> \include <sup>commands in the master document. For</sup> example,

The master document for this <sup>book has a lot of</sup> \include <sup>commands...</sup>

## 17.4 Logical design

The discussion of logical and visual design in Section 2.3 applies to books even more than to articles. Since books are long and complex documents, errors in the logical design are much harder to correct. 

Let us review some common sense rules. 

Rule 1 Stick with the sectioning commands provided by the document class. Define the nonstandard structures you wish to use as environments. 

Here is an example which is obviously bad: 

\vspace{18pt} 

<table><tr><td>If you use small caps for acronyms, do not type</td></tr><tr><td>\textsc{ibm}</td></tr><tr><td>but rather define</td></tr><tr><td>\newcommand{\ibm}{\textsc{ibm}}</td></tr><tr><td>and then</td></tr><tr><td>\ibm</td></tr></table>

And a good way to achieve the same result: 

\begin{theorem}\label{T:Goodtheorem} 

This is a good theorem. 

\end{theorem} 

The bad example creates a number of dificulties. 

You have to number the theorems yourself. Adding, deleting, and rearranging theorems becomes dificult and updating cross-references is even harder. 

It is dificult to keep such constructs consistent. 

If the publisher decides to increase the white space before and after the theorems to 20 points, finding and changing all the appropriate commands becomes a tedious and error prone task. 

<table><tr><td>Rather than</td></tr><tr><td>\textbf{Warning! Do not exceed this amount!}</td></tr><tr><td>define</td></tr><tr><td>\newcommand{\important}[1]{\textbf{#1}}</td></tr><tr><td>and type your warnings as</td></tr><tr><td>\important{Warning! Do not exceed this amount!}</td></tr><tr><td>You or your editor can then change all the warnings to a different style with ease.</td></tr></table>

or more generally 

\newcommand{\acronym}[1]{\textsc{#1}} 

and then 

\verb+\acronym{ibm}+ 

Rule 4 Avoid white space commands. 

Occasionally, you may feel that there should be some white space separating two paragraphs, so you do the following: 

paragraph 1 

\medskip 

paragraph 2 

<sup>It would be better to define a new command</sup>, <sup>sa</sup>y \separate, <sup>as</sup> 

\newcommand{\separate}{\medskip} 

and type the previous example as 

paragraph 1 

\separate 

paragraph 2 

Now such white space can be adjusted throughout the entire document by simply re-<sup>definin</sup>g <sup>one command. Note that redefinin</sup>g \medskip <sup>itself ma</sup>y <sup>have unintended side</sup> efects: 

<sup>Man</sup>y <sup>environments de</sup>p<sup>end on LAT</sup>E<sup>X’s definition of</sup> \medskip<sup>.</sup> 

<sup>You ma</sup>y <sup>have used</sup> \medskip <sup>in other situations as well.</sup> 

Here is a short list of commands should not redefine: 

<table><tr><td>\bigskip</td><td>\hfil</td><td>\hspace</td><td>\parskip</td><td>\vfill</td><td>\vspace</td></tr><tr><td>\break</td><td>\hfill</td><td>\kern</td><td>\smallskip</td><td>\vglue</td><td></td></tr><tr><td>\eject</td><td>\hglue</td><td>\medskip</td><td>\vfil</td><td>\vskip</td><td></td></tr></table>

## 17.5 Final preparations for the publisher

Throughout this book, there are a number of “don’ts”. Most are practices you should avoid while writing articles. When writing a book, it is even more important not to violate these rules. 

When the editors, including the copy editor, are finished with your manuscript and you have the document class designed for the book, then you can start on the final preparations. 

Step 1 Eliminate all T<sub>E</sub>X commands. 

T<sub>E</sub>X commands, that is, Plain T<sub>E</sub>X commands that are not part of L<sup>A</sup>T<sub>E</sub>X (not listed as L<sup>A</sup>TEX commands in the index of this book) may interfere with L<sup>A</sup>TEX in unexpected ways. They may also cause problems with the style file that is created for your book. 

Step 2 Collect all your custom commands and environments together in one place, preferably in a separate command file (see Section 14.3). 

Step 3 Make sure that custom commands for notations and custom environments for structures are used consistently throughout your document. 

<sup>This book uses the command</sup> \doc <sup>for document names</sup>, <sup>so</sup> firstarticle <sup>is</sup> <sup>t</sup>yp<sup>ed as</sup> \doc{firstarticle}<sup>. Ofcourse</sup>, \texttt{firstarticle} g<sup>ives the same</sup> <sup>result</sup>,<sup>but if</sup>y<sup>ou intermix</sup> \doc{firstarticle} <sup>and</sup> \texttt{firstarticle} <sup>com-</sup> mands, you lose the ability to easily change the way document names are displayed. 

Step 4 Watch out for vertical white space adding up. 

Do not directly follow one displayed math environment with another. Multiple adjacent lines of displayed mathematics should all be in the same environment. 

If your style file uses interparagraph spacing, avoid beginning paragraphs with displayed math. 

For instance, 

\[ x=y \] 

```txt
[ x=z ] 
```

<sup>is</sup> <sup>wron</sup>g<sup>.</sup> <sup>Use</sup>, <sup>instead</sup>, <sup>an</sup> align <sup>or</sup> gather <sup>environment.</sup> 

Step 5 If possible, do not place “tall” mathematical formulas inline. All formulas that might change the interline spacing, as a rule, should be displayed. 

You can find examples on pages 138 and 368. Here is one more example, double hat accents used inline: <sup>̂</sup>�<sup>̂</sup>. 

Step 6 Read the log file. 

Watch for line-too-wide warnings (see Section 1.4). 

Check for font substitutions (see Section 3.6.7). 

Adobe Acrobat Professional has a preflight utility. It will check whether the PDF version of your typeset document has all the fonts it requires. 

Step 7 Do not assume that gray boxes or color illustrations appear when published exactly the way that they look on your monitor or printer. 

Color work requires calibration of monitors and printers. It is often best left to the experts at the publisher. 

Step 8 Do not assume that the application that created your PDF files (see Section 8.4.3) can create high-quality PDF files. 

Many applications can create PDF files or convert files to PDF format. Very few do it right. Ask your publisher what applications they recommend. 

Font substitutions can also cause problems: 

A font that was used in typesetting the document may not be the font you intended. Missing fonts are substituted and the substitute fonts are rarely satisfactory. 

A special trap: Your publisher may have more, or maybe fewer, fonts than you do! As a result, the font substitutions on your publisher’s system may be diferent from those on yours. Make sure that the fonts you use are not substituted. 

## 17.6 If you create the PDF file for your book

Many publishers take your manuscript, prepared as described in Section 17.5, and guide it through the final steps for printing. Some books, however, are prepared by the authors for printing using a custom document class for books and submitted to the publisher as PDF files. If your book falls into this category, there are a few more things you should do before you create the final PDF file for your book. 

## Adjust the pages

Make sure that you are satisfied with the way the document is broken into pages by L<sup>A</sup>TEX <sup>and with the</sup> p<sup>lacement of the</sup> figure <sup>and</sup> table <sup>environments</sup> (<sup>see Section 8.4.3</sup>)<sup>.</sup> If necessary, you should make last-minute changes to adjust page breaks.
